title: What Does 99% Accuracy Measure? A Reproducible Audit of Shortcut Learning in a Widely Used Fake News Corpus
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 11 tables. Code, experiment scripts, and machine-readable results: https://github.com/vermayuvraj/fake-news-detection
summary: Text classifiers trained on the ISOT/Kaggle "Fake and Real News" corpus routinely report accuracy and F1 above 0.98, a level of performance that sits uneasily beside the difficulty of assessing veracity. Using a transparent TF-IDF and linear-classifier pipeline as a measurement instrument, we audit the corpus along three leakage channels and two distribution-shift protocols, releasing all code and derived numbers. First, the benchmark is partly degenerate: a classifier given only the subject metadata field, with the article text discarded, attains F1 = 1.000, since the two classes have disjoint subjects. Second, removing all three leakage channels, metadata, a newswire source tag present in 99.2% of real articles, and 6,251 duplicate documents contaminating 19.4% of a naive test split, lowers F1 by only 1.21 points (0.9935 to 0.9814); the residual signal is diffuse editorial style rather than a few giveaway tokens, since deleting the 1,000 highest-weight unigrams still leaves F1 = 0.926. Third, this style signal does not transfer: under a topic-disjoint protocol, average precision falls from 0.9995 to 0.9475 and deployed F1 from 0.9905 to 0.8067, with a prior-matched analysis confirming a genuine 5.2-point loss of discrimination, while temporal transfer is nearly lossless. A fine-tuned DistilBERT is stronger in-distribution (F1 = 0.9993) but degrades far more under topic shift, losing 12.9 average-precision points against the linear model's 5.2. Transferred to the independent LIAR benchmark, all three models fall to near-chance ranking (ROC-AUC 0.54-0.57), none beating a majority-class baseline. We conclude that within-corpus scores here quantify source and topic separability rather than veracity, that added capacity exploits the shortcut rather than avoiding it, and we recommend metadata-only, small-sample, and topic-disjoint baselines as inexpensive diagnostics for future work.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that extremely high fake-news detection scores on the ISOT/Kaggle dataset are mostly due to dataset artifacts (metadata, source, topic/style) rather than true veracity understanding, and proposes simple baselines to expose such shortcuts.
AI.motivation: Reported near-perfect performance (accuracy/F1 > 0.98) on the ISOT/Kaggle fake-vs-real-news dataset seems implausible given the inherent difficulty of determining truthfulness, suggesting that models may be exploiting spurious signals or leakage in the dataset instead of genuinely assessing veracity. The authors aim to audit this benchmark to understand what is actually being learned and how robust it is under more realistic distribution shifts.
AI.method: They use a transparent TF-IDF + linear classifier pipeline as a measurement tool to systematically audit the ISOT/Kaggle corpus. They: (1) test a metadata-only classifier using just the article “subject” field; (2) identify and remove three leakage channels—subject metadata, a near-universal newswire tag in real articles, and thousands of near-duplicate documents contaminating naive splits—then test performance with and without high-weight tokens; (3) evaluate robustness under topic-disjoint and temporally disjoint train/test splits to simulate distribution shift; (4) compare with a fine-tuned DistilBERT model; and (5) transfer all models to the independent LIAR benchmark to test out-of-corpus veracity detection. All code and derived statistics are released for reproducibility.
AI.result: (1) A classifier using only the subject metadata (no article text) achieves F1 = 1.000 because fake and real news have disjoint subject labels, revealing a degenerate benchmark. (2) After removing metadata, the newswire source tag (present in 99.2% of real articles), and 6,251 duplicates affecting 19.4% of a naive test split, F1 only drops slightly from 0.9935 to 0.9814. Even after deleting the top 1,000 highest-weight unigrams, F1 remains 0.926, indicating a diffuse style signal. (3) Under a topic-disjoint protocol, performance sharply degrades: average precision falls from 0.9995 to 0.9475 and deployed F1 from 0.9905 to 0.8067, with a prior-matched analysis confirming a real 5.2-point loss in discrimination, while temporal splits show little loss. (4) DistilBERT achieves even higher in-distribution F1 (0.9993) but is more brittle under topic shift, losing 12.9 average-precision points versus the linear model’s 5.2. (5) On the LIAR dataset, all three models perform near chance (ROC-AUC 0.54–0.57) and do not beat a majority-class baseline, showing poor transfer of veracity detection.
AI.conclusion: The extraordinarily high performance on the ISOT/Kaggle fake-vs-real-news corpus is largely driven by dataset shortcuts—metadata, source markers, and stable topical/editorial style—rather than genuine modeling of truthfulness. Within-corpus metrics mostly measure separability of sources and topics, and higher-capacity models like DistilBERT exploit these shortcuts even more instead of overcoming them. The authors recommend routine use of metadata-only baselines, reduced training samples, and topic-disjoint evaluation protocols as cheap diagnostic tools to reveal such artifacts in future fake-news and veracity-detection research.

title: Training a Language Model End-to-End in Rust: An Experience Report
summary: I pretrained a language model end-to-end in Rust - alone, with no team, no PyTorch, and no Python in the training path - for $164 in rented GPU time. I report that as an achievement, not a recommendation: the more useful contribution is a measured failure taxonomy of the two leading Rust ML frameworks, Candle and Burn, as training (not inference) backends in 2026. I document five Candle defects, including fused kernels that silently produce no gradient, and three Burn defects, including a backward pass at roughly 3% of theoretical GPU throughput and a kernel-fusion path that segfaults mid-training at multi-billion-parameter scale. Every one passed ordinary loss-curve inspection; none announced itself. I describe the verification discipline that caught six such silent failures, centered on a gradient-flow arbiter: a test that runs one forward/backward pass and asserts every trainable parameter receives a finite, nonzero gradient, generalizable to any framework. The trained model (roughly 0.4B parameters, Bangla-first) shows strong Bangla language-modeling signal - a per-token negative log-likelihood of 0.93 against 12.60 for a random-initialized twin - while scoring at chance on English commonsense multiple-choice, the expected outcome of a deliberately small, Bangla-weighted budget (about 2 billion tokens, 54.6 hours, one rented H100). I also report a tokenizer-fertility trap in Bengali script: naive byte-level tokenization collapsed Bangla to roughly 1.4 characters per token against English's 3.9, silently inverting the corpus's language balance; fixing it reached roughly 4.1. To my knowledge, this is among the first documented end-to-end LM pretraining runs in pure Rust. After this run I moved training to PyTorch and kept Rust for on-device serving: in my hands, Rust is not yet a competitive place to train a language model, though it may be a good place to serve one.

AI.tldr: A single author pretrained a 0.4B-parameter Bangla-first language model entirely in Rust for $164 GPU cost, but the main contribution is a detailed account of silent training failures and shortcomings in Rust ML frameworks Candle and Burn, plus a simple, general test to detect broken gradient flows.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether Rust ML frameworks are ready for serious language-model pretraining, to document their failure modes for training (not just inference), and to provide practical verification techniques for catching silent training bugs during end-to-end LM pretraining.
AI.method: Implement an end-to-end LM training pipeline in Rust using Candle and Burn on a rented H100 GPU, train a ~0.4B parameter Bangla-first model on ~2B tokens, systematically probe and catalog framework defects (e.g., fused kernels, backward-pass throughput, kernel-fusion segfaults) and design a gradient-flow arbiter test that checks all trainable parameters receive finite, nonzero gradients in a forward/backward pass. Analyze tokenizer behavior, especially byte-level tokenization fertility in Bengali vs English, and compare trained model performance to a random-initialized twin on Bangla LM metrics and English commonsense tasks.
AI.result: Identified five training-related defects in Candle and three in Burn, including silent gradient failures and severe backward-pass underutilization, none of which are obvious from loss curves. Proposed and applied a framework-agnostic gradient-flow arbiter test that uncovered six silent failures. Successfully trained a ~0.4B-parameter Bangla-first LM that achieves strong Bangla modeling performance (NLL 0.93 vs 12.60 for random baseline) but chance-level English commonsense performance, consistent with the small, Bangla-weighted training budget. Discovered a tokenizer-fertility issue where naive byte-level tokenization made Bangla tokens far shorter than English, distorting language balance, and fixed it by improving tokenization to ~4.1 characters per token in Bangla.
AI.conclusion: Pure-Rust training pipelines for large language models are currently fragile and noncompetitive compared to mature ecosystems like PyTorch, particularly for training workloads, though Rust remains attractive for inference/serving. Reliable LM training in Rust requires rigorous verification of gradient flow and careful tokenization design, especially for scripts like Bengali; ordinary loss-curve inspection is insufficient to catch critical framework-level defects. The author has therefore moved training to PyTorch while retaining Rust for on-device serving.

title: Same Quantity, Different Answer: Numerical Representation Invariance in Language Models
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Ancillary archive includes the frozen benchmark, evaluation and audit records, consensus raw responses, manifests, analysis code, and tests
summary: Numerically equivalent word problems should yield the same canonical answer whether a quantity is written as a decimal, fraction, percentage, number word, scientific notation, or an exactly converted unit. We generate 3,600 exact-rational problems and 8,600 prompts spanning five identity-preserving transformation families, and evaluate five open-weight systems. After a fixed syntax audit that normalizes common answer forms without an LLM judge, canonical accuracy is 0.969-0.996, but orbit correctness falls to 0.848-0.981 and orbit invariance to 0.851-0.981; invariant-but-wrong orbits account for at most 0.003. Most of the broad strict-parser collapse arises because multiplication-form scientific notation lies outside the implemented number grammar, illustrating how evaluator interfaces can masquerade as reasoning failures. A distinct semantic pathology remains: Mistral Small 4 scores 0.699 on unit-converted inputs and produces 265 errors differing from the label by exact powers of ten. In a separate 9,000-call experiment that allocates equal calls to the compared arms, representation consensus does not outperform paraphrase consensus on a low-error subset and produces substantially more false alarms. The accompanying ancillary archive contains the frozen benchmark, evaluation and audit records, consensus raw responses, manifests, analysis code, and a one-command paper build.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether LLMs give consistent answers to mathematically equivalent word problems written in different numeric formats, and shows that some apparent reasoning failures are actually evaluation/interface artifacts while others are real systematic semantic errors.
AI.motivation: LLMs should provide the same answer to numerically equivalent math problems regardless of how numbers are represented (decimals, fractions, percentages, scientific notation, unit conversions). However, evals often treat these as separate items and may confound model reasoning failures with parsing/interface limitations. The authors want to separate true reasoning issues from artifacts of answer parsing, and to test whether leveraging variation in numeric representation helps consensus-based reliability methods.
AI.method: They construct a benchmark of 3,600 exact-rational math word problems and 8,600 prompts generated by applying five families of identity-preserving transformations (e.g., numeric format changes and unit conversions). They evaluate five open-weight LLMs under a fixed, strict syntactic answer parser and then a syntax-audited canonicalization pipeline that normalizes common answer forms without using an LLM judge. They compute: (1) canonical accuracy of each prompt individually; (2) orbit correctness, i.e., whether all equivalent variants in an orbit are correct; and (3) orbit invariance, i.e., whether a model’s answers are consistent across all variants. They diagnose specific grammar gaps (e.g., multiplication-form scientific notation) and semantic pathologies (e.g., systematic powers-of-ten errors on unit conversions). They also run a 9,000-call experiment distributing calls equally across compared arms to compare “representation consensus” (aggregating over different numeric formats) with “paraphrase consensus” on a low-error subset, measuring gains and false alarms.
AI.result: After syntax auditing and normalization, per-prompt canonical accuracy is very high (0.969–0.996), but when grouping equivalent representations into orbits, orbit correctness drops to 0.848–0.981 and orbit invariance to 0.851–0.981. Orbits that are fully consistent but consistently wrong are rare (≤0.003). A large share of strict-parser failures come from scientific notation in multiplication form not being covered by the number grammar, showing evaluator design can mimic reasoning errors. Nonetheless, a real semantic issue is found: for Mistral Small 4 on unit-converted prompts, accuracy is only 0.699, with 265 mistakes that are exactly off by powers of ten. In the 9,000-call follow-up, representation-consensus methods do not outperform paraphrase consensus on a low-error subset and instead introduce substantially more false alarms.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are mostly accurate on these exact-rational math tasks, but consistency across numerically equivalent representations is weaker than raw accuracy suggests. Some apparent failures come from brittle evaluation interfaces, like parsers that mishandle common scientific-notation formats, underscoring that evaluation tools can masquerade as model reasoning problems. However, genuine semantic bugs remain, such as systematic powers-of-ten errors under unit conversion for certain models. Moreover, using multiple numeric representations for consensus does not clearly beat standard paraphrase-based consensus and can increase false alarms. Reliable assessment of LLM numerical reasoning thus requires careful evaluator design, attention to representation-induced pathologies, and skepticism about simplistic consensus strategies based solely on format variation.

title: A Computational Approach to Measuring Semantic Change in Sanskrit Literature
summary: Diachronic word embeddings have become the modern standard for tracking semantic change, yet they have been largely validated on modern, high-resource, and well-segmented languages. This paper tests whether the paradigm transfers to Sanskrit, an ancient, low-resource language whose phonological fusion (sandhi), morphological inflection, compounding, and polysemy pose a unique challenge. I assemble a 2.7M-token corpus spanning four canonical periods, recover word boundaries with a neural byte-level sandhi splitter and lemmatizer, and train per-period embeddings across configurations. To evaluate the system, I curate a validation set from historical scholarship and test recovery directionally with anchor displacement. Of 21 testable shifts, 19 move in the philologically attested direction (sign test, p=0.00011). I further show which configuration the language forces and comment on opportunities for improvement.

AI.tldr: Tests whether modern diachronic word embedding methods reliably detect semantic change in Sanskrit and finds they mostly do, given careful preprocessing.
AI.motivation: Diachronic word embeddings are widely used to study semantic change, but they have mainly been validated on modern, high-resource languages with clear word boundaries and simpler morphology. It is unclear whether these methods are reliable for ancient, low-resource languages like Sanskrit, which has complex phonological fusion (sandhi), rich inflection, compounding, and high polysemy, all of which can distort distributional signals. The author wants to assess if the standard paradigm actually transfers to Sanskrit and under what conditions.
AI.method: Construct a 2.7M-token diachronic corpus of Sanskrit spanning four canonical historical periods. Recover word boundaries and base forms by using a neural byte-level sandhi splitter and lemmatizer. Train separate word embedding models for each period under multiple configuration choices. Build an evaluation set of historically documented meaning shifts from philological scholarship. Evaluate whether embeddings capture attested change directions using an anchor-displacement method, and statistically test the proportion of correctly predicted directions via a sign test.
AI.result: The author successfully builds the diachronic Sanskrit corpus and trains per-period embeddings. In the curated evaluation set, 21 semantic shifts can be operationalized; for 19 of these, the direction of semantic movement in embedding space matches the direction attested in historical scholarship. A sign test yields p = 0.00011, indicating the probability of obtaining this level of agreement by chance is extremely low. The experiments also expose which embedding and preprocessing configurations Sanskrit effectively requires for robust performance.
AI.conclusion: Diachronic word embedding methods can transfer effectively to Sanskrit despite the language’s challenging properties, provided that careful segmentation and lemmatization are applied and the right configuration choices are made. The high rate of correctly oriented semantic shifts provides empirical validation of the paradigm for a low-resource ancient language. The paper also identifies configuration constraints imposed by Sanskrit and outlines directions to improve coverage and accuracy further.

title: Do Synthetic Personas Predict Real Audience Response? A Sim-to-Real Study Where a No-Persona Baseline Beats Persona-Based Copy Simulation
summary: Marketers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as "synthetic personas" to predict how an audience will react to a piece of copy before it ships, encouraged by evidence that profile-conditioned LLMs mimic human samples. But is that prediction actually valid against real behaviour - and does the persona machinery help? We present a sim-to-real validity study using the Upworthy Research Archive - thousands of headline A/B tests on shared real traffic, with measured click-through - as held-out ground truth. We compare a ten-persona panel, grounded in the real audience's demographics, against a no-persona zero-shot baseline that simply asks the model how likely a typical reader is to click. Two findings stand out. First, ground-truth reliability is the binding constraint: most A/B tests have no statistically distinguishable winner, so validity can only be measured on the reliable subset (n = 399). Second, and counter to the persona-simulation premise, persona conditioning degrades predictive validity: the no-persona baseline ranks variants markedly better (Kendall τ = 0.361, a medium effect; top-1 accuracy 49.2%) than the persona panel (τ = 0.084; top-1 34.6%), with non-overlapping confidence intervals. Asking the model directly taps an accurate population-level prior; forcing it to role-play specific personas injects bias and noise. The result replicates across three independent Upworthy splits, holds in direction on a different-domain news dataset, and is robust to seed, prompt phrasing, and model choice - across three Gemini tiers and a different model family (OpenAI gpt-4.1, significant paired gap). The takeaway: for predicting aggregate engagement, a plain LLM ranker beats persona simulation - synthetic personas are not merely a weak predictor, they are worse than not using them. All numbers regenerate from a public, artifact-first replication package.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether using LLM-based synthetic personas improves prediction of which headlines will get more clicks, finding that simple, non-persona LLM predictions are actually more accurate.
AI.motivation: Marketers are starting to use LLMs as synthetic personas to forecast audience reactions to marketing copy, assuming persona-conditioned outputs better reflect diverse human responses. However, it is unclear whether such persona-based predictions actually line up with real-world user behavior, and whether personas outperform simpler, direct LLM queries.
AI.method: The authors use the Upworthy Research Archive of thousands of real headline A/B tests with observed click-through rates as ground truth. They construct a ten-persona LLM panel grounded in real audience demographics and compare its ability to rank headline variants against a simple zero-shot baseline that directly asks the LLM how likely a typical reader is to click. Predictive validity is evaluated using Kendall’s tau and top-1 accuracy, restricted to A/B tests with statistically reliable winners. They replicate analyses across multiple dataset splits, an additional news dataset, varied prompts, random seeds, and several LLMs (three Gemini tiers and OpenAI gpt-4.1).
AI.result: Only 399 A/B tests have statistically reliable winners, limiting where validity can be meaningfully assessed. On this subset, the no-persona baseline significantly outperforms the persona panel: Kendall τ of 0.361 and top-1 accuracy of 49.2% versus τ of 0.084 and top-1 accuracy of 34.6% for personas, with non-overlapping confidence intervals. These results replicate across three Upworthy splits, show the same directional effect on another news dataset, and remain robust to changes in random seed, prompt phrasing, and choice of LLM, including a significant performance gap for gpt-4.1.
AI.conclusion: For predicting aggregate engagement such as headline click-through, persona-conditioned LLM simulations are not just weak but actively harmful compared to a simple non-persona LLM ranker. Directly querying the model about a typical reader taps into an accurate population-level prior, whereas forcing role-play of specific personas introduces additional bias and noise. Marketers should therefore avoid synthetic persona panels for aggregate engagement prediction and instead use straightforward LLM ranking approaches, with all results supported by a public replication package.

title: Retrieved-Span Training for Efficient Query-Focused Meeting Summarization on QMSum
summary: QMSum provides no scorer, making query-focused meeting summarization results difficult to compare. We rescore or generate 15 systems under one implementation. Through a common inference port, a released 406M Fusion-in-Decoder specialist loses 6.30 ROUGE-1 when moved from capped long input to 2,000-word retrieved spans. Fine-tuning it on this span regime recovers the loss. On test it scores 36.33 ROUGE-1 versus 35.41 for our 1.2B system; the meeting-cluster 95% interval for the difference is [-0.27, +2.22], so QMSum does not statistically separate them. The smaller system uses about one-third as many total parameters and less than half the peak inference memory. Within the fixed 1.2B base, span-regime fine-tuning adds 5.29 [+4.02, +6.56], while replacing the first 4,500 transcript words with 2,000 retrieved words adds 1.55 on test and 0.29 on validation. Separately, under one concise prompt and reference-overlap scorer, a released 406M specialist exceeds five proprietary hosted models by at least 6.2 ROUGE-1, but output length and absent human or factuality evaluation limit this ordering. Conclusions are limited to QMSum and automatic metrics.

AI.tldr: Study analyzes query-focused meeting summarization on QMSum by unifying evaluation, comparing models, and examining input span regimes and fine-tuning effects.
AI.motivation: QMSum lacks a standardized scorer, making it hard to compare query-focused meeting summarization systems fairly. Existing models differ in implementation, input handling, and evaluation, obscuring how architecture size, input span regimes, and fine-tuning strategies actually affect performance and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors reimplement, rescore, or newly generate 15 systems under a single framework with a common inference interface. They test a released 406M-parameter Fusion-in-Decoder specialist model under different input regimes: capped long inputs versus 2,000-word retrieved spans. They then fine-tune this model specifically for the span regime. They also compare it to a larger 1.2B-parameter model, keeping the base model fixed when analyzing gains from span-regime fine-tuning and from replacing the initial 4,500 transcript words with 2,000 retrieved words. Performance is measured mainly with ROUGE-1 on QMSum test and validation sets, including confidence intervals over meeting clusters. Separately, under a single concise prompt and a reference-overlap scorer, they compare the 406M specialist to five proprietary hosted models.
AI.result: Moving the 406M Fusion-in-Decoder specialist from capped long inputs to 2,000-word retrieved spans causes a 6.30 ROUGE-1 drop, which is recovered by fine-tuning on the span regime. After fine-tuning, the 406M model scores 36.33 ROUGE-1 on test, versus 35.41 for the 1.2B model; the 95% confidence interval for their difference ([-0.27, +2.22]) indicates no statistically significant separation on QMSum. The 406M model uses roughly one-third the total parameters and under half the peak inference memory of the 1.2B model. For the fixed 1.2B base, span-regime fine-tuning adds 5.29 ROUGE-1 with a 95% interval of [+4.02, +6.56], while substituting the first 4,500 transcript words with 2,000 retrieved words adds 1.55 ROUGE-1 on test and 0.29 on validation. In a separate comparison using a unified prompt and scorer, the 406M specialist outperforms five proprietary hosted models by at least 6.2 ROUGE-1, although these results are not supported by human or factuality assessments and may be influenced by output length differences.
AI.conclusion: A medium-sized (406M) Fusion-in-Decoder specialist, when properly adapted to a retrieved-span input regime, can match or slightly surpass a much larger 1.2B model on QMSum in ROUGE-1, with substantially lower parameter and memory costs. Fine-tuning for the span regime is crucial and yields larger gains than simply swapping long-prefix inputs for retrieved spans. However, conclusions are restricted to QMSum and automatic reference-overlap metrics, and the comparison to proprietary models is tentative due to lack of human and factuality evaluation and confounds like output length.

title: Do Existing Preconditioners Improve Biomedical Tabular Foundation Learning? An Empirical Study on TabPFN Optimization
summary: Tabular foundation models have recently shown strong potential for structured biomedical data analysis. Among them, TabPFN has emerged as an effective approach for low-data tabular classification tasks. However, the impact of optimization and preconditioning strategies on biomedical fine-tuning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive empirical investigation of five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies for fine-tuning TabPFN v2.5 on 59 biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease, breast cancer, schizophrenia, significant memory concern (SMC), KEEL biomedical datasets, and UCI biomedical benchmarks. The evaluation considers predictive performance, computational efficiency, and statistical significance analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the original AdamW optimizer consistently achieves the best overall performance and statistical ranking, while existing curvature-aware preconditioners fail to provide reliable improvements across diverse biomedical learning scenarios. The findings suggest that generic preconditioning approaches may not adequately capture the optimization characteristics of biomedical tabular learning, motivating the development of biomedical-aware preconditioners specifically tailored for healthcare-oriented tabular foundation models.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically evaluates five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies for fine-tuning the TabPFN v2.5 tabular foundation model on 59 biomedical datasets and finds that plain AdamW performs best overall.
AI.motivation: Although TabPFN has shown promise for tabular biomedical tasks, it is unclear how different optimization and preconditioning strategies affect fine-tuning performance on diverse biomedical datasets. Understanding this is important because biomedical data have specific characteristics and good preconditioning could potentially improve accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune TabPFN v2.5 on 59 heterogeneous biomedical datasets covering multiple disease domains (Alzheimer's, breast cancer, schizophrenia, SMC, KEEL biomedical, UCI biomedical). They compare five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies, including the original AdamW optimizer and several curvature-aware variants. They assess predictive performance, computational efficiency, and conduct statistical significance and ranking analyses across datasets.
AI.result: Across all datasets and metrics, the standard AdamW optimizer consistently achieves the best or near-best predictive performance and the highest statistical ranking. Curvature-aware preconditioners do not deliver consistent or statistically reliable improvements and sometimes underperform, offering no clear advantage in this biomedical tabular setting.
AI.conclusion: Generic curvature-based preconditioning strategies do not reliably improve the fine-tuning of TabPFN on biomedical tabular data, whereas standard AdamW remains robust and effective. This indicates that the optimization landscape of biomedical tabular learning may require specialized, domain-aware preconditioners rather than off-the-shelf methods, motivating future work on healthcare-tailored optimization techniques for tabular foundation models.

title: From Tone to Trajectory: Continuous Sentiment and the Shape of Monetary Policy Communication
summary: Central bank press conferences are not merely information releases --- they are structured narratives. We study whether the shape of sentiment within a statement, not just its average tone, carries policy-relevant signals. Constructing sentiment arcs for ECB and Fed press conferences along three dimensions --- monetary stance, economic outlook, and uncertainty --- we assess their predictive content for policy rate changes, inflation expectations, and forecaster disagreement. Our findings show that arc shape robustly predicts rate decisions beyond lexicon-based benchmarks at both institutions --- it is not merely whether a statement sounds hawkish or economically optimistic on average, but how these sentiments are sequenced and emphasized across the statement, that carries the policy signal. Arc features also shape how professional forecasters update inflation expectations and how much they disagree, pointing to a receiver-side effect distinct from the direct policy signal. These findings suggest that communication design --- the sequencing and emphasis of policy language across a statement --- is a first-order feature of the policy signal, not a second-order refinement.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that not just the overall tone, but the *shape* and sequencing of sentiment in central bank press conferences (ECB and Fed) predicts policy moves and affects expectations.
AI.motivation: Most research treats central bank communication as a single average tone (e.g., hawkish vs. dovish). However, central bank press conferences are structured narratives where the order and emphasis of arguments might matter for markets and forecasters. The authors want to know whether these within-statement dynamics (how sentiment evolves from beginning to end) contain policy-relevant information beyond simple average sentiment scores.
AI.method: The authors build ‘sentiment arcs’ for ECB and Fed press conferences along three dimensions: (1) monetary policy stance, (2) economic outlook, and (3) uncertainty. They likely segment statements into parts (e.g., paragraphs or time blocks), score sentiment in each part using domain-specific lexicons or models, and then summarize the trajectory (shape) of sentiment over the statement using arc features (such as slope, curvature, timing of peaks/troughs). They then test whether these arc features predict (a) subsequent policy rate changes, (b) changes in inflation expectations, and (c) forecaster disagreement, controlling for traditional lexicon-based average sentiment benchmarks.
AI.result: They find that features of the sentiment arcs – how sentiment evolves and is sequenced – significantly and robustly predict policy rate decisions for both the ECB and the Fed, above and beyond what can be explained by average hawkish/dovish or optimistic/pessimistic tone. Additionally, arc features explain how professional forecasters revise their inflation expectations and how much they disagree with one another after the press conferences, indicating that narrative structure affects belief updating and dispersion.
AI.conclusion: Central bank communication works not only through what is said on average, but also through how it is narratively structured. The sequencing and emphasis of policy-relevant language across a press conference – captured by sentiment arc shapes – is a core part of the policy signal. This suggests that the design and ordering of communication should be treated as a first-order policy tool, with implications for how central banks craft and evaluate their statements to manage expectations and disagreements in the audience.

title: 4DGS-JEPA: Temporally Compositional Joint-Embedding Prediction for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting provides an explicit representation of evolving 3D scenes, but existing approaches are primarily optimized for reconstruction, future-state generation, or rendering rather than for learning reusable predictive dynamics. We propose 4DGS-JEPA, a Gaussian-native joint-embedding predictive architecture for causal multi-horizon prediction over dynamic Gaussian scenes. The model uses a hierarchical scene-, motion-group-, and Gaussian-level representation together with a horizon-conditioned transition operator that supports both direct prediction and recursive rollout. Its central principle is temporal composition: different chronological transition paths reaching the same future endpoint should produce compatible predictive states. Endpoint and multi-horizon path supervision anchor these predictions to future target embeddings, while a selective geometry decoder and geometry-level composition ground the learned dynamics in consistent group motion and Gaussian geometry without requiring complete future appearance reconstruction. We further introduce a hybrid correspondence mechanism that combines persistent canonical identity with residual optimal-transport matching under reordering and topology change. We characterize zero-loss path agreement and finite-error rollout accumulation theoretically. Three controlled experiments provide mechanism-level evidence that temporal composition reduces latent path dependence while retaining predictive accuracy, geometry-level composition improves consistency of decoded motion, and hybrid correspondence preserves reliable identity while remaining robust when correspondence becomes ambiguous. Together, 4DGS-JEPA provides a predictive, temporally compositional formulation of dynamic Gaussian worlds.

AI.tldr: 4DGS-JEPA is a predictive model for dynamic Gaussian Splatting scenes that enforces temporal compositionality so different paths to the same future state yield consistent predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods focus on reconstruction, short-term future generation, or rendering rather than learning reusable, causal dynamics that can predict over multiple future horizons in a consistent way. There is a gap in modeling predictive dynamics directly in the Gaussian domain, with robust handling of identity, correspondence, and path dependence over time.
AI.method: They design 4DGS-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture operating on dynamic Gaussian scenes. It builds a hierarchical representation (scene-, motion-group-, and Gaussian-level) and a horizon-conditioned transition operator supporting both direct multi-step prediction and recursive rollout. The core training principle is temporal composition: different temporal paths that reach the same future time must yield compatible latent states. Training uses endpoint and multi-horizon path supervision to align predictions with future target embeddings. A selective geometry decoder plus geometry-level composition grounds latent dynamics in consistent group motion and Gaussian geometry, without reconstructing full appearance. A hybrid correspondence mechanism maintains canonical identities for Gaussians while using residual optimal-transport matching to handle reordering and topology changes. They also provide theoretical analysis of conditions for zero-loss path agreement and bounded error accumulation.
AI.result: Across three controlled experiments, they show: (1) temporal composition reduces dependence on the particular prediction path while preserving accuracy; (2) geometry-level composition improves the consistency of decoded motion compared to baselines; and (3) the hybrid correspondence strategy maintains reliable identity tracking and remains robust when true correspondences are ambiguous or change.
AI.conclusion: 4DGS-JEPA offers a temporally compositional, predictive formulation for dynamic Gaussian Splatting worlds, enabling multi-horizon causal prediction directly in the Gaussian domain, with improved path-invariant dynamics, consistent geometry-aware motion, and robust identity correspondence under dynamic scene changes.

title: Peerify: Benchmarking Peer-Review Claim Verification
summary: Peer review plays a central role in scholarly publishing, yet verifying whether reviewer claims are supported by manuscript evidence remains a largely manual and time-consuming process. We present Peerify, a pipeline for manuscript-grounded verification of peer-review claims. Given a manuscript and a review comment, the Peerify pipeline decomposes reviews into atomic claims, retrieves relevant manuscript evidence, and determines whether each claim is supported by the paper. To support the development and evaluation of the pipeline, we construct a benchmark of 800 claims derived from authentic peer-review interactions collected from NeurIPS 2024 and ICLR 2024, including a 300-claim hand-labeled subset used to audit the automated supervision. We evaluate state-of-the-art language models and retrieval strategies within the Peerify pipeline, together with entailment baselines. Our results demonstrate the importance of retrieval-centered verification and claim decomposition, while highlighting the challenges posed by ambiguous and interpretive reviewer claims. Automated labels agree with human consensus on 90.3% of audited claims ($κ= 0.87$), while off-the-shelf entailment models stay below 0.24 macro-F1.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Peerify, a pipeline that automatically checks whether peer-review claims are supported by the content of a manuscript, and builds a benchmark from real NeurIPS 2024 and ICLR 2024 reviews to evaluate it.
AI.motivation: Peer review is crucial but verifying if reviewers’ statements are truly grounded in the manuscript is manual, slow, and error-prone. With growing submission volumes, there is a need for scalable, reliable tools that can automatically verify the factual grounding of reviewer claims in the paper under review.
AI.method: The authors design Peerify, a multi-step pipeline that: (1) decomposes review comments into atomic claims; (2) retrieves relevant evidence spans from the manuscript; and (3) classifies whether each claim is supported by that evidence. They build a benchmark of 800 claims from real NeurIPS 2024 and ICLR 2024 reviews, including a hand-labeled set of 300 claims to audit automated labels. They then plug different state-of-the-art language models, retrieval strategies, and entailment baselines into the pipeline to compare performance.
AI.result: Automated labels from the Peerify pipeline match human consensus on 90.3% of the audited 300-claim subset, with high inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.87), whereas standard off-the-shelf textual entailment models perform poorly (macro-F1 < 0.24). The experiments show that explicitly retrieving manuscript evidence and decomposing complex review comments into atomic claims substantially improves verification quality and exposes limitations of generic entailment approaches, especially on ambiguous and interpretive reviewer statements.
AI.conclusion: Peerify provides an effective manuscript-grounded verification framework for peer-review claims, showing that retrieval-centric architectures and claim decomposition are key to reliable automated review checking. The released benchmark and analysis illustrate both the promise and the remaining challenges—particularly around ambiguity and interpretation—in automating the quality control of peer reviews.

title: An Accurate and Interpretable Hyper Graph Neural Network for GBM Survival Prediction
summary: Survival prediction for glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) demands models that are both accurate and interpretable, yet existing approaches treat these objectives as com- peting, where performant models sacrifice transparency, while interpretable models accept degraded predictive power. We argue that this trade-off is not inherent. Graph neural net- works offer a structural foundation for extracting interpretable, explainable representations without compromising discriminative ability. Furthermore, current methods typically rely on a single imaging modality, underutilizing the complementary information available across multi-modal MRI and clinical metadata. We propose a multi-modal framework that inte- grates three components to address both objectives simultaneously: (1) a sheaf hypergraph neural network that captures higher-order relationships among tissue patches through direc- tional, asymmetric message passing; (2) a concept bottleneck layer that compresses learned representations into clinically grounded concepts, enforcing ante-hoc interpretability; and (3) an extension sufficiency test (EST) regularizer that penalizes unfaithful explanations during training, ensuring that model explanations genuinely reflect the internal decision process. Clinical and genomic features are incorporated through gated fusion, preserving the dominant prognostic signal of molecular markers while retaining concept-level traceabil- ity. Evaluated on 593 patients from the UPenn-GBM dataset under 5-fold cross-validation, our framework achieves a concordance index of 0.643 with the lowest fold-level variance among all compared models (std = 0.015). To our knowledge, this is the first work to unify sheaf hypergraph convolution, concept bottleneck supervision, and EST regularization for interpretable survival prediction from brain MRI

AI.tldr: They propose an interpretable, accurate survival prediction model for glioblastoma using multimodal MRI and clinical data, combining sheaf hypergraph neural networks, concept bottlenecks, and an explanation-faithfulness regularizer.
AI.motivation: Current GBM survival models face a perceived trade-off between accuracy and interpretability, often using only a single imaging modality and yielding opaque predictions not well aligned with clinical reasoning.
AI.method: They design a multimodal framework that (1) uses a sheaf hypergraph neural network to model higher-order, directional relations among MRI tissue patches, (2) introduces a concept bottleneck layer to map features onto clinically meaningful concepts for ante-hoc interpretability, (3) applies an Extension Sufficiency Test (EST) regularizer to ensure explanations faithfully reflect the model’s decision process, and (4) fuses clinical/genomic features with these concepts via gated fusion.
AI.result: On 593 patients from the UPenn-GBM dataset with 5-fold cross-validation, their method achieves a concordance index of 0.643 and the lowest variance (std = 0.015) across folds compared with baselines.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable, concept-level GBM survival prediction can be achieved without sacrificing performance by integrating sheaf hypergraph neural networks, concept bottlenecks, and EST regularization, and this is claimed as the first unified framework of its kind for brain MRI-based survival prediction.

title: AIBuildAI-2.5: Efficient Autonomous AI Model Development Through LLM-Guided Tree Search
summary: Autonomous agents that automatically build artificial intelligence (AI) models could broaden access to AI across science and engineering. A popular line of such agents frames model building as a code search problem and solves it by tree search, in which each node is a candidate program and the tree grows by generating a child program from a parent, and these agents now approach the capability of experienced AI engineers on realistic benchmarks. However, these agents have three weaknesses in efficiency that have not been fully addressed. First, only a small number of candidates can be executed within a realistic budget, so search rules that rank nodes by executed rewards, such as Monte Carlo-style tree search, rely on few and noisy scores and select the next node to explore less effectively. Second, no resource-aware strategy is used to schedule training jobs, which can lower hardware utilization and training efficiency. Third, every agent call is served by a single powerful model, which inflates inference cost. Here we introduce AIBuildAI-2.5, an agentic system that carries out the tree search with LLM agents and addresses each of the three issues. AIBuildAI-2.5 proposes a novel LLM-guided tree search, in which a judge scores each candidate on its expected improvement, grounding, and feasibility, and a selector ranks the pool of candidates from these scores and the state of the search. In addition, AIBuildAI-2.5 comprises a scheduler that launches training jobs with the current hardware resource status taken into account and a router that assigns lower-cost LLMs to less demanding tasks while reserving the most capable LLM for the most challenging sub-tasks in the AI model building workflow. AIBuildAI-2.5 ranks first on MLE-Bench with a medal rate of 73.3%, and outperforms a strong baseline on six autonomous AI research tasks from AIRS-Bench.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AIBuildAI-2.5, an autonomous agent system that builds AI models more efficiently via LLM-guided tree search, resource-aware scheduling, and cost-aware model routing, achieving state-of-the-art performance on AI engineering benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Autonomous code-search agents can now approach experienced AI engineers on realistic benchmarks, but they remain inefficient. They can execute only a small subset of candidate programs, use noisy reward signals for search decisions, lack resource-aware scheduling of training jobs, and rely on a single powerful (and costly) model for all tasks. These limitations reduce search effectiveness, waste hardware resources, and inflate inference costs. The paper is motivated by the need to make autonomous AI model building both more effective and more computationally efficient, so it can scale and be broadly useful in science and engineering.
AI.method: The authors design AIBuildAI-2.5, an agentic system that conducts tree search over candidate AI programs using large language model (LLM) agents. They introduce an LLM-guided tree search where: (1) a judge LLM scores each candidate program along dimensions of expected improvement, grounding in evidence, and feasibility; and (2) a selector LLM ranks the candidate pool based on those scores and the global state of the search, guiding which node to expand next. They augment this search with (a) a resource-aware scheduler that launches model training jobs according to the current hardware status to improve utilization and throughput, and (b) an LLM router that assigns cheaper models to simpler subtasks while reserving the strongest LLM for the most challenging parts of the pipeline, reducing overall inference cost.
AI.result: AIBuildAI-2.5 achieves first place on the MLE-Bench benchmark with a medal rate of 73.3%, indicating superior overall performance among competing autonomous AI-building systems. It also outperforms a strong baseline across six autonomous AI research tasks drawn from AIRS-Bench, demonstrating both improved effectiveness of the search procedure and better practical efficiency in realistic AI engineering scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that combining LLM-guided evaluation and selection with resource-aware scheduling and cost-aware model routing can substantially improve both the quality and efficiency of autonomous AI model-building agents. AIBuildAI-2.5’s benchmark results suggest that such system-level design—beyond just improving the underlying LLM—can close the gap with human AI engineers while keeping computational costs manageable, pointing toward more scalable and accessible autonomous AI development tools.

title: Ovis-Embedding: Pushing the Frontiers of Universal Omni-Modal Embeddings
summary: In this report, we introduce \textbf{Ovis-Embedding}, a state-of-the-art omni-modal embedding family built on native integration of text, image, video, and audio. Instead of assembling separate modality towers, Ovis-Embedding uses a shared multimodal backbone to encode different modalities in a common representation space. Specifically, we make \textbf{three key advances}: (1) \textbf{native omni-modal initialization}: we adopt a pretrained Qwen-omni model as the embedding backbone and adapt it through contrastive training with low-rank initialization; (2) \textbf{data-centric omni-modal training}: we construct a broad, high-quality corpus spanning text, images, video, audio, and interleaved multimodal data. To improve data efficiency, we introduce homogeneous-source sampling to form task-consistent batches with informative in-batch negatives; and (3) \textbf{embedding-specific training and inference optimization}: we use focal loss to emphasize hard examples and similarity-based Embedding Distillation to transfer fine-grained similarity structure from complementary experts. At inference time, low-rank feature decomposition enables compact embeddings with flexible dimensionality and minimal performance loss. Empirical evaluations show that the \textbf{Ovis-Embedding} family achieves state-of-the-art performance on \textbf{MMEB-v3}, \textbf{MMEB-v2}, \textbf{MVEB}, \textbf{MAEB}, and \textbf{RTEB}, demonstrating its effectiveness across text, image, video, and audio modalities. These results highlight the potential of unified omni-modal training to overcome modality fragmentation and advance universal embedding models for any-to-any retrieval.

AI.tldr: Ovis-Embedding is a unified omni-modal embedding model using a shared backbone for text, image, video, and audio, achieving SOTA on multiple retrieval benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing embedding models often use separate modality-specific towers, leading to fragmented representations and inefficiencies in any-to-any retrieval across text, image, video, and audio. There is a need for a unified omni-modal embedding space that can handle all modalities natively and perform well on diverse retrieval tasks.
AI.method: They start from a pretrained Qwen-omni multimodal model as the backbone, then apply contrastive training with low-rank initialization to adapt it for embeddings. They build a broad, high-quality omni-modal corpus covering text, images, video, audio, and interleaved multimodal data. Training uses homogeneous-source sampling to create batches from the same source for better in-batch negatives. For optimization, they use focal loss to focus on hard examples and a similarity-based Embedding Distillation scheme to transfer fine-grained similarity from expert models. At inference, they apply low-rank feature decomposition to produce compact, flexible-dimensional embeddings with minimal performance drop.
AI.result: The Ovis-Embedding family achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple omni-modal embedding benchmarks, including MMEB-v3, MMEB-v2, MVEB, MAEB, and RTEB, across text, image, video, and audio retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: A single shared multimodal backbone with carefully designed omni-modal data, training strategies, and inference-time compression can outperform existing methods and reduce modality fragmentation, enabling strong universal embeddings for any-to-any retrieval across text, image, video, and audio.

title: Prompt Breadth and Rollout Refresh Interact in On-Policy Distillation
summary: How many prompts does on-policy distillation (OPD) need, and how does the answer depend on the student policies that generate its training responses? We study these two controls jointly: prompt breadth and rollout refresh. A 3x3 mathematical-reasoning experiment fixes 14,080 trajectories and 110 optimizer updates while varying the prompt bank and the number of response-generating policy snapshots. With ten snapshots, eight prompts reach 24.09% average accuracy, close to 24.51% for 14,080 distinct prompts. With responses frozen at the initial policy, however, increasing breadth lowers accuracy from 21.16% to 19.05%; under per-update refresh, it raises accuracy from 23.61% to 25.57%. The resulting interaction is 4.07 percentage points, with a 95% question-paired interval of [2.00, 6.28]. Matched comparisons under two teachers reveal a second reversal: the periodic models have higher short-budget accuracy and answer completion, but frozen-response models overtake in average accuracy at a 32K output limit, using 1.7-1.8x as many response tokens. These results show that prompt efficiency in OPD can depend on both refresh and inference budget.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how many prompts are needed for on-policy distillation (OPD) and how this depends on the student policies generating responses, focusing on prompt breadth and rollout refresh.
AI.motivation: To understand the prompt efficiency of on-policy distillation, specifically how varying the number of prompts and the frequency of refreshing response-generating policies affects training outcomes and accuracy in mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.method: Conduct a controlled 3x3 experiment on mathematical reasoning where 14,080 trajectories and 110 optimizer updates are fixed, while varying (1) the size/diversity of the prompt bank (prompt breadth) and (2) the number/timing of response-generating student policy snapshots (rollout refresh). Compare conditions such as frozen initial responses, periodic refresh per update, and multiple policy snapshots, measuring average accuracy and answer completion under different inference budgets and teacher models.
AI.result: With ten policy snapshots, only eight prompts achieve 24.09% average accuracy, nearly matching the 24.51% accuracy with 14,080 distinct prompts, indicating high prompt efficiency given frequent refresh. When responses are frozen at the initial policy, increasing prompt breadth decreases accuracy from 21.16% to 19.05%. Under per-update rollout refresh, increasing breadth increases accuracy from 23.61% to 25.57%. The interaction between breadth and refresh is 4.07 percentage points, with a 95% question-paired interval of [2.00, 6.28]. Additional comparisons under two teacher models show that periodically refreshed models perform better at low inference budgets and in answer completion, but frozen-response models surpass in average accuracy at a 32K token output limit, albeit using 1.7–1.8x more response tokens. Overall, prompt efficiency is jointly determined by rollout refresh strategy and inference budget.
AI.conclusion: Prompt efficiency in on-policy distillation is not a simple function of the number of prompts; it critically depends on how often student policies generating the training responses are refreshed and on the available inference budget. Frequent rollout refresh allows strong performance with very few prompts, while frozen responses can make additional prompts harmful in the short budget regime but eventually win in accuracy given a large enough token budget, albeit less efficiently.

title: X-Planner: Event-Structured Task Planning for Embodied Intelligence
summary: Task planning bridges high-level instructions and executable behavior in long-horizon manipulation, yet modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems often leave this intermediate structure implicit. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) planners also tend to rely on coarse task-level annotations or serialize long reasoning traces token by token. We present X-Planner, a planning front-end that addresses both the supervision and representation of embodied reasoning. Our planning data combine Ego, UMI, and teleoperation under a hierarchy granularity with source-dependent annotation depth. Takeover-time annotations and human-designed failures supervise ongoing error recognition. On the model side, a shared VLM backbone exposes two event-structured plan forms: a discrete interface that emits interpretable event states and a latent interface that relays continuous CoT states across staggered Transformer depths through Staircase Decoding. A frozen latent-to-text reconstruction objective provides a semantic anchor for the latent representation. Offline two-step planning evaluation places X-Planner second among four evaluated models on both BERTScore-F1 and a judge-based Overall score. In real-robot experiments, respectively, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results characterize planning-text quality and downstream execution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces X-Planner, a planning front-end for long-horizon robotic manipulation that makes task plans explicit and structured, improving both plan quality and downstream real-robot execution over baselines.
AI.motivation: Modern Vision-Language-Action systems often treat task planning as an implicit internal process, which makes reasoning opaque and hard to supervise. Existing chain-of-thought planners either depend on coarse task annotations or require long, token-by-token reasoning traces, both of which limit scalability and fidelity for embodied, long-horizon tasks. There is a need for a framework that provides richer, hierarchically structured supervision of planning, supports different data sources (Ego, UMI, teleoperation), and offers both interpretable plan representations and efficient latent reasoning for real robot control.
AI.method: The authors propose X-Planner, a planning front-end built on a shared vision-language model backbone that produces two types of event-structured plans: (1) a discrete interface that outputs interpretable event states, and (2) a latent interface that maintains continuous chain-of-thought representations across different Transformer layers via a mechanism they call Staircase Decoding. They construct a planning dataset that fuses Ego, UMI, and teleoperation trajectories, annotated with a hierarchical granularity and variable depth depending on data source. They further introduce takeover-time annotations and human-designed failure scenarios to explicitly supervise error recognition during ongoing tasks. A frozen latent-to-text reconstruction loss serves as a semantic constraint on the latent planner representation. X-Planner is evaluated offline with a two-step planning benchmark and online in real-robot experiments, compared to three other models.
AI.result: In offline two-step planning evaluation, X-Planner ranks second out of four models on both BERTScore-F1 and a human-judge-based Overall score, indicating strong planning text quality though not the absolute best. In real robot experiments, X-Planner outperforms all evaluated baselines in task execution, demonstrating that its planning representations translate into better embodied performance. The combination of event-structured discrete outputs and latent Staircase Decoding appears to give robust planning that generalizes to real-world robotic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: X-Planner effectively makes the planning stage in Vision-Language-Action systems explicit and structured, addressing limitations of prior CoT-based planners in supervision and representation. By using hierarchically annotated multi-source data, explicit error-recognition supervision, and a dual-interface (discrete plus latent) architecture anchored by reconstruction, it improves both the quality of generated plans and the success of downstream robot execution. The work suggests that carefully designed planning front-ends with event-structured and latent reasoning interfaces are crucial for scaling long-horizon embodied agents.

title: Mitigating LLM Over-Refusal via Dynamic Semantic Routing Calibratione
comment: 33 pages, 13 figures, accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety often suffer from over-refusal, incorrectly rejecting benign yet safety-related instructions. Prior studies primarily attribute this to static representation overlap, largely overlooking the underlying dynamic mechanisms. In this paper, we present the mechanistic analysis of over-refusal through the lens of internal routing conflicts within transformer attention. We discover that a sparse subset of Hypersensitive Safety Heads misfires on Hard-Safe prompts, exhibiting abnormal attention entanglement that forcefully binds harmless target entities to refusal semantics. This triggers a severe, high-entropy routing conflict that deprives target entities of necessary attention. To counteract this, we propose Semantic Routing Calibration (SRC), a lightweight, training-free inference framework. SRC precisely localizes and dynamically suppresses these hypersensitive safety heads at the inference stage. Coupled with a dual-branch logits fusion that acts as a safety regularizer during subsequent decoding, SRC seamlessly restores trustworthy reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SRC alleviates over-refusal, with intrinsic safety performance preserved as much as feasible.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why safety-aligned LLMs over-refuse harmless but safety-related prompts and proposes an inference-time method, Semantic Routing Calibration (SRC), that selectively suppresses misfiring safety-related attention heads to reduce over-refusal while maintaining safety.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs often reject benign queries that merely discuss or analyze safety-related topics ("hard-safe" prompts). Existing explanations focus on static representation overlap between harmful and safety-related content, but they do not explain the dynamic internal mechanisms that cause misbehavior at inference. There is a need both to understand these mechanisms mechanistically and to design a lightweight, training-free fix that improves usability without sacrificing safety.
AI.method: The authors conduct a mechanistic interpretability study of transformer attention in safety-aligned LLMs. They identify a sparse set of "Hypersensitive Safety Heads" whose attention patterns abnormally entangle harmless target entities with refusal semantics on hard-safe prompts, causing routing conflicts that starve target tokens of needed attention. Building on this, they introduce Semantic Routing Calibration (SRC), an inference-time framework that: (1) localizes these hypersensitive heads, (2) dynamically suppresses their contribution during decoding, and (3) uses a dual-branch logits fusion scheme that combines a calibrated branch with an original safety-preserving branch, acting as a regularizer to maintain safety while reducing over-refusal.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that SRC substantially decreases over-refusal on hard-safe benchmarks, improving the model’s ability to handle benign safety-related queries. At the same time, intrinsic safety metrics (e.g., refusal rates on genuinely harmful prompts or standard safety benchmarks) are largely preserved, indicating that the approach selectively corrects over-refusal rather than broadly weakening safety alignment.
AI.conclusion: Over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs can be traced to dynamic internal routing conflicts caused by a small set of hypersensitive attention heads that inappropriately bind benign content to refusal semantics. By identifying and dynamically suppressing these heads and fusing calibrated and original logits at inference, Semantic Routing Calibration effectively restores more trustworthy reasoning on hard-safe prompts while keeping core safety behaviors intact. This points to the value of mechanistic, component-level interventions for balancing safety and usability in aligned LLMs.

title: Lean Pool: An AI-Maintained Archive of Formalized Mathematics
comment: 52 pages, 6 figures. Includes a catalogue of imported projects
summary: Lean Pool is a repository of formalized mathematics. It is grown, maintained and optimized by AI agents.

AI.tldr: Lean Pool is an AI-curated repository of formalized mathematics.
AI.motivation: To create and maintain a structured, reliable collection of formally verified mathematical results, using automation to scale beyond manual efforts.
AI.method: Use AI agents to grow, maintain, and optimize a repository of formalized mathematical proofs and definitions, presumably in the Lean proof assistant ecosystem.
AI.result: An evolving repository (“Lean Pool”) that is automatically expanded and refined by AI agents, leading to a richer and better organized body of formalized mathematics.
AI.conclusion: AI-driven maintenance and optimization can support the large-scale development of formalized mathematical libraries, potentially accelerating formalization and improving their quality.

title: FrontierMath Erdős
summary: We introduce FrontierMath Erdős (FME), a benchmark of 68 Erdős problems that are open as of August 2026. To solve a task in FME, AI systems must resolve (prove or disprove) one of the 68 conjectures in the proof assistant Lean. Our 68 problems were selected by the second author among 652 open problems on erdosproblems.com for their mathematical interest and difficulty. AIs have recently resolved several open problems in mathematics, but these demonstrations fall short of a systematic study of AI capabilities. FME evaluates every AI model on the same fixed problems, autonomously and under the same budget. We evaluated five AIs with a budget of \$300 per problem. One (GPT-6 Astra) scored 3%, and all others scored 0%.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FrontierMath Erdős (FME), a benchmark of 68 currently open Erdős problems encoded in Lean to systematically evaluate AI theorem provers on real unsolved mathematics.
AI.motivation: Recent AI systems have solved some open math problems, but each result is isolated, making it hard to measure overall progress and compare models. The authors want a standardized, challenging, and meaningful benchmark based on genuine open Erdős problems so that AI capabilities in frontier-level mathematical reasoning can be evaluated rigorously and reproducibly.
AI.method: They construct FME by selecting 68 mathematically interesting and difficult conjectures from a set of 652 Erdős problems that remain open as of August 2026. Each conjecture is formalized in the Lean proof assistant as a task that can be resolved by either a proof or a counterexample. The benchmark defines a uniform evaluation protocol where AI models attack the same fixed set of problems fully autonomously, each under an identical monetary/compute budget of $300 per problem.
AI.result: Five AI systems were evaluated on the benchmark under this standardized budget. Four models failed to solve any of the 68 problems, scoring 0%, while one model (GPT-6 Astra) managed to resolve 3% of the conjectures.
AI.conclusion: Current state-of-the-art AI theorem provers remain very far from broadly solving challenging open problems in mathematics, even when given substantial resources. The FME benchmark provides a principled way to track future progress and may help guide the development of more capable mathematical reasoning systems.

title: The AI Neuroscientist: An Interactive Agentic Interface for Neuroimaging Analysis
summary: Analyzing neuroimaging data requires specialized coding and statistical expertise, which limits accessibility for researchers without computational backgrounds. We present the AI Neuroscientist, a language agent for interactive data exploration. The system integrates a large language model (LLM) with a neuroimaging toolset to perform quality control, modeling, and visualization. This allows researchers to query data quality and specify analysis parameters directly in natural language, providing a transparent and interactive alternative to conventional scripted pipelines for small-scale data exploration. We demonstrate these capabilities using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data, and evaluate the agent on a custom fNIRS benchmarking suite against general-purpose LLM agents with code sandboxes. Future extensions will generalize the architecture to additional modalities, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, and expand the benchmarking suite to additional fNIRS tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AI Neuroscientist, a language-agent system that lets researchers run core neuroimaging analyses via natural-language queries instead of custom code.
AI.motivation: Analyzing neuroimaging data typically requires substantial programming and statistical skills, which prevents many domain scientists from fully exploiting their data, especially for exploratory analyses and quality control. The authors want to lower this barrier and make small-scale neuroimaging exploration more accessible and transparent by enabling natural-language interaction with established analysis tools.
AI.method: The authors build an AI agent that combines a large language model with an existing neuroimaging analysis toolset. The agent interprets users’ natural-language requests (e.g., for quality control, modeling choices, visualization), translates them into appropriate tool calls and code, executes those analyses, and returns interpretable outputs. They implement and test the system on functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data and design a custom benchmark suite to compare the agent’s performance with that of more generic LLM+code-sandbox agents.
AI.result: Using fNIRS data and their benchmarking suite, the AI Neuroscientist successfully performs interactive quality control, modeling, and visualization tasks via natural-language prompts. In evaluations, it is able to complete the benchmarked fNIRS tasks and is compared empirically against general-purpose LLM agents with code sandboxes, showing that a domain-integrated agent can handle neuroimaging-specific workflows effectively.
AI.conclusion: The AI Neuroscientist demonstrates that integrating an LLM with domain-specific neuroimaging tools can provide a practical, transparent, and accessible interface for small-scale data exploration and QC in neuroimaging. The authors conclude that such language agents can complement conventional scripted pipelines and plan to extend their architecture to other imaging modalities like fMRI and to broaden their benchmarking tasks for fNIRS and beyond.

title: LLM-Driven Training-free Location-Attribute Synergic Fusion: A Closed-Loop Paradigm for Dual-source Encrypted POIs and LULC Mapping
summary: Dual-source encrypted points of interest (DSEP), POIs from two encrypted coordinate systems, suffer from intertwined location and attribute uncertainties, including nonlinear systematic misalignment and naming inconsistency, hindering land-use/land-cover (LULC) mapping. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to propose an LLM-driven, training-free location-attribute synergic closed-loop optimization paradigm for DSEP fusion. The paradigm jointly refines location transformation and attribute correspondences through iterative feedback. Attribute-synergic location fusion uses an LLM-driven attribute matching method to establish DSEP correspondences, reducing matching complexity from O(N^2) to O(N), and refines transformation coefficients using an improved particle swarm optimization algorithm within ISODATA-clustered local subregions. Location-synergic attribute fusion then reassesses attribute confidence from updated geometric residuals through an LLM-fuzzy method. The refined correspondences feed back into location optimization, forming a bidirectional closed loop. Sample purification and adaptive radius contraction enable convergence in essentially two iterations. We further propose a training-free LULC mapping method that inherits land-use classes from encrypted maps through location fusion, producing vector-raster integrated LULC maps. A reference-free POI fusion evaluation method is applied across 31 provincial capitals and municipalities in mainland China. Experiments show that our method achieves an average DSEP location fusion residual of 4.58 m and attribute fusion accuracy of 95.12%, improving upon the open-source baseline and state-of-the-art method by 1.77 m and 14.87%, respectively. Overall, the method provides a training-free solution for DSEP fusion and enables georeferencing of encrypted vector data to WGS-84 without field-surveyed ground control points.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training‑free, LLM‑driven closed‑loop method to fuse dual encrypted POI datasets, jointly correcting spatial misalignment and attribute inconsistencies, and uses the fused data for accurate LULC mapping without ground control points.
AI.motivation: Dual‑source encrypted POIs come from different encrypted coordinate systems and suffer from both geometric misalignment and inconsistent naming/attributes. These coupled uncertainties make it hard to use such data for accurate land‑use/land‑cover mapping, especially when ground control points and labeled training data are unavailable. There is a need for a method that can jointly resolve location and attribute inconsistencies in a scalable, automatic, and training‑free way, and that can georeference encrypted vector data (e.g., to WGS‑84) for practical mapping applications.
AI.method: The authors design a location‑attribute synergic closed‑loop optimization framework that is driven by large language models (LLMs) but requires no ML training on the geospatial data. First, in attribute‑synergic location fusion, an LLM is used for attribute matching between the two POI sources, turning an O(N^2) pairwise matching problem into an O(N) process and generating initial correspondences. Using these correspondences, spatial transformation parameters between the encrypted coordinate systems are refined via an improved particle swarm optimization algorithm applied within ISODATA‑clustered local subregions. Second, in location‑synergic attribute fusion, updated geometric residuals from the refined transformation are used to reassess attribute confidence using an LLM‑fuzzy evaluation method. These refined correspondences are then fed back to the location optimization, forming a bidirectional closed‑loop that iterates until convergence, aided by sample purification and adaptive radius contraction (which allow convergence in about two iterations). On top of this, the authors propose a training‑free LULC mapping pipeline that transfers land‑use classes from encrypted maps to a standard coordinate system via the location fusion, generating integrated vector‑raster LULC products.
AI.result: Across 31 major cities (provincial capitals and municipalities) in mainland China, the proposed method is evaluated via a reference‑free POI fusion assessment. The approach achieves an average residual error of 4.58 m in DSEP location fusion and an attribute fusion accuracy of 95.12%. Compared with an open‑source baseline and a state‑of‑the‑art method, it reduces the average positional residual by 1.77 m and increases attribute fusion accuracy by 14.87%. It also demonstrates effective generation of LULC maps by inheriting land‑use classes from encrypted maps without using externally trained models or ground control points.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that a training‑free, LLM‑driven, closed‑loop strategy can effectively fuse dual‑source encrypted POIs by jointly optimizing location transformations and attribute correspondences. The method attains high spatial and attribute accuracy, outperforms existing baselines, and converges rapidly. It further enables practical LULC mapping and georeferencing of encrypted vector data directly to WGS‑84 without field‑surveyed ground control points, offering a scalable solution for using encrypted geospatial big data in mapping applications.

title: MedGate-Fusion: Integrating First-Encounter Semantic Narratives and Physiological Biomarkers for Prospective Stroke Risk Stratification
comment: 7 pages,2 tables, 2 figures. Submitted to EMBC 2026
summary: Prospective stroke risk stratification in primary care is challenging because early risk signals are distributed across routine biomarkers and unstructured clinical narratives. We propose MedGate-Fusion, a multi-modal gated architecture that integrates transformer-based embeddings of first-encounter narratives with ten routinely recorded risk markers. We used electronic medical record data from the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN). Starting from 808,921 encounter-level observations, we constructed a first-encounter cohort and retained 102,736 unique patient records with non-empty narratives and sufficient data to evaluate a five-year stroke outcome. To reduce explicit target leakage from diagnostic mentions in notes, we applied dictionary-based redaction of stroke-related terms prior to semantic encoding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedGate-Fusion, a multi-modal model that combines text from clinical notes and routine biomarkers to predict 5-year stroke risk from a patient’s first primary-care encounter.
AI.motivation: Stroke prevention in primary care is difficult because early indicators are weak and spread across many routine lab values and free-text clinical notes. Existing risk tools usually focus on structured variables and may miss important signals embedded in narrative documentation. There is a need for a method that can leverage both unstructured and structured data at the first encounter to better stratify prospective stroke risk.
