AI.method: The authors build MedGate-Fusion, a gated fusion architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings of first-encounter clinical narratives with ten standard stroke risk markers from electronic medical records. They assemble a cohort from the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN), starting from 808,921 encounters and filtering to 102,736 unique patients with adequate narrative and follow-up to ascertain 5-year stroke outcomes. To prevent label leakage, stroke-related terms in the notes are removed via a dictionary-based redaction before being encoded by the transformer.
AI.result: Within the selected cohort of 102,736 patients with first-encounter notes and complete data, MedGate-Fusion is trained to predict 5-year stroke events using both narrative embeddings and structured risk markers. Although specific performance metrics are not reported in the abstract segment, the result is the successful construction of a large, de-duplicated first-encounter dataset and an implemented multi-modal model that can exploit both text and routine biomarkers while controlling for explicit diagnostic leakage in the narratives.
AI.conclusion: The abstract suggests that integrating semantically encoded first-encounter narratives with routine risk markers in a gated multi-modal architecture is a feasible approach to prospective stroke risk stratification in primary care. The preprocessing step of redacting explicit stroke terms reduces direct label leakage, supporting a more realistic evaluation of how early narrative information contributes to medium-term risk prediction.

title: Self-Cleaning and Captured Anyway: One Measured Primitive for Error in a Store an Agent Writes to Itself, and What a Falling Score Actually Measures
summary: "An agent that writes its conclusions into a store it later retrieves from closes a loop usually reported as one-way contamination. Taking the loop to the infinite-tenure limit against an append-only store gives a different picture: because writing never deletes, the reachable state space has a hard upper edge at (n-1)/n, so the outcome is a choice between two edges rather than a decay. At f_0 = 0.9 the interval between the two modes holds 3.6% of 220 runs where a uniform spread would put 20.6%, and is strictly empty on the first 15; the pooled mean describes 8.2% of the runs it summarises, the median 68.2%. Everything the model contributes is carried by one measured primitive with no fitted parameter, the copy function γ(φ): on 36 Wikidata facts, sign(\hatγ - γ_{crit}), with γ_{crit} = 1/k at r = 0, w = 1, predicts the direction of drift on 353 of 360 real-fact runs (39 of 40 synthetic in the same batch). Scale does not rescue the store: pooled frontier capture is 0.850, with claude-sonnet-4.5 captured on 20 of 20 seeds against our registered prediction of <0.5. What the interval tests is distinguishability rather than count: on the real facts, multi-valued runs have 6.4x its occupancy of the rest. It survives at f_0 in {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, capture peaks at f_0 = 0.5, and of four interventions with criteria frozen first, timing dominates fraction at matched budget while a consistency gate drives every model to 0.993. The resampling unit is the seed, at a design effect of 3.75 on a pooled level: under a 44-seed control the ordering supporting claim 4 collapses from Spearman +0.98 at three seeds to +0.31-0.80 at forty-four, while claim 2's ordering is exact there (+1.00, p = 0.017). All 87 graded rows are in Appendix W, 37 of them graded withdrawn, failed, self-correcting, undecidable or an acknowledged limit, against 50 that are not."

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes feedback loops where an AI agent writes to and later reads from a shared store, showing that contamination behaves like convergence to one of two stable extremes rather than gradual decay, and validates a simple copy-function-based predictor of drift direction on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify how much an AI system contaminates a shared knowledge store when it repeatedly reads and writes to it, especially in the infinite-use limit, and to test whether simple, measurable system primitives can predict this contamination and its direction.
AI.method: They model the feedback loop as an agent interacting with an append-only store, derive a theoretical upper bound on contamination using a single primitive copy function γ(φ), run hundreds of simulations (both synthetic and on 36 real Wikidata facts) across many random seeds and initial truth fractions f0, and test various interventions (timing of writes, fraction of data written, consistency gates). They also carefully account for statistical dependence via a design effect and resampling by seed, and report graded results with withdrawals and limits in an appendix.
AI.result: The system’s state space has a hard upper edge at (n-1)/n, so the long-run behavior typically jumps between two modes (edges) instead of gradually decaying. A single measurable primitive, the copy function γ(φ), with critical value γ_crit = 1/k at r = 0, w = 1, correctly predicts the direction of drift in 353/360 real-fact runs and 39/40 synthetic ones. Pooled frontier capture is 0.850; a specific model (claude-sonnet-4.5) is captured in 20/20 seeds, contrary to a prior prediction of <0.5. The ambiguous interval between modes is sparsely populated (3.6% vs 20.6% expected under uniform, empty for the first 15 runs). Multi-valued runs occupy this interval 6.4x more than other runs. Effects persist across different initial truth levels f0 ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, capture peaks at f0 = 0.5, timing of interventions matters more than fraction written, and a consistency gate drives capture to 0.993 for all models. Under more robust 44-seed resampling, one claimed ordering weakens substantially while another is statistically confirmed (Spearman ρ = 1.0, p = 0.017).
AI.conclusion: AI–store feedback contamination in an append-only setting is best understood as convergence to one of two stable extremes rather than smooth degradation, and this behavior is largely governed by a single measurable copy parameter. Simple interventions like timing and consistency gating can strongly affect capture, but scale alone does not prevent it. The authors emphasize statistical rigor by resampling over seeds and openly grading claims, including many withdrawn or limited ones, to give a transparent picture of what their model and experiments do and do not support.

title: When LLM Agents Fail to Read the Room: ReAdapt for Relational Social Reasoning
summary: A social agent's most basic decisions (should I react to this post? who should I reach out to?) are not purely content problems. The right action often hinges on the latent relationship between people -- tie strength, reciprocity, mutual connections -- rather than on which content is most salient. Standard LLM agent loops do not explicitly represent how new relational evidence should revise the agent's current social hypothesis, leaving them prone to surface-obvious choices when relational and content cues diverge. We formalize this failure mode with a relationship-reasoning benchmark: 500 synthetic social worlds with friendships, follows, reaction histories, and feeds, yielding 1,000 queries over two tasks, reaction selection and warm introduction (finding the best bridge to a target person). By construction, the surface-obvious candidate differs from the relationship-grounded oracle in about 53% of queries, forming an overturn subset where the agent must use relational evidence to revise an initially plausible choice. We propose ReAdapt (Relationship-Adaptive Agent with Policy-driven sTate), which augments the ReAct loop with an explicit structured social state z = (G, B, R, N, D) capturing goal, belief, relationship, norm, and disclosure. After each tool observation, ReAdapt runs a typed Adapt step that updates this state and emits a policy operation (continue, switch, abandon, or clarify) before choosing the next action. With Gemini-3-Flash on a stratified subset of n = 150 queries per task, ReAdapt improves warm-introduction accuracy from 37% to 51% (+14 points) and reaction-selection accuracy from 69% to 77% (+8 points). Oracle regret drops from 0.260 to 0.152 and from 0.095 to 0.053, respectively. Holding the model, tools, and environments fixed, these results suggest that explicit relational-state adaptation helps LLM agents turn retrieved social evidence into revised decisions.

AI.tldr: They build a benchmark and an agent architecture to test and improve how LLM agents reason about social relationships, not just content, in social-media-like tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents acting in social environments (e.g., social media) often make decisions based only on surface content cues, ignoring latent relationship factors like tie strength, reciprocity, and network structure. This causes them to choose actions that look obvious from content but are suboptimal socially, especially when social and content cues diverge. There is a lack of formal benchmarks and agent designs that explicitly test and support relationship-aware reasoning.
AI.method:
1) Construct a relationship-reasoning benchmark: 500 synthetic social worlds containing friendship and follow graphs, interaction histories, and feeds. From these, derive 1,000 queries across two tasks: (a) reaction selection (deciding how to react to posts) and (b) warm introduction (choosing the best intermediary to reach a target). The benchmark is designed so that in about 53% of cases, the content-obvious choice differs from a relationship-grounded oracle, creating an overturn subset requiring relational reasoning.
2) Analyze the failure mode of standard ReAct-style LLM agent loops, which don't maintain or update an explicit representation of social relationships and thus tend to stick with surface-obvious actions.
3) Propose ReAdapt, a modified agent loop that introduces an explicit structured social state z = (G, B, R, N, D) representing goal, belief, relationship, norm, and disclosure. After each tool call, the agent performs a typed Adapt step that (i) updates this state based on new evidence, and (ii) emits a policy operation (continue, switch, abandon, clarify) before choosing the next tool or action. They evaluate ReAdapt using Gemini-3-Flash on a stratified subset of 150 queries per task, holding model, tools, and environment constant relative to a baseline ReAct setup.
AI.result: On the benchmark subset (n = 150 per task) with Gemini-3-Flash, ReAdapt significantly improves performance over a standard agent loop. For the warm-introduction task, accuracy increases from 37% to 51% (+14 percentage points), and oracle regret decreases from 0.260 to 0.152. For reaction selection, accuracy rises from 69% to 77% (+8 points), with oracle regret dropping from 0.095 to 0.053. These gains occur despite keeping the underlying LLM, tools, and synthetic environment fixed, isolating the benefit to the explicit relational-state adaptation mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and updating a structured social/relational state within the agent loop enables LLM agents to use retrieved social evidence more effectively, leading to better decisions when relational cues conflict with surface content cues. The benchmark and ReAdapt architecture jointly demonstrate that relationship-aware state representations and adaptation policies can substantially reduce regret and improve accuracy on socially grounded tasks, indicating a promising direction for building more socially competent LLM agents.

title: LatentPort: Beyond KV Cache - Cross-Model Transfer of Recurrent Memory in Hybrid Language Models: A 4B-to-9B Hybrid-State Handoff Without Target Prefix Replay
summary: Can one language model hand its live memory to another without the receiver rereading the context? We demonstrate useful persistent hybrid-state transfer across one architecture-matched Qwen3.5 4B-to-9B sibling pair. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstrated cross-model handoff of persistent recurrent inference state between differently sized hybrid language models without target prefix replay. Translated attention KV alone leaves a large gap; adding the Gated DeltaNet (GDN) persistent-state package lowers teacher-forced negative log-likelihood (NLL), the average next-token log-loss, by 0.747 nats/token (95% paired document bootstrap CI [0.6921, 0.8047]), improving all 64 PG19 documents. Direct recurrent and convolution reuse outperforms the tested learned GDN maps, consistent with partial functional compatibility of persistent-state coordinates. A fresh component factorial selects translated KV with direct recurrent and convolution state. An additional 434,176-parameter correction improves that base on 64 fresh web documents: continuation loss is 0.076 nats/token above native 9B (excess NLL), Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence is 0.022, and native context recovery (NCR) is 0.918. Corrected 9B significantly beats continued 4B inference while processing zero historical prefix tokens. Evidence covers one direction, one geometry-matched Base-model pair, and 4K teacher-forced continuation; the near-native gate failed, the 16K branch was not run, and free-generation equivalence and a general state interface remain unproven.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that one language model can hand over its internal recurrent state to a larger sibling model without replaying the whole context, achieving near-native performance on the receiver.
AI.motivation: Long-context inference with large models is expensive because they must repeatedly process long prefixes. If a smaller model can process the long history and then transfer its internal state to a larger model, the larger model could continue generation cheaply without rereading the entire context. It was unclear whether such cross-model persistent state transfer was possible in practice, especially between models of different sizes.
AI.method: The authors study a pair of architecture-matched Qwen3.5 hybrid models (4B and 9B parameters). They attempt to transfer the full hybrid recurrent state (attention KV cache plus Gated DeltaNet—GDN—persistent state) from the 4B to the 9B model, so that the 9B can continue generation without seeing the prior tokens. They compare several state-transfer variants: translated attention KV alone, direct reuse vs. learned mappings of recurrent and convolutional components, and an additional small correction module. Evaluation uses teacher-forced continuation on PG19 and fresh web documents, measuring negative log-likelihood (NLL), Jensen-Shannon divergence, and native context recovery (NCR).
AI.result: Using only translated attention KV leads to a substantial performance gap relative to the native 9B model. Adding the GDN persistent-state package reduces NLL by 0.747 nats/token on PG19 (with tight bootstrap CIs) and improves all 64 test documents. Direct reuse of recurrent and convolution states outperforms learned GDN mappings, indicating partial compatibility between state spaces of the two models. A factorial gating mechanism selects between translated KV and directly reused recurrent/convolutional state. With an extra ~434k-parameter correction layer, the transferred 4B→9B state yields continuation NLL only 0.076 nats/token worse than native 9B, JS divergence of 0.022, and NCR of 0.918 on fresh web data. The corrected 9B continuation is significantly better than just continuing inference with the 4B model, despite never seeing the historical tokens.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first empirical evidence that persistent hybrid state—attention plus recurrent components—can be transferred across differently sized but architecture-matched language models without replaying the prefix, while retaining near-native performance for the larger model. This suggests a practical path toward computation-efficient multi-model pipelines, where smaller models handle long histories and larger models take over using state handoff. However, results are limited to a single architecture-matched Base pair, one transfer direction, and teacher-forced 4K-token continuations. The authors emphasize that broader generalization, free-generation behavior, longer contexts, and a universal state interface remain open problems.

title: Attention as a Routing Graph: Live Circuit Extraction from a Single Forward Pass
summary:
Finding circuits in language models usually means running many careful interventions. We try something simpler: treat attention as a routing map from one forward pass, keep a small set of routes that point toward the answer, and ask whether those routes actually matter.
  They often do. On induction and IOI (tasks where the "right" circuit is already known), ablating our extracted edges hurts the model much more than ablating a random set of the same size. We evaluate n=100 prompts per cell on GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and Pythia-410M, with paired gap tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. The extract step costs one forward; a head-by-head patch sweep costs about two orders of magnitude more.
  We are not claiming a complete circuit atlas. We are claiming a cheap sketch that carries real causal signal on known tasks, with clear failure modes when it does not. Code and evaluation artifacts are at https://github.com/Aquinf03/live-circuit-routing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cheap, single-forward-pass method to approximate causal circuits in language models by using attention as routing, and shows these extracted routes are meaningfully important on known mechanistic interpretability benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing circuit-finding in language models relies on many expensive, carefully designed interventions and patching sweeps. The authors want a cheaper, automated way to sketch important computation pathways (circuits) that still carry real causal information, making circuit analysis more scalable and practical.
AI.method: In one forward pass, they interpret attention as a routing map, then select a small subset of attention edges (routes) that appear to point toward the answer token. They then ablate (remove or zero out) just these extracted edges and compare the performance drop to ablating random edges of the same number. They run this on induction and IOI tasks, using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and Pythia-410M, testing 100 prompts per model-layer cell and reporting paired performance gaps with bootstrap confidence intervals. They compare the cost to standard head-by-head patch sweeps, which are around 100x more expensive.
AI.result: Across induction and IOI tasks, ablating the extracted attention routes typically hurts model performance much more than ablating a random subset of edges of the same size, indicating that the routing-based extraction captures truly important causal paths. The extraction requires only a single forward pass per prompt, whereas full head-sweep patching is about two orders of magnitude more computationally expensive.
AI.conclusion: The proposed routing-based extraction method does not produce a full, detailed circuit atlas but provides a fast, approximate "live" sketch of important causal pathways in language models. This sketch often aligns with known circuits on benchmark tasks and carries genuine causal signal, while also exhibiting clear, observable failure modes when it does not work. This makes it a practical, low-cost tool for mechanistic interpretability workflows, complementing more expensive and precise circuit-mapping methods.

title: MoM: Memory of Memory
summary: For a long-horizon LLM agent, the memory question is not what was once recorded but what \emph{currently holds}. Most designs answer it only indirectly: every interaction is stored, and the present is reconstructed at query time by retrieving and reconciling records, so stale values re-enter and the same conflicts are re-litigated. Committing the current value at write time avoids this, but existing write-time (CRUD) memories overwrite, so a wrong update is unrecoverable and prior state is lost. We take the missing combination---\emph{commit on arrival while retaining what is displaced}---and formalize it as \textsc{Memory of Memory} (MoM): memory tracks not only content but the provenance, status, and history of its own entries. We instantiate MoM as \textsc{Provenant Memory} (P-Mem), a typed provenance graph whose \emph{active frontier} exposes one current value per resolved key while displaced values are retained as provenance; typed operations decide whether a new observation supports, supersedes, contests, rejects, revokes, or resolves an existing value. P-Mem's decisive gain is validity rather than accuracy: its turn-level read matches the strongest retrieval memory in accuracy at $\sim$4$\times$ fewer read tokens---a retrieval-granularity effect---while graph-guided turn pruning cuts the knowledge-update stale-answer rate (19.4\%$\rightarrow$10.9\%); on revision chains it stays at 100\% where query-time reading collapses to 25\%, and, because displaced values are retained rather than overwritten, it recovers committed errors a CRUD memory cannot (100\% vs.\ 0\%).

AI.tldr: Introduces Memory of Memory (MoM) and a concrete implementation, Provenant Memory (P-Mem), which maintains both current values and their provenance/history for long-horizon LLM agents, enabling valid, efficient, and correctable memory updates.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents need a notion of "what currently holds" rather than a raw log of past interactions. Existing retrieval-based memories repeatedly re-hash stale or conflicting information at query time, while CRUD-style write-time memories overwrite state, making wrong updates unrecoverable and discarding history. A new memory model is needed that both commits the current state and preserves displaced information and its provenance.
AI.method: Define Memory of Memory (MoM) as a memory architecture that tracks not only content but provenance, status, and history. Instantiate MoM as Provenant Memory (P-Mem), a typed provenance graph. The graph maintains an active frontier with one current value per key, while displaced values are preserved as provenance. Typed update operations (support, supersede, contest, reject, revoke, resolve) determine how new observations modify the graph and active frontier. Evaluate P-Mem against strong retrieval baselines on accuracy, token usage, stale-answer rates, revision chains, and error recovery.
AI.result: P-Mem achieves similar turn-level accuracy to strong retrieval memories while using about four times fewer read tokens due to more efficient retrieval granularity. Graph-guided turn pruning reduces stale-answer rate from 19.4% to 10.9% on knowledge updates. On revision chains, P-Mem maintains 100% performance while query-time reading drops to 25%. Because it retains displaced values, P-Mem can fully recover from committed errors (100% recovery) whereas CRUD memories cannot recover at all (0%).
AI.conclusion: Tracking provenance and history in memory, rather than only current content or raw logs, yields more valid and robust behavior for long-horizon LLM agents. Provenant Memory (P-Mem), as an instance of Memory of Memory, offers efficient reads, lower stale-answer rates, robustness on revision chains, and the ability to recover from incorrect updates—all without sacrificing accuracy relative to strong retrieval-based approaches.

title: Learned Enterprise Data Comprehension: Compression and Routing for Data Agents
summary: Structured-data agents in enterprise settings must reason over complex data environments whose relevant evidence is distributed across schemas, relationships, policies, and recurring business roles. Modern agentic systems often address this burden through reusable markdown-style memory or skill files that preserve previously discovered information for later queries, reducing the need to rediscover the same structure repeatedly. This is useful, but it obscures a natural division of labor: agents are well suited to semantic reasoning, while learned systems are well suited to predicting and organizing recurring structure. We introduce latent equivalence learning to bridge this gap. The framework separates persistent task-relevant identities from their dataset-relative realizations. In our realization, supporting and opposing evidence shape support-realized Gaussian prototypes that learn how those identities are expressed in a particular data environment, while soft-membership profiles retain distinctions lost under a hard assignment. A separate learned query-prototype system represents recurring evidential requirements and maps them through a learned compatibility function into the same persistent identity structure. This identity-factorized, query-conditioned routing materializes the relevant dataset-specific evidence for downstream reasoning, allowing the agent to operate over an already organized evidential state rather than reconstructing cross-schema structure at every query. On the Data Agent Benchmark, spanning 54 queries across 12 heterogeneous datasets, our full implementation achieves 94.67% dataset-macro stratified Pass@1 over five complete trials and 258/270 successful raw query attempts, compared with 55.51% for the benchmark's Claude Opus 4.6 reference agent, ranking first among 40 leaderboard entries at submission.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework, latent equivalence learning, to help structured-data agents reason more effectively in complex enterprise data environments by separating persistent task identities from their dataset-specific realizations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a data agent benchmark.
AI.motivation: Enterprise data environments are complex, with relevant information scattered across schemas, relationships, policies, and business roles. Current agentic systems use reusable markdown-style memory or skill files to store previously discovered structure, but this mixes semantic reasoning with pattern discovery and obscures a natural division of labor between agents and learned systems. The authors are motivated to create a framework that lets agents focus on semantic reasoning while a learned component captures and organizes recurring structural patterns across datasets and queries.
AI.method: The paper introduces latent equivalence learning, which separates persistent, task-relevant identities from their dataset-relative realizations. In the proposed realization, evidence in a given dataset shapes Gaussian prototypes that represent how each identity is expressed in that environment, with soft-membership profiles preserving nuanced membership rather than hard assignments. A separate learned query-prototype subsystem models recurring evidential requirements and maps them, via a learned compatibility function, into the same persistent identity space. This enables identity-factorized, query-conditioned routing that selects and organizes the relevant dataset-specific evidence for the agent.
AI.result: On the Data Agent Benchmark, which comprises 54 queries across 12 heterogeneous datasets, the full implementation of the proposed framework achieves 94.67% dataset-macro stratified Pass@1 over five trials, successfully answering 258 out of 270 raw query attempts. This significantly outperforms the benchmark's Claude Opus 4.6 reference agent, which achieves 55.51% Pass@1, and places the method first among 40 leaderboard entries at the time of submission.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that latent equivalence learning effectively bridges the gap between semantic reasoning and structural pattern learning in structured-data agents. By factorizing persistent identities from their dataset-specific realizations and using learned query prototypes for routing, the approach allows agents to operate over pre-organized evidential states instead of repeatedly reconstructing cross-schema structure. This leads to substantial performance gains on a challenging benchmark, suggesting that identity-based organization is a powerful abstraction for complex enterprise data reasoning tasks.

title: ICDAR2026 Competition on Multimodal Reasoning over Documents in Multiple Domains
summary: In this report we present results of the ICDAR2026 Competition on Multimodal Reasoning over Documents in Multiple Domains. This competition aimed to advance research in document understanding through the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA). Building upon previous DocVQA benchmarks, this competition introduces challenging reasoning questions over a diverse collection of documents spanning eight domains, including business reports, scientific papers, slides, posters, maps, comics, infographics, and engineering drawings. The competition concluded with 20 valid submissions from 8 teams spanning zero-shot VLMs, OCR and parser-augmented pipelines, agentic retrieval systems, multi-agent ensembles, and fine-tuned multimodal models. The results show that the strongest systems move beyond single-pass prompting and instead rely on structured evidence extraction, retrieval, verification, and orchestration across multiple components.

AI.tldr: Competition report on multimodal document VQA across eight document domains, evaluating diverse system architectures and highlighting the importance of multi-step, structured reasoning pipelines.
AI.motivation: To push forward research in multimodal document understanding by creating a more challenging and diverse benchmark for visual question answering over real-world documents from many domains, beyond previous DocVQA setups.
AI.method: Organized an ICDAR2026 competition with a new benchmark of multimodal reasoning questions over documents in eight domains; collected and evaluated 20 valid system submissions using different paradigms, including zero-shot vision-language models, OCR+parser pipelines, retrieval-augmented and agentic systems, multi-agent ensembles, and fine-tuned multimodal models.
AI.result: 20 submissions from 8 teams were benchmarked; systems employing more sophisticated, multi-step pipelines with explicit evidence extraction and retrieval generally outperformed simpler single-pass prompting approaches.
AI.conclusion: Effective multimodal document VQA, especially for complex reasoning over diverse document types, benefits from moving beyond single-pass models to structured, multi-component pipelines that orchestrate evidence extraction, retrieval, and verification.

title: Making Agents More Consistent: Skills Should Form Habits for Repeat Tasks
summary:
On repeated work, agents are inconsistent. We ran 42 tasks three times each and found that, depending on the model, 38% to 74% returned answers that did not agree. Consistency is what a buyer, an auditor, or a regulator requires, and agents do not have it. They are wasteful too: 95.3% to 97.2% of what an agent generates goes to re-deriving a plan the system already knows.
  We propose skill habit formation. An agent mines its own execution history for candidate skills, deterministic variants that compete against the incumbent rather than replacing it. A candidate declares the region of input space it claims, so the common case runs as a script and the rest falls through to reasoning. Four gates of ascending cost admit candidates; the central one tests a candidate's execution trace against a retained reference, within a tolerance measured from that reference's own run-to-run variability.
  On text-to-SQL, three of four reasoning arms reproduced their own output on 11 to 13 of 42 repeated questions and the fourth on 26 of 42, while a habit-formed variant reproduced on all 456 dispatches we repeated and was non-inferior to every arm it replaced (p<0.0001). It also used 14% to 56% fewer tokens, turning net positive after 7 to 53 reuses.
  We measured what this costs in accuracy. The guard admitted work it should have deferred on 2.6% of natural paraphrases and 26% of inputs near its boundary, and 11 of 13 such failures were invisible to the trace-conformance gate at any threshold. Deterministic errors repeat exactly: a bad habit is as reliable as a good one, and that is the price of the property that makes the system auditable. Separating routing from parameter extraction raised end-to-end accuracy from 0.888 to 0.952 at 43% of the cost.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that LLM-based agents are inconsistent and wasteful when repeatedly solving similar tasks, and proposes “skill habit formation,” a mechanism that mines past executions to create deterministic skills that improve consistency, efficiency, and auditability with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents show large run-to-run variability on identical inputs and repeatedly spend tokens and computation re-deriving solutions they already know. This undermines trust for buyers, auditors, and regulators who need consistent, auditable behavior, and it is resource-inefficient. The authors aim to provide a way for agents to become both more consistent and cheaper to operate without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: The authors introduce skill habit formation: the agent analyzes its own execution history to extract deterministic “skills” (habits) that capture common patterns of reasoning. These skills are added as competing variants rather than replacements and are invoked when the input falls into a declared region of input space. Execution then uses a four-stage gating system of increasing cost to decide whether to apply a learned habit or fall back to full reasoning, with a key gate that checks the candidate habit’s execution trace against a reference run, using a tolerance calibrated by the reference’s own variability. They evaluate this on text-to-SQL tasks with multiple reasoning arms, comparing baseline repeated runs to habit-formed variants in terms of consistency, token usage, and accuracy under various input perturbations and boundary conditions.
AI.result: On text-to-SQL benchmarks, standard reasoning arms only reproduced their own outputs on a subset of repeated questions (11–13 out of 42 for three arms and 26 out of 42 for the fourth), whereas the habit-formed system reproduced its outputs on all 456 repeated dispatches tested. It matched or exceeded the accuracy of all arms it replaced (non-inferior with p<0.0001) while using 14%–56% fewer tokens and becoming net beneficial after 7–53 reuses of a given habit. However, the guard sometimes admitted cases it should have deferred: 2.6% of natural paraphrases and 26% of boundary-near inputs, and most of these failures (11 of 13) could not be detected by the trace-conformance gate at any threshold. Deterministic habits thus repeated both good and bad decisions.
AI.conclusion: Skill habit formation makes LLM agents more consistent, auditable, and efficient by turning frequently repeated reasoning patterns into deterministic skills gated by execution-trace conformance tests. While this introduces the risk of reliably repeating systematic errors, it substantially improves run-to-run determinism, reduces token cost, and can even raise overall accuracy when routing is separated from parameter extraction, as shown by an increase in end-to-end accuracy from 0.888 to 0.952 at 43% of the original cost.

title: Graph-Based Inference for Feedback-Driven Word Deduction: A Scalable Framework for the Jotto Problem
summary:
A feedback-based word deduction framework based on the Jotto problem is proposed, and the problem space is represented as a weighted graph where all valid words correspond to nodes, and the edge weight is defined by the number of common letters between the two words. Finally, the gameplay is defined as an iterative constraint propagation mechanism where feedback is used to iteratively narrow the incompatible space of the graph, facilitating the reduction of the hypothesis space in a structured and interpretable manner.
  In contrast to existing approaches, where the problem space is typically defined for fixed-length isograms, the proposed framework generalizes to variable-length words (between 3 and 8 letters) and naturally extends to repeated letter cases, facilitating the treatment of realistic Jotto problem instances within a unified framework for the first time. The proposed framework's applicability and solver dynamics are also discussed through an interactive implementation and a qualitative case study, respectively.
  Significant automated tests on approximately 3,000 simulated gameplay scenarios identify a novel convergence behavior: the expected number of iterations diminishes with increasing word length. A strong relationship is confirmed using statistical tests to verify a logarithmic relationship, which is also verified using regression modeling and goodness-of-fit tests.
  In addition to the initial problem statement, this formulation introduces graph pruning as a viable paradigm for feedback-driven inference with interpretability and its association with symbolic reasoning and interactive intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: They propose a graph-based, feedback-driven framework to solve generalized Jotto word deduction problems, showing a surprising logarithmic drop in required guesses as word length increases, and framing this as interpretable graph pruning for symbolic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing Jotto solvers usually assume fixed-length, no-repetition isogram words, which is unrealistic and limits analysis; there is a need for a unified, interpretable framework that can handle variable word lengths and repeated letters, and to better understand solver dynamics statistically.
AI.method: Model the Jotto problem as a weighted graph where each valid word is a node and edge weights reflect the number of shared letters. Use feedback from guesses as constraints to iteratively prune incompatible nodes/edges, thereby shrinking the hypothesis space. Evaluate the framework via an interactive implementation, a qualitative case study, and large-scale simulations (~3,000 games), then analyze convergence behavior using statistical tests, regression, and goodness-of-fit for a hypothesized logarithmic relationship between word length and iterations to solution.
AI.result: Empirical tests on about 3,000 simulated games reveal a new convergence pattern: as the target word length increases from 3 to 8 letters, the expected number of iterations to solve the puzzle actually decreases, following a strong and statistically supported logarithmic relationship. The framework successfully handles variable-length and repeated-letter words within one unified model and exhibits interpretable pruning dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first unified, graph-based, feedback-driven Jotto framework that accommodates realistic word constraints and yields interpretable inference via graph pruning. It uncovers a logarithmic convergence behavior where longer words require fewer iterations on average, and positions graph pruning as a general, interpretable paradigm for feedback-driven inference, connecting Jotto-style gameplay to symbolic reasoning and interactive intelligent systems.

title: Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as course-specific tutors, but their usefulness depends on grounding in vetted instructional materials that are often revised mid-semester. Our prior work built a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over an authentic machine learning course corpus (Foundations of Machine Learning) and found that retrieval improved contextual grounding, but that fixed retrieval strategies were suboptimal. That motivates a different question: whether how a corpus is structured at ingest time matters more than how much is retrieved at query time. We present a controlled head-to-head comparison of two knowledge representations over an identical classroom corpus: (A) vector RAG, replicating the best-performing configuration from our prior study, and (B) an LLM-compiled wiki (Karpathy framework), in which the corpus is synthesized at ingest into linked concept pages with explicit cross-references and citations back to source materials. We evaluate 59 questions spanning single-fact recall, cross-unit concept linking, synthesis and explanation, and currency after a syllabus revision, scored by an LLM judge against a human-authored rubric. Both representations answered single-fact questions about equally well (9.33 vs. 9.96 of 10), but diverged sharply on questions requiring links across course units. The compiled wiki remained accurate and grounded (9.93; 100% grounded in cited sources), while retrieval scored lower and was markedly less grounded (8.14; 64%). The wiki's citations let students and instructors trace any claim back to the lecture that introduced it, adding a layer of dynamic retrieval that machine learning courses require. While further testing is needed, instructors using AI to support learning in ML courses should consider wiki-based structure for its potential to support foundational elements of best practice.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two ways of structuring course materials for large language model tutors—a standard vector-based RAG system vs. an LLM-compiled wiki—and finds that while both handle simple factual questions similarly, the wiki structure is much better for questions requiring connections across course units and offers superior grounding via explicit citations.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that multimodal RAG over course materials improves grounding but that fixed retrieval strategies are not ideal. This raises the question of whether the way the corpus is organized when ingested might matter more than tuning retrieval at query time, especially for dynamic, evolving course content. The authors aim to understand which knowledge representation better supports different types of learning queries in a real machine learning course setting.
AI.method: Using the same machine learning course corpus, the authors construct two knowledge representations: (A) a strong baseline vector RAG system based on their previous best configuration, and (B) an LLM-compiled wiki using the Karpathy framework, where content is synthesized into linked concept pages with explicit cross-references and citations. They evaluate performance on 59 questions covering single-fact recall, cross-unit concept linking, synthesis/explanation, and handling updated material after a syllabus change. Answers from each system are scored by an LLM judge using a human-authored rubric, including both accuracy and grounding in cited sources.
AI.result: Both systems perform similarly on single-fact recall questions (scores of 9.33 vs. 9.96 out of 10). However, on questions requiring linking concepts across course units, the wiki representation substantially outperforms vector RAG: it achieves a score of 9.93 with 100% of answers grounded in cited sources, while the RAG system scores 8.14 with only 64% of answers grounded. The wiki's structured pages and explicit citations enable better cross-unit reasoning and traceability to original lectures.
AI.conclusion: The way instructional corpora are structured at ingest time has a strong effect on LLM tutor performance, especially for higher-level and cross-unit reasoning tasks. An LLM-compiled wiki organization, with linked concept pages and explicit citations, offers better grounding and accuracy than a purely vector-based RAG approach for complex queries in a machine learning course. This structure also supports traceability of claims back to lectures, aligning with best practices in ML education. The authors recommend that instructors using AI tutors consider wiki-based corpus structuring, while noting that more extensive testing is still needed.

title: ChainDoRA: Tensor-Train Factorized Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks while updating only a small fraction of their pretrained parameters. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) uses two trainable low-rank matrices, while Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) further separates weight magnitude and direction but retains the dense LoRA-style factorization in its directional branch. We propose ChainDoRA, a weight-decomposed adaptation framework that constructs the directional low-rank factors from a connected Tensor-Train (TT) chain, where the adapter rank forms the boundary rank between input- and output-side TT contractions and an independent TT rank controls representation capacity and parameter cost. Under a controlled 15,119-example response-only adaptation setting with LLaMA-7B, ChainDoRA is evaluated against matched LoRA and DoRA baselines on seven commonsense reasoning benchmarks. ChainDoRA with TT rank 16 achieves a seven-task average accuracy of 72.30%, compared with 69.88% for LoRA and 69.39% for DoRA, while requiring only 5.35M trainable parameters versus 56.10M for LoRA and 56.98M for DoRA, corresponding to a 90.62% reduction relative to DoRA. Ablations over TT rank and adapter placement show controllable parameter-accuracy trade-offs, indicating that connected TT parameterization can substantially reduce the parameter cost of magnitude-direction adaptation while preserving, and in this setting improving, downstream reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces ChainDoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method using tensor-train-structured low-rank adapters that outperform LoRA and DoRA on reasoning tasks with far fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Standard PEFT methods like LoRA and DoRA still require tens of millions of trainable parameters when adapting large language models, limiting scalability and deployment in resource-constrained settings. The authors aim to reduce the parameter footprint of magnitude-direction (weight-decomposed) adaptation while maintaining or improving downstream performance, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks.
AI.method: They propose ChainDoRA, which keeps DoRA’s weight-decomposition (separating magnitude and direction) but replaces the dense low-rank matrices in the directional branch with a connected Tensor-Train (TT) factorization. The adapter rank becomes the boundary rank between input-side and output-side TT contractions, while an independent TT rank directly controls model capacity and parameter count. They adapt LLaMA-7B on a 15,119-example response-only setting and evaluate ChainDoRA versus rank-matched LoRA and DoRA across seven commonsense reasoning benchmarks, along with ablations over TT rank and where adapters are placed in the network.
AI.result: With TT rank 16, ChainDoRA attains an average accuracy of 72.30% across seven reasoning benchmarks, outperforming LoRA (69.88%) and DoRA (69.39%). It uses only 5.35M trainable parameters compared to 56.10M for LoRA and 56.98M for DoRA, corresponding to about a 90.6% reduction in parameter count relative to DoRA. Ablations confirm that increasing TT rank and changing adapter placement provide a smooth trade-off between parameter count and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Connected Tensor-Train parameterization within a weight-decomposed adapter (ChainDoRA) can drastically cut the number of trainable parameters needed for PEFT while preserving or even improving reasoning performance. The method offers a tunable parameter-accuracy trade-off via TT rank and adapter placement, demonstrating that tensorized low-rank structures are an effective design choice for scalable, parameter-efficient LLM adaptation.

title: Clarification Is Not Correction: LLMs Fail to Let Go
summary: Dialogue failures in language models are usually framed as memory failures: context too long, summaries lossy, a constraint forgotten. We argue this misses a deeper problem: in many conversations the model does not forget, it commits too early. An ambiguous early turn collapses into a single hidden interpretation, and later clarification is filtered through that commitment. We call this early posterior collapse: unresolved user intent collapsing into a committed task state before ambiguity is resolved. We study it with controlled dialogue tasks in writing, planning, and coding using Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Across thousands of trials, the same information in different orders yields different outcomes, even when the final dialogue contains equivalent task-relevant information. This order effect suggests later clarification is treated as extra context rather than a corrective signal: it refines a stale task state without invalidating it. Coding tasks are especially vulnerable, suggesting early assumptions get embedded in structured artifacts such as interfaces and control flow. Standard prompting and memory strategies do not reliably help: summaries can collapse ambiguity, and chain-of-thought can reduce explicit wrong commitment in reasoning traces without improving final task success. These findings motivate uncertainty-preserving state management. If assistants cannot let go of early interpretations, robustness cannot rely on post hoc correction alone; it must keep ambiguous early turns from hardening into one task state. Assistants should hold tentative hypotheses while ambiguity remains, ask before executing when high-impact ambiguity persists, and rebuild from a revised state when later evidence invalidates an earlier reading. Rather than one prompting fix, we aim to redirect research for interactive LLMs from retaining more context toward preserving uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and analyzes a core failure mode of dialogue LLMs called early posterior collapse, where models commit too quickly to a single interpretation of ambiguous user input, causing later clarifications to be misused and reducing robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing work tends to treat dialogue failures as memory or context problems (forgetting constraints, lossy summaries, limited context windows). However, the authors observe that even when models do remember, they often lock into an early, incorrect interpretation of the user’s intent and fail to properly revise it. There is little systematic study of how information order and ambiguity affect interactive performance and how models manage internal task state over a multi-turn exchange. This gap motivates a focused examination of early commitment and its consequences, with the goal of shifting research from purely context retention toward uncertainty management in interactive systems.
AI.method: The authors define and operationalize the notion of early posterior collapse: the model prematurely collapsing multiple plausible interpretations of the user’s intent into a single internal task state. They construct controlled dialogue tasks in three domains—writing, planning, and coding—and run thousands of multi-turn interactions with Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash. They manipulate the order in which equivalent task-relevant information is presented while ensuring the final dialogue turns contain the same information content. They then measure differences in outcomes as evidence of order effects and state-commitment issues. They also test standard prompting and memory strategies (e.g., summaries, chain-of-thought) to see whether they mitigate the problem.
AI.result: The experiments show strong order effects: presenting the same information in different sequences leads to systematically different outcomes, even when the final context available to the model is informationally equivalent. This indicates that the model treats later clarification as additional context that refines but does not invalidate the early internal task state. Coding tasks exhibit the strongest vulnerability, suggesting that early assumptions, once encoded into structured artifacts such as APIs, interfaces, or control flow, are hard for the model to revise. Conventional remedies like better summaries or chain-of-thought prompting fail to consistently alleviate the issue: summaries can themselves prematurely collapse ambiguity, and chain-of-thought can reduce explicit wrong commitments in the reasoning trace without improving actual task success.
AI.conclusion: The central issue in many dialogue failures is not just limited memory or context, but the model’s inability to preserve and revise uncertainty about user intent over time. Once an ambiguous early turn drives the model into a specific task state, later turns are processed as refinements rather than possible corrections, leading to persistent misalignment. To build more robust interactive assistants, systems must adopt uncertainty-preserving state management: maintaining multiple tentative hypotheses when intent is unclear, explicitly asking users before acting when high-impact ambiguity remains, and rebuilding from a revised state when new evidence contradicts earlier assumptions. The paper argues that research on interactive LLMs should pivot from a narrow focus on retaining more context to designing mechanisms and interfaces that prevent premature task-state hardening and support principled revision under uncertainty.

title: Understanding Reliability in LLM-based Human Behavior Simulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human survey responses and behavioral reactions, yet unreliable simulations can mislead social science conclusions. However, existing evaluations focus on end-to-end scores, leaving it unclear how different aspects of the simulation process interact to determine reliability. We propose ReliMap, which decomposes LLM-based human behavior simulation into three structured layers and evaluates reliability at both the individual level (R1) and population level (R2) across three configuration dimensions: model capacity, profile completeness, and population coverage. Through experiments across four simulation tasks and eleven LLMs, we find that all models exhibit substantial distributional bias without profile conditioning. Profile conditioning reduces this bias with diminishing returns. Larger models benefit more, and attribute informativeness matters more than quantity. Critically, R1 gains do not reliably transfer to R2--individual and population-level reliability can move in opposite directions. At the population layer, increasing coverage reduces variance but not systematic bias, with R2 stabilizing at around 50-100 individuals. These findings highlight that reliable simulation cannot be achieved by optimizing any single layer in isolation, but requires coordinated improvement across all three.

AI.tldr: ReliMap is a framework to systematically evaluate how reliably large language models can simulate human behavior, by decomposing the process into layers and examining both individual and population-level reliability under different configurations.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as substitutes for human participants in social science surveys and behavioral experiments, but their reliability as simulators is not well understood. Existing work usually reports only aggregate end-to-end performance, which obscures how different parts of the simulation pipeline (e.g., individual response generation vs. population aggregation) contribute to errors and biases. Social scientists need principled guidance on when and how LLM-based simulations can be trusted, and what configurations (model size, participant profiles, population sampling) most affect validity.
AI.method: The authors introduce ReliMap, a structured evaluation framework that decomposes LLM-based human behavior simulation into three layers and defines reliability metrics at two levels: R1 for individual-level reliability and R2 for population-level reliability. They systematically vary three key configuration dimensions: (1) model capacity (different LLM sizes and architectures), (2) profile completeness (amount and informativeness of demographic/psychological attributes used to condition the model), and (3) population coverage (number of simulated individuals). Using four different simulation tasks and eleven distinct LLMs, they run controlled experiments to measure how these factors affect R1 and R2, and how improvements at one layer propagate—or fail to propagate—across layers.
AI.result: Across tasks and models, all evaluated LLMs show substantial distributional bias when generating responses without any profile conditioning, meaning the simulated populations do not match real human distributions. Adding profile information systematically reduces this bias, but with diminishing returns as more attributes are added. Larger-capacity models gain more from profile conditioning, and the informativeness of attributes is more important than sheer number. A key empirical finding is that improvements in individual-level reliability (R1) do not consistently translate into improvements at the population level (R2); they can even move in opposite directions. At the population layer, increasing the number of simulated individuals mainly reduces variance in the estimates but does not remove systematic bias, and R2 tends to plateau once around 50–100 simulated individuals are included.
AI.conclusion: ReliMap reveals that reliable LLM-based human behavior simulation is a multi-layer problem: focusing on any single aspect—such as using a larger model, better individual prompts, or simply simulating more agents—is insufficient. Profile conditioning is necessary to reduce distributional bias but exhibits diminishing returns and interacts with model capacity and attribute informativeness. Population-level reliability is not guaranteed even when individual-level behavior looks plausible, and expanding simulated sample size cannot correct systematic biases inherent in the model or setup. Therefore, social scientists and practitioners must jointly optimize all three layers of the ReliMap framework and validate both R1 and R2 when using LLMs as proxies for human populations.

title: From Decorative to Load-Bearing: Task Difficulty Shapes the Causal Role of Chain-of-Thought
comment: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), September 2026. Code/ dataset available at the project repository and huggingface
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is only meaningful if written reasoning causally constrains the answer. We introduce continuation-based causal testing, an ablation-patch intervention that perturbs one reasoning step, truncates the chain, and forces the model to continue from the corrupted prefix. It measures how load-bearing a CoT is for the final answer, a behavioral notion distinct from mechanistic faithfulness. Across Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K, MMLU, and BIG-Bench Hard, CoT load-bearingness tracks model-relative task difficulty: on easy tasks models silently bypass their own reasoning; on hard tasks they follow corrupted steps and propagate errors. A matched 2x2 analysis shows task difficulty dominates perturbation type: error propagation rises 16x from GSM8K to BBH multistep arithmetic, and a variance partition over 28,584 continuations attributes 98.8% of explained deviance to task difficulty versus 0.8% to perturbation type. Reasoning-specific RL suppresses error propagation and compresses the gradient. A four-variant judge-sensitivity analysis and blind two-annotator study (n=500) show the error-propagation vs. non-propagation label is invariant to judge prompt, with perfect inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa = 1.00). This gradient creates a structural problem for CoT-based oversight and AI safety monitoring: where the trace is easy to read it carries little signal, and where it matters errors propagate before a monitor can intervene. Linear probes on hidden states separate silent bypass, self-correction, and error propagation, but additive activation steering provides limited causal control, flipping only about 25% of error-propagation cases at best. Behavioral mode is readable but not reliably controllable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a causal test to measure when a model’s chain-of-thought (CoT) actually constrains its final answer and shows that CoT is most load-bearing on hard tasks, creating challenges for CoT-based oversight.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT monitoring and oversight assume that written reasoning meaningfully causes a model’s final answer, but models can often ignore or bypass their own chains. The authors want a behavioral, task-level way to test when CoT truly matters for outputs, and to understand implications for AI safety and monitoring.
AI.method: They propose continuation-based causal testing: corrupt a single reasoning step in the CoT, truncate the chain there, and force the model to continue from the corrupted prefix. They then measure whether the model propagates the injected error into its final answer versus bypassing or correcting it. They run this on multiple instruction-tuned 7B–9B models (Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) and benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, BIG-Bench Hard), perform a 2x2 matched analysis over task difficulty and perturbation type, variance partitioning over tens of thousands of continuations, judge-sensitivity and inter-annotator reliability tests, and linear-probe plus activation-steering experiments on hidden states.
AI.result: They find that CoT “load-bearingness” correlates with model-relative task difficulty: on easier problems, models often silently bypass corrupted reasoning and still answer correctly, but on harder ones they follow the corrupted step and errors cascade. Task difficulty explains nearly all the variance in error propagation (about 98.8%), while the specific perturbation type contributes negligibly (~0.8%). Reasoning-optimized RL reduces error propagation and compresses the difficulty gradient. Human labeling of propagation vs non-propagation is robust to prompt changes and shows perfect inter-annotator agreement. Linear probes can distinguish behavioral modes like silent bypass, self-correction, and error propagation, but activation steering only flips a minority (~25%) of propagation cases, limiting causal control.
AI.conclusion: CoT behavior forms a difficulty-dependent gradient: where reasoning traces are easy to interpret they often don’t causally govern answers, but where they do govern answers (hard tasks) the model tends to propagate errors before any oversight can meaningfully intervene. This undermines the reliability of CoT-based safety monitoring and suggests that while internal behavioral modes are decodable, directly steering them with simple activation edits is weak, motivating more robust causal-control methods and alternative oversight strategies.

title: ufakzeka-1: Building and Evaluating a 151M-Parameter Turkish Language Model from Scratch
comment: 8 pages. Model, code, evaluation results and demo: https://ufakzeka.com, https://huggingface.co/ufakai, https://github.com/ufakai/ufakzeka
summary: We describe ufakzeka-1, a 151M-parameter (182M with embeddings) decoder-only Turkish language model pretrained from scratch on 13.5B tokens of openly licensed text and instruction-tuned for chat, at a total cost of about \$286 in cloud GPU, API and notebook time. The contribution is not the model's capability, which is what a model this size can be expected to have, but the record of building and measuring it: a Turkish byte-level tokenizer at 1.77 tokens per word, a three-stage pretraining schedule, a post-training mixture of openly licensed and generated data, and an evaluation battery of release gates, a rule-checked sweep of 5,508 conversations, judged conversations and hand tests, all with prompts held out from the training data, enforced by decontamination inside the data build and by a checked-in invariant script we run before each build. We report three findings that we believe transfer to other small-model efforts: a safety gate that had been "fixed" with training data written from its own questions read 64/64 while the honest figure was 34/64; training-seed variance was as large as the spread across every recipe we tried, so single-seed comparisons at this scale are uninformative; and data rounds repaired only what was absent from the data, while identity tracking over long context and multi-turn arithmetic did not move across any data change we tried, which we read as limits of the model size rather than gaps in the data, a reading the next, larger model will test. Weights, the data recipe, the evaluation code and the spend ledger are released under Apache-2.0.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ufakzeka-1, a small, fully open Turkish chat LLM, focusing on documenting its construction, data, evaluation, safety gates, and lessons for low-cost small-model development rather than on state-of-the-art capability.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of well-documented, openly licensed, and reproducible small language models for low-resource or non-English languages like Turkish. Existing work often omits detailed build, data, cost, and evaluation procedures, making it hard for others to replicate or extend. The authors aim to show how to build a capable Turkish chat model on a very small budget, while rigorously tracking safety, contamination, and evaluation, and to extract general lessons for other small-model efforts.
AI.method: They train a 151M-parameter (182M including embeddings) decoder-only Turkish language model from scratch on 13.5B tokens using a custom byte-level tokenizer (1.77 tokens per word). Training follows a three-stage pretraining schedule, followed by instruction tuning for chat using a mixture of openly licensed and model-generated data. They enforce strict decontamination to keep evaluation prompts out of the training set, including an invariant script that is run before each build. Evaluation uses a multi-part battery: release gates, rule-checked sweeps of 5,508 conversations, judged conversations, and manual tests, all using held-out prompts. They also perform multiple training runs with different seeds and data rounds to study variance and the effect of data changes.
AI.result: The model achieves performance in line with expectations for its size as a small Turkish chat LLM. More importantly, they obtain three key empirical findings: (1) A safety gate that had been “fixed” using data generated from its own questions appeared to pass 64/64 tests, but its actual performance when honestly evaluated was only 34/64, revealing how self-contaminated training can vastly overestimate safety. (2) Training-seed variance is as large as the difference between all the recipe variations they tried, implying that single-seed experiments at this scale are unreliable for comparing methods. (3) Additional data rounds only improve behaviors that were missing from the data; capabilities like long-context identity tracking and multi-turn arithmetic did not improve under any data modification, suggesting they are limited by model size rather than data quality.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that for small language models, careful experimental methodology is crucial: safety evaluations must be protected from contamination, multiple seeds are needed to obtain reliable comparisons, and some shortcomings are fundamentally due to model capacity rather than data gaps. They provide ufakzeka-1’s weights, data recipe, evaluation code, and cost ledger under Apache-2.0 to promote transparent, reproducible small-model development, and propose testing their interpretation of capacity limits with a subsequent larger model.

title: Robust Failure, Conservative Repair: Textual Knowledge Distillation from Cross-Model Failures
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main track)
summary: Failure-based textual knowledge distillation aims to discover gaps in a model's knowledge by examining its task errors. The distilled knowledge can be useful for the reasoning of both this model ("source model") and other models. However, this transfer of knowledge may not be stable. We define a rule atom to be a standalone rule injected into a model's textual input at inference time. A rule atom can encode transferable task knowledge or model-specific reasoning patches that can confuse other models. Also, the injected rule atoms can be misapplied to unrelated cases, causing the model to incorrectly flip its answer based on irrelevant information. Building on a pipeline that distills training examples into task-specific cheat sheets that aid model reasoning, we examine when failure-derived rules can improve these cheat sheets. Our early experiment shows rule distillation from a single model's failures underperforms the baseline cheat sheet on non-source model families. This motivates Robust Failure, Conservative Repair (RFCR), a textual distillation procedure that derives rules from failures shared across models, sharpens their application boundaries using boundary cases, and abstains when no useful rule is found. On a 400-item BIG-Bench Hard task set, RFCR improves the baseline cheat sheets from 68.50% to 71.25% (+2.75 pp; 95% CI [+1.25,+4.50]) without performance degradation on previously correct cases. Ablations and cross-model diagnostics support that accuracy gains come from both new knowledge injection and strict rule-application control.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to more safely and effectively distill textual rules from model failures so they help multiple models without causing harmful side effects, and proposes RFCR, which uses shared failures and boundary cases to create conservative, robust rules that improve performance on hard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing failure-based textual knowledge distillation finds rules from a model’s own mistakes and injects them into prompts as guidance. But these distilled rules can be unstable: (1) they may be model-specific patches that confuse other models, (2) they may be applied inappropriately to unrelated cases, flipping correct answers to wrong ones, and (3) naively distilling from a single model’s failures underperforms when transferred across model families. The paper aims to understand and fix these robustness and transferability issues so that distilled rules genuinely encode task knowledge rather than fragile, model-specific tricks.
AI.method: The authors formalize “rule atoms” as standalone textual rules injected at inference time. They build on an existing pipeline that distills training examples into task-specific cheat sheets, then ask when failure-derived rules can enhance these cheat sheets. After observing poor cross-model transfer from single-model failure distillation, they design Robust Failure, Conservative Repair (RFCR). RFCR: (1) collects failures shared across multiple models to focus on robust gaps in knowledge; (2) distills rules from these shared failures; (3) refines and narrows the scope of each rule using boundary cases that clarify when it should and should not apply; and (4) abstains from adding a rule when it cannot be made both useful and safe. They evaluate RFCR on a 400-item BIG-Bench Hard task subset and perform ablation and cross-model diagnostics to understand the source of gains.
AI.result: On a 400-item subset of BIG-Bench Hard, RFCR applied on top of baseline cheat sheets raises accuracy from 68.50% to 71.25%, a +2.75 percentage point gain with 95% CI [+1.25, +4.50]. Importantly, this improvement comes without degrading accuracy on instances that were already correct before adding RFCR-derived rules. Diagnostic and ablation experiments indicate that the improvements stem both from injecting genuinely new task-relevant knowledge and from tight control over when rules are applied, which reduces harmful misapplication and transfer issues.
AI.conclusion: Failure-based rule distillation must be handled carefully: naive rules from a single model’s errors can be unstable, model-specific, and harmful when transferred. By focusing on failures shared across models, sharpening rule application with boundary cases, and abstaining when rules cannot be safely applied, RFCR creates conservative, robust rule atoms that enhance existing cheat sheets. This yields statistically significant accuracy gains on challenging benchmarks without sacrificing performance on previously solved cases, suggesting that conservative, cross-model-aware failure distillation is a promising direction for safer textual knowledge transfer between models.

title: Impact Is Not Invalidation: Ask About the Claim, Not the Diff
summary: Memory systems for coding agents must decide, when a repository changes, which of their stored claims have become false. Content anchoring invalidates a claim whenever the artifact it came from changes, which fires constantly. Semantic-equivalence classification asks whether a diff preserves behavior, a question about the diff rather than about any stored claim. We show the second signal fails for a reason unrelated to model capability: asked whether a commit preserves behavior, five models spanning a 40x price range fire on 59-72% of real commits and reach precisions of only 0.291 to 0.329 against a 0.25 base rate. Asked instead whether one specific claim still holds, the same models on the same diffs reach 0.705 to 0.974. A control that hands the behavior-preservation judge the claim text, changing only the question, moves precision by 0.010 and 0.016; changing the question moves it by 0.49 and 0.65. We also compare against pytest-testmon, a deployed regression-test selector with coverage-derived dependency data: it reaches 0.868 recall at 0.415 precision, so near-complete knowledge of what a change can reach does not identify what it falsifies. Ground truth is execution, not annotation: a claim is a test function passing at commit t, and it has flipped if that same assertion text fails at t+1. Building this required an observation we did not find in prior work. On a CI-gated mainline a commit that leaves a pre-existing test failing cannot merge, so the naive construction has an empty positive class by design. We report 10,369 claims with 184 execution-verified flips mined from 23 Python libraries, splits held out by repository, a post-knowledge-cutoff split, a shuffled-diff null, a paraphrase control, and a leave-one-repository-out analysis over 17 repositories.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how coding agents should decide which stored claims become invalid when code changes, finding that asking models directly about specific claims is far more reliable than asking whether a commit preserves overall behavior.
AI.motivation: In evolving codebases, AI coding agents and memory systems need to know which previously true statements about a repository become false after new commits. Existing strategies either invalidate everything from any changed artifact (content anchoring) or try to classify whether a diff preserves behavior overall (semantic-equivalence classification). Both are problematic: content anchoring is overly conservative and fires constantly, and behavior-preservation judgments are difficult and noisy. The authors want a more precise and reliable signal for claim invalidation and a realistic ground truth for evaluating such signals.
AI.method: They compare two question formulations posed to multiple LLMs across the same real-world code diffs from 23 Python libraries. (1) Behavior-preservation: ask the model whether a given commit preserves behavior. (2) Claim-specific: ask the model whether a particular previously true claim (represented as a test function assertion) still holds after the commit. They use execution as ground truth: a “claim” is defined as a test function that passes at commit t; it has ‘flipped’ if the exact same assertion text fails at t+1. They carefully construct a dataset that avoids the CI-gated-mainline issue, mine 10,369 such claims with 184 verified flips, and define splits (by repository, post-knowledge-cutoff, shuffled-diff null, paraphrase control, leave-one-repo-out) to ensure robustness. They also run a control where the behavior-preservation judge is given the claim text (changing only the question wording) to isolate the effect of question formulation, and they compare LLM-based signals to pytest-testmon, a coverage-based regression-test selector.
AI.result: For behavior-preservation classification, five LLMs with a 40x price range label 59–72% of real commits as behavior-preserving but achieve only 0.291–0.329 precision against a 0.25 base rate, indicating only marginal usefulness. When asked the claim-specific question—whether a particular claim still holds on the new commit—the same models on the same diffs achieve much higher precision: 0.705–0.974. A control experiment where the behavior-preservation model is also given the claim text but asked the original ‘preserve behavior?’ question changes precision only slightly (+0.010 and +0.016), whereas switching to the claim-specific question yields large gains (+0.49 and +0.65), showing that question formulation, not just context, drives the improvement. pytest-testmon, using coverage-derived dependency information, attains 0.868 recall at 0.415 precision, demonstrating that even near-complete knowledge of what code a change can reach does not suffice to infer which specific claims are falsified.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-preservation as a global property of a diff is a poor signal for deciding which stored claims in an AI coding agent’s memory have become invalid. In contrast, asking targeted, claim-specific questions—“does this particular claim still hold?”—is far more reliable, even with the same models and diffs. The large performance gap is mainly due to how the question is posed, not lack of model capability or missing context. Moreover, even strong dependency-coverage tools like pytest-testmon cannot reliably infer which precise assertions flip, so structural reachability alone is insufficient. For robust memory management in coding agents, systems should rely on claim-level evaluation grounded in execution-based truth, not coarse behavior-preservation judgments or simple content anchoring.

title: Efficient Iterative Retrieval with Heterogeneous Batching
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: Modern information retrieval increasingly employs both embedding and generative models to handle complex queries. However, current serving systems suffer from low throughput and poor GPU utilization because they execute these models in isolation. Coarse-grained partitioning, such as dedicating GPUs to specific tasks, fails to adapt to dynamic workloads and creates computational "bubbles". To address these, we present Orthrus, a serving system that performs heterogeneous batching within a unified inference loop. The primary challenge lies in unifying embedding and generation workloads with conflicting computational patterns while optimizing batch composition for high performance. Orthrus addresses these challenges through chunked embedding with incremental pooling and by adjusting batch composition in a workload-aware manner. Evaluation on four A100 GPUs shows that, relative to baseline deployments, Orthrus achieves 1.28$\times$--4.52$\times$ higher throughput on controlled workloads and up to 55.8% lower end-to-end p99 latency on an iterative-RAG benchmark. We release our code at https://github.com/illinoisdata/Orthrus .

AI.tldr: Orthrus is a GPU serving system that jointly batches embedding and generative model queries to boost throughput and reduce latency for IR/RAG workloads.
AI.motivation: Existing IR/RAG serving pipelines run embedding and generative models separately, often on dedicated GPUs or coarse partitions.
