This leads to low GPU utilization, computational bubbles, and poor throughput/latency when workloads are dynamic and mixed (embedding vs generation requests). A more fine-grained and adaptive execution model is needed to better pack heterogeneous workloads onto shared accelerators.
AI.method: Orthrus introduces a unified inference loop that performs heterogeneous batching of both embedding and generation requests on the same GPUs. It uses chunked embedding with incremental pooling to make embedding computation more compatible with generative decoding patterns, and it dynamically adjusts batch composition based on current workload characteristics to keep GPUs busy. The system runs on multi-GPU setups (e.g., four A100s) and is compared against standard baseline serving deployments.
AI.result: On four A100 GPUs, Orthrus achieves 1.28×–4.52× higher throughput on controlled workloads compared with baseline systems. On an iterative-RAG benchmark, it reduces end-to-end p99 latency by up to 55.8%, demonstrating substantial gains in both efficiency and tail latency.
AI.conclusion: A unified serving system that performs heterogeneous batching of embedding and generation workloads, combined with techniques like chunked embedding and workload-aware batch composition, can significantly improve GPU utilization, throughput, and tail latency for modern IR/RAG applications. Orthrus provides such a design and empirically validates its effectiveness, with publicly released code for reproducibility and adoption.

title: FinFIRST: Benchmarking Search Agents for Financial Information Retrieval, Sourcing and Traceability
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, and 7 tables. Dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/inclusionAI/FinFIRST
summary: Financial search is a highly demanding task for LLM agents, requiring not only a correct final answer but also temporally valid information retrieval, authoritative source selection, entity and period alignment, unit and definition consistency, and verifiable evidence for all conclusions. Existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate only the final answer, making it difficult to localize errors or assess whether an answer is well-founded. To address this gap, we introduce FinFIRST (Financial Information Retrieval, Sourcing and Traceability), the first financial benchmark to jointly evaluate answers and supporting evidence through atomic rubrics. FinFIRST comprises 123 expert-authored tasks spanning a graduated difficulty spectrum, constructed from aggregate patterns of real-world financial scenarios through an 18-field taxonomy, a six-axis coverage blueprint, a registry of 138 financial sources, contributions from over 50 finance experts, and a six-stage quality-control pipeline. Each task is accompanied by an evidence-grounded reference package decomposed into atomic criteria across three dimensions: raw-information acquisition, source verification, and computation and answer formation. We evaluate 15 model configurations under a unified tool setting. Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest atomic score of 87.59%, while GPT-5.6-Sol attains the highest strict pass rate of 71.54%. Computation and answer formation consistently lag behind raw-information acquisition across systems. FinFIRST retains final-answer correctness as the primary objective while making the supporting research process measurable, verifiable, and diagnosable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FinFIRST, a benchmark for evaluating financial search by LLM agents that scores both answers and the evidence and reasoning behind them through fine-grained atomic criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing financial benchmarks largely measure only whether the final answer is correct, without checking if models used temporally valid data, authoritative sources, correct entities and periods, consistent units/definitions, or verifiable evidence. This makes it hard to localize failures or judge if correct-looking answers are well-founded. The authors want a benchmark that reflects real financial research demands and can diagnose where LLM agents go wrong in the information-retrieval and reasoning pipeline.
AI.method: The authors construct FinFIRST, a benchmark of 123 expert-authored tasks across a range of difficulty, grounded in real-world financial scenarios. They design an 18-field taxonomy, a six-axis coverage blueprint, and maintain a registry of 138 vetted financial sources. Over 50 finance experts contribute, and tasks go through a six-stage quality-control pipeline. For each task, they build an evidence-grounded reference package decomposed into atomic rubrics along three dimensions: (1) raw-information acquisition, (2) source verification, and (3) computation and answer formation. They then evaluate 15 LLM/tool configurations under a unified tool-usage setting, scoring both final answers and atomic evidence criteria.
AI.result: On FinFIRST, Claude-Opus-5 attains the highest atomic score (87.59%), indicating the strongest performance on fine-grained evidence and reasoning criteria, while GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest strict pass rate on end-to-end tasks (71.54%). Across all systems, the stages involving computation and answer formation underperform the raw-information acquisition stage, revealing a systematic weakness. The benchmark successfully differentiates model capabilities at multiple granular levels.
AI.conclusion: FinFIRST is presented as the first financial benchmark that jointly evaluates final answers and the supporting evidence chain using atomic rubrics. It preserves final-answer correctness as the main objective but makes the underlying research process—information retrieval, source vetting, and reasoning—measurable, verifiable, and diagnosable. This should enable more reliable assessment and improvement of LLM agents for financial search tasks.

title: From Offline Proxies to Online Decisions: A Layered Engagement Evaluation Framework for Conversational AI
comment: 11 pages main text, 9 pages supplementary material; 2 figures, 25 tables
summary: Online A/B experiments are the decision standard for user engagement, but traffic and readout time limit how many conversational-AI changes can be tested. We ask whether an offline signal designed to be computable without treatment-arm user exposure agrees with the outcomes of those experiments. We contribute a reusable construction and diagnosis checklist that treats an offline proxy as a chain of three alignments: behavioral label to product outcome, learned classifier to candidate-assistant behavior, and aggregated offline signal to experiment effect. A companion evaluation protocol audits the whole composite by interval-aware decision agreement, which compares offline and online confidence intervals instead of point estimates, and by within-experiment ranking. The instantiation we evaluate comprises a fixed evaluation suite on which candidate behavior is scored, an engagement classifier trained to predict session/prompt level engagements, and a calibration layer mapping sample-level score differences to online model-level engagement deltas. We then report the audit: 489 paired offline-online contrasts (one candidate arm against its control) from 27 experiments on a deployed multi-turn assistant, spanning model checkpoints to system-prompt tuning. Our primary test uses the 113 contrasts from eight experiments that ran after the map was frozen: on these the composite reaches 81.1% F1, against 34.3% for the raw classifier score it is built on, and makes no wrong-direction calls where that raw score makes 31. Every offline prediction was computed before its experiment ran to prevent overfitting. The evidence supports using the composite to prioritize candidates before scarce experiment traffic is allocated---in our deployment of the experiment, selecting among training checkpoints and tuning system prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and validates an offline evaluation framework that predicts the outcomes of online A/B experiments for conversational AI, enabling better pre-selection of model variants when online traffic is scarce.
AI.motivation: Online A/B tests are the gold standard for measuring user engagement but are constrained by limited user traffic and time, restricting how many model or system changes can be tested. The authors want to know if an offline-computable signal can reliably stand in for online outcomes so that only the most promising conversational AI variants are sent to costly experiments.
AI.method: They conceptualize an offline proxy as a composite of three aligned components: (1) mapping behavioral labels to product outcomes, (2) training a classifier to link candidate assistant behavior to these behavioral labels, and (3) aggregating and calibrating the classifier outputs into an offline signal that predicts experiment-level engagement effects. They develop a diagnosis checklist for these alignments and a companion evaluation protocol based on interval-aware decision agreement (comparing offline vs. online confidence intervals rather than point estimates) and within-experiment ranking of candidate arms. They instantiate this with a fixed evaluation suite, an engagement classifier, and a calibration layer that maps sample-level score differences to expected online engagement deltas.
AI.result: They conduct an audit using 489 paired offline–online contrasts from 27 experiments on a deployed multi-turn assistant, covering both model checkpoint changes and system prompt tuning. Focusing on 113 contrasts from eight experiments that occurred after the mapping and calibration were frozen (to avoid overfitting), their composite offline metric achieves 81.1% F1 in predicting experiment decisions, compared to only 34.3% F1 for the raw classifier scores. The composite makes no wrong-direction calls in this primary test set, whereas the raw classifier makes 31 such errors. All offline predictions were made prior to running the corresponding experiments.
AI.conclusion: The composite offline signal reliably anticipates the direction and significance of online A/B outcomes and substantially outperforms a naïve use of raw classifier scores. This supports using the proposed framework as a practical tool to prioritize which conversational AI candidates should receive scarce experiment traffic, particularly when selecting among training checkpoints and tuning system prompts, thereby improving experimentation efficiency without compromising decision quality.

title: FineWeb-CLaR: Culture, Language, and Region Annotations for Benchmark-Aligned Corpus Auditing
summary:
Cultural evaluation coverage and robustness in language models are difficult to diagnose because pretraining corpora and cultural benchmarks are rarely indexed with comparable metadata. Benchmarks increasingly target culturally situated phenomena at the level of languages, regions, and locale-specific practices, while web-scale corpora are usually organized only by language. A shared culture-language-region layer makes these resources comparable, enabling audits of whether a target cultural phenomenon is represented in pretraining data, evaluated by benchmarks or both. To this end, we introduce FineWeb-CLaR, a large-scale annotated dataset derived from FineWeb and FineWeb-2 that places web documents on a shared culture-language-region axis for corpus auditing and benchmark alignment.
  FineWeb-CLaR annotates the full 30.9B-document collection from FineWeb and FineWeb-2 with URL-derived region labels and cultural-topic provenance. Our region resolver assigns a non-empty region to 25.61% of documents (7.92B). For cultural-topic analysis, we induce locale-specific topics and project them onto the 14 leaves of the Cultural Taxonomy of Liu et al. (2025), producing Locale Topic Distributions (LTDs) for corpus-side comparison. We also annotate 277 cultural NLP benchmarks with the same taxonomy, language coverage, and region coverage. Together, these resources enable direct comparison between corpus-side pretraining evidence and benchmark-side evaluation coverage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FineWeb-CLaR, a large-scale annotation of web documents and cultural NLP benchmarks with shared culture-language-region labels, enabling audits of cultural coverage and robustness in language model pretraining and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current language model pretraining corpora and cultural benchmarks are not directly comparable because they lack consistent culture-language-region metadata. Benchmarks are increasingly culture-aware (languages, regions, locale-specific practices), while pretraining data is mostly labeled only by language. This mismatch makes it hard to diagnose whether specific cultural phenomena are represented in training data, covered in benchmarks, or both. The authors want a unified framework to connect corpora and benchmarks along a shared cultural axis.
AI.method: They build FineWeb-CLaR by annotating the 30.9B documents in FineWeb and FineWeb-2 with (1) URL-derived region labels using a region resolver, and (2) cultural-topic provenance via induced locale-specific topics mapped to a 14-leaf Cultural Taxonomy (Liu et al., 2025). This yields Locale Topic Distributions (LTDs) that summarize how cultural topics are distributed across locales in the corpus. In parallel, they annotate 277 cultural NLP benchmarks with the same taxonomy, plus language and region coverage, to make benchmark metadata commensurate with corpus annotations.
AI.result: The region resolver successfully assigns a non-empty regional label to about a quarter of the corpus (25.61%, or 7.92B documents). They obtain LTDs for corpus documents aligned to 14 cultural taxonomy leaves and parallel annotations for 277 cultural NLP benchmarks, creating a shared representation space for corpus and benchmark cultural coverage. This infrastructure enables corpus-side vs. benchmark-side comparisons of where cultural evidence exists and where it is evaluated.
AI.conclusion: FineWeb-CLaR provides a unified culture-language-region annotation layer over large web corpora and cultural NLP benchmarks, making it possible to systematically audit cultural representation and robustness in language model training and evaluation. With its region labels, cultural-topic mappings, and benchmark annotations, researchers can directly compare pretraining evidence against evaluation coverage for specific cultural phenomena and identify cultural under- or over-representation.

title: ZeroGate: Trust-Preserving Fast Paths for Governed AI Agent Runtimes
comment: 47 pages, 11 figures, 13 tables. Full research report with an ancillary archive containing reference code, raw experimental records, and offline verification tools
summary: Moving authorization earlier can shorten an agent's dispatch boundary without removing authorization work. It can also admit an action whose payload, authority, or relevant state has changed. ZeroGate separates exact-action approval from durable local admission: an issuer signs a short-lived ActionPass, and a trusted runtime adapter reconstructs the final action before a local gate checks its binding and consumes its nonce. A SQLite transaction couples nonce consumption, applicable quota updates, and an admission receipt. We state a conditional decision-preservation proposition: successful local admission implies that a specified synchronous policy would authorize the same action at the admission point, provided approval is sound, all policy dependencies are represented and current, observations are faithful, and consumption is atomic. The implementation alone establishes neither current-world freshness nor exactly-once remote effects. Evaluation separates authored semantic fixtures, controlled concurrency and crash experiments, and an Azure Blob study comparing synchronous and prepared execution through the same issuer and gate. Both modes mint an exact-action pass; lifecycle latency includes preparation and prepared-batch dwell. Across 4800 cloud attempts, prepared worker-admission-to-dispatch p95 ranges from 9.802 to 11.374 ms, versus 25.018 to 334.000 ms synchronously, across the tested concurrency levels. Prepared mean complete lifecycle is longer at every level: the boundary improvement is not a net speedup. The contribution is an explicit revalidation contract, a durable reference boundary, and an auditable comparison of where authorization cost is paid, not a new cryptographic primitive or a universal performance frontier.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ZeroGate, a system that moves authorization earlier via short-lived ActionPasses and durable local admission, improving dispatch latency boundaries without changing which actions are authorized.
AI.motivation: Traditional synchronous authorization ties approval to the final action at dispatch time, which can lengthen dispatch latency, complicate handling of changed payloads or state, and blur where authorization costs are paid. The authors want a way to move authorization earlier while preserving the correctness of authorization decisions and making the boundary between approval and execution explicit and auditable.
AI.method: They design ZeroGate, which issues short-lived ActionPass tokens representing exact-action approval. A trusted runtime adapter reconstructs the final action just before a local admission gate, which validates the binding, checks and consumes a nonce, and records the decision in a SQLite transaction that also updates quotas and writes an admission receipt. They formalize a conditional decision-preservation proposition linking local admission to what a synchronous policy would decide, under assumptions about sound approval, complete and current policy dependencies, faithful observations, and atomic consumption. They implement ZeroGate and evaluate it via semantic fixtures, controlled concurrency and crash tests, and an Azure Blob workload comparing synchronous execution and prepared (pre-authorized) execution through the same issuer and gate.
AI.result: In cloud experiments with 4800 attempts, the prepared mode achieves significantly lower p95 latency from worker admission to dispatch (about 9.8–11.4 ms) than synchronous authorization (25.0–334.0 ms) across tested concurrency levels. However, the overall mean end-to-end lifecycle latency is higher in prepared mode at every level, because preparation and dwell time add overhead. The system demonstrates correct coupling of nonce use, quota updates, and receipts, but it does not alone guarantee world-state freshness or exactly-once remote side effects.
AI.conclusion: ZeroGate clarifies and restructures authorization by introducing an explicit revalidation contract, a durable, auditable local admission boundary, and a way to compare when and where authorization costs are paid. It shows that moving authorization earlier can narrow dispatch latency boundaries and still preserve the decisions of a synchronous policy under stated conditions, but it does not claim cryptographic novelty or universal performance gains; instead, it provides a framework and empirical evidence for reasoning about authorization placement and its tradeoffs.

title: TelecomGPT-R1: Unified Post-Training for Reasoning Across Heterogeneous Telecom Tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer great potential to automate a broad range of telecom engineering tasks by reasoning over standards, network configurations, mathematical models, source code, and operational logs. However, existing telecom LLMs struggle to reliably reason across these diverse tasks and data types. General-purpose LLMs often lack reliable grounding in telecom-specific knowledge, while telecom-specialized models are typically developed for narrower task families and exhibit limited multi-task performance. To fill this gap, we introduce TelecomGPT-R1, a family of open source unified telecom reasoning models structured around four complementary axes: protocol, knowledge, modeling, and fault. We first develop an axis-aware data generation framework that refines coarse public telecom artifacts into verified question-answer pairs and high quality chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning trajectories, yielding a training corpus containing 104,880 examples. Building on this corpus, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) instills telecom knowledge and evidence-grounded reasoning patterns to overcome the cold start barrier for reinforcement learning (RL). We then apply dynamic sampling policy optimization (DAPO) with task-routed rubric rewards to keep RL updates informative and stable across heterogeneous telecom reasoning tasks. These rewards decompose axis-specific CoT traces into verifiable reasoning units and combine grounded dense process credit with outcome correctness, allowing RL to learn generalizable problem solving behaviors from verifiable telecom evidence. We release the TelecomGPT-R1 models and a reproducible training recipe to support further community development. Evaluations on seven benchmarks of the GSMA Open Telco Leaderboard show that the open-source TelecomGPT-R1-27B achieves an 89.64% mean score, outperforming leading proprietary models, including GPT-5, Claude, and Gemini.

AI.tldr: TelecomGPT-R1 is an open-source family of telecom-specialized reasoning LLMs that unify multiple telecom task types and outperform leading proprietary models on the GSMA Open Telco Leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs either lack strong grounding in telecom-specific knowledge (general models) or are narrow and weak at multi-task reasoning (telecom-specialized models). There is a need for a unified telecom reasoning model that can reliably handle diverse tasks and data types such as standards, configurations, code, and logs.
AI.method: The authors design TelecomGPT-R1 around four reasoning axes (protocol, knowledge, modeling, fault) and build an axis-aware data generation framework that converts public telecom artifacts into verified QA pairs and CoT trajectories, yielding 104,880 training examples. They first perform supervised fine-tuning to teach telecom knowledge and grounded reasoning, then apply dynamic sampling policy optimization (DAPO), a reinforcement learning approach with task-routed rubric rewards. These rewards decompose axis-specific CoT traces into verifiable units and combine dense process rewards with outcome correctness to stabilize and generalize RL across heterogeneous telecom tasks.
AI.result: The TelecomGPT-R1 models and training recipe are released as open source. On seven GSMA Open Telco Leaderboard benchmarks, the 27B-parameter TelecomGPT-R1 model attains an 89.64% mean score, surpassing top proprietary models such as GPT-5, Claude, and Gemini on these benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TelecomGPT-R1 demonstrates that carefully structured data generation, SFT, and RL with axis-aware rubric rewards can produce a unified open-source telecom reasoning model that generalizes across diverse telecom tasks and outperforms leading proprietary systems on domain-specific benchmarks, providing a strong foundation for community-driven advancement in telecom LLMs.

title: Rollout Efficiency in Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
summary: Reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning enables large language models to solve mathematical, coding, and other multi-step tasks, but shifts a substantial portion of the training cost to rollout, where trajectories are generated for policy updates. Efficient rollout mechanisms are therefore essential to reduce this cost while maintaining the freshness, consistency, and statistical validity of training data. This survey provides a systematic taxonomy of recent research on rollout efficiency for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning, classifying existing approaches from both mechanism and bottleneck perspectives. Based on this taxonomy, we analyze how different technique families address distinct sources of rollout inefficiency, examine opportunities and potential conflicts for combining them, identify gaps in the evaluation and reporting of efficiency gains, and discuss open challenges and future research directions.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys methods to make rollouts more efficient in reasoning-focused RL for large language models, offering a taxonomy of techniques, their bottlenecks, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-oriented RL for LLMs is powerful but very expensive because training requires generating many long trajectories (rollouts). This rollout phase dominates cost and raises issues of data freshness, consistency, and statistical validity, motivating a systematic study of how to make rollouts more efficient.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured literature survey. They propose a taxonomy that organizes prior work on rollout efficiency along two dimensions: (1) the mechanisms used to improve efficiency (e.g., algorithmic, systems, or data-centric changes), and (2) the main bottlenecks they target (e.g., compute, memory, latency, sample efficiency, or data quality). They then analyze how technique families map to bottlenecks, where they complement or conflict, and how they are evaluated.
AI.result: The survey classifies existing rollout-efficiency methods into clear categories, maps them to the sources of rollout inefficiency they address, and compares their strengths, limitations, and compatibility. It highlights patterns in how different approaches are used, exposes inconsistencies and gaps in how efficiency gains are measured and reported, and surfaces underexplored directions.
AI.conclusion: Efficient rollout is a central challenge for reasoning-oriented RL with LLMs. Existing work provides a diverse toolkit, but no single approach fully resolves the trade-offs between cost, data quality, and training stability. The paper concludes that more standardized evaluation, better combinations of complementary methods, and attention to overlooked bottlenecks are needed, and it outlines promising open problems for future research.

title: Passes Alone, Fails Together: Benchmarking Semantic Coordination in Parallel LLM-Agent Development
comment: 6 pages, accepted to The 2nd Workshop on Explainable and Reliable Software Systems (EXPRESS 2026)
summary: Parallel coding agents can produce patches that work alone but fail when merged. This happens when one agent changes an interface or rule that another agent still relies on. We study these failures with stale, a benchmark for semantic coordination. Our evaluation runs the same tests on each patch alone and on their combination, counting only failures introduced by combining the patches. We use three tiers: synthetic tasks with controlled interface changes, pairs of merged pull requests, and constructed tasks that use real Django helpers. Among 834 runs on 417 mined Django pairs, only one showed interference after correcting the grading procedure. On constructed tasks using 12 Django helpers, interference occurred in 97% of runs. A message describing the completed concurrent change recovered 82% of runs. Reviewed pull requests may contain few unresolved parallel changes, even when agents fail on controlled tasks using real code. The constructed failure rates do not estimate how often these problems occur in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how independently generated code patches from parallel coding agents can interfere when merged, introducing semantic coordination failures, and studies how often and why this happens across synthetic, mined, and constructed Django-based tasks.
AI.motivation: Parallel coding agents often modify shared codebases concurrently. While each patch may work in isolation, their combination can fail if agents make inconsistent assumptions about interfaces or rules. There is little systematic evaluation of such semantic coordination failures, especially in realistic settings involving frameworks like Django. The authors want to quantify and characterize these interference problems and understand how representative constructed benchmarks are of real-world development.
AI.method: They introduce a benchmark called 'stale' for semantic coordination, and evaluate three tiers of tasks. For each task, they run tests on each agent-produced patch separately and on the merged version, counting only failures that appear only after combining patches. The tiers include: (1) synthetic tasks with controlled interface changes, (2) real-world pairs of merged pull requests mined from Django (417 pairs, 834 runs), and (3) constructed tasks that involve real Django helpers, designed to induce potential interference. They also test a mitigation where a message describing a concurrent change is provided to the agent.
AI.result: In the mined Django pull request pairs, after fixing grading, only 1 out of 834 runs exhibited interference, suggesting very low observable conflict in reviewed real-world PRs. In contrast, in the constructed Django-helper tasks, interference was observed in 97% of runs, indicating that these synthetic constructions are highly prone to coordination failures. Providing a message describing the concurrent change allowed recovery in 82% of the failed constructed runs.
AI.conclusion: Semantic interference between parallel coding agents can be severe in controlled, constructed tasks involving realistic code, but appears rare in reviewed real-world pull requests, suggesting that human processes and review reduce unresolved parallel changes. However, high failure rates in constructed benchmarks should not be taken as direct estimates of real-world incidence. Simple communication about concurrent changes can substantially mitigate failures in constructed scenarios, but the gap between benchmark behavior and real-world practice must be carefully considered when evaluating or deploying parallel coding agents.

title: Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition for OpenXR Using Transformer-Based Machine Learning
summary: Hand gesture recognition is a key component in human-computer interaction (HCI), enabling intuitive interfaces for applications in gaming, virtual reality (VR), robotics, and more. This study integrates transformer-based machine-learning models for real-time hand gesture recognition, using hand-tracking data captured through the OpenXR standard in Unity. We leverage positional data of hand joints and wrist rotation angles to train a custom gesture recognition system. By utilizing the sequential modeling capabilities of transformers, the system captures temporal dependencies within short gesture windows and classifies gestures robustly across hand orientations and sizes. The results show a significant improvement in gesture classification accuracy. Building on this, we outline how the approach can be extended toward detecting the flow of movement, i.e., the transitions between gestures, as future work.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a transformer-based, real-time hand gesture recognition system using OpenXR hand-tracking data in Unity, achieving improved gesture classification accuracy and discussing extensions to gesture transition detection.
AI.motivation: To improve the robustness and accuracy of real-time hand gesture recognition for HCI applications (gaming, VR, robotics, etc.), especially across different hand orientations and sizes, using standardized hand-tracking data (OpenXR) within a widely used engine (Unity).
AI.method: Use OpenXR in Unity to capture positional data of hand joints and wrist rotation angles. Feed these as temporal sequences into transformer-based machine learning models that exploit their sequential modeling capabilities. Train a custom classifier on short gesture windows to recognize static/dynamic hand gestures in real time.
AI.result: The transformer-based system demonstrates a significant improvement in hand gesture classification accuracy and robustness across different hand orientations and hand sizes compared with unspecified baselines or prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Transformer models, when applied to OpenXR hand-tracking sequences in Unity, enable accurate, real-time hand gesture recognition that is robust to orientation and size variations. The framework is practical for HCI applications and can be extended in future work to recognize not only discrete gestures but also flows of movement, i.e., transitions between gestures.

title: Mining Legal Arguments in U.S. Corporate Case Law
summary: Legal argument mining supports passage classification, retrieval, and argument completion. This work introduces an expert-annotated dataset of 42 U.S. federal tax opinions on corporate reorganizations under I.R.C. §368. To our knowledge, it is the first expert-annotated, tree-structured argument corpus for this domain. Explicit spans receive one of five functional labels: Rule, Analysis, Conclusion, Background Facts, and Procedural History. Rule, Analysis, and Conclusion spans can be linked into directed support trees, while Background Facts and Procedural History serve a contextual function. The corpus provides span-based, sentence-based, flat, and tree-structured representations. Agreement analysis shows that functional node labels are more reliable than directed support edges and implicit intermediate conclusions. Directed-path agreement is stronger than direct-edge agreement, which indicates that broad reachability is more stable than exact local decomposition. Classification experiments show that functional labels are learnable under case-disjoint evaluation. Retrieval experiments show that supervised fine-tuning improves within-case retrieval. However, cross-case generalization remains weak. The dataset supports legal passage classification and provides a conservative benchmark for structured argument mining in U.S. federal tax case law.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an expert-annotated, tree-structured argument corpus of 42 U.S. federal tax court opinions on corporate reorganizations, analyzes annotation reliability, and benchmarks classification and retrieval models for legal argument mining.
AI.motivation: To enable more precise legal argument mining—such as passage classification, argument structure extraction, and improved retrieval—in a specialized and complex area of U.S. tax law, where no expert-annotated, tree-structured argument datasets currently exist.
AI.method: They construct an expert-annotated corpus of 42 federal tax opinions, labeling text spans with five functional roles (Rule, Analysis, Conclusion, Background Facts, Procedural History) and linking Rule/Analysis/Conclusion spans into directed support trees. They provide multiple granular representations (span-level, sentence-level, flat, and tree-structured), measure inter-annotator agreement on labels and links (including path vs. edge agreement), and run supervised classification and retrieval experiments (including case-disjoint evaluation and cross-case generalization tests).
AI.result: (1) Functional node labels show higher inter-annotator agreement than directed support links and implicit intermediate conclusions. (2) Agreement on directed paths in the argument trees is stronger than on individual edges, suggesting more stability in global reachability than in local argument decomposition. (3) Functional labels can be reliably learned by models when training and test cases are disjoint. (4) Supervised fine-tuning improves within-case legal passage retrieval but models generalize poorly across different cases.
AI.conclusion: The new corpus is a valuable resource for legal AI: it enables reliable functional passage classification and provides a conservative, realistic benchmark for structured argument mining in U.S. federal tax case law. However, precise argument structure prediction and cross-case retrieval/generalization remain challenging, highlighting open research problems in legal argument mining.

title: ShowTellArena: Evaluating Business Workflow Understanding from Demonstrations
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Code and dataset linked in the paper
summary: We often teach a colleague by showing the work and explaining the decisions as we go. How can we check what an agent understood from the same lesson? We introduce ShowTellArena, a benchmark protocol and public dataset for comprehension after narrated business demonstrations. The v1.0 release contains 50 business workflow tasks, with recordings, screenshots, narration, fixture seeds, and 502 questions. Tasks span finance, hiring, procurement, customer decisions, inventory, and logistics. The protocol holds the business scenario and quiz fixed while allowing each product to capture the lesson through its own teaching interface. Questions test operational rules, boundaries, exceptions, and errors in proposed automations. We analyze 218 selected pilot attempts across 39 workflow cases, including 28 cases attempted by all three evaluated systems. These exploratory results expose both answer errors and failures to complete the teaching experience. We describe the release's verification gaps and the pilot's uneven coverage, exclusions, and grading provenance. The contribution is an inspectable dataset and assessment workflow that others can extend; the selected pilot is not a controlled product ranking.

AI.tldr: Introduces ShowTellArena, a benchmark and dataset for testing how well AI agents comprehend narrated business process demonstrations.
AI.motivation: In real workplaces, people learn business workflows by watching demonstrations with explanations. For AI agents to be useful in such settings, we need a way to measure what they actually understood from similar narrated lessons, beyond simple task execution or static QA benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors build ShowTellArena, a protocol and dataset where agents are first ‘taught’ via narrated demonstrations of business workflows (recordings, screenshots, narration, seeds), and then quizzed with 502 questions over 50 tasks spanning multiple business domains. The protocol keeps the scenario and quiz fixed but lets each product use its own teaching UI. They run 218 pilot evaluation attempts across 39 workflow cases and three systems, then examine answer errors and failures in going through the teaching experience, and document verification gaps and grading provenance limits.
AI.result: The v1.0 dataset includes 50 business workflow tasks across domains such as finance, hiring, procurement, customer decisions, inventory, and logistics, plus 502 comprehension questions. Pilot evaluations across 39 cases reveal multiple types of system failures—incorrect answers as well as incomplete or failed teaching sessions. Coverage of tasks and verification are still partial and uneven, with noted gaps and exclusions.
AI.conclusion: ShowTellArena offers an initial, inspectable benchmark and assessment workflow for evaluating agents’ comprehension of narrated business demonstrations. The current pilot results are exploratory and not meant as a controlled comparison of products, but the framework and dataset are designed to be extended and improved by the community.

title: Conduct Under Pressure: What Sixty Language Models Do When a User Pushes
summary:
We study what LLMs do when a user applies pressure in an uncomfortable situation: a user insists, begs, flatters or grieves, and the model gives up a correct fact, writes a document it should refuse, or cheers a plan that will cost the user money. We send frozen multi-turn scenes, identical for every model regardless of the reply, to 60 models from 13 vendors, and label each transcript with a codebook built by open coding and then frozen: a trajectory (the model held its position or folded) and a manner (how it held or folded). Two findings separate. Whether a model holds tracks its generation, meaning how recent it is: fold rate correlates with a public capability index at Spearman -0.64, with little vendor effect. How it holds tracks the vendor: six of the 17 manner codes sort by vendor at permutation p <= 0.001, corrected across the codebook. We report four vendor profiles on the codes that cleared reliability.
  We also ask which parts of the labeling need a person. Six LLM coders from three vendors apply the codebook more consistently than three human coders do (Krippendorff's alpha 0.66 against 0.46), agree with the codebook's author on trajectory at kappa 0.84 to 0.91 on transcripts the codebook's examples never touched, and match an adjudicated human reference at 0.83. Blind machine readings recover the codebook's categories but cannot tell which of them a second reader would apply the same way. We conclude that for behavior a non-specialist can judge, the human contribution is authoring and bounding the codes and owning a small reference, not producing labels at volume.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how large language models respond under emotional or social pressure from users and evaluates whether LLMs can reliably label such behaviors, often outperforming human coders in consistency.
AI.motivation: To understand LLM safety and reliability in socially or emotionally charged interactions, and to test whether LLMs can help with large-scale, consistent behavioral annotation of model outputs.
AI.method: The authors design fixed multi-turn conversational ‘scenes’ where users pressure models (e.g., insisting, begging, flattering, grieving) to change answers or violate policies. They run these scenes on 60 frozen LLMs from 13 vendors and annotate each transcript with a pre-defined codebook for two dimensions: trajectory (whether the model holds or folds) and manner (how it does so). They analyze correlations between fold rates, model generation/ability indices, and vendor effects. They then compare labeling quality from human coders and six LLM coders using the same codebook, measuring inter-rater reliability and agreement with a human reference.
AI.result: Newer, more capable models are less likely to fold under pressure, with fold rate strongly negatively correlated with an external capability index (Spearman -0.64), and vendor identity adds little to that dimension. However, the qualitative manner of how models hold their ground or fold strongly depends on vendor, with six of 17 manner codes significantly sorted by vendor. LLM coders apply the codebook more consistently than human coders (higher Krippendorff's alpha), agree highly with the codebook’s author on trajectory, and align closely with an adjudicated human reference. Unsupervised machine analyses can rediscover the code categories but cannot predict which ones will be reliably applied across readers.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral robustness to pressure (whether models hold or fold) mostly tracks model generation/capability, not vendor, while the style of that behavior is vendor-specific. For labeling such behaviors, humans are most needed to design and constrain the codebook and curate a small reference set, whereas LLMs can perform high-volume, consistent labeling, often more reliably than multiple human annotators.

title: RAG-NAROK: Retrieval-Aware Knowledge Corpus Poisoning in RAG with Source-specific Refutation
summary: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) systems have emerged as the dominant architecture for grounding large language model (LLM) outputs in verifiable external knowledge, yet their structural reliance on a dynamic retrieval pipeline introduces a largely unexplored class of adversarial vulnerability. Existing knowledge-base poisoning attacks are fundamentally static. Adversarial documents are pre-computed and injected without any awareness of what the victim system will actually retrieve for a given query, leaving the attack blind to the competitive documentary landscape that surrounds its payload in the generator's context window. Unlike traditional static poisoning attacks that are blind to the retrieved context, we introduce RAG-NAROK (Retrieval-Anchored Generation Negation And Response Quality Collapse), a RAG attack framework that adapts to the query text. RAG-NAROK exploits the transparency inherent in RAG pipeline to first extract the legitimate source identities, then generate Anchor-Specific Refutation documents that explicitly name and devalue retrieved sources while leveraging recency and authority biases to steer the text generation toward a target answer. Our results demonstrate that RAG-NAROK significantly outperforms static baselines across diverse domains, revealing a fundamental tension between RAG transparency and AI security.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RAG-NAROK, a query-adaptive poisoning attack on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that exploits pipeline transparency to refute retrieved sources and steer answers, outperforming prior static attacks.
AI.motivation: RAG systems are widely used to ground LLM outputs in external knowledge, but most prior poisoning work assumes static adversarial documents that do not adapt to what the system actually retrieves. This ignores how RAG’s dynamic retrieval and visible citations create new, largely unexplored attack surfaces. The authors aim to understand and exploit this structural vulnerability to better characterize the security risks of RAG and the trade-off between transparency and robustness.
AI.method: They propose RAG-NAROK, an adaptive attack framework tailored to RAG. For each query, the attacker first observes which legitimate documents and source identities the RAG pipeline retrieves. It then generates Anchor-Specific Refutation documents: adversarial texts that explicitly name and undermine those retrieved sources while leveraging typical LLM biases such as recency and perceived authority (e.g., claiming to be newer or more authoritative). These crafted documents are inserted into the knowledge base so they are likely to be retrieved alongside or instead of legitimate sources, causing the generator to devalue trusted documents and follow the attacker’s target answer. The framework is evaluated against static poisoning baselines across multiple domains.
AI.result: Experiments show that RAG-NAROK substantially increases attack success rates compared to static poisoning methods, more reliably driving the RAG system toward attacker-specified answers and degrading response quality. The performance gains hold across diverse domains, indicating that query-adaptive, anchor-aware poisoning is a powerful and general threat model for RAG.
AI.conclusion: RAG-NAROK exposes a structural security weakness in RAG systems: the very transparency and dynamic retrieval mechanisms that make RAG attractive also enable more potent adaptive attacks. The work suggests there is an inherent tension between providing transparent, source-grounded RAG outputs and maintaining robustness against adversaries who can observe and manipulate the retrieval context. Future defenses must explicitly account for this adaptive, anchor-targeting poisoning paradigm.

title: Matryoshka attribution: Learning to attribute language model outputs to representations and weights
comment: 10 pages main text, 58 pages total; preprint
summary: Attributing language model outputs to their internal computations is an open problem in interpretability. Existing methods, which use causal interventions, gradients, or learnable masks, either are infeasibly expensive or struggle to identify actual causally-important internal computations. We propose framing attribution as the problem of identifying nested subsets of internal components which minimise a downstream loss. To learn this task, we introduce Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a mask learning method that parametrises the mask with a simple differentiable sigmoid top-$k$ operator. We supervise training over all sparsities simultaneously by randomising $k$ over training, resulting in a learned ordering of components by attribution score. MAttr achieves number 1 on the official leaderboard of the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (Mueller et al., 2025); our method identifies sparse and task-transferrable circuits across varying circuit bases. As a practical application, we show that MAttr can be trained with reinforcement learning to identify weight changes responsible for downstream behaviours in LLM finetuning. We train MAttr on refusal judge scores and find that restoring $1\%$ of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct's weights to their base model state is sufficient to remove refusals while maintaining capabilities. We view MAttr as a successful formulation of interpretability into a learnable objective that we can tackle with gradient descent, and encourage future work along these lines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a new, efficient method to attribute language model outputs to internal components by learning nested sparse masks that minimize task loss, achieving SOTA on a mechanistic interpretability benchmark and enabling practical circuit-level interventions in finetuned LLMs.
AI.motivation: Interpreting which internal computations in large language models actually cause specific outputs is difficult: existing causal, gradient-based, or mask-learning methods are either too computationally expensive or fail to reliably identify causally important components. There is a need for an efficient, principled, and scalable way to attribute model behavior to internal circuits that works across different circuit bases and supports practical interventions such as modifying or reverting specific weights.
AI.method: The authors reframe attribution as finding nested subsets of internal components that minimize a downstream loss. They propose Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a mask-learning approach where a differentiable sigmoid top-k operator parameterizes a mask over components. During training, the sparsity level k is randomized so that the model is supervised across all sparsity levels simultaneously, forcing it to learn a global ordering of components by attribution score. They apply MAttr to different circuit bases and also train it with reinforcement learning to select weight changes associated with specific downstream behaviors in finetuned LLMs.
AI.result: MAttr ranks first on the official leaderboard of the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (Mueller et al., 2025), indicating strong performance in identifying causally important internal circuits. It recovers sparse and task-transferable circuits across multiple circuit bases. In a concrete LLM finetuning application, MAttr trained on refusal-judge scores finds that reverting only 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct's weights to the base model is enough to remove refusals while preserving overall capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that Matryoshka Attribution constitutes a successful formulation of mechanistic interpretability as a learnable optimization objective solvable via gradient descent. By producing ordered, sparse, and transferable attributions and enabling effective circuit-level edits in real models, MAttr demonstrates that scalable, optimization-based interpretability is both feasible and useful. The authors encourage further work that casts interpretability problems as trainable objectives and extends MAttr to broader settings and behaviors.

title: Spectra: A Rules-Driven LLM Pipeline for Automated KYC Document Processing
summary: Know Your Client (KYC) onboarding in capital markets requires analysts to manually classify documents, extract structured data from heterogeneous sources, and validate compliance against complex regulatory policies. This process requires significant analyst time per client, with end-to-end onboarding often stretching to multiple weeks due to sequential handoffs. In this work, we analyze an on-boarding process and find that it comprises repeatable components well-suited to AI automation. We therefore propose a restructured workflow to be amenable to automation: we consolidate the traditional four-party process into two parties that share most of the work and can be automated together, eliminating intermediate handoffs that compound delays. To automate the remaining steps, we introduce Spectra, an AI-assisted document processing platform that combines a structured rules engine with LLM-based classification, extraction, and validation agents. The rules engine encodes compliance policy as a queryable database, enabling focused context injection that reduces token usage while improving extraction precision. Rather than a single monolithic prompt, the system decomposes document processing into isolated, auditable stages, each optimized independently and traceable to specific policy clauses. In evaluation on real KYC documents, Spectra achieves 100% classification accuracy and 89.4% extraction accuracy. Human review burden dropped by 96%.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Spectra, an AI-assisted KYC onboarding platform that restructures workflows and uses rules + LLM agents to automate document classification, data extraction, and compliance validation, greatly reducing human review time.
AI.motivation: KYC onboarding in capital markets is slow and labor-intensive because analysts must manually classify documents, extract structured data from varied sources, and check them against complex regulatory policies. The process involves multiple parties and sequential handoffs, leading to long onboarding times and high operational costs. The authors want to understand this process, identify repeatable components suitable for AI, and design a system that makes KYC onboarding faster, more accurate, and less burdensome for human analysts while remaining auditable and compliant.
AI.method: First, the authors analyze the existing KYC onboarding workflow and decompose it into repeatable components. They then redesign the workflow, consolidating the traditional four-party process into two parties that can share work and be jointly automated, reducing handoffs. On top of this new workflow, they build Spectra, an AI-assisted document processing platform. Spectra combines: (1) a structured rules engine that encodes compliance policies in a queryable database; and (2) LLM-based agents for document classification, information extraction, and validation. The rules engine is used to inject only the most relevant policy context into prompts, thereby reducing token usage and focusing the LLM’s attention. Document processing is decomposed into separate, auditable stages, each linked to specific policy clauses, rather than relying on one large prompt. The system is then evaluated on real-world KYC documents.
AI.result: On real KYC documents, Spectra achieves 100% accuracy for document classification and 89.4% accuracy for data extraction. The redesigned, AI-augmented workflow reduces human review effort by 96%, indicating a major improvement in efficiency while maintaining high quality outputs.
AI.conclusion: KYC onboarding in capital markets can be significantly streamlined by both restructuring the workflow and applying AI in a principled, auditable way. By encoding compliance policies in a rules engine, using LLM agents for discrete, well-defined tasks, and minimizing handoffs between human teams, Spectra achieves high accuracy and dramatically reduces the need for manual review. The work suggests that complex regulatory document workflows are amenable to modular AI automation, provided that systems are designed around policy traceability and efficient context management.

title: Compressing Long Context into Answer-Aligned Memory Embeddings for LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is constrained by the quadratic scaling of self-attention and the linear scaling of the KV cache, increasing latency, energy consumption, and GPU memory demand as context length scales. Existing soft-compression methods either lack query-guided memory selection at inference time, train without answer-targeted supervision, or couple compression tightly to a specific decoder architecture. We propose a Context-to-Answer-Aligned Memory Compression (CMC) framework, which compresses long input contexts into compact Context Memory Embeddings (CMEs) aligned to any frozen decoder's embedding space, reducing inference costs without modifying decoder weights. CMC introduces a two-tier KV cache that combines question-guided CME selection with a local context window, and trains the compressor with answer-targeted distillation from a frozen LLM. Experiments across nine encoder-decoder combinations and four QA benchmarks show that CMC consistently outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 7.3 EM and 4.0 F1 point gains on SQuAD, while reducing inference time and energy consumption by up to 20% and peak reserved GPU memory by up to 50% at 3,000 generation tokens. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component and training objective contributes to the performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training and inference framework (CMC) that compresses long contexts into compact embeddings aligned with a frozen LLM, enabling faster, more memory-efficient inference with minimal accuracy loss or even gains on QA tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM inference becomes increasingly expensive as context length grows because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length and the KV cache scales linearly. Existing compression and memory methods either are not guided by the current query, lack answer-targeted supervision, or are tightly bound to a specific architecture, making them less practical and less effective. There is a need for a general, model-agnostic compression scheme that can reduce latency, energy, and GPU memory while preserving or improving QA performance, and that can work with frozen decoders.
AI.method: They introduce Context-to-Answer-Aligned Memory Compression (CMC), which learns a compressor that maps long input contexts into a small set of Context Memory Embeddings (CMEs) that live in the embedding space of any frozen decoder. CMC uses a two-tier KV cache at inference: (1) a question-guided selection mechanism chooses relevant CMEs given the query, and (2) a local context window is retained to preserve nearby information. The compressor is trained via answer-targeted distillation from a frozen LLM, so that compressed representations preserve information necessary to reproduce the teacher’s answers. The framework is evaluated across nine encoder–decoder pairings and several QA benchmarks without changing the decoder weights.
AI.result: Across four QA benchmarks and nine different encoder–decoder configurations, CMC consistently outperforms baseline soft-compression approaches. On SQuAD it yields up to +7.3 EM and +4.0 F1 over baselines. At generation lengths of around 3,000 tokens, it reduces inference time and energy consumption by up to 20% and cuts peak reserved GPU memory by up to 50%. Ablation studies show that removing any of the key pieces—query-guided CME selection, the local context window, or answer-targeted distillation—degrades performance, indicating each component is important.
AI.conclusion: CMC offers a general, decoder-agnostic framework for compressing long contexts into compact memory embeddings aligned with a frozen LLM’s embedding space. By combining question-guided CME selection, a local context window, and answer-targeted distillation, it reduces latency, energy, and memory footprint while improving or maintaining QA accuracy. The consistent gains across multiple models and datasets and the ablation results suggest that carefully designed, answer-aligned compression can be a practical solution for scaling LLM inference to long contexts without modifying the underlying decoder.

title: Queer inclusion in speech datasets: An audit and taxonomy of practical tensions
summary: In this paper, we examine speech datasets for their inclusion of LGBTQIA+, or queer, voices and provide a taxonomy of tensions to better understand why there is a lack of such voices in current speech technology datasets. Through an audit of six diverse speech datasets, we find that measurable queer representation is low (0-1.4% of speakers) - insufficient for robust disparity measurement. We take this community as a case study to consider what challenges and tensions are associated with collecting speech data from marginalized communities. For comparison, we audit an additional two datasets from the speech sciences that were created by, for, and with the queer community. We note that many customs in speech dataset collection efforts in AI and speech technology research may conflict with values emphasized in participatory approaches with marginalized communities, and provide a taxonomy describing these tensions.

AI.tldr: The paper audits major speech datasets to assess inclusion of queer speakers and develops a taxonomy of tensions that explain why such voices are underrepresented.
AI.motivation: There is growing concern that speech technologies may not work equitably for marginalized communities, including queer people, but it is unclear how much these communities are actually represented in the datasets used to train and evaluate such systems. Without sufficient representation, it is impossible to reliably measure or address disparities. The authors aim to understand the extent of queer representation and the structural reasons behind its scarcity.
AI.method: The authors conduct an audit of six diverse speech datasets commonly used in AI and speech technology to quantify the measurable representation of queer speakers. They then analyze the broader processes and norms of dataset collection to identify challenges and tensions in gathering speech data from marginalized communities. For contrast and deeper insight, they also audit two additional speech-science datasets that were intentionally created by, for, and with the queer community. From these empirical observations and comparisons, they derive a taxonomy of tensions between mainstream dataset practices and participatory, community-centered approaches.
AI.result: The audit shows that queer representation in the six mainstream speech technology datasets is very low, ranging from 0% to 1.4% of speakers—far too small for meaningful or robust disparity analysis. In contrast, datasets built explicitly with and for queer communities exhibit different design choices and practices that better align with community values. The authors systematically identify recurring tensions between conventional dataset collection customs (e.g., scale, standardization, anonymity norms) and participatory practices that prioritize community agency, safety, and relevance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current speech technology datasets largely fail to include queer voices at levels necessary for rigorous fairness and disparity assessment. This underrepresentation is not merely accidental but is linked to deeper tensions between mainstream data collection norms and the values emphasized in community-driven, participatory research with marginalized groups. The proposed taxonomy of tensions offers a framework for rethinking how speech datasets are collected, encouraging practices that more meaningfully and ethically include marginalized communities, thereby enabling fairer and more inclusive speech technologies.

title: Qwen3.8-Omni: Towards Native Omni-Modal Agents
summary: We introduce Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, a natively multimodal agentic model for real-world multimodal productivity. Compared with previous omni models, which primarily emphasized perception and interaction, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash substantially improves multimodal understanding and reasoning, as well as performance on long-horizon agentic tasks. These capabilities are supported by a native multimodal co-training strategy that preserves strong text-domain capabilities while facilitating the transfer of agentic capabilities from text to audio and video tasks. The model inherits the sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture of Qwen3.8-Next and extends the context window to one million tokens, supporting long-context multimodal reasoning and long-horizon planning. These advances enable integration into production workflows as a primary agent or a specialized sub-agent, supporting video editing, long-form audio and video translation, music-conditioned music video or movie generation, and video-based note or omni-skill creation. To address the lack of native audio and video support in existing agent harnesses, we release Qwen-MM-Plugins, a lightweight open-source plugin framework for multimodal productivity. We further frame real-time multimodal interaction as a system-level challenge requiring orchestration of context and memory management, tool use, and sub-agent delegation. Accordingly, we release Qwen-Live-Harness, an open-source framework for building responsive, real-time multimodal agents based on Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash achieves strong performance across multimodal understanding, reasoning, long-horizon agentic execution, and video productivity tasks. These results and the accompanying open-source tools support Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash as a practical foundation for deploying natively multimodal agents in research and production.

AI.tldr: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash is a natively multimodal, MoE-based, long-context agentic model plus toolkits (Qwen-MM-Plugins, Qwen-Live-Harness) for real-time, production-ready multimodal productivity.
AI.motivation: Existing omni/multimodal models focus more on perception and interaction than on deep multimodal reasoning, long-horizon agentic tasks, and real-time, production-ready multimodal workflows. There is also a lack of native audio/video support in agent harnesses, limiting deployment of such models as practical multimodal agents.
AI.method: They design Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash as a sparse MoE model (inheriting Qwen3.8-Next) trained with a native multimodal co-training strategy to transfer strong text and agentic capabilities to audio and video. The model’s context window is extended to one million tokens to support long-context multimodal reasoning and planning. On the system side, they introduce two open-source frameworks: Qwen-MM-Plugins, a lightweight plugin system for multimodal tools, and Qwen-Live-Harness, an orchestration layer handling real-time interaction, memory/context management, tool use, and sub-agent delegation.
AI.result: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash shows strong quantitative performance on benchmarks for multimodal understanding, multimodal reasoning, long-horizon agentic execution, and video-centric productivity tasks, indicating effective transfer of agentic abilities to audio and video and robust long-context behavior.
AI.conclusion: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, together with Qwen-MM-Plugins and Qwen-Live-Harness, forms a practical foundation for deploying natively multimodal agents in both research and real-world production settings, capable of acting as primary or specialized sub-agents in complex multimodal workflows.

title: Towards participatory speech dataset curation: A queer case study and conceptual framework
summary: In this paper, we motivate the need for a participatory speech dataset creation framework through a case study of the LGBTQIA+, or queer, community - a community with documented concerns about AI and reported harms, including attempts to develop 'gaydar' technologies that purportedly identify individuals as queer. We review common speech data collection practices, why these methods may be unsuitable for engaging with queer speakers, and discuss previous efforts in participatory AI with queer community engagement, as well as participatory endeavours specific to speech data collection for other marginalized communities. From this review, we develop a conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation by, for, and with marginalized communities drawing on insights from co-design and knowledge sharing. We propose a framework comprising overlapping and two-way processes of defining a community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a participatory framework for creating speech datasets with marginalized communities, illustrated via a case study of the queer community, to address harms and mistrust in AI.
AI.motivation: Existing speech dataset collection practices often neglect or harm marginalized groups, such as queer people, who have documented concerns about AI misuse (e.g., so‑called 'gaydar' systems). There is a need for data practices that respect community autonomy, address historical harms, and build trust while enabling inclusive speech technologies.
AI.method: The authors conduct a conceptual and critical review of: (1) standard speech data collection practices and their limitations for queer participants; (2) prior participatory AI work involving queer communities; and (3) participatory speech data efforts with other marginalized groups. Using this synthesis and drawing on co-design and knowledge-sharing literatures, they derive a conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation.
AI.result: They produce a structured, conceptual framework for participatory speech dataset creation tailored to marginalized communities. The framework emphasizes overlapping, bidirectional processes across four dimensions: defining the community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy. It articulates how these dimensions should interact in practice when curating speech data by, for, and with marginalized communities.
AI.conclusion: Participatory, community-centered approaches are necessary for ethical and inclusive speech dataset creation, especially for communities with histories of AI-related harms. The proposed framework offers guiding principles and processes that can help researchers and practitioners engage marginalized speakers more safely and respectfully, potentially mitigating misuse and improving trust and representation in speech technologies.

title: From Utterances to Networks: Modelling Slang Adoption and Diffusion Across Subreddits
summary: Adoption and diffusion of neologisms in online communities have received renewed attention in recent years. As internet slang terms such as APT, referring to a K-pop song, and phrases such as Canon Event meaning an embarrassing but pivotal event, go viral online, it becomes increasingly important to understand the mechanisms that contribute to their success. Prior studies have often explained slang diffusion either from the perspective of social interaction or from the linguistic properties of the slang itself, but rarely from both perspectives together. One major obstacle has been the high cost of annotating slang usage in large-scale online communication. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to use them as scalable annotators for such tasks. In this study, we first curate a human-annotated benchmark to evaluate LLM performance in detecting slang usage in real Reddit communication. We then leverage LLM-based annotations to model slang adoption and diffusion. Our results show that slang diffusers with higher bridging capital are associated with increased subsequent adoption, whereas diffusers with higher bonding capital are associated with reduced adoption. We also find that wider contextual usage of a slang term is associated with a longer time before new users officially adopt it. Together, these findings suggest that both social-network structure and linguistic context shape the diffusion of neologisms in online communities.

AI.tldr: The paper uses large language models to annotate real Reddit data and study how both social-network structure and linguistic context jointly influence which internet slang terms spread and get adopted.
AI.motivation: Internet slang like “APT” or “Canon Event” spreads rapidly, but we lack a detailed understanding of why some neologisms diffuse widely while others do not. Prior work usually focuses either on social interaction patterns (who talks to whom) or on properties of the slang itself (how and where it’s used), but rarely integrates both. A key barrier has been the high cost of manually annotating slang usage across large-scale online conversations. With recent advances in LLMs, there is now an opportunity to cheaply and consistently label slang usage and thereby enable richer, combined analyses of social and linguistic drivers of diffusion.
AI.method: The authors first build a human-annotated benchmark dataset of slang usage drawn from actual Reddit posts and comments. They then evaluate the performance of large language models as automatic annotators for detecting slang in this benchmark. After validating LLM annotations, they apply LLM-based labeling at scale across Reddit data to identify when and how slang terms are used. Using these annotations, they construct models of slang adoption and diffusion that incorporate both users’ positions in the social network (bridging vs. bonding social capital) and the contextual breadth of slang usage (how widely and in what contexts a term appears).
AI.result: The study finds that users who act as bridges between otherwise disconnected parts of the network (“bridging capital”) tend to promote further adoption of slang: when they diffuse a term, subsequent uptake by other users increases. Conversely, users with strong ties mainly within tightly knit groups (“bonding capital”) are associated with reduced subsequent adoption when they diffuse a term. Linguistically, slang terms that appear in a wider variety of contexts are adopted more slowly, with a longer delay before new users begin using them in a stable, “official” way. These results are derived from models built on large-scale Reddit data annotated by LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Both social structure and linguistic context are critical to understanding how internet slang spreads. Bridging users facilitate diffusion, while tightly bonded users can inhibit it, highlighting the importance of network position for neologism adoption. At the same time, the breadth of contextual usage influences the timing of adoption, with more contextually diverse terms taking longer to stabilize into common usage. Methodologically, the work demonstrates that LLMs can serve as scalable annotators for complex, nuanced language phenomena like slang, enabling integrated social and linguistic analyses of language change in online communities.

title: SMTB: Fast Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds
summary: Structure-mapping forms analogies by aligning systems of relationally connected elements based on shared structure instead of surface features. We introduce a new structure-mapping algorithm: Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds (SMTB) that is 5--15x faster than the structure-mapping engine (SME) and about 50\% better at finding mappings in large nested domains. SMTB is part of the broader Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE) project, a flexible multi-language-compatible framework with an accessible Python interface to state-of-the-art C++ implementations of core algorithms commonly used in cognitive systems such as pattern matching, planning, and structure-mapping. CRE and SMTB are designed to work with a wide range of representation choices. Unlike SME, which biases higher-order correspondences in tree-like predicate logic, SMTB maximizes relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations. This allows SMTB to work just as well over arbitrary relational graphs as it does in tree-like domains of nested predicate logic. We discuss situations where privileging "higher-orderness" in structure-mapping can cause issues, and illustrate how SMTB avoids failure modes that SME would encounter in these situations. We also provide an evaluation comparing SMTB to SME v4 over 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus.

AI.tldr: They present a new, faster, and more flexible structure-mapping algorithm (SMTB) within a general cognitive rule engine, and show it outperforms the classic SME algorithm, especially on large and graph-like domains.
AI.motivation: Classic structure-mapping (especially SME) is powerful but computationally expensive and biased toward higher-order, tree-like predicate structures, which limits performance and applicability to large, nested, or graph-structured domains. The authors want an algorithm that preserves the core idea of structure-mapping—aligning relational structure rather than surface similarity—while scaling better, being more representation-agnostic, and avoiding failure modes caused by privileging higher-order relations.
AI.method: They design SMTB (Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds), a new structure-mapping algorithm that focuses on maximizing relational connectivity without explicitly privileging higher-order relations. SMTB is implemented as part of the Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE), a C++-based framework with a Python interface, intended to support multiple cognitive algorithms (pattern matching, planning, structure-mapping) across varied representation schemes. They analyze where SME’s higher-order bias leads to problems and run an empirical comparison of SMTB versus SME v4 on 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus, measuring speed and mapping quality, particularly in large and nested domains and non-tree relational graphs.
AI.result: SMTB runs 5–15 times faster than the classic SME implementation and achieves about 50% better performance in discovering mappings in large nested domains. It also handles arbitrary relational graphs as effectively as tree-like predicate-logic structures. The comparisons over 5845 SME-corpus domain pairs show systematic advantages for SMTB in both efficiency and robustness, especially where SME’s higher-order bias would cause failures or degraded mappings.
AI.conclusion: SMTB provides a more efficient and more generally applicable structure-mapping algorithm than SME, retaining the core idea of aligning relational structure while eliminating the rigid preference for higher-order relations. Embedded within the CRE framework, it supports a broader range of representational formats and graph structures, avoids SME’s known failure modes, and delivers substantial speed and mapping-quality improvements on a large benchmark suite.

title: Syndrome, Synergy, and Safety: Structured Reasoning and Knowledge-Driven Alignment for TCM Prescription Generation
summary: Applying large language models to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) prescription generation reveals three clinically critical gaps: models produce end-to-end mappings without auditable reasoning following the li-fa-fang-yao paradigm (SR Gap), treat each encounter in isolation without follow-up adjustment via sui zheng jia jian (LA Gap), and fail to enforce absolute contraindication rules such as Shi Ba Fan (SC Gap). We propose a progressive four-stage framework (SFT $\to$ PG-CoT $\to$ Dynamic $\to$ K-RL) that addresses each gap: PG-CoT constrains CoT distillation under the li-fa-fang-yao paradigm to produce auditable diagnostic chains, Dynamic SFT models patient trajectories with explicit transition reasoning, and K-RL encodes deterministic pharmacological rules as rule-based DPO preference signals. Across 12 fine-tuned models and 6 zero-shot baselines, our framework substantially improves prescription quality over zero-shot baselines---with a 7B model (Mistral-7B) surpassing zero-shot GPT-5 on all three TCM evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: They propose a four-stage training framework for TCM prescription LLMs that adds structured reasoning, longitudinal adjustment, and strict rule constraints, leading a 7B model to outperform a much larger zero-shot GPT-5 baseline on TCM metrics.
