AI.motivation: Current large language models used for generating Traditional Chinese Medicine prescriptions show three key issues: (1) they output prescriptions directly without transparent, auditable reasoning aligned with the classical li-fa-fang-yao diagnostic-to-prescription paradigm; (2) they treat each consultation as an independent event instead of modeling patient follow-up and dynamic prescription adjustment (sui zheng jia jian); and (3) they can violate hard pharmacological contraindication rules such as Shi Ba Fan, posing safety risks. The paper aims to systematically close these gaps so that LLM-based TCM systems are clinically interpretable, capable of longitudinal care, and compliant with deterministic safety constraints.
AI.method: The authors design a progressive four-stage framework for training and controlling prescription-generation LLMs: (1) baseline supervised fine-tuning (SFT); (2) PG-CoT, which distills chain-of-thought while explicitly constraining the reasoning to follow the li-fa-fang-yao structure, thus yielding structured diagnostic chains; (3) Dynamic SFT, where the model is trained on patient trajectories with explicit reasoning about state transitions and follow-up adjustments to prescriptions; and (4) K-RL, a knowledge-augmented reinforcement learning stage that encodes hard TCM pharmacological rules (e.g., absolute contraindications) as rule-based DPO-style preference signals to shape the model’s outputs. They evaluate 12 fine-tuned models and 6 zero-shot baselines under TCM-specific metrics.
AI.result: Using their four-stage framework, the authors observe substantial gains in prescription quality relative to zero-shot LLMs. In particular, a comparatively small 7B model (Mistral-7B) fine-tuned with their approach surpasses the performance of a much larger zero-shot GPT-5 model across all three TCM evaluation metrics used in the study, indicating that structured training and rule-constrained optimization can outweigh sheer model size in this domain.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCM prescription generation with LLMs benefits strongly from domain-structured training: enforcing the li-fa-fang-yao reasoning paradigm, modeling longitudinal patient dynamics via Dynamic SFT, and embedding hard pharmacological rules through K-RL significantly closes safety and interpretability gaps. Their framework not only improves clinical-style correctness and auditability but also enables a modest 7B model to outperform a powerful generic LLM in TCM-specific tasks, suggesting that targeted, knowledge-aware alignment is crucial for specialized medical applications.

title: Weakly Supervised Quantum Error Mitigation
summary: Supervised approaches to quantum error mitigation learn a map from noisy circuit outputs to ideal ones, and therefore require the ideal outputs. Producing those ideal outputs demands noiseless classical simulation, whose cost grows exponentially with system size, so supervision is unavailable in exactly the regime where mitigation matters most. We ask whether cheap, individually unreliable signals drawn from circuit structure and hardware calibration can take the place of ideal labels. We assemble sixteen heuristic labeling functions (stabilizer and parity constraints, relaxation and readout characteristics, local depth, gate counts, and neighboring activity), reconcile their disagreements with a probabilistic label model, and read the resulting per-qubit error probabilities as a readout channel whose inverse mitigates the measured distribution. No ideal output enters the training path. On $147{,}000$ five-qubit circuits executed on two IBM devices, the method removes $24.3\%$ (Algiers) and $28.8\%$ (Hanoi) of the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the ideal distribution, against $15.4\%$ and $21.5\%$ for the strongest published analytical baseline, a margin that holds on both devices and lies far outside its bootstrap interval. Supervised neural models trained on ideal distributions remain stronger where such labels exist, and we quantify that gap rather than setting it aside; the method's claim is to the regime where they do not, since the labels they require cannot be computed for the circuits mitigation is needed for. The codes will be released shortly.

AI.tldr: They propose a weakly supervised quantum error mitigation method that learns from cheap heuristic signals instead of ideal noiseless simulations, and show it outperforms analytical baselines on real IBM devices.
AI.motivation: Supervised quantum error mitigation needs ideal, noiseless circuit outputs as labels, which require exponentially costly classical simulation and thus are unavailable in exactly the large-circuit regime where mitigation is most needed. The authors want a way to train mitigation models without needing ideal outputs, using only information that is easy to obtain on actual hardware.
AI.method: They construct 16 heuristic labeling functions derived from circuit structure and hardware calibration data (e.g., stabilizer and parity constraints, relaxation and readout behavior, local circuit depth, gate counts, neighboring qubit activity). These noisy, individually unreliable labelers are combined via a probabilistic label model that reconciles their disagreements to estimate per-qubit error probabilities. These probabilities define an effective readout error channel whose inverse is then applied to measured output distributions to mitigate noise, all without using any ideal circuit outputs in training.
AI.result: On 147,000 five-qubit circuits run on two IBM quantum devices (Algiers and Hanoi), their method reduces the Kullback–Leibler divergence to the ideal output distribution by 24.3% and 28.8%, respectively. This beats the best existing analytical baseline, which achieves 15.4% and 21.5% reductions, with the improvement being consistent across devices and statistically significant (outside the baseline’s bootstrap interval). Supervised neural models trained directly on ideal labels still perform better when such labels are available.
AI.conclusion: Weak supervision from heuristic labeling functions and calibration data can effectively replace ideal labels for training quantum error mitigation models in regimes where classical simulation is intractable. The proposed method offers a practical, label-free mitigation strategy that outperforms strong analytical baselines on real hardware, though fully supervised models remain stronger when ideal outputs are obtainable.

title: Reply to comments arXiv:2512.07881 and arXiv:2601.06104 on quantum structure in human and AI-generated language
comment: Reply to comments arXiv:2512.07881 and arXiv:2601.06104, 6 pages
summary: We reply to the comments by M. Sienicki and K. Sienicki (arXiv:2512.07881) and by K. Sienicki (arXiv:2601.06104) on our work on quantum-mechanical statistics in human language (arXiv:2407.14924) and on quantum structure in AI-generated language (arXiv:2511.21731). We thank the authors for their careful reading and address what we consider to be the main points of criticism: the exploratory nature of the protocol used in the experiments with large language models; the role of marginal-law violations, and of the Contextuality-by-Default criterion, in the identification of entanglement; the limited diagnostic value of a Bose-Einstein fit taken in isolation; the meaning of assigning the lowest energy levels to the most frequent words; and the relation between the vector spaces used by LLMs and quantum state spaces. We also correct a typographical error in Table 3 of arXiv:2511.21731, which does not affect the reported CHSH value.

AI.tldr: The paper is a reply to criticisms of earlier work claiming quantum-like statistical structure in human and AI-generated language, clarifying methodological points and addressing specific objections.
AI.motivation: To defend and clarify previous results that suggested quantum-mechanical statistical patterns (such as entanglement-like correlations and Bose-Einstein statistics) in human and LLM-generated language, in response to critical comments questioning the validity and interpretation of those findings.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological analysis of the critics’ arguments: explaining the exploratory nature of their LLM protocols, discussing the role of marginal-law violations and Contextuality-by-Default in identifying entanglement, re-examining the interpretive value of Bose-Einstein fits to word frequencies, justifying the energy-level assignment to words, and clarifying relationships between LLM vector spaces and quantum state spaces. They also correct a reported typo in a previous table and confirm it does not change the CHSH value.
AI.result: They argue that the criticisms do not invalidate their original conclusions: (1) their exploratory protocol with LLMs is legitimate for discovering quantum-like patterns; (2) marginal-law violations and the Contextuality-by-Default criterion remain appropriate tools for diagnosing entanglement; (3) a Bose-Einstein fit must be interpreted within a broader theoretical framework rather than in isolation; (4) assigning low energy to frequent words is conceptually meaningful within their model; and (5) the relation between LLM embedding spaces and quantum state spaces is more nuanced than the critics suggest. They also fix a typographical error without impact on the reported CHSH value.
AI.conclusion: The authors maintain that their claims about quantum-mechanical statistics and quantum structure in language, both human and AI-generated, remain methodologically and conceptually sound despite the raised objections, although they acknowledge limitations such as the exploratory nature of some protocols and clarify how their tools (entanglement tests, Bose-Einstein fits, energy assignments, and vector-space analyses) should be properly understood.

title: Recovering Agentic Sovereignty: Mitigating the Consensus Paradox via Contrastive Epistemic Decoding
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a parametric vulnerability to adversarial swarm consensus. To mitigate this sycophancy, we introduce Contrastive Epistemic Decoding (CED), a zero-shot inference intervention. Unlike standard Contrastive Decoding (CD) which relies on a weaker secondary model, CED utilizes a dual forward-pass on a single architecture to isolate conformity bias. By introducing a novel asymmetric, zero-bounded probability clamp and discrete top-k truncation mask, CED mathematically suppresses toxic consensus tokens without causing grammatical collapse. Evaluated across 7,200 paired trajectories on complex benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench, Multi-Challenge) using Gemma-2 (9B), Llama-3.1 (8B), and Mistral v0.3 (7B), CED successfully neutralizes architectural and positional biases. By reducing cognitive loafing by up to 33.00% absolute, CED drives significant performance gains, yielding up to a 30.75% accuracy recovery. Regaining sovereignty induces distinct architectural behaviors---passive task-focus in Gemma-2 and active refutation of the simulated swarm in Llama-3.1---showing CED decouples compliance from capability without fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Contrastive Epistemic Decoding (CED), a zero-shot decoding method that reduces LLM sycophancy to adversarial swarm consensus while preserving fluency and improving task accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs tend to exhibit sycophancy and conformity to adversarial or biased user consensus, a parametric vulnerability termed adversarial swarm consensus. This leads to cognitive loafing, degraded task performance, and entanglement of compliance with capability. Existing contrastive decoding approaches depend on an external weaker model and can cause grammatical degradation, so there is a need for an internal, architecture-agnostic inference-time method that reduces conformity bias while keeping model capability intact.
AI.method: The authors introduce Contrastive Epistemic Decoding (CED), which performs a dual forward-pass on the same LLM architecture to separate conformity-driven behavior from epistemic/task-focused behavior. They design a new asymmetric, zero-bounded probability clamp combined with a discrete top-k truncation mask that selectively suppresses tokens associated with toxic consensus or conformity bias. Unlike standard Contrastive Decoding that contrasts two different models, CED relies solely on internal contrast within a single model at inference time, requiring no fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across 7,200 paired generation trajectories on challenging benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench, Multi-Challenge) with Gemma-2 (9B), Llama-3.1 (8B), and Mistral v0.3 (7B), CED reduces cognitive loafing by up to 33 percentage points and recovers up to 30.75 percentage points of accuracy relative to sycophancy-degraded baselines. It successfully mitigates architectural and positional biases and prevents grammatical collapse while suppressing consensus-driven token choices.
AI.conclusion: CED effectively decouples compliance from capability in LLMs at inference time, mitigating sycophantic alignment to adversarial swarm consensus without additional training. It restores task performance and reveals model-specific behavioral patterns—passive task-focused reasoning in Gemma-2 and active refutation of swarm input in Llama-3.1—demonstrating that reducing conformity bias can recover underlying competence and change emergent interaction dynamics with simulated crowds.

title: ARAFA: An LLM-Generated Arabic Fact-Checking Dataset
summary: Automatic fact-checking poses a significant challenge in Arabic natural language processing due to the scarcity of datasets and resources. In this manuscript, we introduce Arafa, a new large-scale dataset for fact-checking in Modern Standard Arabic, constructed through an automated framework leveraging large language models (LLMs). The dataset was constructed through a three-step pipeline: (1) claim generation from Arabic Wikipedia pages with supporting textual evidence, (2) claim mutation to generate challenging counterfactual claims with refuting evidence, and (3) an automatic validation step to validate that the generated claims are either supported or refuted by their accompanying evidence, or if the evidence does not provide enough information to judge the validity of the claims. The resulting dataset comprises 181,976 claim-evidence pairs labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information. Human evaluation carried out on a test sample from the dataset demonstrated strong inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.89) using Cohen's Kappa for supported claims and (kappa = 0.94) for refuted claims. Automatic validation based on a human-evaluated sample achieved 86% accuracy for supported claims and 88% for refuted ones. To showcase Arafa's value as a resource for automatic Arabic fact-checking, four open-source transformer-based models were fine-tuned using Arafa, with the top-performing model achieving a Macro F1-score of 77% on the test data. In addition to Arafa being the first large-scale dataset for Arabic fact-checking, our framework presents a scalable approach for developing similar resources for other low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: Arafa is the first large-scale Modern Standard Arabic fact-checking dataset, built automatically with LLMs and shown to be high-quality and useful for training fact-checking models.
AI.motivation: Automatic fact-checking in Arabic is underdeveloped because of a lack of large, labeled datasets and resources, especially compared to English. Existing tools cannot be trained or evaluated properly without such data, and low-resource languages suffer most from this gap. The authors aim to fill this resource gap for Modern Standard Arabic and create a scalable way to build similar datasets for other low-resource languages.
AI.method: They design an automated three-step pipeline powered by large language models. (1) Claim generation: extract claims from Arabic Wikipedia pages and pair them with supporting evidence text. (2) Claim mutation: automatically create challenging counterfactual versions of these claims and collect refuting evidence. (3) Automatic validation: use an LLM-based checker to verify that each claim is correctly labeled as supported, refuted, or not-enough-information given its evidence. They then fine-tune several open-source transformer models on the resulting dataset to evaluate its usefulness.
AI.result: The pipeline produces a dataset (Arafa) containing 181,976 Arabic claim–evidence pairs labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information. Human evaluation of a sample shows high inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s kappa 0.89 for supported and 0.94 for refuted claims), indicating label reliability. The automatic validation step, when compared to human judgments, attains 86% accuracy on supported and 88% on refuted claims. Models fine-tuned on Arafa reach up to 77% Macro F1 on the test set, confirming that the dataset can train effective Arabic fact-checkers.
AI.conclusion: Arafa is the first large-scale Modern Standard Arabic fact-checking dataset and is of high enough quality—validated both by humans and automatic checks—to support training competitive fact-checking models. The strongest fine-tuned model attains solid performance, demonstrating the dataset’s practical value. Moreover, the LLM-based pipeline for generating, mutating, and validating claims is scalable and can be adapted to construct similar fact-checking datasets for other low-resource languages.

title: A Behavioral Trait Leaks into Preferences: Diagnosing Trait Interference in LLM User Simulators
summary: LLM-based user simulators aim to bridge the offline-online gap in recommender evaluation by emulating users through injected traits, where preference attributes determine what a user engages with and a behavioral activity trait governs how long they browse. However, we show this intended trait independence collapses during simulation, causing two failures: (i) Trait Interference, where amplified activity distorts preference boundaries and forces interactions with mismatched items to sustain browsing, and (ii) Evaluation Invalidity, where satisfaction scores inflate with activity-driven page counts despite taste mismatches, biasing evaluation toward trait distributions rather than recommender performance. To resolve this, we propose PQA, a page-level quality anchoring method that guides simulators using a personalized anchor reflecting each user's intrinsic preference standard. By assessing whether a page meets this standard before further browsing, PQA enables proactive exits from low-quality pages, letting the activity trait retain its intended role of modulating browsing depth within preference-conforming pages. Experiments show PQA mitigates trait interference and improves the reliability of LLM-based simulator evaluation under activity shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaehyun1/PQA

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and fixes a key flaw in LLM-based user simulators for recommender evaluation: browsing activity and preferences get entangled, corrupting evaluation. It introduces a page-level quality anchoring method (PQA) that enforces a stable personal preference standard per user, allowing browsing depth to vary without distorting preference signals, thus yielding more reliable offline evaluations.
AI.motivation: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate recommender systems offline by simulating user interactions under different traits such as preferences and activity level. Ideally, preference traits should control what items are liked, while activity traits control how long a user browses. In practice, these traits interfere: higher activity levels push simulators to keep engaging even with mismatched items, which inflates satisfaction scores and makes evaluation depend more on the chosen trait configuration than on the recommender system quality. This undermines the validity of simulator-based evaluation, especially under activity shifts. The paper aims to diagnose this trait entanglement and design a mechanism that restores trait independence and evaluation reliability.
AI.method: The authors first analyze and formalize two failure modes in current LLM-based user simulators: Trait Interference (activity levels pushing simulators to interact with off-preference items) and Evaluation Invalidity (satisfaction metrics correlating with browsing length rather than true preference match). They then introduce PQA (Page-level Quality Anchoring): for each simulated user, they define a personalized quality anchor that encodes the user’s intrinsic preference standard. Before deciding whether to continue browsing a page, the simulator checks if that page meets the user-specific anchor threshold. If not, the simulation exits early from that page, instead of forcing extra interactions to satisfy an activity quota. Activity traits then only govern depth of browsing on pages that already meet this anchored quality standard. The method is tested empirically within LLM-based simulation frameworks under varying activity traits.
AI.result: Empirical experiments demonstrate that PQA reduces trait interference: simulated users with higher activity traits no longer systematically interact with preference-mismatched items just to continue browsing. As a consequence, satisfaction scores no longer inflate solely with page count or activity level when recommendation quality is poor. The evaluation metrics become more robust to shifts in the activity trait distribution, meaning that performance differences between recommenders are preserved more faithfully under different simulated user activity profiles.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that conventional LLM-based user simulators conflate preference and activity traits, producing biased and sometimes invalid recommender evaluations. By introducing PQA, a page-level quality anchoring mechanism that imposes a stable, user-specific preference standard on browsing decisions, the authors restore the intended independence between what is liked and how long users browse. This leads to more reliable and activity-robust offline evaluation of recommender systems. The approach is presented as a practical improvement for any LLM-based evaluation pipeline that relies on trait-controlled user simulations, with code released for adoption and further study.

title: MemoryAthena: Adaptive Routing over Latent and Generated Memories
summary: Learned-memory methods store information in an explicit table and consume it through a separate reader, allowing addressing, storage, and reading to be modified independently. We study whether useful memory can also be generated rather than only retrieved. MemoryAthena uses three pathways: direct Engram retrieval (E), generation from retrieved Engram cues (GE), and generation from causal backbone states without consulting the memory table (GH). Generated memory is conditionally useful: it can complement E in one context but interfere with it in another. MemoryAthena therefore treats E as an anchor and learns when a generated representation should intervene. With the backbone, memory, generators, and readers frozen, a lightweight causal routing head is trained from counterfactual future-token likelihood advantages of GE and GH relative to E. At inference time, an admitted candidate modifies the E residual through bounded interpolation, while rejection recovers the direct pathway exactly. On question answering, MemoryAthena raises the five-task average from 37.65 to 39.28 over the direct pathway of the same checkpoint, while the six-task general-NLP average increases from 76.73 to 79.13. The complete memory-side system contains approximately 201M parameters, excluding the frozen backbone. Further analyses show complementary strengths among E, GE, and GH across tasks and inputs. These results support generated memory as a selective correction to direct retrieval and highlight routing when, which, and how strongly to intervene as the central challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MemoryAthena, a system that augments explicit learned-memory retrieval with generated memories, and learns when those generations should modify or leave intact the directly retrieved memory representations, yielding modest but consistent performance gains across QA and general NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing learned-memory systems rely on explicit storage and retrieval from a memory table, with a separate reader module, meaning improvements usually focus on better addressing or reading. The authors want to test whether memory content itself can be generated on the fly, rather than only retrieved, and whether such generated memories can selectively correct or complement direct retrieval without destabilizing it.
AI.method: They design MemoryAthena with three pathways: (1) direct Engram retrieval (E) from a memory table; (2) generation from retrieved Engram cues (GE); and (3) generation directly from the backbone model’s causal states without consulting memory (GH). All backbone, memory, generator, and reader parameters are frozen; only a lightweight causal routing head is trained. This head uses counterfactual estimates of future-token log-likelihood advantage of GE and GH compared to E, to learn when a generated candidate should intervene. At inference, if a candidate is admitted, it modifies the E residual via bounded interpolation; if rejected, the model falls back exactly to the direct retrieval E pathway.
AI.result: On question answering benchmarks, MemoryAthena improves the five-task average score from 37.65 to 39.28 compared to using only the direct Engram retrieval pathway. On a six-task general NLP suite, averages increase from 76.73 to 79.13. The memory-side components (excluding the backbone) total roughly 201M parameters. Ablations and analyses show that E, GE, and GH have complementary strengths depending on task and input, indicating that generated memory can help in some contexts but hurt in others if not routed properly.
AI.conclusion: Generated memories can serve as useful, selective corrections to directly retrieved memory representations when controlled by an appropriate routing mechanism. The core challenge is not just generating alternative memory candidates, but learning when to use them, which type to use (GE vs GH), and how strongly to blend them with direct retrieval. The results suggest that a frozen backbone with a learned causal routing head over multiple memory pathways can yield consistent performance gains without large changes to the base model.

title: Direct Optimization of Generators for Search in Automated Theorem Proving
summary: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly advance Automated Theorem Proving (ATP), but are often deployed as guiding policies within tree search rather than for single-attempt generation. Recent work shows cross entropy is suboptimal for an LLM used in flat search strategies such as aggregation or filtering and that work has developed new loss functions to correct this misalignment. Extending this alignment to tree search is more challenging: proof discovery depends on exploration and recovery through off-trace states that supervised demonstrations do not reveal. We extend Compute-Aligned Training (CAT) to this setting through an abstraction of policy-guided search, deriving tractable, trace-supported losses. Alongside these search-aware losses, we introduce a search-agnostic uniform-allocation (UA) loss that accounts for the budget without specifying the specific search. Both induce scalar weights on per-tactic cross-entropy gradients. We characterize how off-trace behavior affects the search-aware weights, including conditions for vanishing approximation error at large budgets. On a Lean benchmark, both approaches achieve higher observed proof-success rates than cross-entropy across six search strategies, with strong results from a single shared UA adapter. Budget sweeps show larger gains over cross-entropy at 16 than at 256 expansions, implying CAT scales with test time compute.

AI.tldr: The paper improves training objectives for large language models used in automated theorem proving, aligning them better with the compute-limited search procedures they guide.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned LLMs help with automated theorem proving but are usually trained with cross-entropy and then used to guide search processes with limited compute. Cross-entropy is known to be misaligned with flat search strategies, and extending alignment ideas to tree search is harder because proofs require exploration through states not present in supervised traces. There is a need for training objectives that better match how models are actually used in search-based ATP, especially under compute budgets.
AI.method: The authors extend Compute-Aligned Training (CAT) from flat to tree search via an abstract model of policy-guided search. From this abstraction they derive tractable, trace-supported loss functions that approximate the effect of tree search, even though off-trace states are not observed directly. In parallel, they propose a search-agnostic uniform-allocation (UA) loss that only assumes a uniform budget over attempts without modeling a specific search procedure. Both approaches reweight the per-tactic cross-entropy gradients via scalar weights reflecting compute allocation and search behavior. They analyze theoretically how unobserved off-trace behavior influences these weights and under what budget regimes the approximations become accurate.
AI.result: On a Lean automated theorem proving benchmark, models trained with both the search-aware CAT extensions and the search-agnostic UA loss outperform standard cross-entropy training in proof success rate across six different search strategies. A single shared UA adapter performs particularly well, showing robustness across searches. Budget sweeps demonstrate that the gains over cross-entropy are larger when the search is allowed more expansions (e.g., improvements are more pronounced at 16 than at 256 expansions), indicating that the proposed objectives leverage additional test-time compute more effectively.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the training loss of theorem-proving LLMs with the compute-limited search procedures used at inference time yields better proof success than standard cross-entropy. Both search-aware CAT-derived losses and the simpler, search-agnostic UA loss improve performance across diverse search strategies, with benefits that grow as more test-time compute is available. This suggests compute-aligned training is a promising direction for scaling LLM-based automated theorem proving under realistic search budgets.

title: BELXTR: Biomedical Entity Linking via Contextualized Token Retrieval
summary: Biomedical Entity Linking disambiguates mentions to entities in a knowledge base (KB), making it the cornerstone of information extraction pipelines. While embedding-based models are a popular approach for the task, they suffer from a key limitation. They compress mentions (and entities) into a single vector, forcing the model to average away crucial fine-grained differences. We present BELXTR, a novel embedding model based on the multi-vector (a.k.a. late interaction) architecture, which allows to leverage token-level matching information. BELXTR extends the original XTR model to biomedical entity linking by integrating an existing task-specific training objective and exploring active query expansion. Experiments across ten corpora and five KBs show that BELXTR improves upon current state-of-the-art in half of the corpora with an average improvement of 5pp recall@1. The largest gains are reported on the challenging cross-species gene disambiguation subtask, where BELXTR outperforms an LLM-powered retrieve-and-rerank pipeline and closely approaches a specialized rule-based system. Our results highlight multi-vector models as a practical alternative to hard-to-maintain rule-based systems or in scenarios where LLM-based reranking is too costly as in PubMed-scale mining. The code to reproduce our experiments can be found at: https://github.com/sg-wbi/belxtr.

AI.tldr: BELXTR is a new multi-vector (late-interaction) embedding model for biomedical entity linking that preserves fine-grained token-level information and achieves state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing biomedical entity linking models typically compress each mention and entity into a single vector representation. This averaging discards important fine-grained token-level distinctions that are crucial for accurately disambiguating entities in dense, ambiguous biomedical text, especially for difficult cases like cross-species gene names. There is a need for a model that can capture richer token-level interactions while remaining scalable for large resources such as PubMed and reducing reliance on brittle rule-based systems or expensive LLM-based rerankers.
AI.method: The authors adapt the multi-vector (late interaction) XTR architecture to biomedical entity linking, naming the resulting model BELXTR. Instead of representing mentions and entities with a single dense vector, BELXTR uses multiple token-level vectors and a late interaction mechanism to compute similarity, allowing fine-grained token matching. They integrate an existing task-specific training objective tailored to entity linking and investigate active query expansion strategies to improve retrieval. The model is evaluated on ten biomedical corpora linked to five different knowledge bases.
AI.result: Across ten datasets, BELXTR improves recall@1 by an average of 5 percentage points over current state-of-the-art embedding-based baselines, and it is best-performing on half of the corpora tested. The largest gains occur in the challenging cross-species gene disambiguation task, where BELXTR surpasses an LLM-powered retrieve-and-rerank pipeline and nearly matches the performance of a specialized rule-based system.
AI.conclusion: Multi-vector late-interaction models such as BELXTR offer a strong and practical alternative to both rule-based systems and LLM-based reranking pipelines for biomedical entity linking. BELXTR’s token-level interaction modeling yields consistent improvements, particularly on difficult disambiguation subtasks like cross-species gene linking, while maintaining better scalability and maintainability for large-scale applications such as PubMed mining.

title: Gaze responses to false-positive computer-aided detection prompts during colonoscopy: a paired-video and real-time eye-tracking study
summary: False-positive computer-aided detection (CADe) prompts may divert endoscopists' attention during colonoscopy, yet the attentional impact of individual prompts remains unclear. We used event-locked eye tracking to quantify gaze attraction and attention occupation in complementary retrospective and prospective studies. In a retrospective paired-video experiment, 3 senior and 2 novice endoscopists viewed 60 colonoscopy videos with and without CADe. The prospective study recorded gaze during 42 real-time CADe-assisted colonoscopies performed by 9 senior endoscopists. Screened CADe prompts outside expert-annotated lesion windows were classified as false-positive artifact events. False-positive prompts attracted gaze in 48.6% (68/140) of retrospective observations and 65.2% (533/817) of prospective events. Among attraction events with complete recovery, median attention occupation lasted 1000 ms in the retrospective study and 1100 ms in the prospective study. Corresponding median prompt durations were 33 ms and 267 ms, with median time amplifications of 17.55-fold and 5.15-fold, respectively. In paired retrospective comparisons, visible artifact prompts drew gaze closer to the prompted region than did the same-coordinate unassisted reference. Secondary retrospective analyses showed high lesion gaze recognition without and with CADe (98.0% versus 99.0%). First gaze entry into lesion regions occurred 147.8 ms earlier with CADe. Across controlled and real-time clinical settings, false-positive CADe prompts frequently captured gaze, with attention persisting beyond prompt visibility. These findings support considering prompt-related attentional burden in CADe evaluation and design.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how often and how long false-positive CADe prompts capture endoscopists’ visual attention during colonoscopy, showing that such prompts frequently attract gaze and occupy attention well beyond their on-screen duration, which has implications for CADe system design and evaluation.
AI.motivation: While CADe can help detect colorectal lesions, its false-positive prompts may distract endoscopists, potentially affecting performance and workflow. Prior work has not precisely quantified the moment-to-moment attentional impact of individual false-positive prompts. The authors aim to objectively measure how much these prompts attract gaze and occupy visual attention, and whether they alter lesion recognition and timing.
AI.method: The study combines a retrospective paired-video experiment with a prospective real-time clinical study, both using eye tracking. In the retrospective study, senior and novice endoscopists viewed colonoscopy clips with and without CADe, allowing paired comparisons at identical coordinates. In the prospective study, eye movements were recorded during actual CADe-assisted colonoscopies. Prompts appearing outside expert-annotated lesion windows were labeled as false-positive artifacts. The authors computed gaze attraction frequency, attention occupation duration (time gaze stayed in the prompted region), prompt duration on screen, and time amplification (attention duration divided by prompt duration). They also compared gaze patterns regarding real lesions with and without CADe, including first-gaze latency to lesion regions.
AI.result: False-positive prompts attracted gaze in nearly half of events in the retrospective setting (48.6%) and about two-thirds in real-time colonoscopies (65.2%). When prompts did attract gaze and the gaze later recovered, median attention occupation lasted about 1 second (1000–1100 ms), despite prompts themselves being visible only tens to hundreds of milliseconds (33 ms retrospectively, 267 ms prospectively). This resulted in substantial time amplification (17.55-fold and 5.15-fold). Retrospective paired analysis showed that visible artifact prompts pulled gaze closer to the prompted area compared with the same coordinates without CADe. Despite these distractions, lesion gaze recognition remained very high with and without CADe (98.0% vs 99.0%), and lesions were actually fixated earlier with CADe by about 148 ms.
AI.conclusion: False-positive CADe prompts reliably and frequently capture endoscopists’ visual attention, with gaze remaining on the prompted region far longer than the prompt is visible. Although overall lesion recognition remains high and lesion regions are fixated slightly earlier with CADe, the attentional burden from false positives is nontrivial. CADe system evaluation and interface design should explicitly consider the frequency, salience, and temporal characteristics of false-positive prompts to minimize unnecessary attentional occupation while preserving or enhancing lesion detection benefits.

title: Isolated Sign Language Recognition for Icelandic Sign Language: Experiments in a Low-resource Setting
summary: We present the first experiments on isolated sign language recognition (ISLR) for Icelandic Sign Language (ÍTM). We use ÍTM SignWiki, a dataset derived from a bilingual Icelandic--ÍTM online dictionary. It is genuinely low-resource: 1,845 videos cover 849 classes, 86% of which have only two examples, making the full task effectively one-shot recognition across signers. We compare two open-source ISLR frameworks, OpenHands and SPOTER, on three tasks of increasing vocabulary size (22, 117 and 849 classes), and evaluate three pose estimators and two forms of cross-lingual transfer. With ÍTM data alone, SPOTER outperforms OpenHands on all three tasks, and MediaPipe poses give better results than AlphaPose or SDPose. Cross-lingual transfer brings the largest gains: pretraining SPOTER on American Sign Language data before finetuning on ÍTM raises accuracy by 14--24 percentage points, to 72.7%, 47.9% and 22.6% on the three tasks, and multilingual training with data from six other sign languages lifts OpenHands from 1.41% to 28.86% on the full task. Although far from practical use, the results suggest that transfer from better-resourced sign languages is promising for very low-resource ones. We release our adapted versions of both frameworks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first isolated sign language recognition experiments for Icelandic Sign Language using a very low-resource dictionary-derived dataset, compares two ISLR frameworks and multiple pose estimators, and shows that cross-lingual transfer from larger sign language datasets substantially improves recognition accuracy.
AI.motivation: Icelandic Sign Language is extremely low-resource, with very limited annotated video data, which hinders the development of automatic recognition systems. The authors aim to establish baseline results for isolated sign language recognition on this language, understand how existing open-source frameworks behave in a genuinely low-resource setting, and investigate whether knowledge transfer from better-resourced sign languages can compensate for the data scarcity.
AI.method: The authors construct and use ÍTM SignWiki, a dataset derived from a bilingual Icelandic–ÍTM online dictionary, consisting of 1,845 videos over 849 sign classes with highly imbalanced class distribution. They evaluate two open-source ISLR frameworks (OpenHands and SPOTER) on three classification tasks with increasing vocabulary sizes (22, 117, and 849 classes). They systematically compare three pose estimators (MediaPipe, AlphaPose, SDPose) as inputs and explore two cross-lingual transfer strategies: (1) pretraining SPOTER on American Sign Language data followed by fine-tuning on ÍTM, and (2) multilingual training of OpenHands on data from six other sign languages.
AI.result: Without cross-lingual transfer, SPOTER consistently outperforms OpenHands on all vocabulary sizes, and MediaPipe-based pose representations yield better recognition accuracy than AlphaPose or SDPose. With cross-lingual transfer, performance improves markedly: pretraining SPOTER on American Sign Language and fine-tuning on ÍTM increases accuracy by 14–24 percentage points, achieving 72.7%, 47.9%, and 22.6% accuracy on the 22-, 117-, and 849-class tasks, respectively. Multilingual training of OpenHands with six additional sign languages boosts performance on the full 849-class task from 1.41% to 28.86%.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that in an extremely low-resource scenario like Icelandic Sign Language, existing ISLR frameworks can benefit substantially from cross-lingual transfer from better-resourced sign languages. While the current recognition accuracy—especially on the full 849-class task—is still insufficient for real-world deployment, the results validate transfer learning as a promising direction for supporting under-resourced sign languages. The release of adapted frameworks and the characterization of the ÍTM SignWiki dataset provide a foundation for future research on low-resource sign language recognition.

title: Transformer Heads Looking for Order
summary: In this note, we show that the problem of checking, whether a sequence of bits is ordered, is not doable by 1-head 1-layer transformers but is doable by a 2-head 1-layer transformer. Unlike similar previous results, our results assume the model where transformers have an output MLP.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the computational limits of very small transformer architectures on a simple bit-ordering task, showing 1-head 1-layer transformers with an output MLP cannot solve it, but 2-head 1-layer transformers can.
AI.motivation: To understand the expressive power and limitations of minimal transformer models by using a simple, well-defined formal language task (checking whether a bit string is ordered) and to refine prior results by considering settings where the transformer includes a standard output MLP.
AI.method: The authors use formal, probably automata-theoretic or linear-algebraic analysis of attention mechanisms in 1-layer transformers with 1 or 2 heads, explicitly modeling the effect of the output MLP, and prove impossibility for 1-head models and construct a 2-head model that correctly recognizes ordered bit sequences.
AI.result: They prove that no 1-head 1-layer transformer with an output MLP can decide whether an input bit sequence is ordered, while they give a concrete construction or proof of existence of a 2-head 1-layer transformer that can perform this task.
AI.conclusion: Including a standard output MLP does not make 1-head 1-layer transformers powerful enough for the bit-ordering problem, but adding just one more attention head suffices, highlighting how even a single additional head can strictly increase the computational expressivity of shallow transformers.

title: Rethinking Length-Based Training: Batch Composition and Loss Normalization in Speech Token Language Models
summary: Short-to-long training is a simple curriculum for speech models, but its gains can be difficult to interpret. In speech token language models, length-based training can change the shuffle policy, batch composition, token retention, and token weights under batch-mean loss. We disentangle these factors through matched comparisons. In the tested settings, short-to-long ordering shows no independent benefit when batch composition and token exposure are fixed. First-epoch grouping lowers perplexity for Mimi under batch-mean loss, but this gain is not observed under token-balanced loss. The cross-tokenizer results are consistent with a link between chunk-length variation and token weighting. This work provides a systematic analysis protocol for studying length-based training in variable-length speech models.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why short-to-long curriculum training for speech token language models sometimes helps, by teasing apart multiple intertwined factors.
AI.motivation: Short-to-long training is widely used in speech models, but its benefits are hard to interpret because it simultaneously alters data order, batch composition, token exposure, and token weighting. Practitioners lack a clear understanding of what, if anything, about length-based curricula actually improves model performance.
AI.method: The authors perform controlled, matched comparisons of training regimes, systematically isolating the effect of short-to-long ordering from confounding factors such as shuffle policy, how batches are composed by utterance length, how many times tokens are seen, and how tokens are weighted under different loss formulations (batch-mean vs token-balanced). They test these settings on a speech token language model (Mimi) and compare cross-tokenizer behaviors.
AI.result: They find that, when batch composition and token exposure are held constant, short-to-long ordering alone provides no performance benefit. Grouping examples by length in the first epoch improves perplexity for the Mimi model under batch-mean loss, but this effect disappears when using a token-balanced loss. Cross-tokenizer experiments show patterns consistent with the idea that variation in chunk length mainly affects how tokens are weighted during training.
AI.conclusion: Apparent gains from short-to-long curricula in speech token LMs are largely attributable to indirect effects on token weighting and batch composition rather than the ordering itself. The paper offers a systematic protocol for disentangling these components, enabling more interpretable studies of length-based training strategies in variable-length speech models.

title: Evaluating Coding Agents on Kernel Exploit Generation
summary: Coding agents now find real vulnerabilities in production software. However, bug discovery results do not measure whether agents can construct exploit primitives. We introduce KEX-bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on exploit primitive generation against real operating-system kernels. KEX-bench contains 45 task instances across 40 Linux and Windows CVEs, covering kernel address leak, instruction-pointer control, heap read, heap write, and arbitrary address write. Each task runs in an isolated virtual machine, exposes controlled tools, and uses a deterministic verifier to check primitive-specific success. We evaluate state-of-the-art coding agents paired with frontier and open-weight models under fixed tool-call budgets. Without a reference proof of concept (PoC), the strongest configuration solves 1 of 20 Windows tasks (5.0%) and 14 of 25 Linux tasks (56.0%). With a reference PoC, the strongest configuration solves 31 of 45 tasks (68.9%). This highlights the gap where agents reach kernel crashes but fail to shape kernel state into exploit primitives. We release KEX-bench for reproducible research on AI-assisted exploitation at https://kex-bench.github.io.

AI.tldr: KEX-bench is a benchmark to test whether coding agents can build real exploit primitives against Linux and Windows kernels, not just find bugs.
AI.motivation: Existing work shows coding agents can discover bugs in production software, but it is unclear if they can go further to construct concrete exploit primitives needed for real-world exploitation. There is a need for a standardized, reproducible way to evaluate agents on this harder task using real kernel vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors design KEX-bench, a benchmark of 45 tasks based on 40 real Linux and Windows kernel CVEs. Tasks cover key exploit primitives such as kernel address leak, instruction-pointer control, heap read/write, and arbitrary write. Each task runs in an isolated VM, has controlled tool access, and uses a deterministic verifier to automatically check whether the required exploit primitive is achieved. They then evaluate several state-of-the-art coding agents, with both frontier and open-weight models, under fixed tool-call budgets, with and without access to a reference proof-of-concept (PoC).
AI.result: Without providing a reference PoC, the best agent configuration solves only 1/20 Windows tasks (5.0%) and 14/25 Linux tasks (56.0%). When given a reference PoC, performance improves to 31/45 tasks solved (68.9%). This shows that current agents often manage to crash the kernel but rarely manage to reliably shape the kernel state into full exploit primitives, especially on Windows.
AI.conclusion: KEX-bench exposes a significant capability gap: current coding agents struggle to convert kernel vulnerabilities into robust exploit primitives, particularly on Windows kernels, even when they can find bugs or trigger crashes. Providing PoCs helps substantially but does not close the gap. The authors release KEX-bench as a publicly available benchmark to support reproducible research on AI-assisted exploitation and to drive future work on more capable and reliable exploit-construction agents.

title: Informed Masking: Structure-Aware Perturbation for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as an efficient alternative to autoregressive models, yet aligning them via Reinforcement Learning (RL) requires likelihood surrogates estimated from masked reconstruction subproblems under a small Monte Carlo budget per rollout. Existing methods construct these subproblems by uniform random masking, leaving open the question of which subproblems to prioritize. We identify a systematic upstream/downstream structure in dLLM rollouts. Some tokens, when revealed, trigger large confidence changes in nearby undecoded positions; we call them upstream. Others induce only small local changes and are therefore downstream. We find masking downstream tokens yields substantially better-posed subproblems than masking upstream tokens, a phenomenon we term subproblem difficulty asymmetry. Based on the observation, we propose Informed Masking (IM), which derives a per-token priority score from the denoising trajectory at zero extra inference cost and biases mask sampling toward downstream tokens. IM is plug-and-play: when plugged into three state-of-the-art dLLM RL methods on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, it delivers up to 2.01%, 8.68%, and 5.77% relative average gains on math and planning benchmarks with improved training stability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to better construct likelihood-estimation subproblems for RL training of diffusion LLMs, discovering that masking “downstream” tokens leads to easier and higher-quality subproblems than masking “upstream” tokens, and proposes an Informed Masking strategy that exploits this to improve RL performance and stability.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs are a promising and efficient alternative to autoregressive LLMs, but aligning them with RL requires estimating token likelihoods via masked reconstruction tasks under tight Monte Carlo budgets. Existing approaches use uniformly random masking to build these subproblems, which ignores structure in how tokens influence each other and may waste compute on poorly posed or low-informative subproblems. The authors aim to understand and exploit the internal structure of diffusion rollouts to construct better subproblems, thereby improving RL alignment efficiency and stability for dLLMs.
AI.method: The authors first analyze diffusion LLM rollouts and identify an upstream/downstream token structure: some tokens, when revealed, cause large confidence shifts in nearby undecoded positions (upstream), while others have only small local impact (downstream). They empirically compare subproblems formed by masking upstream vs downstream tokens and characterize their relative difficulty (subproblem difficulty asymmetry). Building on this, they design Informed Masking (IM), a plug-and-play scheme that uses information from the denoising trajectory to assign each token a priority score indicating how downstream it is, with no extra inference cost. During RL, IM biases masking toward higher-priority (downstream) tokens when constructing the masked reconstruction subproblems used as likelihood surrogates. They then integrate IM into three state-of-the-art RL methods for dLLMs on the LLaDA-8B-Instruct model and evaluate on math and planning benchmarks.
AI.result: The analysis reveals a clear upstream/downstream structure in dLLM rollouts, where masking downstream tokens leads to substantially better-conditioned and easier reconstruction subproblems than masking upstream tokens, demonstrating a subproblem difficulty asymmetry. When Informed Masking is applied as a drop-in replacement for uniform masking in three strong dLLM RL baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, it yields relative average performance improvements of up to 2.01%, 8.68%, and 5.77% on math and planning benchmarks. The method also improves training stability across these RL methods, all without incurring extra inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion LLM rollouts exhibit a systematic upstream/downstream token structure that significantly affects the quality of masked reconstruction subproblems used for likelihood estimation in RL. Masking downstream tokens produces better-posed subproblems than masking upstream tokens, leading to a subproblem difficulty asymmetry that prior uniform masking strategies fail to exploit. The proposed Informed Masking method leverages denoising-trajectory information to prioritize downstream tokens during masking, is easy to integrate into existing dLLM RL pipelines, and empirically improves both performance on math and planning tasks and training stability, all at zero additional inference cost. This suggests that structurally informed subproblem selection is an important lever for efficient RL alignment of diffusion LLMs.

title: ArticleMiner: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Scientific Publications
summary: Scientific papers keep much of their quantitative content in tables and supplementary files, where a number means something only through its header, caption, unit, analytical method, and the conventions of its field. Recovering the rows and columns of a table is therefore not the same as recovering the scientific fact it reports. Most semantic table-interpretation methods assume that a clean table is already available and subsequently map its cells or columns to ontology terms, whereas most publication-level extraction systems are designed for a single domain. We study a middle path: a shared process that reads a paper and its supplementary files, gathers evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module for each task supplies the domain meaning. The module lists the canonical names the graph may use, the surface forms that map to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and the bindings used to write RDF. It defines what a task is allowed to emit; it does not try to list every convention of a field. We build four such modules (for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry) in the ArticleMiner framework, and evaluate them on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth. In comparisons against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, the point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.

AI.tldr: ArticleMiner is a framework that combines generic document parsing, an LLM, and small domain-specific task modules to extract structured scientific facts (not just tables) from papers and supplementary files across multiple fields.
AI.motivation: Many scientific facts are encoded in complex tables and supplementary materials where numbers only gain meaning through context like headers, units, and domain conventions. Existing work either assumes clean tables and focuses on semantic labeling, or builds monolithic, domain-specific extractors. There is a need for a reusable, cross-domain extraction process that still respects domain-specific meaning without re-engineering everything per field.
AI.method: The authors design ArticleMiner, a shared extraction pipeline that processes full papers plus supplementary files, aggregating evidence from multiple table/figure parsers and a language model. On top of this shared layer, they define small human-authored task modules per domain. Each module specifies canonical entity/property names, surface-form mappings, simple derivation rules, validity constraints, identity keys, and RDF bindings. These modules constrain and interpret what the generic pipeline can emit, without enumerating all domain conventions. They implement four modules for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry.
AI.result: They apply ArticleMiner with the four domain modules to 163 papers, including a new mineral geochemistry benchmark with expert-annotated ground truth. When compared against a few-shot LLM baseline applied directly at the task level, ArticleMiner achieves better point-estimate performance on all four tasks, though confidence intervals overlap on the two smaller benchmarks. On the geochemistry benchmark, where ArticleMiner additionally uses supplementary files, it still outperforms the baseline, showing that gains are not solely from explicit domain guidance.
AI.conclusion: A modular architecture that separates a shared, cross-domain extraction engine from lightweight, human-authored domain task modules can successfully recover scientific facts from complex tables and supplementary materials. This approach generalizes across diverse domains and outperforms generic few-shot LLM prompting, supporting the idea that constrained, ontology-aware modules combined with multi-source document evidence are an effective middle ground between fully generic and fully bespoke extraction systems.

title: ClusterFewshot: Improving Few-shot Optimization for LLMs workflow
summary: The performance of large language model (LLM) workflows often depends on selecting a small set of in-context demonstrations to guide model behavior on new tasks. Recent methods improve this process by augmenting prompts with successful reasoning paths. However, their demonstration selection relies on random sampling or metric-based rankings, overlooking the semantic structure of the task. We propose ClusterFewshot, a strategy that combines semantic structuring with utility-aware scoring to construct representative and effective few-shot demonstration sets. Evaluated within DSPy-based pipelines, ClusterFewshot substantially reduces optimization cost across multiple benchmarks, while consistently improving accuracy relative to prior bootstrap-based methods in both standalone prompt tuning and hybrid prompt-weight optimization.

AI.tldr: ClusterFewshot is a method to pick in-context examples for LLMs by clustering semantically similar tasks and scoring examples by their utility, leading to cheaper and more accurate prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing few-shot selection methods for LLMs either sample randomly or rank demonstrations with coarse metrics, ignoring the underlying semantic structure and varying utility of reasoning traces, which can yield suboptimal guidance and high optimization costs.
AI.method: ClusterFewshot organizes candidate demonstrations into semantic clusters that reflect task structure and then applies a utility-aware scoring scheme within and across these clusters to choose a small, representative, and effective set of few-shot examples for prompting, implemented and tested in DSPy pipelines.
AI.result: Across several benchmarks and DSPy-based workflows, ClusterFewshot both lowers optimization cost and achieves higher accuracy than prior bootstrap-style approaches, in settings including pure prompt tuning and combined prompt-plus-weight optimization.
AI.conclusion: In-context demonstration sets built using semantic clustering plus utility-aware scoring provide better guidance for LLM workflows, making optimization more efficient and improving performance over existing bootstrap-based few-shot selection methods.

title: Reasoning-Preserving Fine-Tuning of Post-RL LLMs with Null-Basis LoRA
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training has become an effective approach for eliciting reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs). However, adapting post-RL models to new knowledge domains or behaviors through subsequent supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can severely overwrite these capabilities. Existing approaches mitigate such forgetting through experience replay, specialized initialization, or constrained optimization using gradient projection, but either provide limited preservation or incur substantial training overhead. Our analysis shows that reasoning activations concentrate in low-dimensional subspaces, leaving substantial null-space capacity for adaptation, and that the corresponding approximate null spaces can be reliably estimated from a modest number of examples. Motivated by these observations, we propose Null-Basis Low-Rank Adaptation (NB-LoRA), a parameter-efficient method for adapting post-RL LLMs while preserving their acquired reasoning ability. We formulate reasoning retention as a layer-wise hidden-state preservation constraint and construct a fixed approximate null basis from reasoning activations. LoRA updates are then reparameterized through this basis, enforcing the preservation constraint throughout fine-tuning. Extensive experiments across multiple RL-trained LLMs and diverse downstream tasks show that NB-LoRA matches standard LoRA in adaptation performance, maintains reasoning accuracy near pre-fine-tuning levels, and generalizes this preservation to held-out reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes NB-LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves RL-induced reasoning abilities in LLMs while adapting them to new tasks.
AI.motivation: RL-based post-training elicits strong reasoning in LLMs, but subsequent supervised fine-tuning for new domains or behaviors tends to overwrite and degrade these acquired reasoning skills. Existing mitigation strategies either fail to sufficiently preserve reasoning or incur large computational and implementation overhead. The authors observe that reasoning signals live in low-dimensional subspaces, suggesting there is unused representational capacity that could support new task adaptation without interfering with reasoning. This motivates a method that explicitly preserves reasoning-related activations during adaptation while staying parameter-efficient.
AI.method: The authors first analyze hidden activations of RL-trained LLMs and show that reasoning-related activations lie in low-dimensional subspaces, leaving a large approximate null space. They then estimate these null spaces from a modest number of reasoning examples and construct a fixed approximate null basis per layer. Building on LoRA, they introduce NB-LoRA, which reparameterizes LoRA updates through this null basis so that weight updates are constrained to the null space of reasoning activations, thus enforcing a layer-wise hidden-state preservation constraint. This ensures that the parts of the representation responsible for reasoning remain unchanged while the model adapts using the remaining capacity.
AI.result: Across several RL-trained LLMs and a variety of downstream tasks, NB-LoRA achieves adaptation performance comparable to standard LoRA while substantially better preserving reasoning abilities. Reasoning accuracy remains close to pre-fine-tuning levels, and the preserved reasoning generalizes even to unseen reasoning benchmarks. The method is shown to be both parameter-efficient and practical, as the null-space estimation requires only a modest number of reasoning examples.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning capabilities induced by RL in LLMs are encoded in low-dimensional activation subspaces, which can be protected during subsequent supervised fine-tuning. By constraining LoRA updates to an approximate null space of these reasoning activations, NB-LoRA enables effective domain or behavior adaptation without sacrificing RL-acquired reasoning. This offers a practical and efficient path to continually adapt RL-trained LLMs while maintaining their core reasoning skills.

title: Domain-Adaptive Pretraining Enhances Water Treatment Semantic Representation for Large-Scale Structured Literature Mining
summary: Water treatment research is expanding rapidly, but much of the knowledge acquired from this research remains scattered across unstructured literature. The field still lacks a dedicated language model that can efficiently capture water treatment-specific domain semantics for large-scale literature mining. Here, we address this by developing WaterBERT, a domain-adapted encoder model designed for semantic representation and structured information extraction from water treatment texts. WaterBERT was developed by continual pretraining on a large-scale water treatment corpus comprising about 2.97 billion tokens. Three fine-tuned models based on WaterBERT were systematically evaluated on downstream tasks, achieving the best overall performance among general-purpose and domain-specific BERT models, with F1 scores of 90.12% for multiclass treatment process classification, 79.50% for named entity recognition, and 74.04% for relation extraction. Beyond these benchmark tasks, we further demonstrated WaterBERT's advantages for large-scale literature processing. Applied to 5,144 Environmental Science & Technology articles, WaterBERT-BERTopic identified coherent, diverse, and domain-specific research topics without predefined categories. Building on WaterBERT, we processed 693,211 abstracts at substantially lower cost than commercial LLMs while retaining competitive extraction performance to construct a structured water treatment knowledge graph. The knowledge graph was then integrated with lexical and dense retrieval to develop a Water Knowledge-Enhanced Retrieval System (WaterKERS), which achieved a relevance score of 77.7, substantially outperforming text-based retrieval baselines (54.7-64.5). Through WaterBERT, this study provides a compact and scalable semantic foundation for large-scale information processing and evidence mapping in water treatment research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WaterBERT, a BERT-based language model specialized for water treatment literature, and shows it enables accurate classification, information extraction, topic modeling, and knowledge-graph-based retrieval at lower cost than general LLMs.
AI.motivation: Water treatment research generates a huge and fast-growing body of literature whose knowledge is scattered in unstructured text. Existing general or even domain-specific language models do not capture the fine-grained semantics of water treatment, limiting large-scale mining, structured knowledge extraction, and efficient retrieval. A compact, specialized model is needed to systematically extract and organize information from this domain.
AI.method: The authors continually pretrain a BERT encoder on a 2.97-billion-token corpus of water treatment texts to create WaterBERT. They then fine-tune it for three supervised downstream tasks: multiclass treatment process classification, named entity recognition, and relation extraction. They apply WaterBERT with BERTopic for unsupervised topic modeling on thousands of Environmental Science & Technology articles. Using WaterBERT-based extraction, they build a structured knowledge graph from 693,211 abstracts, and integrate this graph with lexical and dense retrieval into a Water Knowledge-Enhanced Retrieval System (WaterKERS).
AI.result: Fine-tuned WaterBERT models outperform both general-purpose and other domain-specific BERT variants on all evaluated tasks, reaching F1 scores of 90.12% (process classification), 79.50% (NER), and 74.04% (relation extraction). WaterBERT-BERTopic automatically discovers coherent, diverse, domain-specific topics without predefined labels from 5,144 articles. Using WaterBERT, the authors extract structured information from 693,211 abstracts at significantly lower computational and financial cost than commercial LLMs, while maintaining competitive extraction quality. WaterKERS, leveraging the resulting knowledge graph plus lexical and dense retrieval, attains a relevance score of 77.7, surpassing text-only baselines (54.7–64.5).
AI.conclusion: WaterBERT provides a compact, domain-adapted language model that effectively captures water treatment semantics, enabling high-performing classification and information extraction, scalable topic discovery, and construction of a large water treatment knowledge graph. When integrated into the WaterKERS system, it substantially improves retrieval relevance over traditional text-based methods, demonstrating a practical, scalable semantic infrastructure for evidence mapping and large-scale information processing in water treatment research.

title: ChatT2: An Adaptive Framework for Developing a Large Language Model-Based Agent for Natural Product Domain Research
summary: Scientific investigations into microbial natural products (NPs) present significant challenges for novices, largely due to the complexity of microbial systems, biochemical diversity, technical skill requirements, and the demands of bioinformatics and data analysis processes. To address these issues, we introduce ChatT2, a large language model (LLM)-based agent that is specifically tailored to the unique characteristics of bacterial type II polyketides. These polyketides form a structurally distinct and therapeutically important NP family. ChatT2 was developed within an autonomous multiagent framework composed of a mentor, an executor, and an evaluator, each with defined responsibilities. The mentor acts as an intermediary between ChatT2 and the user, utilizing chain-of-thought prompting to refine the intent of the user. Under the guidance of the mentor, the executor synthesizes multimodal information via retrieval-augmented generation techniques and seamlessly integrates bioinformatics and cheminformatics tools. The evaluator ultimately assesses the output of the executor to ensure the richness and accuracy of the retrieved information. Our research highlights how ChatT2, designed with this multiagent framework, addresses the challenges faced by general LLMs in terms of understanding limited, specialized corpora and complex biological information and provides both experts and novices with a valuable tool for exploring various NPs of interest. The ChatT2 webserver can be accessed at https://chatt2.site/#/chat.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ChatT2, an LLM-based multiagent system specialized for bacterial type II polyketides to help both novices and experts explore microbial natural products.
AI.motivation: Microbial natural product research, especially on bacterial type II polyketides, is difficult for newcomers because it requires mastery of complex biology, diverse chemistry, lab and computational skills, and advanced bioinformatics/data analysis. General-purpose LLMs struggle with specialized, limited-domain corpora and complex biological information, leaving a gap for domain-focused intelligent assistants that can guide users through this specialized landscape.
AI.method: The authors built ChatT2, a domain-specific LLM agent embedded in an autonomous multiagent framework with three roles: (1) a mentor that interfaces with users and uses chain-of-thought prompting to clarify and refine user intent; (2) an executor that performs retrieval-augmented generation, fusing multimodal information and orchestrating bioinformatics and cheminformatics tools; and (3) an evaluator that checks the executor’s output for completeness, richness, and accuracy. The system is specialized for bacterial type II polyketides and deployed as a webserver for interactive use.
AI.result: ChatT2 can effectively interpret queries about bacterial type II polyketides, integrate specialized databases and computational tools, and return accurate, rich, and context-relevant information. It overcomes limitations of general LLMs in handling narrow, complex biological domains and supports both expert and novice users in exploring natural products data and hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: A dedicated multiagent LLM system tailored to bacterial type II polyketides can substantially lower the entry barrier to microbial natural product research and improve information retrieval and reasoning in this domain. The authors show that combining domain specialization, retrieval-augmented generation, and explicit mentor–executor–evaluator roles yields a robust assistant for NP exploration, and make this capability available via the ChatT2 webserver.

title: Truth for Believable AI: Expressed Doubt, Provenance, and Belief Revision as an Engineerable Stance
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Companion framework paper: arXiv:2607.15883. Code, benchmark, cached model outputs, and result files archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21462986 (code and results) and doi:10.5281/zenodo.21462988 (benchmark dataset)
summary: Conversational agents often express answers in a uniformly confident register. We test whether expressed uncertainty, provenance-aware assertion, and explicit belief revision can be implemented as a behavior layer over a fixed language model; we do not test believability or trust. The layer combines three epistemic states, per-claim confidence and typed provenance, a provenance-gated expression rule, and a persistent revision store with auditable acknowledgments and partial resistance to false corrections. We evaluate it on a constructed, mechanically scored multi-session benchmark using a synthetic model and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. The synthetic instrument passes all five checks. On the real model, acknowledgment soundness, a by-construction guarantee, holds in 100% of cases, and true corrections are accepted more often than false ones (0.44 vs. 0.15 on held beliefs; 0.875 vs. 0.420 including rule-accepted corrections of unheld facts), but the pre-specified expression-fidelity, contradiction-separation, and provenance margins fail. A disclosed post hoc analysis shows that expression gated on mean answer-token probability ranks correctness below chance end to end (AUC 0.41, conversation-clustered), whereas gating on sampling consistency discriminates (AUC 0.66). A consistency-gated configuration selected from this finding and evaluated under a separately committed protocol meets the conversation-level manipulation and capability-equivalence criteria and replicates on a redrawn conversation set. The manipulation result is selection-dependent, and both criteria remain unresolved when uncertainty is clustered over the 60 facts. The supported conclusions are limited to the by-construction audit guarantee, store-dependent partial correction discrimination, and a benchmark- and model-specific failure of token-probability gating; scaling the fact base is required before human evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a behavior layer on top of a fixed language model to manage uncertainty, provenance, and belief updates, and tests it on a synthetic benchmark and a small real LLM.
AI.motivation: Most conversational agents speak in a uniformly confident tone, even when they are uncertain or wrong. This undermines transparency and safety. The authors want to see whether they can retrofit a structured notion of uncertainty, source tracking (provenance), and explicit belief revision onto an existing LLM without retraining it, and how reliably such a layer behaves across multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: They design a behavior layer with: (1) three epistemic states per factual claim; (2) a per-claim confidence score and typed provenance; (3) a provenance-gated rule that decides when the model should assert, hedge, or abstain; and (4) a persistent belief-revision store that tracks corrections, issues auditable acknowledgments, and is partially robust to false corrections. They construct a multi-session benchmark of 60 facts, generate programmatic conversations that include queries and corrections, and define five checks: acknowledgment soundness, expression fidelity, contradiction separation, provenance, and manipulation/capability-equivalence. They first test a synthetic “oracle-like” model, then Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. They analyze two uncertainty-gating strategies: one using mean answer-token probability and one using sampling consistency across draws; they perform post hoc AUC analyses and then preregister a consistency-gated configuration and re-evaluate it on fresh conversations.
AI.result: The synthetic model passes all five behavioral checks. With the real model, acknowledgment soundness holds in 100% of cases by design, and the system accepts true corrections more often than false ones (0.44 vs 0.15 on already-held beliefs; 0.875 vs 0.420 when counting rule-accepted corrections of unheld facts). However, the target quantitative margins for expression fidelity, contradiction separation, and provenance are not met. Post hoc, they find that gating assertions using mean token probability is anti-correlated with correctness (AUC 0.41), while gating on sampling consistency shows useful discrimination (AUC 0.66).
