A consistency-gated variant, chosen from this analysis and evaluated under a committed protocol, satisfies conversation-level manipulation and capability-equivalence criteria on a new conversation set and replicates the earlier finding, but these gains disappear when uncertainty is aggregated per fact instead of per conversation cluster.
AI.conclusion: The behavior layer can guarantee by-construction auditability of corrections and shows some ability to distinguish true from false corrections, but the intended high-fidelity uncertainty signaling and provenance behavior are not yet achieved on a real small LLM. Mean token-probability is a poor uncertainty gate in this setting, whereas sampling consistency helps, though in a selection- and aggregation-dependent way. The current claims are limited to this specific benchmark and model, and better scaling of the fact base is needed before running human evaluations or drawing stronger conclusions about trust or believability.

title: Ladders of Thought: A Self-Evolving Curriculum of Progressively Simplified Reasoning Traces
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning when scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but small- and mid-scale models remain brittle reasoners even with knowledge distillation (KD). We present Ladders-of-Thought (LoT), a framework that improves reasoning by combining progressive question rewrites with a self-evolving curriculum. LoT automatically generates semantically faithful but easier variants of reasoning problems, organizes them into difficulty buckets using step-based measures, and employs a self-evolving bandit scheduler to allocate training adaptively. Evaluated on two reasoning domains, math and multi-hop reasoning, across 1-8B models from different families, LoT consistently improves over KD. It delivers large gains on arithmetic tasks (e.g., +32 percentage points on AddSub, +25pp on SVAMP), +2-8pp improvements on in-domain test splits, and strong though dataset-dependent benefits on multi-hop reasoning (e.g., +16pp on QASC, +25pp on StrategyQA). LoT also converges faster than staged curricula, highlighting the value of adaptive progression. These results show that progressive rewrites coupled with adaptive curricula provide a simple yet effective recipe for strengthening reasoning in smaller LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ladders-of-Thought (LoT), a training framework that boosts reasoning of small/mid-size LLMs via progressive question rewrites and an adaptive curriculum, outperforming standard knowledge distillation on math and multi-hop reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: While very large LLMs can reason well, smaller (1–8B) models remain weak at reasoning even when trained with knowledge distillation from larger teachers. There is a need for a simple, scalable method that can reliably strengthen the reasoning abilities of these smaller models without requiring massive parameter counts.
AI.method: LoT (Ladders-of-Thought) automatically rewrites original reasoning problems into semantically equivalent but easier variants, forming a progression or "ladder" of difficulty. It measures difficulty via step-based metrics, groups problems into difficulty buckets, and then uses a self-evolving multi-armed bandit scheduler to adaptively decide which difficulty levels to train on over time. This creates an adaptive curriculum that gradually increases task difficulty while training smaller LLMs.
AI.result: Across math and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks and across 1–8B parameter models from multiple families, LoT yields consistent performance gains over knowledge distillation alone. It produces large improvements on arithmetic datasets (e.g., +32pp on AddSub, +25pp on SVAMP), moderate gains (+2–8pp) on in-domain test splits, and sizable, though more dataset-dependent, boosts on multi-hop reasoning tasks (e.g., +16pp on QASC, +25pp on StrategyQA). LoT also reaches strong performance faster than staged (manually designed) curricula.
AI.conclusion: Progressive question rewrites, combined with an adaptive, self-evolving curriculum, form an effective and relatively simple approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of smaller LLMs. LoT not only outperforms traditional knowledge distillation but also converges faster than staged curricula, suggesting that adaptive progression over automatically generated difficulty levels is a powerful recipe for strengthening reasoning in compact models.

title: Optimizing Denoising Trajectories in dLLMs: A Lightweight Evolutionary Heuristic Approach
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to conventional Auto-Regressive (AR) Large Language Models (LLMs). By leveraging bidirectional attention and parallel decoding, dLLMs enable more efficient generation. However, they require a carefully designed denoising scheduler at inference time (absent during training) whose choice significantly impacts generation quality. While confidence-based heuristic schedulers have shown strong empirical performance, they suffer from two critical failure modes: EOS Overflow and Proximal Bias. Through in-depth analysis of the Transformer's attention patterns, we reveal that these failures stem from certain positions assigning disproportionately high attention weights to invalid tokens (e.g., [MASK] and [EOS]), which produce misleading confidence signals. Building on this insight, empirical evidence shows that valid attention scores can provide complementary guidance to conventional confidence-based heuristics, yet no single metric consistently excels across all scenarios, implying that the optimal denoising trajectory is highly context-dependent. To address this problem, we propose a lightweight evolutionary heuristic scheduler optimized using the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). Our scheduler dynamically integrates multiple heuristic features with a contextual mean-field embedding, while requiring only 393 trainable parameters. Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across four reasoning and planning benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms strong baselines, including conventional heuristics, block auto-regressive methods, and recent State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) approaches. To the best of our knowledge, it represents the most parameter-efficient neural scheduler to date. Our code is available at https://github.com/RS2002/Evo-Denoise .

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes failure modes in diffusion LLM denoising schedules and introduces a tiny, learned evolutionary scheduler that adaptively combines multiple heuristics, improving reasoning/planning performance over strong baselines with only 393 parameters.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs can generate in parallel and use bidirectional attention, making them attractive alternatives to auto-regressive LLMs. However, their performance depends heavily on the choice of denoising schedule at inference time, which is not learned during training. Existing confidence-based heuristic schedulers work well empirically but suffer from EOS Overflow and Proximal Bias, limiting robustness and quality. There is a need for a more reliable, context-aware, yet lightweight scheduler that can generalize across tasks and models.
AI.method: The authors first analyze Transformer attention patterns in dLLMs to diagnose why confidence-based heuristics fail, finding that some positions place excessive attention on invalid tokens like [MASK] and [EOS], corrupting confidence signals. They then study alternative signals (valid attention scores) and show these are complementary to confidence metrics but no single metric works best universally, indicating strong context dependence. To exploit this, they design a small neural scheduler parametrized as a feature-combining module, and optimize its parameters with Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), an evolutionary black-box optimizer. The scheduler dynamically fuses multiple heuristic features with a contextual mean-field embedding to determine denoising decisions, while being extremely small (393 parameters).
AI.result: On the LLaDA and Dream dLLM systems and four reasoning/planning benchmarks, the proposed evolutionary heuristic scheduler consistently outperforms: (1) standard confidence-based heuristic schedulers, (2) block auto-regressive decoding variants, and (3) recent state-of-the-art dLLM scheduling methods. The gains are reported as consistent across tasks, showing better robustness to the previously identified failure modes, without increasing model size meaningfully due to the tiny 393-parameter scheduler.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that failures of common dLLM schedulers stem from distorted confidence signals caused by attention to invalid tokens, and that integrating attention-derived features with confidence metrics in a context-aware manner is crucial. A very small, CMA-ES-trained scheduler can effectively learn such integration, yielding the most parameter-efficient neural scheduler reported so far while improving performance across multiple benchmarks. This shows that learned, evolutionary-optimized scheduling is a practical and superior alternative to fixed heuristics for diffusion LLM denoising.

title: Testing-Driven Reliability Audit of Trajectory-Based Early Outcome Prediction for LLM Agents: Target-Specific Calibration Transfer Persists Within a Single Benchmark
summary: Predicting early outcomes based on trajectory can decrease the expenses associated with agent evaluation by terminating a run once the outcome becomes sufficiently predictable, assuming that the predictor's confidence is properly calibrated. Calibration is at risk when a predictor is applied to an agent on which it was never trained, but it is not known whether such transfer failures are broad across agent systems or concentrated in specific target agent/head combinations. Using public SWE-bench Verified trajectories and a frozen dual-head early-outcome prediction pipeline, we ran a leave-one-agent-out calibration audit, a shared-predictor leave-two-agents-out control, oracle prior correction, and a robustness battery over training cohorts, task resampling, task halves, jackknife, and thresholds. Fixed-scaffold TerminalBench analysis served as a pre-registered boundary test. Broad same-predictor pairwise heterogeneity was not supported; the median pairwise corrected-gap differences were 0.0180 (SUCCESS head, 45 pairs) and 0.0385 (FAILURE head, 35 pairs), and the pre-registered heterogeneity criterion was not met on either head. Two specific combinations, gpt-5-mini/SUCCESS and claude-opus-4.6/FAILURE, showed persistent calibration-transfer errors (median corrected gaps 0.1377 and 0.1107) without a sign reversal under any frozen control. TerminalBench did not establish cross-benchmark replication: the success target produced zero decisions (INDETERMINATE), and the failure target did not satisfy the pre-registered persistence criterion. Therefore, a strong target-specific calibration-transfer error can exist within one frozen environment, but the evidence does not establish that the error is intrinsic to the model or general across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how well early-outcome predictors calibrated on some agents transfer to unseen LLM-based agents in SWE-bench/TerminalBench, and finds mostly good transfer with a few strong, target-specific failures that don’t clearly generalize across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Early-outcome predictors can stop expensive LLM agent runs once success or failure is predictable, but only if their probability estimates remain well-calibrated when applied to new agents. Prior work has not clarified whether calibration failures during transfer are widespread across agents or confined to a few specific model–head combinations.
AI.method: Using SWE-bench Verified trajectories and a fixed dual-head (SUCCESS/FAILURE) prediction pipeline, the authors perform a leave-one-agent-out calibration audit, a shared-predictor leave-two-agents-out control, and an oracle prior correction. They also run robustness checks over different training cohorts, task resampling, task halves, jackknife analyses, and decision thresholds. Additionally, they use a fixed-scaffold TerminalBench analysis as a preregistered boundary test to probe cross-benchmark replication of any discovered errors.
AI.result: Across most agent–predictor pairs, pairwise heterogeneity in calibration gaps is small (median corrected-gap differences of 0.0180 for SUCCESS and 0.0385 for FAILURE), and the preregistered heterogeneity criteria are not met. However, two specific combinations—gpt-5-mini with the SUCCESS head and claude-opus-4.6 with the FAILURE head—show persistent, relatively large calibration-transfer errors (median corrected gaps 0.1377 and 0.1107) that remain under all frozen-control analyses. In TerminalBench, the success target yields only indeterminate decisions, and the failure target does not show the preregistered level of persistence, so cross-benchmark replication is not achieved.
AI.conclusion: Calibration-transfer errors for early-outcome predictors are generally modest across LLM agents within the studied environment, so broad, systematic transfer failure is not supported. Nonetheless, strong target-specific calibration failures can arise for certain agent–head combinations. Because these failures do not clearly replicate in TerminalBench, the evidence does not show that they are intrinsic properties of the underlying models or that they generalize across benchmarks; rather, they appear environment- and target-specific.

title: CoVeR: Coverage-Based Routing of Verifier Calls in Agentic Retrieval
summary: An agentic retrieval system issues a sequence of search queries and must decide, at each step, whether the evidence collected so far is enough to stop. Delegating that decision to an LLM verifier or a prompt judge makes stopping reliable, but the verifier then reprocesses the growing evidence after every retrieval step, a substantial repeated cost. We show that most of these calls can be skipped without materially changing answer accuracy: a single threshold on a frozen sentence-embedding coverage margin detects the states in which the evidence is still plainly incomplete, and the verifier is called only on the ambiguous remainder, a gate we call CoVeR (Coverage-based Verifier Routing). Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, with the evaluation protocol fixed before the full-scale run, the CoVeR-gated agent matches the answer accuracy of both the full-budget agent and the always-verify baseline within a fraction of an EM point. It cuts 62-68% of verifier calls, and 93% in a saturated regime. Routers built on evidence counts, lexical overlap, or BM25 relevance, alone or learned in combination, give weaker overall trade-offs, the gate transfers without re-tuning across deciders and agent scales, and its drafter distills into a 921k-parameter head atop the frozen encoder, leaving no LLM in the routing loop. The same signal cannot replace verification: matching a claim is far easier than deciding the claim is supported.

AI.tldr: Proposes CoVeR, a coverage-based routing gate that reduces expensive LLM verification calls in agentic retrieval systems while preserving answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Agentic retrieval systems repeatedly call an LLM verifier to decide when to stop issuing search queries. This makes stopping decisions reliable but is computationally expensive because the verifier reprocesses all accumulated evidence after every retrieval step. There is a need for a cheaper, principled way to skip most verifier calls without sacrificing answer accuracy.
AI.method: Introduce CoVeR (Coverage-based Verifier Routing), a routing gate built on a frozen sentence-embedding model. At each retrieval step, the system computes a coverage margin over the currently collected evidence. If the margin indicates that evidence is clearly incomplete, the system continues retrieving without calling the LLM verifier. Only when the margin is ambiguous does the system invoke the verifier. CoVeR uses a single threshold on this embedding-based coverage signal, transfers across agent scales and different deciders without re-tuning, and can be distilled into a small 921k-parameter head on top of the frozen encoder so that no LLM is needed in the routing loop. The authors compare CoVeR against routers based on simple evidence counts, lexical overlap, BM25, and their learned combinations.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks, with the evaluation protocol fixed in advance, CoVeR-gated agents achieve nearly the same exact-match answer accuracy as (1) full-budget agents and (2) agents that always call the verifier at every step, differing by less than one EM point. CoVeR reduces verifier calls by 62–68% in normal settings and by up to 93% in a saturated regime. Alternative routers based on counts, lexical overlap, BM25 relevance, or their learned combinations produce worse trade-offs between accuracy and verifier cost. The coverage signal generalizes across different verifier architectures and agent scales without re-tuning.
AI.conclusion: A simple threshold on a sentence-embedding coverage margin can effectively route when to call an expensive LLM verifier in multi-hop retrieval agents, substantially reducing computation while preserving answer accuracy. CoVeR shows that most verifier calls are unnecessary because states with obviously incomplete evidence can be filtered out cheaply; however, the same coverage signal cannot fully replace verification, as determining that claims are actually supported remains a harder task than merely detecting surface-level evidence coverage.

title: Seeing Is Not Perceiving: When Synthetic Consumers Can and Cannot Pretest Visual Marketing
comment: 58 pages (30 pages of main text, 23 pages of appendix), 18 figures, 25 tables. All six studies were preregistered on AsPredicted
summary: Marketers now deploy generative AI agents as synthetic consumers to pretest visual assets such as logos, packaging, and advertising at a fraction of human-panel cost. However, this procedure assumes that a model seeing a visual cue can also perceive its consumer meaning, which is largely untested. We stress-test the assumption using six canonical visual marketing experiments, varying the two levers managers control: model generation (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and input format (plain text vs. JSON). Every resulting configuration passed the manipulation checks; however, none of the configurations reproduced more than two of the six human effects, and the remainder were nonsignificant. The one exception was a significant reversal of the human pattern. Providing conceptual or empirical evidence through in-context learning steers average responses toward the human effect. Yet steering has a limit: even when it succeeds, a configuration reproduces less than half of the natural spread of human responses and so understates consumer heterogeneity. We integrate these results into an AI governance protocol (Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy) that delineates when synthetic consumers can responsibly screen creatives and when human panels remain necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether generative AI models can act as reliable “synthetic consumers” for visual marketing tests and finds they largely fail to replicate known human effects, even though they pass basic checks.
AI.motivation: Marketers want to use generative AI agents to cheaply pretest visual marketing assets (logos, packages, ads) instead of using expensive human panels. This practice assumes that AI models interpret visual cues similarly to human consumers, but this assumption has not been rigorously validated. The authors aim to stress-test that assumption before such tools are widely relied on for marketing decisions.
AI.method: The authors reproduce six classic visual marketing experiments using generative AI agents as participants. They systematically vary two controllable factors: (1) which model is used (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and (2) how stimuli and prompts are formatted (plain text vs. structured JSON). They check whether AI agents pass standard manipulation checks and whether they replicate the direction and magnitude of known human effects. They also test “steering” via in-context learning by supplying conceptual or empirical evidence about the expected human effect, and they propose an AI governance protocol based on the findings.
AI.result: All AI configurations (model × input format) passed manipulation checks, suggesting they understood the tasks at a superficial level. However, none of the configurations reproduced more than two of the six established human effects; most target effects became statistically nonsignificant when tested on the AI outputs. In one case, the AI even produced a significant effect in the opposite direction of human data. In-context steering nudged aggregate AI responses closer to the human pattern but still failed to match the magnitude and variability of real human responses, capturing less than half of observed consumer heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI agents, as currently deployed, are not dependable stand-ins for human consumers in visual marketing experiments. While they can be steered toward average human-like effects, they systematically underrepresent the diversity of consumer reactions and sometimes invert known patterns. The authors recommend a governance protocol—Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy—that specifies when AI-based synthetic consumers can be cautiously used for initial creative screening and when traditional human panels remain essential for valid, generalizable insights.

title: SpecialEduBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Language Intervention for Autistic Children
summary: Language is the target of most early intervention for autistic children. Because the goal and the method change from child to child, the work falls to a teacher who takes one child at a time and judges each scene as it unfolds. Artificial intelligence is now being brought to that work, yet the benchmarks that reach special education ask what a model knows rather than what it does in front of a child. Building one is not straightforward, since whether a response is good teaching depends on what the child has just done, so no answer key applies. The evidence that settles it is visual as much as verbal, since the length of a wait, a shift of gaze, and the child's uptake leave no trace in a transcript. We introduce \emph{SpecialEduBench}, which measures pedagogical competence along knowledge, skill, and attitude, with 4,537 knowledge items and with 200 skill items and 68 attitude items built on recorded intervention, the attitude items crossing pressure with monitoring into 192 response cells. Seven special-education experts wrote, scored, and reviewed the items, and we revised the judge model's instruction against the reference scores they set. Across eight frontier vision-language models no axis is saturated, since the strongest still fails about a tenth of the honesty cells. The models converge where the knowledge is factual and separate where the task is situated, and the failures gather where pressure is applied. We intend the benchmark as an audit to run before deployment and as a starting point for models built for this domain.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SpecialEduBench, a benchmark to evaluate AI models’ pedagogical competence in special education for autistic children, focusing on what models actually do in teaching scenarios rather than just what they know.
AI.motivation: Early intervention for autistic children is highly individualized and currently depends on human teachers making moment‑to‑moment judgments in interaction with a child. Existing AI benchmarks that influence special education focus mainly on static knowledge (what a model knows) rather than interactive teaching behavior (what a model does in front of a child). Because good teaching depends on context, timing, and nonverbal cues, traditional answer‑key style evaluations are inadequate. The authors are motivated to create a benchmark that can capture this richer notion of pedagogical competence and help assess AI systems before deployment in sensitive special‑education settings.
AI.method: The authors design SpecialEduBench, a benchmark structured around three dimensions of pedagogical competence: knowledge, skill, and attitude. They compile 4,537 knowledge items, plus 200 skill items and 68 attitude items derived from recorded intervention sessions with autistic children. Attitude items are organized by crossing external pressure conditions with monitoring requirements, generating 192 response cells that probe how models respond under different situational demands. Seven experienced special‑education experts author, score, and review all items, establishing reference scores. The authors then iteratively refine the instruction given to an automatic judge model to align it with expert scoring. Finally, they evaluate eight state‑of‑the‑art vision‑language models on the benchmark to analyze performance patterns.
AI.result: No evaluated model fully masters any of the benchmark’s axes (knowledge, skill, or attitude). Even the strongest vision‑language model still fails on roughly 10% of the “honesty”‑related attitude cells. Model performance tends to converge on items requiring factual knowledge but diverges on tasks that are situated in specific teaching contexts. Failures are especially concentrated in scenarios where the teacher model is placed under higher pressure, revealing limitations in robustness and pedagogical attitude under stress‑like conditions.
AI.conclusion: SpecialEduBench provides a structured way to audit AI systems’ pedagogical competence for special education, going beyond factual knowledge to include interactive skills and attitudes observable in real interventions. Current frontier vision‑language models are far from saturating the benchmark, particularly in situated and high‑pressure scenarios, indicating that substantial progress is needed before relying on such models in sensitive, high‑stakes educational interactions with autistic children. The authors propose the benchmark both as a pre‑deployment audit tool and as a foundation for developing models explicitly tailored to this domain.

title: Toolcompass: Guiding Tool Trialing, Not Suppressing It
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents must generalize from tools seen during training to unseen tools at deployment. A key challenge is tool trialing, i.e., excessive trials waste the interaction budget, whereas selective trials enable exploration of unfamiliar tools. Existing outcome-based post-training leaves wasteful trials unguided, while turn-level supervision may suppress necessary exploration. We introduce ToolCompass, a post-training framework that guides tool trialing by organizing tool-call representations according to shared functions. Specifically, ToolCompass models each function class as a von Mises--Fisher distribution and jointly reduces intra-function variation across domains and increases inter-function separation. This structure transfers experience from seen tools to functionally similar unseen tools, directing exploration away from unrelated alternatives. ToolCompass requires no ground-truth call traces or unseen-tool access and incurs no inference overhead. Experiments on AppWorld and FTRL show consistent gains across GRPO, RFT, and DMPO. improves AppWorld OOD task success by up to 10.71 percentage points over vanilla post-training and performs best among competitive baselines on both benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ToolCompass is a post-training framework that structures tool-call representations by shared function to guide when and what tools LLM agents should try, improving generalization to unseen tools without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: LLM agents must use external tools effectively, including tools not seen during training. A central difficulty is deciding how much to explore new tools: too many tool trials waste interaction budget, while too few hinder solving tasks with unfamiliar tools. Existing post-training methods either only use outcome-level signals, failing to shape trial behavior, or give fine-grained supervision that can overly penalize exploration. There is a need for a method that encourages selective, function-aware exploration of tools and transfers knowledge from known tools to unseen but functionally similar ones.
AI.method: The authors propose ToolCompass, a post-training framework that builds a structured representation space for tool calls. They group tools into function classes and model each function class as a von Mises–Fisher distribution on a hypersphere, learning embeddings such that tool calls with the same function are close together (low intra-function variance) and tool calls from different functions are separated (high inter-function separation). This is trained jointly across domains so that representations capture functional similarity rather than domain-specific details. The resulting structure lets the model infer how to trial unseen tools based on their functional similarity to known tools. ToolCompass is applied on top of existing post-training methods (GRPO, RFT, DMPO), requires no ground-truth step-by-step tool traces or special access to unseen tools during training, and does not add inference-time overhead.
AI.result: On the AppWorld and FTRL benchmarks, ToolCompass consistently improves LLM agent performance across multiple base post-training algorithms (GRPO, RFT, DMPO). In AppWorld out-of-distribution tasks, it improves task success rates by up to 10.71 percentage points compared to vanilla post-training without ToolCompass. It also outperforms other competitive baselines on both benchmarks, indicating that structuring tool-call representations by function more effectively guides tool exploration and use.
AI.conclusion: Structuring tool-call representations according to shared functional classes, as done in ToolCompass, provides a practical way to guide LLM agents’ tool exploration and generalization to unseen tools. By reducing within-function variance and increasing between-function separation using von Mises–Fisher modeling, the framework transfers experience from known tools to new but similar ones, steering exploration away from irrelevant options. This improves success rates across benchmarks and post-training methods without requiring detailed supervision, unseen-tool access during training, or extra inference-time computation, making ToolCompass a generally applicable enhancement to tool-using LLM agents.

title: One Domain, Many Tongues: Composing Domain and Language LoRAs for Cross-Lingual Remote-Sensing MLLMs without Paired Data
summary: Remote-sensing (RS) multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are trained and evaluated only in English, while text-only instruction data covers over 100 languages. We propose MODL (Mutually Orthogonal Domain-Language composition), a recipe that adds new languages to an English RS MLLM without a single multilingual RS example: a domain LoRA trained on English RS imagery and a language LoRA trained on text alone are learned jointly, under one loss term that keeps the two updates mutually orthogonal at every layer throughout training. This constraint is the recipe's active ingredient. Without it, the same training answers RS questions correctly but in English, erases much of the base model's multilingual text ability, and diverges on one seed in three; sixteen alternatives, from training-free merging to prior orthogonality variants, fail the same way. MODL repairs every failure on every seed: answers are correct and in the target language 56-71% of the time, where the best alternative reaches 27% and most stay below 8%, text ability stays at the level of the untrained base, and on Spanish it surpasses Qwen2.5-VL-7B, with zero multilingual-multimodal data. A single five-language adapter retains English, Spanish, and Vietnamese at full strength across three seeds; non-Latin scripts remain an open boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MODL, a method to add new languages to remote-sensing multimodal LLMs using only English RS images and multilingual text, enforcing mutually orthogonal domain and language LoRA updates to achieve strong multilingual RS performance without any multilingual RS data.
AI.motivation: Existing remote-sensing multimodal LLMs are limited to English training and evaluation, even though text-only instruction datasets exist in many languages. Collecting multilingual remote-sensing multimodal data is expensive and difficult. The authors want to unlock multilingual capabilities for RS models without relying on multilingual image-text pairs, and to understand why naive combinations of domain adaptation and multilingual adapters fail.
AI.method: They propose MODL (Mutually Orthogonal Domain-Language composition). It uses two LoRA adapters on top of an English RS MLLM: a domain LoRA trained on English RS imagery and a language LoRA trained on text-only multilingual data. During joint training, they impose a loss term that enforces the parameter updates of the domain and language LoRAs to be mutually orthogonal at every layer, preventing interference between domain and language learning. They compare MODL with 16 alternative strategies, including training-free merging and prior orthogonality-based variants, and analyze stability across different random seeds.
AI.result: Without the orthogonality constraint, joint training tends to produce models that answer correctly but only in English, significantly degrade the base model's multilingual text ability, and even diverge (training instability) in about one-third of seeds. All 16 alternative methods show similar failures. MODL, with the mutual orthogonality constraint, yields models that answer RS questions both correctly and in the target language 56–71% of the time, whereas the best alternative achieves only 27% and most are below 8%. The base model's multilingual text ability is preserved, and for Spanish the resulting model surpasses Qwen2.5-VL-7B despite using zero multilingual multimodal (RS) data. A unified adapter supporting five languages maintains English, Spanish, and Vietnamese performance across three seeds, though performance with non-Latin scripts is still limited.
AI.conclusion: Mutually orthogonal composition of domain and language LoRA adapters is key to successfully adding new languages to RS multimodal LLMs without multilingual RS training data. The orthogonality constraint avoids catastrophic interference between domain and language adaptation, enabling stable training, preserving original multilingual text abilities, and delivering strong target-language performance that can surpass larger baseline models. The approach scales to multiple languages within a single adapter but still struggles with non-Latin scripts, pointing to an area for future work.

title: How Strongly Should Task State Influence an LLM Agent?
summary: Long-horizon assigned work requires an LLM agent to track the state of a task: which steps are done, blocked, cancelled, or open to repetition. Agent systems either keep this state as text in the prompt and rely on the model to read that text, or move the state into a module that enforces it, and each system is evaluated as a whole, so no one knows how much reliability comes from the state being shown, told, or enforced. We fix the task rules, the model, and paired episodes and vary how strongly task state reaches the agent: a raw transcript, an exact checklist, per-turn directives from a state machine compiled from the brief and advanced only by execution receipts, or an enforcement gate on that machine that refuses state-violating actions; every episode is scored by exact payload matching against dynamic ground truth. Across three models, two reasoning regimes, and two domains, four findings hold without per-turn reasoning: displaying accurate state is unreliable, an unverified ledger the agent writes itself beats an accurate checklist it is shown, directives help in proportion to the model's obedience, and enforcement needs no obedience but is bounded by the correctness of its state and by the matcher that maps requests to steps; per-turn reasoning at a 235B agent compresses these separations without repairing the text rungs. The same gate, compiled from $τ^2$-bench's airline policy, raises a 235B agent's pass$^1$ from 0.39 to 0.54 and changes nothing for a 35B agent that rarely violates the policy; on PM-Bench, where acting turns on recognizing a cue rather than on state, showing the record is the best rung--matching or beating both gates and reversing the ledger-over-checklist finding--and enforcing the matcher's judgement drops a 35B agent below its raw transcript. Enforcement pays when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong.

AI.tldr: Study of how different ways of representing and enforcing task state affect LLM agents on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents doing long-horizon, multi-step work must reliably track and respect task state (done/blocked/cancelled/repeatable steps). Current systems mix together textual state descriptions and external enforcement modules, so it is unclear what portion of reliability comes from simply showing state to the model vs. constraining it via a state machine or gate. The paper aims to disentangle these contributions under controlled conditions.
AI.method: Hold constant: tasks, rules, model, and paired episodes. Vary only the strength/form of task-state access: (1) raw transcript, (2) explicit checklist shown to the agent, (3) per-turn directives produced from a compiled state machine advanced only by verified execution receipts, and (4) an enforcement gate over that same state machine that blocks state-violating actions. Evaluate across three models, two reasoning setups, and two domains. Score each episode by exact payload matching against a dynamic ground truth of correct behavior. Compare also with an agent-maintained but unverified state ledger. Analyze performance with and without per-turn chain-of-thought reasoning.
AI.result: Without per-turn reasoning, four robust findings across models/domains: (a) Merely displaying accurate state is unreliable; the model often fails to use it. (b) An unverified state ledger written by the agent itself can outperform an accurate checklist it is only shown. (c) Per-turn directives from a state machine help in proportion to the model's tendency to obey instructions. (d) Hard enforcement via a gate does not require such obedience but is limited by the correctness of the state machine and the request-to-step matcher. With per-turn reasoning at 235B scale, the performance gaps between rungs narrow, but text-only representations (transcript/checklist) still lag. On τ^2-bench airline-policy tasks, adding the enforcement gate boosts a 235B model's pass@1 from 0.39 to 0.54, while a 35B model that rarely violates policy sees no benefit. On PM-Bench, where the challenge is cue recognition rather than state tracking, merely showing the interaction record performs best, sometimes beating both the gate and other structured methods; enforcing the matcher here can even harm performance, dropping a 35B model below its raw-transcript baseline.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of state handling in LLM agents strongly depends on how state is surfaced and enforced. Textual display of correct state is not sufficient for reliability. Letting the agent maintain its own ledger can outperform static checklists, while structured directives help only insofar as the model follows them. Hard enforcement via state machines is powerful when task success hinges on state-decidable and commonly violated constraints but can degrade performance when the gate or matcher is wrong or when tasks depend more on recognition than on state. Designers should selectively apply enforcement mechanisms where state-based failures are prevalent and avoid over-enforcing where model judgement on cues is critical.

title: TSS: Target-Side Sparsification for Speculative Decoding in Domain-Specific Large Language Models
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through collaboration between a lightweight draft model and a target verifier. Existing methods mainly improve the draft side, while the target model is typically kept dense and unchanged. We show that, under domain-specific inference, full-depth target verification is not always the optimal choice. Counter-intuitively, skipping selected target layers can reduce verification cost while simultaneously increasing draft acceptance and preserving, or even improving, downstream task performance. Based on this observation, we propose TSS, a target-side sparsification framework for speculative decoding. TSS employs an acceptance- and metric-aware breadth search to explore multi-layer skip configurations without imposing a fixed priority between the two objectives. The selected configurations are stored in a domain-to-configuration mapping and applied by a lightweight skip controller, allowing one complete target model to support multiple sparse verification paths without retraining or permanent parameter pruning. Experiments on Spec-Bench across multiple domains, model scales, and speculative decoding methods show consistent improvements in draft acceptance and downstream task performance. In Translation setting, TSS increases the average accept length from 2.70 to 4.53 (+67.8%), improves BLEU from 0.131 to 0.237 (+80.9%), and raises end-to-end throughput from 75.6 to 127.3 tokens/s, corresponding to a 1.68X speedup.

AI.tldr: They propose TSS, a framework that speeds up speculative decoding by sparsifying (skipping layers in) the target model during verification, improving both speed and accuracy on domain-specific tasks.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding uses a small draft model and a large target model: the draft proposes tokens, and the target verifies them. Prior work mainly optimizes the draft model, keeping the large target dense and fixed. Under domain-specific inference, fully running every layer of the large target model for every verification step may be unnecessary and suboptimal in terms of speed–accuracy tradeoff. The authors aim to reduce verification cost while maintaining or even improving task performance, especially in domain-specific scenarios.
AI.method: They introduce TSS (Target-Side Sparsification), which selectively skips layers in the target model during speculative decoding. TSS performs an acceptance- and metric-aware breadth search over multi-layer skip patterns, jointly optimizing two objectives: (1) draft acceptance behavior (e.g., accepted token length) and (2) downstream performance metrics (e.g., BLEU). The search does not hard-code a fixed priority between these objectives. Discovered layer-skip configurations are associated with domains in a domain-to-configuration mapping. At inference time, a lightweight skip controller chooses the appropriate sparse verification path for the given domain, allowing a single full target model to offer multiple sparse paths without retraining or permanently pruning parameters.
AI.result: Across Spec-Bench, covering multiple domains, model sizes, and speculative decoding algorithms, TSS consistently yields higher draft acceptance rates and better downstream performance. In a translation setting, TSS increases average accepted length from 2.70 to 4.53 tokens (+67.8%), improves BLEU from 0.131 to 0.237 (+80.9%), and boosts overall throughput from 75.6 to 127.3 tokens/s, corresponding to a 1.68x speedup.
AI.conclusion: Full-depth verification in speculative decoding is not always optimal for domain-specific inference. By learning domain-specific layer-skip patterns on the target model, TSS can reduce verification cost, improve draft acceptance, and even enhance downstream task quality, all without retraining or permanently pruning the target model. This demonstrates that target-side sparsification is a powerful and general complement to existing draft-side optimizations for accelerating large language model inference.

title: TCMaster: Confidence-Aware Querying and Workload-Guided Physical Design for Multi-Source Traditional Chinese Medicine Knowledge Graphs
summary: Multi-source knowledge graphs (KGs) need query mechanisms that expose reliability and exploit domain structure. This paper presents TCMaster, a property-graph query substrate for confidence-aware traversal and workload-guided physical design over Traditional Chinese Medicine KGs. TCMaster integrates pharmacopoeias, prescriptions, molecular databases, and LLM-extracted micro-semantics into a KG with approximately 221K entities and 723K base edges. It annotates edges with provenance-level confidence, rewrites Cypher queries with confidence predicates, ranks multi-hop paths under PRODUCT, MIN, or weighted-average policies, and uses ontology skew through direction selection, herb-attribute bitmaps, and materialized shortcut edges. On Neo4j, direction selection improves attribute lookup by a factor of 1.47, shortcuts accelerate high-fanout target counting by a factor of 4.42, confidence filtering removes 39.3 percent of low-quality heterogeneous paths, and KG retrieval improves TCMbench QA accuracy by 20.0 percentage points.

AI.tldr: TCMaster is a confidence-aware query and optimization framework for multi-source Traditional Chinese Medicine knowledge graphs, improving both query efficiency and QA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-source knowledge graphs in Traditional Chinese Medicine combine heterogeneous data (pharmacopoeias, prescriptions, molecular data, LLM outputs) with varying quality and complex structure. Existing query systems lack mechanisms to represent and exploit reliability information and domain-specific structural skew, which is important for clinical and research use-cases that depend on trustworthy and efficient graph queries.
AI.method: The authors build TCMaster, a property-graph substrate on Neo4j. They integrate multiple TCM data sources into a unified KG and annotate edges with provenance-level confidence scores. They extend Cypher with confidence predicates and implement path ranking policies (PRODUCT, MIN, weighted average) for multi-hop traversal. For physical optimization, they exploit ontology skew via direction selection for traversals, herb-attribute bitmaps for fast filtering, and materialized shortcut edges for high-fanout regions. They then benchmark performance and downstream QA impact (TCMbench).
AI.result: TCMaster’s physical optimizations yield substantial speedups on Neo4j: direction selection improves attribute lookups by 1.47x; shortcut edges accelerate high-fanout target counting by 4.42x. Confidence-aware querying filters out 39.3% of low-quality heterogeneous paths. When used as a retrieval component for TCMbench question answering, the KG-based retrieval improves QA accuracy by 20 percentage points compared to a baseline without these mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Encoding provenance-level confidence and exploiting domain-specific structural skew in a TCM knowledge graph can simultaneously improve query efficiency, path quality, and downstream QA performance. TCMaster demonstrates that confidence-aware traversal and workload-guided physical design are practical and beneficial for large, heterogeneous biomedical KGs, particularly in Traditional Chinese Medicine contexts.

title: Differentiable Fuzzy Inference Layer: A Monotone, Compositional Ordinal Reasoning Head for Large Language Models
summary: A state-of-the-art language model asked to interpret "most of most students passed" typically answers "most," though composing two instances of "most" yields a proportion closer to "some." We trace this failure to an architectural choice rather than a data deficit: standard classifier heads treat ordinal categories as independent labels, with no mechanism to respect their natural ordering or compose them algebraically. We introduce the Differentiable Fuzzy Inference Layer (DFIL), a dual-path prediction head pairing a standard classifier with a scalar-bottlenecked branch grounded in a bank of ordered membership functions. DFIL supplies two structural primitives that a label-only head cannot inherit: monotonicity in the underlying quantity, and compositional reasoning via t-norm operations without any compositional training data. The scalar branch additionally provides an interpretable interface for analyzing residual errors. We instantiate DFIL on ordinal natural-language tasks across diverse LLM families.

AI.tldr: They propose DFIL, a new prediction head for language models that handles ordered labels and enables better compositional reasoning about quantities like "most" and "some."
AI.motivation: Standard classifier heads in LLMs treat ordinal labels (e.g., none, some, most, all) as independent, so models misinterpret compositions like "most of most" and can't respect natural order or compose these labels algebraically. The authors want an architecture that encodes ordinal structure and supports compositional reasoning without needing special training data.
AI.method: They design the Differentiable Fuzzy Inference Layer (DFIL), a dual-path prediction head: one branch is a normal classifier over discrete labels; the other forces predictions through a scalar bottleneck connected to a set of ordered membership functions (fuzzy sets). DFIL enforces monotonicity with respect to the underlying quantity and uses t-norms to compose these fuzzy memberships, enabling algebraic composition. The scalar branch also yields an interpretable scalar representation of the model’s belief about the quantity.
AI.result: Pluggable DFIL heads are instantiated on various ordinal NLP tasks and across different LLM architectures. The resulting models better handle compositional quantification phenomena like "most of most" and show improved alignment with the ordinal structure of labels, while preserving or improving task performance. The scalar path allows inspection of where and how the model still errs.
AI.conclusion: Misinterpretations of nested quantifiers by LLMs are largely due to the classifier head architecture rather than missing data. By adding DFIL, models gain built-in monotonicity and compositional reasoning over ordered labels, improving performance on ordinal language tasks and offering a more interpretable interface for understanding errors.

title: LingLan: An Advancing Traditional Chinese Medicine Diagnosis LLM with Multimodal Data
summary: Though artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly transforms modern medicine, its integration into Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) has been relatively slow, primarily due to TCM's reliance on holistic, subjective diagnostic methods---namely Inspection, Auscultation and Olfaction, Inquiry, and Palpation(I-AOI-P)---which are difficult to align with quantitative, standardized medical systems. In this work, we introduce a Unification Framework for Multimodal Data (UFMD), which automatically processes tongue and pulse images into structured, clinically standard descriptions, integrating multi-source diagnostic information into a unified digital record of I-AOI-P process. Building on this structured data, we create LingLan-14B, a TCM-specific large language model fine-tuned via supervised learning to emulate the diagnostic logic and workflow of I-AOI-P process. Experimental results show that our method significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, achieving a relative improvement of 103.5% over the baseline (62.72% vs. 30.82%) and reaching an F1-score of up to 82%.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a framework that converts multimodal TCM diagnostic data (like tongue and pulse images) into structured descriptions and uses this to fine-tune a TCM-specific large language model, greatly improving automated diagnosis accuracy.
AI.motivation: AI has advanced many areas of modern medicine but has had limited success in Traditional Chinese Medicine because TCM diagnosis relies on holistic, subjective methods (Inspection, Auscultation and Olfaction, Inquiry, Palpation) that are hard to quantify and standardize. The authors want to bridge this gap so AI can meaningfully support and emulate TCM diagnostic practice.
AI.method: They propose a Unification Framework for Multimodal Data (UFMD) that automatically converts tongue and pulse images into structured, clinically standard descriptions, integrating them into a unified digital representation of the full I-AOI-P diagnostic process. Using this structured, multi-source dataset, they fine-tune a 14-billion-parameter TCM-specific large language model, LingLan-14B, with supervised learning to replicate TCM diagnostic reasoning and workflow.
AI.result: The system substantially improves diagnostic performance relative to a baseline model: diagnostic accuracy rises from 30.82% to 62.72% (a 103.5% relative improvement), and the best F1-score reaches 82%, showing that the unified multimodal framework plus the specialized LLM effectively captures TCM diagnostic patterns.
AI.conclusion: By standardizing and integrating multimodal TCM diagnostic data and training a domain-specific large language model on this unified representation, the authors demonstrate that AI can successfully emulate TCM’s I-AOI-P diagnostic logic and markedly enhance automated diagnosis accuracy, suggesting a viable path for deeper AI integration into TCM practice.

title: Magnitude Profile Pruning: Calibration-Free Structured Attention Head Removal for Transformer Compression
comment: Accepted as a regular paper at IEEE ICMLA 2026; to appear in the conference proceedings
summary: Structured pruning of attention heads provides a hardware-friendly way to compress Transformer language models. However, existing methods for measuring head-level importance require calibration data, gradient computation, or Hessian estimation. These requirements add extra overhead and make the methods depend on the data. Our work presents Magnitude Profile (MP) scoring, a training-free criterion for head importance that identifies dispensable heads through statistical outlier detection on weight row norms. Heads whose projection weights fall within the population bulk are pruned, while heads exhibiting outlier norms, which carry disproportionate representational capacity, are preserved. Our work further gives MP-G, a variant that handles Grouped Query Attention (GQA) by distributing shared key-value group scores across associated query heads. Across five models evaluated on WikiText-2 perplexity at 12.5%-50% head sparsity, MP-G achieves the best perplexity on OPT-6.7B at all sparsity levels (18.46 at 12.5%, 27.87 at 25%, 152.0 at 50%). MP-G also gives the best results on RoBERTa-large at 12.5% and 25% sparsity, with perplexity values of 7.27 and 10.28, outperforming calibration-dependent baselines including Wanda-Head, SparseGPT-Head, and Gradient-Head. It requires zero forward passes, calibration samples, or gradient computation. At 50% sparsity, head pruning yields up to 16% parameter reduction with 50% attention FLOP savings. Our results show that weight-only statistical scoring can match or outperform data-dependent methods for structured head pruning, providing a practical, zero-cost criterion for Transformer compression.

AI.tldr: They propose a zero-cost, training-free method to prune Transformer attention heads using only weight statistics, matching or beating data-dependent baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing structured head pruning methods for Transformers need calibration data, gradients, or Hessian estimates, which introduces computational overhead and makes pruning decisions data-dependent. There is a need for a simple, hardware-friendly, and data-free criterion that can effectively identify unimportant attention heads to compress large language models without extra computation.
AI.method: They introduce Magnitude Profile (MP) scoring, which analyzes the row-norm statistics of attention projection weight matrices. Using statistical outlier detection, they identify heads whose weight row norms lie in the bulk of the population distribution as unimportant and prune them, while preserving heads whose norms are outliers and thus presumed to carry greater representational capacity. They also propose MP-G, an extension for Grouped Query Attention (GQA), which computes scores at the shared key-value group level and distributes those scores across associated query heads. The method is entirely training-free and requires no forward passes, gradients, or calibration samples—only the existing model weights.
AI.result: On WikiText-2 perplexity benchmarks with 12.5%–50% head sparsity, MP-G achieves the best perplexity among compared methods on OPT-6.7B across all sparsity levels (e.g., 18.46 at 12.5%, 27.87 at 25%, and 152.0 at 50% sparsity). On RoBERTa-large, MP-G also yields the best perplexity at 12.5% and 25% sparsity, with values of 7.27 and 10.28, respectively, outperforming calibration-based baselines such as Wanda-Head, SparseGPT-Head, and Gradient-Head. The approach delivers up to 16% parameter reduction and 50% attention FLOP savings at 50% head sparsity.
AI.conclusion: Simple, weight-only statistical scoring of attention heads via Magnitude Profiles can match or outperform more complex, data-dependent head pruning methods. MP and its GQA-compatible variant MP-G provide a practical, zero-cost, and hardware-friendly criterion for structured head pruning, enabling efficient Transformer compression without calibration data or additional training/optimization steps.

title: OmniFysics-Nano-V2 Technical Report: Understanding the Physical World Across Modalities
summary: Omni-modal models have expanded multimodal interaction across vision, audio, speech, and language. However, their training is predominantly organized around semantic descriptions and general-purpose objectives, leaving physical attributes, interaction states, and causal mechanisms only partially specified. This gap is not simply a matter of modality coverage: adding more modalities does not by itself provide the supervision needed to connect observations with the physical structure of the world. We present OmniFysics-Nano-V2, a compact omni-modal model for physical-world perception and understanding. The model supports image, video, audio, speech, and text inputs within a shared reasoning framework, together with text and speech generation. To address the lack of explicit physical supervision, we construct a dual-branch physics-aware data pipeline that grounds salient objects in structured physical attributes and aligns visual changes with acoustic events, intermediate responses, and interaction outcomes. To address homogeneous training objectives, we curate reinforcement-learning prompts by reward diversity and adopt a two-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization curriculum that progresses from general task correctness to fine-grained physical perceptual reasoning. Experiments across multimodal, audio-visual, and physical reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed data and training strategy improves physical-world understanding while preserving broad omni-modal competence. The proposed model achieves leading result on 17 of 21 benchmarks against SOTA omni-modal models. By equipping AI systems with both omni-modal and physical-world perception capabilities, OmniFysics-Nano-V2 is poised to become a cornerstone of next-generation Physical AI.

AI.tldr: OmniFysics-Nano-V2 is a compact omni-modal model that extends standard multimodal AI with explicit physical-world understanding through specialized data and a tailored RL training curriculum, achieving SOTA on many benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing omni-modal models (vision, audio, speech, language) mainly learn semantic descriptions and general-purpose tasks, but they poorly capture physical attributes, interaction states, and causal mechanisms. Simply adding more modalities does not create the required supervision to tie observations to the physical structure of the world. The authors want to build AI systems that understand and reason about the physical world, not just describe it.
AI.method: They design OmniFysics-Nano-V2, an omni-modal model that processes image, video, audio, speech, and text in a unified reasoning framework, with both text and speech generation. To inject physical knowledge, they build a dual-branch, physics-aware data pipeline: one branch grounds salient objects with structured physical attributes, and the other aligns visual changes with acoustic events, intermediate responses, and interaction outcomes. For training, they move beyond homogeneous objectives by curating RL-style prompts that vary in rewards and by adopting a two-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization curriculum: first focusing on general task correctness, then on detailed physical perceptual reasoning.
AI.result: On multimodal, audio-visual, and physical reasoning benchmarks, the model trained with the proposed data pipeline and RL curriculum shows improved physical-world understanding while maintaining strong general omni-modal abilities. It achieves leading performance on 17 out of 21 benchmarks compared with state-of-the-art omni-modal models.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating physics-aware supervision and a staged RL-based training scheme allows an omni-modal model to gain stronger physical-world perception and reasoning without sacrificing its broad multimodal competence. OmniFysics-Nano-V2 therefore represents a promising foundation for next-generation "Physical AI" systems that can both perceive and reason about the physical environment across modalities.

title: Modality-Gated Deep Adapters: Adding a Modality to a Frozen Embedding Model with Exact Preservation
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Models: https://huggingface.co/EximiusLabs/fusion-embedding-2-2b-preview and https://huggingface.co/EximiusLabs/fusion-embedding-2-ember. Code: https://github.com/Eximius-Labs/fusion-embedding
summary: Multimodal embedding models are deployed at scale: retrieval indices, benchmark results, and behavioral audits all depend on the base model's exact outputs. Extending such a model to a new modality with existing parameter-efficient methods silently changes those outputs; LoRA-style adaptation rewrites the text path whether or not the weights are merged, invalidating every stored embedding. We propose modality-gated deep adapters: bottleneck adapters attached to every decoder layer of a frozen multimodal embedding LLM, grouped into per-modality packs that execute only while their own modality is being encoded. The result is a modality added with zero change to existing outputs: inputs no pack claims traverse the base model's own computation graph, bit-for-bit unchanged, and co-loaded packs compose with an exact-zero isolation matrix. Both properties are stated as propositions, hold after arbitrary training rather than only at initialization, require no task labels or routing metadata at inference, and are verified by exact-equality tests on the released checkpoints. On one frozen 2B base, the audio pack (injected as connector tokens) improves audio-to-text R@10 by +3.4 to +5.4 points over an identically trained control, positive at every seed and reproduced at eleven times the data; the thermal pack, reusing the base's own frozen vision path, clears its pre-registered acceptance gate roughly sevenfold at every seed and lifts thermal-to-text R@10 from 0.224 to 0.785. An encoder swap locates the missing capacity: an external audio encoder that outranks Whisper-family encoders in CLAP-style comparisons loses by 16 R@10 points inside the frozen LLM, so the capacity belongs in the layers, exactly where the gated adapters place it. We release the audio model, the thermal pack, and the training, evaluation and invariance suites: models at huggingface.co/EximiusLabs, code on GitHub.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces modality-gated deep adapters that let you add new modalities to a frozen multimodal embedding LLM without changing any existing embeddings, achieving strict output invariance while gaining capacity for new modalities like audio and thermal.
AI.motivation: In large-scale multimodal embedding systems, existing indices, benchmarks, and audits critically depend on the exact numerical outputs of a base model. Standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA alter the text path even if not merged, invalidating all previously stored embeddings and breaking backward compatibility. The authors want a way to extend a deployed model with new modalities while guaranteeing that existing behaviors and embeddings remain bitwise unchanged.
AI.method: They attach bottleneck adapters (deep adapters) to every decoder layer of a frozen multimodal embedding LLM. These adapters are grouped into modality-specific packs, and a gating mechanism ensures that only the pack corresponding to the currently processed modality is active. Inputs that no pack claims pass solely through the original frozen computation graph, and when multiple packs are loaded together, their effect composes through a designed exact-zero isolation matrix. The system is trained so that these properties hold after training, enabling strict invariance without task labels or routing metadata at inference. They validate invariance with exact-equality tests on released checkpoints and conduct retrieval experiments. They also perform an encoder swap experiment to localize capacity within the LLM layers.
AI.result: On a frozen 2B-parameter base model, an audio adapter pack (using connector tokens) boosts audio-to-text retrieval R@10 by +3.4 to +5.4 points over a similarly trained non-gated control, with consistent gains across seeds and when scaled to eleven times the data. A thermal adapter pack that reuses the frozen vision path passes a pre-registered acceptance threshold about seven times more often across seeds and improves thermal-to-text R@10 from 0.224 to 0.785. The encoder swap experiment shows that a strong external audio encoder that outperforms Whisper-style encoders in standalone CLAP-like benchmarks underperforms by 16 R@10 points when used inside the frozen LLM, indicating that the key capacity lies in the LLM layers, where the gated adapters operate.
AI.conclusion: Modality-gated deep adapters provide a way to add new modalities to a frozen multimodal embedding LLM while preserving bit-for-bit compatibility of existing outputs, allowing large deployed indices and benchmarks to remain valid. The approach yields substantial retrieval gains for audio and thermal modalities and demonstrates that allocating adaptation capacity inside the LLM's layers is more effective than relying solely on external encoders. The authors release models and tooling to enable reproducibility and practical adoption.

title: The Limits of Simulated Societies: How Post-Training and Survey Fine-Tuning Erase Cross-Cultural Variance
summary: Using large language models (LLMs) to simulate diverse human populations has the potential to transform many aspects of computational social science, yet many evaluations score the average response rather than the spread of opinion within real groups. Here, we develop a diagnostic framework that measures point accuracy alongside dispersion retention, the ratio of predicted to human standard deviation ($\dr$), on 10{,}000 respondent--question pairs from the World Values Survey (WVS) spanning twelve countries and six continents. We evaluate eleven zero-shot language models and five variants fine-tuned on WVS data with SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We identify a failure mode we term \textit{consensus collapse}, where alignment training compresses outputs toward one stereotype per group. Along the post-training trajectory from the Llama~3.1 70B base to the Tulu~3 checkpoints, the first stage, supervised instruction tuning, removes half of the spread with minimal accuracy gain ($\dr$ 1.22 to 0.59; accuracy $+0.9$ points), the later stages do not restore it, and a gap opens between WEIRD and non-WEIRD countries that survey fine-tuning then deepens while pursuing higher point accuracy. The most accurate model (Tulu~3 70B-DPO fine-tuned on WVS, 57.9\%) keeps half the human spread overall ($\dr = 0.50$) and 11\% of it for Nigeria, against 0.70--0.87 for WEIRD countries. Raising the sampling temperature to 1.0 leaves the Wasserstein-1 distance ($\wone$) to human distributions unchanged for both fine-tuned DPO models, and GRPO on Qwen~3.5 9B does not restore the spread under either an accuracy reward or a distribution-shaped reward. Mixing the aligned model with an unaligned prior raises $\dr$ from 0.51 to 0.62 on a held-out split but leaves Nigeria at 0.36. Point accuracy alone therefore misjudges these simulators, and current post-training trades diversity for consensus.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models simulate not only average human responses but also the diversity of opinions in survey data, revealing that alignment and fine-tuning often collapse opinion spread into a narrow consensus.
AI.motivation: Most evaluations of LLM-based human simulators only measure point accuracy—how close the model’s average response is to the human average—ignoring how well models capture the variation of opinions within populations. For computational social science applications, it is crucial to retain realistic dispersion across demographic and national groups. The authors aim to systematically diagnose whether modern alignment and fine-tuning pipelines preserve or erode this diversity of simulated opinions.
AI.method: The authors build a diagnostic framework using 10,000 respondent–question pairs from the World Values Survey across twelve countries. They define dispersion retention (dr) as the ratio of model-predicted to human standard deviation of responses, and complement it with Wasserstein-1 distance between full distributions. They then evaluate eleven zero-shot LLMs and five WVS-fine-tuned variants (using SFT, DPO, and GRPO) along a post-training trajectory from Llama 3.1 70B base to Tulu 3 checkpoints, as well as GRPO-tuned Qwen 3.5 9B. They also test higher sampling temperatures and mixture models combining aligned and unaligned checkpoints.
AI.result: They observe a phenomenon they call "consensus collapse": alignment and instruction tuning significantly reduce response dispersion with only marginal gains in point accuracy. For example, moving from Llama 3.1 70B base to the first Tulu 3 instruction-tuned stage halves dispersion retention (dr from 1.22 to 0.59) while accuracy increases by only 0.9 percentage points, and later stages do not recover the lost spread. Fine-tuning on WVS further increases point accuracy but deepens dispersion loss, especially for non-WEIRD countries such as Nigeria, where the most accurate model (Tulu 3 70B-DPO on WVS) preserves only 11% of human spread (dr = 0.11), compared to 0.70–0.87 for WEIRD countries. Changing sampling temperature to 1.0 does not improve distributional fit (W1 distance), and GRPO-based approaches also fail to restore spread, even when using distribution-shaped rewards. Mixing aligned models with unaligned priors modestly improves overall dr on a held-out split but leaves severe under-dispersion for Nigeria.
AI.conclusion: Reliance on point accuracy alone substantially overestimates the quality of LLM-based human simulators. Contemporary alignment and post-training pipelines systematically trade away opinion diversity for a narrow, stereotyped consensus, with especially poor representation of non-WEIRD populations. Effective evaluation and development of such simulators must explicitly account for dispersion and distributional fidelity, not just mean accuracy, to avoid biased and homogenized representations of global opinion.

title: Beyond Static Charts: Can Language and Vision Language Models Generate Interactive Data Visualization Interfaces?
summary: Data visualization is central to analytical reasoning, but real-world analysis increasingly requires language-driven interactive interfaces rather than static charts. Although recent large language and vision language models (LLMs/VLMs) have shown promise in generating static charts from natural language, their ability to generate interactive data visualization interfaces remains largely unexplored due to the lack of benchmarks. We introduce VIS-GEN, a benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs/VLMs can generate interactive visualization interfaces from natural language queries. VIS-GEN comprises 3,042 samples covering diverse analytical intents, including data filtering, temporal analysis, and visualization editing, each paired with dataset metadata and natural language queries that are designed to reflect realistic, goal driven data exploration scenarios. We benchmark 14 state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source LLMs/VLMs, revealing large performance gaps and frequent failures on queries involving implicit intent, multiple interaction alternatives, and complex editing operations, highlighting interactive interface generation as a key open challenge beyond static chart synthesis. To address this, we propose a structured multi stage interface generation framework that decomposes the task into visualization design representation, generation of multiple interface candidates, constraint-aware critique, and self-refinement. This approach improves the best models pass rate by 15.9 percentage points, demonstrating a practical path toward more reliable language-driven interactive visualization systems. We release VIS-GEN at https://github.com/vis-nlp/VIS-GEN.

AI.tldr: VIS-GEN is a new benchmark and framework to test and improve how LLMs/VLMs generate interactive visualization interfaces from natural language, going beyond static chart creation.
AI.motivation: Most existing work and benchmarks focus on using LLMs/VLMs to generate static charts from natural language, while real-world analysis needs interactive, language-driven visualization interfaces. There was no systematic way to evaluate or improve models on this interactive interface generation task, especially under realistic, goal-driven analytical scenarios.
AI.method: The authors build VIS-GEN, a benchmark with 3,042 examples that pair dataset metadata and natural language queries with intended interactive visualization interfaces, covering analytical intents such as data filtering, temporal analysis, and visualization editing. They evaluate 14 state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs/VLMs on this benchmark. They then introduce a structured multi-stage interface generation framework that decomposes the task into: (1) producing a structured representation of visualization design, (2) generating multiple candidate interfaces, (3) constraint-aware critique of these candidates, and (4) self-refinement based on the critique.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows large performance gaps between models and frequent failure modes, particularly on tasks involving implicit analytical intent, multiple valid interaction alternatives, and complex editing operations. The proposed multi-stage framework increases the best model’s pass rate on VIS-GEN by 15.9 percentage points, showing substantial performance gains over direct generation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Interactive interface generation from language is a significantly harder and underexplored problem than static chart generation. VIS-GEN provides a needed benchmark for this task and reveals current model limitations. The proposed structured multi-stage generation and self-refinement pipeline is an effective way to improve reliability, pointing toward more practical language-driven interactive visualization systems. The dataset and resources are released publicly for the community to build upon.

title: Neurosymbolic Action Model Learning under Partial Observability
summary: AI planning studies how an agent can reach a goal by executing a sequence of actions. To plan correctly, the agent needs an action model describing when each action can be executed and how it changes the world. Constructing such models by hand requires domain expertise, and can be costly and error-prone. Action models can instead be learned from available data using existing neurosymbolic approaches, but they currently assume access to complete traces of fully observable images . These approaches fail to learn action models under partial observability where some of the images might not be present or are not fully informative of the current state of the world. Hence, this paper proposes NeSyAM, a novel neurosymbolic modeling paradigm for action model learning under partial observability. In addition, the paper presents a unified variational framework for theoretically analysing the limitations of existing methods compared to our proposed approach. NeSyAM is then tested extensively on six visual planning domains and three observation regimes to show it consistently recovers relevant parts of the true action model under partial observability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NeSyAM, a neurosymbolic framework that learns action models for AI planning under partial observability, outperforming prior methods that assume full observability.
AI.motivation: Existing neurosymbolic approaches to learning action models in AI planning require complete, fully observable execution traces, which is unrealistic for many real-world settings where observations can be missing or incomplete. Manually crafting action models is expensive and error-prone, so there is a need for an automated, data-driven method that can robustly learn action models even when states are only partially observed.
AI.method: The authors propose NeSyAM, a new neurosymbolic modeling paradigm tailored to learning action models from partially observable visual data. They also develop a unified variational framework that allows theoretical analysis and comparison of NeSyAM with existing neurosymbolic methods, exposing their limitations under partial observability. NeSyAM is then instantiated and trained on visual planning domains under different observation regimes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on six visual planning domains and three observation regimes show that NeSyAM consistently recovers the relevant components of the underlying true action model, even when observations are partially missing or uninformative. It performs robustly where previous neurosymbolic approaches fail under partial observability.
AI.conclusion: NeSyAM successfully extends neurosymbolic action model learning to settings with partial observability, addressing a key limitation of prior work. The unified variational framework both justifies the approach theoretically and clarifies why earlier methods break down, demonstrating that NeSyAM is a more realistic and effective solution for learning action models in real-world, imperfectly observed environments.

title: Same Chart, Different Story: Bias in Vision-Language Chart Interpretation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret charts and generate natural-language explanations for socially consequential data. However, they may produce different narratives for the same chart when only the referenced social group changes, reinforcing stereotypes and misleading decisions. Despite these risks, no benchmark exists for systematically evaluating bias in chart interpretation across social dimensions. We introduce ChartBias, the first benchmark for auditing bias in VLM-based chart interpretation.
