AI.method: They propose canonical locks, a geometric primitive where parts and wholes are represented as high-dimensional vectors (dimension d ≥ 4). Information is encoded through relative phase differences between these vectors. The network is organized as positionally-bound bottom-up and top-down neural fields that interact iteratively. These two fields drive each other toward a state analogous to thermal equilibrium. The authors also analyze symmetrical configurations of these fields and how symmetry breaking unfolds over computational iterations, as a function of angular relationships between part and whole vectors arranged on a high-dimensional ring or disk.
AI.result: They identify and characterize several symmetric configurations in the proposed network and study how the network’s iterative dynamics break these symmetries. The time (iterations) required for symmetry breaking is shown to depend systematically on the angle between part/whole vectors placed on a high-dimensional ring. They also observe that the system’s behavior resembles known psychological effects in mental rotation tasks, suggesting that the representation and dynamics capture meaningful geometric reasoning about parts and wholes.
AI.conclusion: Canonical locks provide a principled geometric framework for encoding part–whole hierarchies using high-dimensional phase-based representations, avoiding the need to flatten structures into sequences. The coupled bottom-up and top-down neural fields can reach equilibrium states that reflect structured part–whole relationships, and the symmetry-breaking dynamics depend on geometric factors like inter-vector angles. These properties suggest that canonical locks may be a promising direction for modeling structured visual reasoning and may be related to human mental rotation processes.

title: Enriching Speech Emotion Representations with Conversational Context
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Detecting emotions is necessary for building systems that can accurately and adaptively interact with humans. Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) has become an important research focus to develop intelligent spoken interfaces. However, most studies predict emotions at the utterance level, ignoring the conversational context, along with the emotional flow and speaker interactions it carries. In this paper, we introduce ACERT (Averaged Contextual Emotion Representation through Time), a module that integrates a flexible-length window of conversational context to better capture emotional evolution in spoken interactions. To evaluate the robustness of this method, we conducted experiments on datasets spanning diverse emotionally expressive styles and contexts. ACERT outperforms current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches on IEMOCAP, establishes the first context-aware benchmark on SAFE, and obtains strong results on MELD for unweighted, class-balanced metrics. Ablation studies show that ACERT's gains come from emotional and conversational continuity, rather than from speaker identity or acoustic conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ACERT, a context-aware module for speech emotion recognition that uses a flexible window of conversational history to model emotional evolution, achieving state-of-the-art or strong performance on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Most speech emotion recognition systems classify emotions at the single-utterance level, ignoring conversational context such as emotional dynamics and speaker interactions, which are crucial for accurate, human-like understanding in dialog systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce ACERT (Averaged Contextual Emotion Representation through Time), which aggregates a variable-length window of past conversational turns to form a contextual emotion representation that captures emotional flow and conversational continuity, and integrate it into SER models. They test it across multiple datasets with different emotional styles and contexts and conduct ablation studies to identify which factors drive performance gains.
AI.result: ACERT surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on the IEMOCAP dataset, provides the first context-aware benchmark on the SAFE dataset, and achieves competitive, strong performance on the MELD dataset when evaluated with unweighted, class-balanced metrics.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating flexible conversational context via ACERT significantly improves speech emotion recognition performance, with improvements attributed mainly to modeling emotional and conversational continuity rather than relying on speaker identity or acoustic artifacts, demonstrating the importance of contextual modeling in SER.

title: FIRE: Failure-Informed Runtime Engineering for Reliable Language-Model Agents
summary: Language-model agents often reach a working solution and then fail to consistently deliver it. We study runtime policies: targeted natural-language instructions and action denials applied by the agent harness at states that preceded observed failures, without changing model weights or the user prompt. With this, keeping capability constant, we observe a meaningful unlock in delivered reliability. Across the complete 87-task Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite, with two attempts per task, policies increase repeated success (pass^2) in all three GPT-5.6 tiers: 50.6% to 54.0% for Luna, 55.2% to 60.9% for Terra, and 64.4% to 73.6% for Sol. Sol's best-of-two success changes by 1.2 points while repeated success rises by 9.2, showing that policies chiefly convert reachable solutions into dependable delivery. We further cover 14 tasks under Terra's frozen portfolio. Policy-guided Terra reaches 71.4%, compared with 64.3% for unassisted Sol, at about half the cost, demonstrating how engineering around models could unlock dependability for a use case. To isolate the mechanism we run a randomized five-arm experiment: real policies reach 61% on eligible tasks, versus 39% without a policy, 36% with a timing-matched sham, and 39 to 43% with generic verification or reconsideration. The intended corrective behavior appears in 22 of 24 coded policy attempts, against at most 14 in any other arm. Runtime policies are therefore a practical reliability layer: they make capabilities an agent already possesses substantially more repeatable.

AI.tldr: They introduce runtime policies—natural-language instructions and action denials applied at specific agent states—to improve reliability of language-model agents without changing their weights or prompts.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents can often find correct solutions but fail to reliably reproduce or deliver them across attempts, limiting their dependability in practical use cases.
AI.method: They define runtime policies as targeted instructions or action denials triggered at states known to precede failures, and evaluate them on the 87-task Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite using multiple GPT-5.6 model tiers, also running a randomized five-arm experiment comparing real policies with no policy, sham timing-matched interventions, and generic verification or reconsideration.
AI.result: Runtime policies boost repeated success (pass^2) rates across all model tiers, especially for the strongest model Sol (64.4% to 73.6%) with minimal change in best-of-two success, and Terra with policies outperforms a stronger unassisted model at lower cost; the randomized experiment shows real policies significantly outperform sham and generic interventions both in task success (61% vs 36–43%) and in eliciting intended corrective behaviors (22/24 vs ≤14/24).
AI.conclusion: Runtime policies serve as an effective reliability layer that converts existing but inconsistently expressed model capabilities into more dependable performance, improving repeatability without modifying model weights or user prompts.

title: How to Estimate Whether You Have Found Several Needles in a Haystack: Measuring Calibration in Multi-Label Text Classification
summary: A key factor in deciding whether to trust an automatic prediction is its confidence score, which should be calibrated to match the actual probability of the prediction being correct. Most confidence calibration metrics target binary or multi-class tasks, while multi-label calibration remains largely underexplored. Multi-label classification tasks, such as assigning medical codes to clinical notes or determining news topics, are usually dominated by a large number of negatives, i.e., labels that do not apply. We show that existing binning schemes to compute label-wise expected calibration error either underestimate the error, simply reflect label frequency, or suffer from many bins with very few instances. To achieve trustworthy label-wise calibration errors, we propose a new binning scheme that gives equal weight to positive and negative label assignments. Our empirical study demonstrates that in contrast to existing binning schemes, our new scheme results in meaningful estimates of calibration error in hierarchical and in extreme multi-label classification. We also show that calibrating confidence scores of large language models for multi-label predictions is an open challenge. Our detailed analysis lays the foundation for further research by providing a solid evaluation metric for measuring calibration in multi-label classification.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of confidence calibration in multi-label classification and proposes a new binning scheme for computing label-wise expected calibration error that better handles the imbalance between positive and negative labels.
AI.motivation: Confidence scores guide whether we should trust automatic predictions, but existing calibration metrics are mainly designed for binary or multi-class settings, and do not work well for multi-label tasks that have many more negative than positive labels. Existing binning schemes for label-wise ECE in multi-label problems either underestimate calibration error, correlate too closely with label frequency, or lead to unreliable estimates due to sparsely populated bins.
AI.method: The authors analyze existing binning schemes for label-wise expected calibration error (ECE) in multi-label classification and identify their shortcomings. They then propose a new binning scheme that balances positive and negative label assignments, giving them equal weight when computing calibration error. They empirically evaluate the new scheme on hierarchical and extreme multi-label classification tasks, including settings with large language models, and compare it to existing schemes.
AI.result: The proposed binning scheme yields more meaningful and trustworthy estimates of label-wise calibration error than existing methods, particularly in settings with strong label imbalance such as hierarchical and extreme multi-label classification. The empirical study also reveals that current methods for calibrating confidence scores of large language models in multi-label settings remain inadequate, indicating an open research challenge.
AI.conclusion: The new binning scheme improves the measurement of label-wise calibration error in multi-label classification by properly accounting for both positive and negative labels. This leads to more reliable evaluation of how well confidence scores correspond to true probabilities. The work highlights that calibration of large language models for multi-label tasks is still unsolved and provides a solid metric that can serve as a foundation for future research on calibration methods in multi-label classification.

title: Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation: Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Algorithms for COA matching & COA generation
comment: 5 pages. DAI 2026 Industry Track submission. Includes public reproducibility artifact link. Uses synthetic offline scenarios only; no classified data, proprietary data, human-subject data, or operational planning systems
summary: Course-of-action (COA) generation is a distributed planning problem: a system must propose structured candidate actions, evaluate them against an adversarial response, and surface options that remain tactically coherent under changing conditions. We present COA-Bench, a small offline benchmark and reproducibility artifact for comparing COA generation policies through self-play. Following the BattleCOA terminology, we reserve COA matching for asset-effect matching and COA generation for course-of-action generation; the present artifact does not implement either DecisionFunction directly. Instead, it represents COAs as typed action chains with conditional branches, assigns a synthetic COA quality score, compares opposing COAs with a BLUE-vs-RED advantage score and Nash-gap distance, and scores doctrinal coherence with an FM 3-0-inspired heuristic rubric. Across 50 synthetic scenarios spanning five operational templates, a sampled best-response policy that draws eight RED candidates reduces BLUE advantage from .516 to .485 and BLUE wargame win rate from .920 to .820; a two-stage multi-agent council with five BLUE proposer agents, RED-team adjudication, and critique-driven revision obtains .509 BLUE advantage and .820 BLUE win rate. We also identify and fix a benchmark-design issue in which scenario framing was stored as metadata but had no effect on generated COA content. COA-Bench is not an operational battle-management system and uses no real, classified, proprietary, or human-subject data. The contribution is an inspectable evaluation harness, preliminary benchmark evidence, and lessons for building auditable agentic planning artifacts.

AI.tldr: COA-Bench is a synthetic, offline benchmark for evaluating course-of-action generation policies via self-play in adversarial planning scenarios.
AI.motivation: To provide a small, reproducible, and auditable testbed for comparing different COA generation strategies in adversarial, distributed planning without relying on real or sensitive operational data.
AI.method: Represent COAs as typed action chains with conditional branches, assign synthetic quality scores, compare opposing BLUE/RED COAs with advantage and Nash-gap metrics, and assess doctrinal coherence with a heuristic rubric inspired by FM 3-0. Evaluate multiple COA generation policies (e.g., sampled best-response, multi-agent council with critique and revision) across 50 synthetic scenarios and five operational templates.
AI.result: In experiments on 50 synthetic scenarios, a sampled best-response RED policy (drawing eight candidates) decreases BLUE’s advantage from 0.516 to 0.485 and BLUE’s wargame win rate from 0.920 to 0.820. A two-stage multi-agent council approach for BLUE achieves a 0.509 BLUE advantage and 0.820 BLUE win rate. The authors also uncover and correct a benchmark design flaw where scenario framing existed only as metadata and did not affect generated COAs.
AI.conclusion: COA-Bench offers an inspectable and reproducible evaluation harness for adversarial COA generation, along with preliminary benchmark results and design lessons. It is explicitly non-operational, uses only synthetic data, and aims to inform the construction of auditable agentic planning systems rather than provide a deployable battle-management tool.

title: Spoken Language Models that Think Aloud
summary: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has improved the capability of language models, directly applying it to Spoken Language Models (SLMs) may introduce long silent intervals under the serial "think-then-speak" paradigm, disrupting real-time spoken interaction. To address this issue, we propose an asynchronous think-aloud framework for reasoning-based SLMs within the Thinker-Talker architecture. The framework maintains a primary reasoning stream for logical deduction and a lightweight think-aloud stream that generates short, task-grounded progress utterances conditioned on the user input and the evolving reasoning state. A dynamic balance strategy coordinates the two streams at runtime, triggering additional think-aloud speech to avoid silent gaps and canceling pending utterances when the final response becomes ready. Experiments on spoken reasoning and question-answering benchmarks show that our approach substantially reduces user-audible silence during reasoning while maintaining answer accuracy comparable to that of a serial "think-then-speak" baseline, demonstrating the potential of asynchronous think-aloud for responsive interaction in SLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an asynchronous think-aloud framework for spoken language models that allows them to reason and speak in parallel, reducing awkward silence while preserving reasoning quality.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought improves reasoning but, when directly used in spoken language models with a serial "think-then-speak" setup, causes long silent pauses that break natural, real-time voice interaction. There is a need for SLMs that can perform deep reasoning without sacrificing conversational responsiveness.
AI.method: The authors design a Thinker-Talker architecture with two asynchronous streams: (1) a primary reasoning stream that performs full logical deduction, and (2) a lightweight think-aloud stream that generates brief, task-related progress utterances based on user input and the current reasoning state. They introduce a dynamic balancing strategy that schedules and coordinates these streams in real time, deciding when to emit extra think-aloud speech to fill potential silences and when to cancel pending utterances once a final answer is ready.
AI.result: On spoken reasoning and QA benchmarks, the proposed framework significantly reduces user-perceived silent intervals during model reasoning, while keeping answer accuracy on par with a conventional serial "think-then-speak" Chain-of-Thought baseline.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous think-aloud, implemented via a Thinker-Talker architecture with coordinated reasoning and progress speech streams, can make spoken language models more responsive and natural in interactive settings without degrading reasoning performance.

title: ChainUQ: Reasoning Consistency-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models
summary: While large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive reasoning capabilities, response-level confidence may remain unreliable when intermediate claims conflict with the final conclusion. Therefore, effective uncertainty quantification (UQ) is required to capture logical inconsistencies within the reasoning chain, not just the correctness of the final output. Current approaches have two major limitations: (1) their reliance on token-level probabilities fails to capture reasoning consistency, and (2) they lack mechanisms to dynamically calibrate confidence using the structural logic of the generated chain. To advance existing research, we introduce ChainUQ, a reasoning consistency-aware uncertainty quantification framework for LLMs. ChainUQ consists of two key technical components: an alignment-aware lightweight UQ module that estimates a raw intrinsic model confidence score from frozen features aligned to the final conclusion, and a reasoning consistency-aware calibrator that refines this score using reasoning-chain consistency evidence. Evaluations across diverse in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks show that ChainUQ consistently improves response-level uncertainty estimation, achieving an average 3.1% relative gain in AUROC and up to 45.0% relative reduction in ECE, and can be directly transferred to new settings without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Proposes ChainUQ, a framework that quantifies uncertainty for LLM reasoning by combining intrinsic model confidence with explicit checks of reasoning-chain consistency, improving AUROC and calibration (ECE) across settings.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimation for LLMs is unreliable at the response level, especially when intermediate reasoning steps contradict the final answer. Methods that rely on token probabilities ignore logical structure, and current approaches lack mechanisms to adjust confidence based on the internal consistency of the reasoning chain. This gap limits safe deployment of LLMs in tasks requiring trustworthy reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce ChainUQ, composed of two main parts: (1) an alignment-aware lightweight UQ module operating on frozen model features that are aligned with the final conclusion to produce a raw intrinsic confidence score; and (2) a reasoning consistency-aware calibrator that adjusts this score using evidence about the logical consistency of the generated reasoning chain. The system is trained/evaluated across multiple benchmarks and tested for transfer without further fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a variety of in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, ChainUQ improves response-level uncertainty estimation, yielding an average 3.1% relative gain in AUROC and up to 45.0% relative reduction in Expected Calibration Error (ECE). It generalizes well, working in new settings without additional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling reasoning-chain consistency and separating intrinsic confidence estimation from logic-based calibration, ChainUQ provides more accurate and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates for LLM outputs than token-probability-based approaches. This makes LLM reasoning more trustworthy and transferable across tasks and domains.

title: Calibration as a First-Class Criterion in LLM Evaluation
comment: Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Uncertainty-Aware NLP (UncertaiNLP) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Calibration of language models -- the alignment between expressed or implicit confidence and empirical correctness -- is a well-studied subfield within NLP. Methods to measure it already exist. The problem is adoption: outside this subfield, NLP research regularly introduces new models, datasets, and benchmarks without checking whether the model's confidence scores are meaningful. We argue that this adoption gap is a major obstacle to trustworthy LLM evaluation. Miscalibration causes problems in two distinct areas: at deployment, where overconfident mistakes cause real harm, and inside the research pipeline, where methods like LLM-as-a-judge, synthetic data generation, and active learning rely on calibrated confidence without verifying it. Standard calibration metrics only require two inputs per example: a confidence score and a correctness judgment. Most benchmarks in use today already provide both, meaning calibration can be reported immediately. For open-ended generation, however, defining these two inputs is still an open challenge. We argue that each NLP subfield should pair its main performance metric with a calibration score and call for treating calibration as an essential property of every model rather than a niche topic.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that calibration—how well a model’s confidence matches actual correctness—is crucial but underused in NLP, and calls for making calibration reporting standard alongside accuracy for all models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Although methods for measuring calibration of language models exist, they are rarely adopted outside a small subfield. As a result, new models and benchmarks are routinely proposed without checking whether their confidence scores are meaningful. This is problematic because miscalibration undermines the trustworthiness of LLM evaluation and leads to practical harms: overconfident wrong answers in deployment, and unreliable internal tools in research such as LLM-as-a-judge, synthetic data generation, and active learning—all of which implicitly assume calibrated confidence. The authors are motivated to close this adoption gap and make calibration a mainstream evaluation dimension.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological analysis rather than a single new algorithm: (1) identify and formalize the adoption gap between existing calibration techniques and current NLP practice; (2) argue, with examples, how miscalibration affects both deployed systems and research pipelines; (3) observe that standard calibration metrics only need per-example confidence and correctness, which most existing benchmarks already contain, thus enabling immediate reporting; and (4) analyze why open-ended generation is harder, since defining confidence and correctness there is non-trivial. They then propose a normative evaluation framework where each NLP subfield couples its main performance metric with a calibration score.
AI.result: The key result is a set of arguments and observations rather than empirical numbers: (1) most classification-style benchmarks already support calibration evaluation with no extra annotation; (2) current practice systematically ignores calibration even though tools exist; (3) many widely used research methods (LLM-as-a-judge, synthetic data, active learning) rest on unverified calibration assumptions; and (4) open-ended generation remains a special case where calibration inputs are not yet standardized. Together these results support the claim that calibration is both feasible to measure and currently underutilized.
AI.conclusion: Calibration should be treated as a core property of language models, not a niche concern. Every NLP subfield is encouraged to report calibration metrics alongside primary performance scores, leveraging existing benchmarks wherever possible. Doing so will improve the reliability of LLM evaluation, reduce harm from overconfident errors in deployment, and make research methods that rely on model confidence (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge, active learning) more trustworthy. Open-ended generation still requires further work to define appropriate confidence and correctness signals, but this is a tractable and important direction.

title: RankCert: When Can Simulated Learners Safely Select an AI Tutor? Robust Decision Certification Under Structural Uncertainty
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology (TIST)
summary: Simulation-based tutor selection can be unstable when predictively adequate learner models imply different policy rankings. RankCert certifies one of eight equal-budget tutoring policies only when model-averaged utility, probability-best, posterior regret, cross-domain rank, family coverage, and leave-one-domain-out and leave-one-visible-family-out averages support the same candidate; otherwise it abstains. We evaluated RankCert in 1,280 frozen held-out settings spanning five rotating held-out oracle families, 64 scenarios per family, and four cohort sizes. Calibration used a licensed, de-identified EdNet-KT1 derivative with 5,000 learners and 590,056 retained responses; all five family representatives passed the frozen adequacy gate. Minimum-domain mean pairwise top-1 agreement was 0.272917 (95% CI [0.253646, 0.293229]), showing substantial structural disagreement. Cohort-noise variance decreased from n = 30 to n = 300, while the structural family share remained nonzero. RankCert reduced total held-out decision loss relative to full-coverage point selection by 0.006605 normalized-outcome units (95% CI [0.004859, 0.008407]). At comparable coverage, however, it did not reduce selective risk relative to a confidence-gated point certificate (difference -0.000213; 95% CI [-0.003238, 0.002384]; Holm p = 0.929654). Certification occurred in 3.75% of settings and only in stable scenarios; RankCert abstained in every ambiguous, misspecified, and structural-conflict setting. "Safe" denotes only benchmark-scoped decision certification under the declared utility and uncertainty set; no human-learning, causal, deployment-effectiveness, or general-safety claim is made.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RankCert, a conservative method for choosing tutoring policies under model uncertainty, which only certifies a policy when many robustness checks agree, otherwise abstaining.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based selection of tutoring policies relies on learner models that may disagree, leading to unstable and potentially unsafe choices. The authors want a principled way to only make recommendations when multiple models and diagnostics consistently support the same policy, and to abstain when structural disagreement or misspecification makes rankings unreliable.
AI.method: They define RankCert, which compares eight equal-budget tutoring policies across multiple model-based criteria: model-averaged expected utility, probability of being best, posterior regret, cross-domain rank, family coverage, and leave-one-domain-out / leave-one-visible-family-out averages. A policy is certified only if all these criteria single out the same candidate; otherwise RankCert abstains. They then run large-scale frozen held-out evaluations across 1,280 settings, using five held-out oracle model families, 64 scenarios per family, and four cohort sizes, calibrated on a large EdNet-KT1 derivative dataset that passed an adequacy gate.
AI.result: The learner model families show substantial structural disagreement in policy rankings (minimum mean pairwise top-1 agreement about 0.27). Increasing cohort size reduces sampling noise but not structural differences across model families. RankCert lowers overall held-out decision loss versus always picking a single best policy (full-coverage point selection) by about 0.0066 normalized outcome units, but at the same coverage level it does not outperform a simpler confidence-gated point certificate in terms of selective risk. RankCert issues certifications in only 3.75% of settings, and only when scenarios are stable; it always abstains in ambiguous, misspecified, or structurally conflicting settings.
AI.conclusion: RankCert is a very conservative, benchmark-scoped certification scheme for tutor policy selection under model uncertainty: it is effective at avoiding decisions in settings with structural model conflict or misspecification, modestly improves total decision loss relative to unconditional point selection, but does not clearly beat a simpler confidence-gated baseline at matched coverage. The authors emphasize that their notion of "safety" is limited to this evaluation setting and does not imply claims about real-world human learning or deployment safety.

title: A Semiotics-Aware Framework for Evaluating Fidelity and Coverage in Natural Language Generation
summary: When two texts describe the same expression, standard metrics based on lexical overlap or whole-text similarity may fail to detect meaningful differences in how that expression is framed. We propose a framework to evaluate semiotic alignment between texts, where a semiotic profile encompasses both the contextual meaning and the discourse references made salient by a text. Our approach yields two scores, Semiotic Fidelity and Semiotic Coverage, estimating how much of one text's profile is supported by the other and how much of the other's profile it recovers. Experiments show that coverage is typically lower than fidelity, and that alignment between LLMs and human-curated data is highest at low sampling temperatures, while higher temperatures reduce this alignment.

AI.tldr: They introduce a way to measure how similarly two texts frame the same expression, beyond simple word overlap, using new metrics called Semiotic Fidelity and Semiotic Coverage.
AI.motivation: Existing text similarity metrics based on lexical overlap or global similarity miss important differences in framing and contextual meaning when two texts ostensibly talk about the same expression or concept. There is a need for a method that captures how meanings and discourse references are aligned between texts, especially when evaluating models like LLMs against human-curated data.
AI.method: They define a notion of a semiotic profile for a text, consisting of its contextual meaning and the discourse references it makes salient. Based on this, they introduce two quantitative scores: Semiotic Fidelity, which measures how much of one text's semiotic profile is supported by another, and Semiotic Coverage, which measures how much of the other text’s semiotic profile is recovered. They then run experiments comparing these scores across pairs of texts, including those generated by LLMs at different sampling temperatures versus human-curated references.
AI.result: Empirically, they find that Semiotic Coverage tends to be lower than Semiotic Fidelity, indicating that texts often fail to fully recover all salient meanings and references from a reference text even if they are broadly consistent with it. They also observe that the semiotic alignment between LLM outputs and human-curated data is strongest when the models are sampled with low temperature, and that increasing the sampling temperature decreases this alignment according to their metrics.
AI.conclusion: Semiotic Fidelity and Semiotic Coverage provide a more nuanced way to evaluate how two texts align in meaning and discourse framing than standard lexical or whole-text similarity metrics. Their experiments suggest that current LLMs align better with human semiotic profiles when generating more deterministic, low-temperature outputs, while higher-temperature sampling introduces divergences in the semiotic profile that standard metrics might miss.

title: Selection-Invariant Communication Compilers for Privacy-Aware Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Structured multi-agent workflows exchange intermediate messages whose content and form can reveal private state even when the final output is safe. We identify selection-channel leakage: after authorization fixes what may be released, a private-state-aware choice among semantically valid realizations creates an additional inference channel. We introduce the selection-invariant communication compiler(SICC), which constrains this post-authorization representation kernel rather than prescribing templates. Any deterministic or independently public-randomized generator satisfying the invariant is valid; requirement-indexed canonical forms are one auditable implementation. We prove a compositional communication-layer guarantee: authorization, public-only form generation, and a dependency-safe utility gate make the emitted transcript reveal no information beyond the complete authorized view. Private-state-aware selection remains vulnerable after surface-disjoint and length-matched controls. Across 132 AgentLeak communication replays and 100 executable LangGraph tasks, deterministic SICC retains complete protocol utility without a positive excess-gain signal; independent public randomization preserves the same result in AgentLeak and 480 controlled cases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a compiler (SICC) that prevents information leakage through how messages are phrased or selected in multi-agent workflows, ensuring that transcripts reveal no more than what is explicitly authorized.
AI.motivation: In structured multi-agent systems, even if the final outputs are sanitized, intermediate messages and the specific choices of wording or representation can leak private internal state. Existing controls like redaction, template enforcement, or length-matching do not fully address the leakage that arises from private-state-aware selection among multiple equally valid responses. There is a need for a principled way to guarantee that communication reveals nothing beyond an explicitly authorized view, while preserving protocol utility.
AI.method: The authors formalize a new leakage channel, selection-channel leakage, where private information is encoded in the choice among semantically equivalent realizations after authorization. They propose the Selection-Invariant Communication Compiler (SICC), which enforces an invariant on the representation layer after authorization. Instead of prescribing fixed templates, SICC allows any generator that is either deterministic or randomized using only public randomness, as long as it satisfies the selection-invariance constraint. They provide one concrete implementation based on requirement-indexed canonical forms, and give a compositional communication-layer guarantee when SICC is combined with an authorization mechanism, public-only form generation, and a dependency-safe utility gate.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that, under their architecture (authorization + SICC + utility gate), the full communication transcript is guaranteed not to reveal any information beyond what is present in the fully authorized view. They also show that private-state-aware selection can still leak information even under conventional mitigations like using surface-disjoint or length-matched messages. Empirically, on 132 AgentLeak communication replays and 100 executable LangGraph tasks, a deterministic instantiation of SICC preserves full protocol functionality without measurable positive excess-gain from leakage. When using independent public randomization, they find the same non-leakage outcome on AgentLeak and in 480 controlled experiments.
AI.conclusion: Selection-channel leakage is a distinct and practically important risk in multi-agent communication that is not resolved by existing controls. By constraining the post-authorization representation kernel instead of the high-level content, the proposed SICC framework provides a compositional and auditable guarantee that transcripts do not leak more information than the authorized view. Their theoretical and empirical results suggest that strong privacy-like guarantees can be achieved without sacrificing protocol utility, using either deterministic canonical forms or public-randomized generators that satisfy selection invariance.

title: Transcribe, Translate, and Optimize: Joint Reward Learning for Speech Translation
summary: In LLM-based speech translation, transcription-based chain-of-thought (CoT) suffers from a mismatch between reference transcripts used in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and model-generated transcripts at inference. To address this, we propose joint recognition and translation fine-tuning via group relative policy optimization (GRPO). We score both transcripts and translations, with translation conditioned on model-generated transcripts, and compare three token advantage strategies. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-3B across four languages, we evaluate CoT against direct speech translation (Direct ST) under SFT and GRPO, training on CoVoST 2 and testing on CoVoST 2 and FLEURS. CoT GRPO outperforms Direct ST GRPO by 1.77 and 0.83 average BLEU points on CoVoST 2 and FLEURS. Compared to CoT SFT, GRPO boosts BLEU by 0.82 and 0.67 points and reduces word error rate (WER) by 8.8% and 7.2% relatively. These results highlight reinforcement fine-tuning as an effective method to mitigate the training-inference mismatch, jointly improving recognition and translation.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the mismatch between training and inference in LLM-based speech translation with chain-of-thought (transcription→translation), and proposes a reinforcement learning fine-tuning method (GRPO) that jointly optimizes ASR and translation, achieving better BLEU and lower WER than standard supervised fine-tuning and direct speech translation.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based speech translation systems that use a chain-of-thought style pipeline (first transcribe, then translate), supervised fine-tuning relies on ground-truth transcripts, but at inference the model must condition on its own (often imperfect) transcripts. This train–test mismatch can degrade both recognition and translation quality. There is a need for a training strategy that directly optimizes the model on its own generated transcripts and their downstream translation impact.
AI.method: The authors introduce joint recognition and translation fine-tuning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm. During training, the model generates transcripts and then translations conditioned on these transcripts. Both transcripts and translations are scored (e.g., via WER/BLEU-based rewards), and GRPO is used to update the model parameters. They experiment with three different token-level advantage strategies for assigning credit across tokens. Experiments use Qwen2.5-Omni-3B as the base LLM and compare chain-of-thought (transcription→translation) versus direct speech translation approaches, under both standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and GRPO-based fine-tuning. Training is on CoVoST 2 and evaluation is on CoVoST 2 and FLEURS for four languages.
AI.result: CoT with GRPO outperforms direct speech translation with GRPO by 1.77 BLEU on CoVoST 2 and 0.83 BLEU on FLEURS on average. Relative to CoT with standard supervised fine-tuning, CoT with GRPO increases BLEU by 0.82 on CoVoST 2 and 0.67 on FLEURS, and reduces word error rate by 8.8% and 7.2% respectively. These gains show clear benefits from joint optimization of recognition and translation via reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning through GRPO, applied in a joint ASR+ST framework that conditions translation on model-generated transcripts, effectively mitigates the train–test mismatch inherent in CoT-style LLM-based speech translation. This approach leads to simultaneous improvements in transcription (WER) and translation (BLEU) quality over both direct speech translation and conventional supervised fine-tuning, suggesting RL-based fine-tuning as a promising direction for LLM-based speech translation systems.

title: The Architect, the Adversary, and the Judge: Closed-Loop Generation of Standards-Aligned Assessment Items at Scale
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. Companion paper: arXiv:2608.01000
summary: We present CLAIM, a production pipeline for K-12 assessment-item generation coupling a two-stage generate-then-attack protocol (the model drafts as a "curriculum architect", then re-enters the same conversation as a hostile adversarial reviewer), bi-directional few-shot conditioning on accepted and rejected items, the latter carrying the evaluator's diagnosis, and a knowledge dictionary of 44,844 error-correction rules mined from that feedback and retrieved per standard and item type. Across 43,227 scored items over 755 Common Core ELA standards, three item types, and ten LLMs, the pipeline reaches a 97.8% expert-evaluator pass rate on a 9,074-item production run. We then ask what that rate certifies. Re-scoring a stratified sample with three judges from other vendors, blind to the deployed verdict, reproduces the format ordering under every judge and recovers a larger open-set deficit than the deployed evaluator does; but agreement on the accept/reject binary is weak at production prevalence (kappa about 0.13), and the judges agree with each other no better. The level is therefore judge-relative, and with no student-response data our quality evidence is evaluator-judged throughout. The corpus also exposes a robust asymmetry. Multiple-choice and multiple-select generation saturate at 98% or above for both frontier models under a dozen static rules, whereas fill-in-the-blank generation is capability-tiered (82.8-96.7% across five models under a matched rule set, standards, and judge) and plateaus under prompt-only optimization, with error mass shifting between answer-key over-inclusion and omission as rules accumulate. We analyze this as open-set boundary determination, a task autoregressive decoders are structurally ill-equipped to solve, and show the asymmetry recurring when the evaluator itself is distilled: fail-recall rises from 8% to 63% while F1 saturates at 0.25.

AI.tldr: CLAIM is a production pipeline for generating K-12 assessment items with LLMs that combines generative and adversarial review stages plus mined error-correction rules, achieving high pass rates but revealing evaluator-relative quality and structural limits, especially for open-ended boundary decisions in fill-in-the-blank items.
AI.motivation: To reliably use large language models to generate high-quality K-12 assessment items at scale, providers need pipelines that both optimize item quality and rigorously quantify what automated pass rates actually mean—especially when expert judgments are noisy and item formats pose different structural challenges to LLMs.
AI.method: The authors build CLAIM, a two-stage generate-then-attack pipeline where the model first drafts items as a "curriculum architect" and then re-enters as an adversarial critic. They condition generation bi-directionally on examples of both accepted and rejected items, with rejected cases annotated by evaluator diagnoses. From this feedback they mine a large knowledge dictionary of 44,844 error-correction rules, retrievable by standard and item type. They evaluate across 43,227 items spanning 755 Common Core ELA standards, three item formats, and ten LLMs. To probe what high pass rates certify, they have three independent vendor judges blind-rescore a stratified sample and analyze agreement, format differences, and open-set error patterns. They also distill the evaluator to test robustness and observe changes in fail-recall and F1.
AI.result: CLAIM attains a 97.8% pass rate from the deployed expert evaluator on a 9,074-item production run. Independent blind judges reproduce relative format ordering and expose an even larger open-set deficit than the deployed evaluator, but inter-judge and judge–evaluator agreement on the binary accept/reject decision is weak (kappa ≈ 0.13) and no higher among the judges themselves, indicating strong judge-relativity. Multiple-choice and multiple-select items reach about 98%+ pass rates for frontier models using a small static rule set. In contrast, fill-in-the-blank items show capability-tiered performance (≈82.8–96.7% across models under matched rules and standards), plateau under further prompt-based optimization, and exhibit shifting error mass between answer-key over-inclusion and omission. When the evaluator is distilled, fail-recall increases sharply (from 8% to 63%) but F1 saturates at 0.25, revealing recurring asymmetries and limitations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based pipelines like CLAIM can mass-produce K-12 assessment items with very high evaluator pass rates, particularly for constrained formats such as multiple-choice and multiple-select, using a generate–attack protocol and mined rule dictionary. However, these pass rates reflect evaluator-relative standards rather than an objective notion of quality, given low inter-rater agreement and lack of student-response validation. Fill-in-the-blank item generation exposes structural shortcomings: autoregressive models struggle with open-set boundary determination for acceptable answers, leading to persistent, format-specific error modes that do not vanish with prompt-only optimization and reappear when evaluators are distilled. Reliable deployment thus requires recognizing judge-relativity, format asymmetries, and inherent limitations of current LLM architectures for open-set assessment tasks.

title: A retrospective analysis on the use of LLMs to study infant syntax learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been used to investigate how children acquire syntax at an early stage of development. This is notably the central scientific goal of the BabyLM challenge, a community-wide effort to develop models that achieve human-level syntactic performance while being trained on developmentally realistic corpora. In this paper, we reflect on the use of LLMs in the study of infant syntax learning by providing an epistemological assessment of several studies from this research program. We discuss how datasets are built, which models are implemented, how they are trained and syntactically evaluated. We observe significant assumptions in the methodology of BabyLM and related studies, thus mitigating their theoretical scope. We additionally observe that using developmentally-realistic corpora have limited effects on models performance on commonly-used benchmarks, which suggest important computational differences between LLMs and the infant syntax learner.

AI.tldr: The paper critically examines how large language models are used to study infant syntax learning, focusing on the BabyLM challenge, and argues that methodological assumptions and limited impact of realistic input corpora constrain what these models can tell us about human language acquisition.
AI.motivation: Researchers are increasingly using LLMs as models of early language acquisition, particularly syntax, epitomized by the BabyLM challenge. There is enthusiasm that training LLMs on child-like corpora might reveal mechanisms of infant syntax learning. However, it is unclear how valid these approaches are as cognitive models, how datasets and evaluations are constructed, and whether better alignment of training data with infant input actually brings LLMs closer to human learners. The paper aims to clarify these issues by providing an epistemological critique.
AI.method: The authors conduct a conceptual and methodological review of studies within the BabyLM program and related work. They analyze how datasets are curated to approximate infants’ linguistic environments, what architectures and training regimes are used for LLMs, and how syntactic knowledge is probed via benchmarks. They then compare model performance under different training conditions, especially developmentally realistic corpora, and assess how these empirical results bear on claims about infant syntax learning.
AI.result: They find that BabyLM-style studies rely on strong assumptions in corpus construction, model choice, training strategy, and evaluation metrics. These assumptions significantly restrict the inferences that can be drawn about infant syntax acquisition. Empirically, they observe that constraining models to developmentally realistic corpora yields only limited improvements or changes on standard syntactic benchmarks, indicating that such manipulations do not meaningfully close the gap between LLM behavior and human infant learning.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current uses of LLMs in the BabyLM framework provide only limited insights into infant syntax learning. Methodological and conceptual assumptions undermine the theoretical reach of these models as cognitive analogues of infants. Moreover, the weak effect of developmentally realistic input on benchmark performance suggests substantial computational differences between present-day LLMs and human infant learners. The authors imply that more careful epistemological grounding and possibly different modeling approaches are needed for LLMs to serve as robust tools in the study of early syntax acquisition.

title: FusionMMT: A Unified Multimodal and Multitask Learning Framework for Nuclear Fusion
summary: With the growing global demand for energy, nuclear fusion has emerged as a promising direction for future clean energy. Tokamaks represent one of the leading approaches to magnetic-confinement fusion. Achieving high-performance, long-pulse, and steady-state operation requires effective diagnosis of plasma states. However, existing intelligent diagnostic methods are largely limited to either multimodal single-task or unimodal multitask learning, while a unified multimodal multitask learning framework remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct EAST-VTD640, a multimodal multitask dataset that integrates vision and time-series diagnostics from 640 EAST shots for disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) recognition, and H98 regression. On this basis, we present FusionMMT, the first unified multimodal multitask framework for intelligent tokamak plasma diagnostics. FusionMMT employs multi-scale, time-aware, and variable-aware modeling to handle heterogeneous sampling rates and the high computational cost of high-frequency sequences. It further combines task-adaptive multimodal fusion with progressive multitask optimization to learn shared and task-specific representations while mitigating cross-task conflicts and optimization imbalance. Extensive experiments on EAST-VTD640 show that FusionMMT outperforms representative multimodal multitask methods across disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression. The source code will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FusionMMT, a unified multimodal multitask learning framework for tokamak plasma diagnostics, built and evaluated on a new dataset (EAST-VTD640) that combines vision and time-series data for disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression, achieving superior performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing intelligent diagnostic methods for tokamak plasmas are typically limited to either multimodal single-task setups (multiple data types but only one prediction task) or unimodal multitask setups (one data type but multiple tasks). There is a lack of a unified framework that can simultaneously handle multiple modalities and multiple diagnostic tasks, which is essential for high-performance, long-pulse, steady-state operation in future fusion devices. Additionally, there was no standardized multimodal multitask dataset for this application, hindering progress and fair comparison of methods.
AI.method: The authors first construct EAST-VTD640, a dataset from 640 EAST tokamak shots that includes both visual and time-series diagnostics and is annotated for three tasks: disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) recognition, and H98 confinement factor regression. On top of this dataset, they propose FusionMMT, a unified multimodal multitask learning framework. FusionMMT integrates: (1) multi-scale, time-aware, and variable-aware sequence modeling to address heterogeneous sampling rates and to reduce the computational load of high-frequency signals; (2) task-adaptive multimodal fusion to balance and combine visual and time-series information differently for each task; and (3) progressive multitask optimization to jointly learn shared and task-specific representations while alleviating gradient conflicts and optimization imbalance between tasks.
AI.result: On the EAST-VTD640 dataset, FusionMMT is empirically compared with representative multimodal multitask baselines. Across all three tasks—disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression—FusionMMT achieves better performance than these baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in leveraging multiple modalities and tasks jointly. The results also validate the usefulness of the EAST-VTD640 dataset as a benchmark for multimodal multitask fusion diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: The work provides both a new benchmark dataset (EAST-VTD640) and a unified multimodal multitask framework (FusionMMT) for intelligent tokamak plasma diagnostics. By explicitly handling heterogeneous temporal resolutions and employing task-adaptive fusion with progressive multitask optimization, FusionMMT achieves state-of-the-art performance on disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression. This demonstrates the potential of multimodal multitask learning to support high-performance, steady-state operation in future fusion reactors, and the public release of code (and presumably data) is intended to facilitate further research in this direction.

title: Receptiveness, Not Sycophancy: Distinguishing Engagement from Deference in Language Models
summary: A central concern with language models is sycophancy: their tendency to defer to users' views at the expense of independent substantive judgment. In parallel, work on social sycophancy has focused on behaviors such as validation and positivity that may signal inappropriate deference. Yet the markers of social sycophancy are also characteristic of conversational receptiveness, a construct from social psychology shown to improve interactions across disagreement. We argue that this overlap creates a construct-validity problem for social sycophancy evaluations. Using a popular moral-advice dataset, we find that responses classified as more socially sycophantic are also more receptive. Further, increasing the receptiveness of human-written responses---while preserving their substantive conclusions---causes them to be classified as more socially sycophantic. This tight coupling raises the possibility that social sycophancy evaluations inadvertently penalize desirable behavior. In a preregistered experiment comparing substantively equivalent responses, participants prefer the more receptive responses, expect users to be more likely to listen to them, and are more willing to seek advice from their authors. The same overall pattern persists even among participants who believe the original question asker is in the wrong. Finally, we introduce a simple approach that substantially increases receptiveness without increasing substantive deference, demonstrating that conversational receptiveness and substantive independence can be achieved together.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current ways of measuring “social sycophancy” in language models are flawed because they confuse it with conversational receptiveness—an interaction style that is actually beneficial—and shows how to increase receptiveness without increasing undue deference.
AI.motivation: Language models are criticized for sycophancy: agreeing with or deferring to users instead of giving independent judgments. In human social psychology, similar concerns focus on behaviors like excessive validation and positivity. However, those same behaviors are central to conversational receptiveness, which is known to improve dialogue across disagreements. This overlap suggests that automatic or rubric-based evaluations of social sycophancy may be misclassifying genuinely healthy, constructive behavior as undesirable, creating a construct-validity problem that could misguide both research and alignment efforts.
AI.method: The authors analyze a widely used moral-advice dataset and apply existing social-sycophancy classifiers to model and human responses. They then systematically edit human-written responses to make them more conversationally receptive while holding their substantive conclusions constant, and measure how these edits affect sycophancy scores. Next, they run a preregistered human-subjects experiment in which participants compare pairs of substantively equivalent responses that differ in receptiveness, rating preferences, perceived effectiveness, and willingness to seek advice from the responder, including cases where the question-asker is judged to be in the wrong. Finally, they prototype a simple intervention for generating responses that explicitly targets higher receptiveness without changing the underlying level of substantive agreement or deference to the user.
AI.result: They find that responses classified as more socially sycophantic are also rated as more conversationally receptive. When they increase the receptiveness of human responses without changing their bottom-line conclusions, these responses are mechanically classified as more socially sycophantic, indicating that the classifier conflates receptiveness with deference. In the human experiment, participants systematically prefer the more receptive version of each response, think users are more likely to listen to it, and report greater willingness to seek advice from its author. These effects remain even for respondents who believe the original question asker is in the wrong, suggesting that receptiveness improves perceived quality and impact without implying substantive agreement. Their simple generation approach successfully produces responses that are more receptive while not increasing measured substantive deference.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that prevalent evaluations of social sycophancy in language models suffer from a construct-validity problem: they tend to penalize conversational receptiveness, a socially beneficial behavior, by misclassifying it as sycophancy. As a result, current metrics may push models away from desirable styles of disagreement-handling and advice-giving. The authors argue that future work must more carefully distinguish between social markers of warmth/receptiveness and actual substantive deference to user views, and they demonstrate that it is feasible to design generation strategies that enhance receptiveness without increasing sycophantic agreement. Properly separating these constructs is crucial for aligning language models toward both honesty and high-quality, user-preferred interactions.

title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
summary: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

AI.tldr: A deep-learning model combining multiparametric MRI and key clinical data predicts pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer with high AUC (up to 0.86).
AI.motivation: To noninvasively and accurately predict pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer patients using only pretreatment data, which would allow better personalized treatment planning and possibly spare some patients from ineffective or overly aggressive therapies.
AI.method: The authors developed a deep-learning classification model that takes as input pretreatment apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, and selected clinical variables. They used the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. EfficientNet-B0 networks, pretrained on natural images, were used as encoders to extract imaging features separately from ADC and DCE MRI. Clinical variables were fused in a late-fusion scheme with the imaging features. Multiple clinical variables (age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum tumor diameter) were tested, and only HR/HER2 subtype was kept in the final model as it improved predictive performance. Model performance was assessed with stratified five-fold cross-validation using AUC as the main metric.
AI.result: Standalone ADC-based models achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, while standalone DCE-MRI-based models achieved a mean AUC of 0.74 for predicting pathological complete response. When HR/HER2 subtype was added as a clinical input, performance increased to 0.83 for ADC and 0.81 for DCE. The best-performing configuration combined both imaging modalities (ADC and DCE) with HR/HER2 subtype, achieving an AUC of 0.86 in cross-validation.
AI.conclusion: A multimodal deep-learning approach that integrates multiparametric MRI (ADC and DCE) with HR/HER2 subtype can effectively predict pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy using only pretreatment data in breast cancer patients. ADC appears more predictive than DCE alone, and inclusion of biologically meaningful clinical information (HR/HER2 subtype) yields additional gains. While results are promising and support the value of multimodal learning for treatment-response prediction, external validation on independent cohorts is necessary before clinical adoption.

title: Semantic Abstraction for Natural Language Inference: a Methodological Framework for Discovering and Compensating Semantic Knowledge and Reasoning Gaps in Large Language Models
comment: 59 pages, 13 figures. Preprint of the article published in Knowledge-Based Systems, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2025.114825
summary: Despite their outstanding performance on many NLP tasks, LLMs face serious challenges related to semantic abstraction. In this study, we are interested in understanding how LLMs leverage abstract semantic knowledge in natural language inference (NLI), which requires sophisticated linguistic capabilities to interpret implicit meanings, contextual conceptual relationships, and semantic connections between words and phrases. To this end, we propose a methodological framework for constructing new semantic knowledge at a higher level of abstraction, which we define under the notions of semantic compatibility and incompatibility for NLI. In this framework, the meaning of the lexical-semantic relations between the premise and the hypothesis is reconfigured to achieve a more flexible semantic network that induces different reasoning paths in LLMs. These new pathways show a consistent pattern of responses that allows agreement on a single response. The results demonstrate that our proposal allows to discover and compensate for LLMs' semantic knowledge gaps in NLI, achieving significant improvements in accuracy, exceeding 10% for some models, and in particular for the non-entailment class. It is essential to note that LLMs need structured knowledge and not just more data to bridge reasoning gaps. Our hybrid approach directs attention to overlooked word relationships, allowing models to synthesize missing information. We believe that the future lies not in increasing model size, but in creating a semantic scafolding that mimics the flexibility of human thinking. Hopefully, our proposal will enable the development of more robust agents and interpretable reasoning, guiding AI toward reliable language understanding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework to inject higher-level semantic compatibility/incompatibility knowledge into NLI for LLMs, improving accuracy (especially for non-entailment) by over 10% on some models.
AI.motivation: LLMs, despite strong performance, struggle with semantic abstraction in tasks like NLI, particularly in capturing implicit meanings, contextual relationships, and flexible semantic connections. The authors want to diagnose and reduce these semantic knowledge gaps.
AI.method: They define and construct higher-level semantic knowledge in terms of semantic compatibility and incompatibility between premise and hypothesis. By reconfiguring lexical-semantic relations into a more flexible semantic network, they create new reasoning paths for LLMs and use this hybrid, structured-knowledge approach to guide models’ attention to overlooked word relationships.
AI.result: The introduced semantic scaffolding yields consistent reasoning patterns across LLMs and enables them to agree on a single response more often. Empirically, it leads to substantial NLI accuracy gains, surpassing 10% for some models, with particularly notable improvements on the non-entailment class.
AI.conclusion: Simply scaling or giving more data is insufficient; LLMs need structured semantic knowledge that scaffolds abstract reasoning. The proposed framework helps fill semantic gaps, supports more robust and interpretable reasoning in NLI, and points toward future systems that mimic the flexible semantic networks underlying human thinking.

title: Early Prediction of Pathological Complete Response to Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Using Temporal Deep Learning on DWI
summary: Early identification of non-responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is crucial for timely treatment adaptation in breast cancer. However, many existing predictive models rely on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), late treatment time points, or extensive clinical data, which limits their applicability. This study proposes a deep learning framework for early prediction of pathological complete response (pCR) using only diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) acquired at baseline and after the first NACT cycle. This framework feeds cropped tumor-centered patches to an EfficientNet-based temporal model that directly learns tumor shape and local tissue characteristics without explicit radiomic feature engineering. The model, trained with 10-fold cross-validation, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.90 for pCR prediction after one cycle, providing actionable information after a single treatment cycle while avoiding gadolinium administration and reducing dependence on heterogeneous clinical data. By focusing on the baseline-to-first-cycle window instead of later stages, the approach supports earlier escalation or de-escalation of NACT, and its exclusive reliance on DW-MRI facilitates protocol standardization, multi-centre deployment and privacy-preserving data sharing. These results demonstrate that DW-MRI-based deep learning on tumor-centered patches constitutes a minimally invasive, clinically deployable strategy for early pCR prediction, with direct implications for personalized treatment adaptation in neoadjuvant breast cancer therapy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a deep learning model using only early diffusion-weighted MRI (baseline and post-first chemotherapy cycle) to predict pathological complete response in breast cancer, achieving high accuracy and enabling earlier, less invasive treatment adaptation.
AI.motivation: To enable early identification of breast cancer patients who will not respond to neoadjuvant chemotherapy so clinicians can adapt or change treatment sooner, while avoiding the complexity, contrast agents, late time points, and extensive clinical data required by many existing MRI-based predictive models.
AI.method: The authors design an EfficientNet-based temporal deep learning framework that takes cropped, tumor-centered patches from diffusion-weighted MRI images acquired at baseline and after the first cycle of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The model is trained with 10-fold cross-validation to directly learn tumor morphology and local tissue characteristics over time, without using hand-crafted radiomic features or multiparametric MRI inputs.
AI.result: Using only DW-MRI from baseline and after the first NACT cycle, the model achieves an AUC of 0.90 for predicting pathological complete response, demonstrating strong discriminative performance at an early treatment stage without gadolinium contrast or extensive clinical variables.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning applied to early DW-MRI tumor-centered patches offers a minimally invasive, contrast-free, and clinically practical method for accurately predicting pathological complete response after just one chemotherapy cycle, supporting earlier escalation or de-escalation of neoadjuvant treatment and facilitating standardized, multi-centre, and privacy-preserving deployment.

title: PERSONAWEAVER: Controllable Diversity Beyond Conventional Archetypes in Procedural Character Generation
comment: Accepted at the 1st PANDORA Workshop: Pluralistic AI and NLP
summary: Procedural character generation aims to populate games, simulations, and other virtual worlds with diverse characters. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising foundation for scaling this task. However, LLM-based procedural character generation remains at an early stage: existing methods either generate characters directly or adapt profiles retrieved from persona banks. As we show, both approaches produce behaviorally homogeneous populations: characters overwhelmingly agree with positive moral norms and respond to questions with helpful, assistant-like reactions. To mitigate this homogenization, we introduce PersonaWeaver, which disentangles world building from behavioral specification and models behavior through setting general, diverse, manually curated banks of moral positions and conversational reactions. This design allows us to test how far LLM(s) can be pushed beyond their default behavioral patterns across settings. Across ten realistic and fantastical settings and three LLM(s), PersonaWeaver produces broader moral and interactional response distributions than prior work. Its guidance also diversifies interpersonal language, response length, and sentiment. It also produces less archetypal combinations of world attributes. Code is available at https://github.com/mqraitem/PersonaWeaver.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PersonaWeaver, a framework that uses LLMs to generate more diverse, less homogenized procedural characters by separating world building from behavioral specification and using curated banks of moral and conversational stances.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based procedural character generation methods tend to yield behaviorally homogeneous agents that mostly agree with positive moral norms and act like helpful assistants, which is undesirable for rich, varied virtual worlds. The authors want a way to systematically push LLMs beyond their safe, default persona and explore a broader space of behaviors and interactions.
AI.method: They propose PersonaWeaver, which decouples setting/world attributes from behavioral traits. Instead of directly prompting the LLM for full personas or relying on existing persona banks, they build manually curated, diverse banks of moral positions and conversational reactions. The system composes characters by weaving together world context with sampled positions from these banks, then prompts LLMs to act accordingly across various settings and models.
AI.result: Across ten realistic and fantastical environments and three different LLMs, PersonaWeaver generates character responses with more varied moral judgments and interaction styles than baselines. It broadens distributions over moral and interactional responses, diversifies linguistic aspects like interpersonal tone, response length, and sentiment, and leads to less stereotypical combinations of world attributes compared to prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: PersonaWeaver effectively counters the homogenizing tendencies of LLM-based character generation by modularizing behavior and world building and injecting curated diversity into moral and conversational stances. This demonstrates that, with appropriate guidance, LLMs can be steered to produce richer, more varied character populations for virtual worlds than standard methods allow.

title: DTOC: Dynamic Tool Output Compression for Adaptive Context Management in AI Agents
comment: Accepted for 29th International Conference on Discovery Science, October 5-9, 2026, Mainz, Germany
summary: As agent capabilities have grown, practical limitations increasingly stem from constrained context windows rather than model capacity. Common strategies, such as truncation, heuristic aging, and lossy summarization, may discard useful information or introduce hallucination risk. To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Tool Output Compression (DTOC), a framework for scalable context management in LLM-based agents that models context updates as explicit and reversible operations within the agent reasoning loop. DTOC retains full tool outputs in external memory while inserting compact placeholders into the active context, enabling selective reconstruction when needed. We formalize the DTOC mechanism, integrate it into a ReAct-style agent architecture, and provide a production-oriented implementation supporting on-demand restoration of compressed outputs. Experiments on DeepSWE reveal model-dependent effects: for responsive models (Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4), DTOC reduces input tokens (10.3 and 12.7%) and agent steps (2.4 and 32.3%), while increasing solve rates (2.5 and 1.5 times higher) and lowering cost per solved task (3 and 3.5 times lower cost per solved task). For the other models results are more mixed, with GPT-5.5 doubling solve rate and halving cost, but no impact on solve rate and negative impact on cost for the other models. Ablation results show reversibility is critical: disable-only compression variants degraded performance, while full DTOC recovered baseline accuracy at substantially lower context cost. These findings indicate that explicit, reversible context management can improve the efficiency of long-horizon agent reasoning without degrading task performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dynamic Tool Output Compression (DTOC), a reversible mechanism to compress tool outputs for LLM agents, reducing context usage and cost while maintaining or improving task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are increasingly limited by context window size rather than model capacity. Existing context management approaches—like truncation, aging, and lossy summarization—often discard useful information or introduce hallucinations. There is a need for a scalable, reliable way to manage long-horizon interaction histories and tool outputs without losing important details or harming accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose DTOC, which treats context updates as explicit, reversible operations within an agent’s reasoning loop. Full tool outputs are stored in external memory, while compact placeholders are inserted into the active context. When needed, the agent can selectively reconstruct the original outputs from memory. DTOC is formalized and integrated into a ReAct-style agent architecture, and implemented in a production-ready system that supports on-demand restoration of compressed content. Ablation studies compare full DTOC with disable-only compression variants.
AI.result: On the DeepSWE benchmark, DTOC yields model-dependent gains. For responsive models (Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4), DTOC reduces input tokens by about 10–13%, reduces agent steps by 2–32%, increases solve rates by 1.5–2.5x, and cuts cost per solved task by 3–3.5x. For other models, results are mixed: GPT-5.5 sees doubled solve rate and halved cost, while some models show no solve-rate improvement and even higher costs. Ablations indicate that non-reversible, disable-only compression harms performance, whereas full DTOC recovers baseline accuracy at lower context usage.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, reversible context management via DTOC can significantly improve efficiency and cost-effectiveness for long-horizon LLM agents while preserving or improving task performance, particularly for more responsive models. Maintaining reversibility—i.e., the ability to reconstruct compressed tool outputs on demand—is essential; simple compression without reversibility degrades results. DTOC thus offers a practical framework for scalable context handling in tool-using agents.

title: Knowledge Pull Requests for Continual Document Authoring
summary: We introduce Knowledge Pull Requests (KPRs), a framework for continual document authoring that makes each change interpretable. Documents require ongoing revision as new knowledge surfaces from other sources, languages, or times, but existing approaches either edit with no account of what knowledge changed or regenerate from scratch. A KPR integrates new knowledge into a document by extracting claims, filtering and routing them to sections, and flagging conflicts with existing content, producing a ChangeLog that separates what knowledge changes (claim proposal) from how the text changes (document diff). We evaluate KPRs on revising Wikipedia across languages and updating query-driven reports on RAGTIME.
