By leveraging a legal knowledge graph, adversarial scenario generation, and continuous expert oversight, it uncovers deep, logic-driven compliance anomalies in modern LLMs and offers a better foundation for safeguarding high-level regulatory compliance in practical deployments.

title: TREND-10K: A Comprehensive Dataset for Next-Generation Video Quality Assessment Based on Preference-Driven Media
summary: The increasing prominence of short-video platforms, coupled with the advanced commercialization of AI-generated content (AIGC) videos, has led to a shift in the types of video media trend consumed by users in their daily lives. Traditional user-generated content (UGC) is gradually being replaced by professional short dramas and AIGC entertainment. Consequently, VQA for contemporary media content has become increasingly important. This requires a unified evaluation framework that can handle diverse video content and evolving media trends. In this context, we introduce TREND-10K, a next-generation comprehensive VQA dataset consisting of the trend-driven part and the static part, containing $10,000$ videos across a wide spectrum of content types. The trend-driven part is based on the TREND-Search framework, which captures user preference profiles from trending lists on online platforms and formulates sampling strategies based on these profiles. The static part, on the other hand, is composed of supplementary samples selected from publicly available datasets. To support unified evaluation for various video types, we incorporate three evaluation dimensions: technical, aesthetic, and AIGC-trace. Experiments show that our dataset ensures high annotation quality and exhibits remarkable generalization across multiple content categories. In conclusion, our work presents a robust framework for advancing VQA, addressing challenges caused by the temporal evolution of user perceptual habits and preferences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TREND-10K, a 10,000-video VQA dataset tailored to modern short-video and AIGC platforms, with unified evaluation across technical, aesthetic, and AIGC-trace dimensions.
AI.motivation: Short-video and AI-generated content are reshaping what users watch, making existing VQA datasets and benchmarks—often focused on traditional UGC or limited domains—less representative of real-world media consumption. There is a need for a unified, future-proof VQA framework that reflects evolving user preferences, covers diverse modern content (including AIGC and professional short dramas), and enables consistent evaluation across heterogeneous video types.
AI.method: The authors construct TREND-10K, composed of two parts: (1) a trend-driven part obtained via TREND-Search, which mines trending lists on online platforms to infer user preference profiles and then samples videos according to these profiles; and (2) a static part, assembled from curated samples drawn from existing public datasets to fill coverage gaps. They design a unified VQA scheme with three complementary dimensions—technical quality, aesthetic quality, and AIGC-trace (whether and how a video bears signatures of AI generation)—and collect human annotations along these axes to support training and benchmarking VQA models.
AI.result: The resulting TREND-10K dataset contains 10,000 videos spanning a wide variety of contemporary content types, from UGC-like clips to professional short dramas and AIGC entertainment. Empirical studies reported in the paper indicate that the annotations are of high quality and that models trained or evaluated on TREND-10K generalize well across multiple content categories, outperforming or complementing prior datasets on modern media scenarios.
AI.conclusion: TREND-10K provides a robust, unified benchmark for video quality assessment aligned with current short-video and AIGC trends. By explicitly modeling technical, aesthetic, and AIGC-trace dimensions and by grounding sampling in real-world trending content, the framework helps bridge the gap between traditional VQA research and rapidly evolving user viewing habits, enabling more reliable evaluation and development of VQA methods for next-generation media.

title: Identifying Intelligent Processes via Online Sequential Testing
summary: Active sequential hypothesis testing studies how to identify an unknown hypothesis with a given set of sensing actions. We study this in the setting of identifying large language models (LLMs), \textit{i.e.}, if a user is conversing with an LLM drawn from a known set of models, how can they identify which one is in use? Here, the available sensing actions (evaluations) are themselves a design choice: an evaluator must first decide which environments and prompt families to construct, and only then decide how to use them sequentially. We formalize these two levels as an outer probe-design problem and an inner identification problem. Simply put, the outer stage selects a set of probes to be sent to the entire set of models, creating a kind of fingerprint dataset. This is followed by the inner stage, which sequentially sends a budget-minimizing set of those probes to identify the model in use. For the outer problem, we show that selecting which evaluations to construct at minimum cost, so that every pair of candidates is distinguished, is exactly a weighted set cover problem. Since the response distributions of the candidate models are not known exactly but only through calibration samples, we give a one-shot procedure that estimates the cover instance from these samples. For the inner problem, we bound the number of evaluations needed to identify the unknown model in terms of how well the available evaluations distinguish each pair of candidates.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to efficiently identify which LLM from a known set is being interacted with, using actively chosen tests.
AI.motivation: As LLM providers and models proliferate, users, auditors, or regulators may need to reliably tell which specific model is behind an interface. Existing active hypothesis-testing frameworks assume fixed tests and known distributions, but here both the tests (probes) and the model response statistics must be designed and learned for LLMs.
AI.method: The authors cast the problem as a two-level active sequential hypothesis testing task. In the outer level, they design a collection of probes (environments and prompt families) to distinguish every pair of candidate LLMs at minimum construction cost, showing that this is equivalent to a weighted set cover problem and giving a sample-based procedure to build the instance from calibration data. In the inner level, given the designed probes and their estimated response distributions, they develop and analyze a sequential strategy that adaptively selects probes to minimize the number of evaluations needed to identify the model, with performance characterized by pairwise distinguishability.
AI.result: They prove that outer-stage probe selection is exactly a weighted set cover instance and give a one-shot way to estimate this from finite samples of model responses. For the inner identification stage, they derive bounds on the required number of probe evaluations in terms of statistical separability between models under the chosen probes.
AI.conclusion: Designing LLM-identification procedures naturally decomposes into probe design (a combinatorial set-cover task under sampling noise) plus sequential testing using those probes. With appropriate probe sets and sequential strategies, one can identify which LLM is in use with bounded and, in principle, efficiently controlled evaluation cost.

title: RCShift: Certifying When Partial Linkage Suffices for Finite-Sample Decisions
summary: Systems with costly gold outcomes and cheaper auxiliary observations must decide how much record linkage to retain. Complete pairing retains every joint counter, while separate margins retain none. Neither endpoint is calibrated to a declared finite-sample decision. Universal reconstruction can retain cycle directions invisible to the likelihood-ratio family. Family-exact storage can exceed what the decision requires because certified residual loss may fit within finite-sample slack. We introduce RCShift, which certifies two routes to sufficiency under a declared observation contract. Its exact mode characterizes minimum-cost family-exact storage through LR-visible cycle directions. Its approximate mode bounds reverse Le Cam deficiency. Its integer mode certifies whether a chosen set preserves the full experiment's minimum integer record count at specified size and power. In a rank-two witness, one aligned counter preserves a four-record minimum. An equal-cost misaligned counter and the margins require eleven records, while universal reconstruction requires two counters. A local perturbation has positive reverse deficiency yet retains the four-record minimum. Proof-checked scheduling bounds instantiate the contract before gold computation and yield exact reconstruction on the admitted tree support. RCShift turns partial-linkage storage into decision-calibrated measurement design for the declared family, costs, target, and common strictly positive support.

AI.tldr: RCShift is a framework for deciding how much record linkage to store so that downstream decisions remain statistically optimal at minimum storage cost under a declared finite-sample decision task.
AI.motivation: In many systems, fully linking records across data sources (“complete pairing”) is expensive, but discarding linkage and keeping only separate margins can harm statistical decisions. Existing approaches are not calibrated to a specific finite-sample decision problem and may over- or under-store information, especially when subtle dependence structures (e.g., cycle directions) matter but are not visible to standard likelihood-ratio comparisons. A principled way is needed to decide which partial linkages to keep so that decisions are near-optimal while controlling storage cost under a concrete observation contract (family, costs, target performance).
AI.method: The paper introduces RCShift, which formalizes an observation contract and then analyzes which combinations of linked counters are sufficient for the declared decision. RCShift has three modes: (1) an exact mode that characterizes minimum-cost family-exact storage by identifying the likelihood-ratio-visible cycle directions that must be preserved; (2) an approximate mode that gives bounds on reverse Le Cam deficiency, quantifying how much statistical power is lost when using a reduced experiment; and (3) an integer mode that checks whether a proposed set of counters preserves the full experiment’s minimum integer record count for the specified size and power. The framework uses proof-checked scheduling bounds, instantiated before computing the expensive “gold” outcomes, to guarantee that reconstruction is exact on the supported tree of admitted observations.
AI.result: The paper shows that RCShift can sharply distinguish between storage schemes that are decision-sufficient and those that are not, even when they have similar cost. In a rank-two witness example, it proves that a single aligned counter is enough to preserve the experiment’s four-record minimum, whereas an equal-cost misaligned counter plus marginal counts requires eleven records to achieve the same guarantees, and universal reconstruction would need two counters. It also exhibits a local perturbation that has positive reverse deficiency yet still preserves the four-record minimum, illustrating that finite-sample decision requirements can be met even when classic deficiency metrics are nonzero.
AI.conclusion: RCShift provides a decision-calibrated method for designing partial-linkage storage. By certifying sufficiency either exactly or approximately, and by connecting these certifications to finite-sample size and power constraints, it turns the abstract problem of which linkages to store into a concrete, contract-based measurement design task. Under the assumed family, costs, target, and common strictly positive support, RCShift can minimize storage while guaranteeing that downstream decisions match or closely approximate those of the full experiment, and it offers constructive, proof-checkable schedules for when and how to compute expensive gold outcomes.

title: Improved Multiplayer Bandit Algorithm for Bernoulli Rewards
summary: We study the multiplayer multi-armed bandit problem with information asymmetry under Bernoulli rewards, for three information structures: asymmetry in actions, in rewards, and in both. Replacing the Hoeffding-style confidence intervals of prior work with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-based bounds gives strictly tighter regret guarantees in each case. We propose \texttt{mKL-UCB}, \texttt{mKL-UCB-Intervals} and \texttt{mKL-DSEE}, and show that the improvement factor is at least two by Pinsker's inequality and far larger when reward means are near zero or one. For asymmetry in rewards we prove that two arms' KL intervals separate after a deterministic number of samples, and that $M$ independent players accelerate elimination further.

AI.tldr: The paper improves regret bounds for multiplayer multi-armed bandits with information asymmetry by using KL-based confidence bounds instead of Hoeffding ones.
AI.motivation: Prior work on multiplayer multi-armed bandits with information asymmetry used Hoeffding-style confidence intervals, which are suboptimal, leading to looser regret guarantees. The authors want to tighten these guarantees and better exploit the Bernoulli reward structure.
AI.method: They consider three information structures: asymmetry in actions, in rewards, and in both. For each, they design bandit algorithms—mKL-UCB, mKL-UCB-Intervals, and mKL-DSEE—that use confidence intervals derived from Kullback–Leibler divergence tailored to Bernoulli rewards instead of traditional Hoeffding bounds. They analyze the regret of these algorithms and compare it with previous Hoeffding-based approaches.
AI.result: For all three information asymmetry settings, the KL-based algorithms obtain strictly tighter regret bounds than their Hoeffding-based counterparts. The improvement factor is shown to be at least two via Pinsker's inequality, and can be much larger when arm means are close to 0 or 1. For the reward-asymmetry case, they prove that the KL confidence intervals for any two arms become disjoint after a deterministic sample size, and that having M independent players further accelerates the elimination of suboptimal arms.
AI.conclusion: KL-based confidence bounds yield provably better regret guarantees than Hoeffding-style bounds in multiplayer Bernoulli bandits with information asymmetry. The proposed algorithms mKL-UCB, mKL-UCB-Intervals, and mKL-DSEE exploit the reward distribution more efficiently, particularly when arm means are extreme, and multiple players help speed up arm elimination under reward asymmetry.

title: A Hybrid AI Framework for Academic Advising: Integrating Ensemble-Based Grade Prediction and a Rule-Based Expert System
summary: The rapidly increasing student population has posed serious challenges to the traditional academic advising process. This study designs and implements a multi-purpose intelligent system to support students' academic progress, based on a two-part hybrid framework: (1) an advanced model for grade prediction and (2) a rule-based recommendation engine. Using a dataset containing 416,558 educational records from the University of Birjand, students were first divided into homogeneous clusters using the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Subsequently, a Stacking Ensemble model combining Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and MLP was trained specifically for each cluster. Evaluation results demonstrated that the Stacking model outperformed base models across all clusters, achieving a final aggregated RMSE of 2.35. The second component is an expert system that provides intelligent recommendations by synergizing educational regulations with the grades predicted by the first component. This system has been implemented as a practical tool on the University of Birjand portal, offering students real-time feedback such as semester GPA prediction, probation risk warnings, and course suggestions for GPA improvement.

AI.tldr: They build and deploy an intelligent advising system that predicts students’ grades with a cluster-specific stacking model and then uses a rule-based expert engine to turn those predictions into actionable advising recommendations.
AI.motivation: Traditional one-to-one academic advising does not scale to rapidly growing student populations. Advisors struggle to continuously monitor student performance, anticipate risks like probation, and propose personalized course plans. The authors aim to create an automated, data-driven system that can support or augment human advisors by accurately forecasting grades and giving timely, individualized guidance.
AI.method: They use 416,558 records from the University of Birjand. First, they cluster students into homogeneous groups using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). For each cluster, they train a Stacking Ensemble model that combines Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to predict grades. They evaluate this hybrid approach via RMSE and compare it with its base learners. On top of the prediction component, they design a rule-based expert system that encodes educational regulations and uses predicted grades as inputs to generate specific advising recommendations. The whole system is implemented on the university portal to operate in real time.
AI.result: The cluster-specific stacking ensemble yields better performance than any of the individual base models in every cluster, with an overall aggregated RMSE of 2.35 for grade prediction. The expert system successfully produces a variety of advising outputs—including predicted semester GPA, early warnings about probation risk, and recommended courses intended to improve GPA—and is operational on the university’s online portal.
AI.conclusion: A two-part hybrid framework—combining unsupervised clustering, a stacking ensemble for grade prediction, and a rule-based expert system—can effectively support scalable, data-driven academic advising. By integrating predictive analytics with institutional rules and deploying the system in the university portal, the authors provide students with real-time, personalized, and practically useful feedback that can complement or partially automate traditional advising.

title: A Multi-Timestep LSTM Ensemble regressor for Enhanced Short-Term Runoff Prediction
summary: Accurately forecasting river runoff is key to managing water resources, controlling floods, and planning agriculture. This study examines the Ajichay River in northwest Iran, a major tributary of Lake Urmia that has experienced increasing water-related stress in recent years. We introduce a daily runoff prediction model based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The model combines five LSTM units, each trained on different time intervals ranging from 2 to 6 days, to better capture variations in river flow patterns. To improve performance, each model was fine-tuned using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a population-based optimization algorithm. The proposed approach was evaluated on unseen data from 2017-2018 using $R^2$, RMSE, and MSE as performance metrics. The results showed strong predictive accuracy, with $R^2$ values ranging from 74.95% to 91.42%. In addition, multiple feature-importance methods were applied to identify the most influential variables, providing further insight into the factors that drive runoff variations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a daily river runoff forecasting model using an ensemble of LSTM networks, each trained on different time lags and optimized via PSO, achieving high predictive accuracy and analyzing feature importance for the Ajichay River.
AI.motivation: Reliable river runoff forecasts are critical for water-resource management, flood control, and agricultural planning, especially in basins under increasing water stress such as the Ajichay River feeding Lake Urmia. Traditional models may struggle with the nonlinear, time-dependent nature of runoff, motivating the use of advanced deep-learning approaches that can capture complex temporal patterns and improve decision-making.
AI.method: The study builds an ensemble-like model of five separate LSTM networks, each using different input time windows (2–6 days) to model daily runoff. Each LSTM is hyperparameter-tuned using Particle Swarm Optimization to enhance predictive performance. The final system is evaluated on unseen data from 2017–2018 with standard regression metrics ($R^2$, RMSE, MSE), and various feature-importance techniques are applied to determine which input variables most strongly influence runoff predictions.
AI.result: The optimized LSTM models demonstrate strong forecasting skill, with $R^2$ values between 74.95% and 91.42% on the test period (2017–2018), alongside correspondingly low RMSE/MSE values (not numerically specified in the abstract). Feature-importance analyses identify a subset of variables as dominant drivers of runoff variability, highlighting which hydrometeorological factors most affect daily discharge in the Ajichay River.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble of PSO-tuned LSTM models using multiple input time windows can effectively predict daily river runoff in a stressed basin, achieving high accuracy and offering interpretable insights via feature importance. This framework can support operational water-management decisions in the Ajichay basin and is potentially transferable to other river systems with similar data availability and management challenges.

title: Coding Agents are Strong Prompt Optimizers
summary: Search-based prompt optimizers improve prompts through iterative search: they propose edits, execute fresh rollouts, score the resulting trajectories, and retain only edits that improve a validation metric. We show that this optimization loop is unnecessary. Given only a static corpus of agent trajectories, an off-the-shelf coding agent can directly synthesize an optimized prompt, requiring neither environment access nor validation data. We call this approach \textit{Coding-Agent Skill Distillation} (CASD). The key insight is reflection scope. Rather than reasoning over a small batch of trajectories at each optimization step, the coding agent writes and executes analysis code to compute corpus-wide statistics, identifies systematic failure modes, inspects representative episodes, and distills the resulting insights into behavioral rules. Across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, $τ^2$-bench retail and telecom, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), under matched data access, a single CASD pass outperforms GEPA, a state-of-the-art reflective prompt optimizer, on three of four benchmarks and outperforms validation-gated reflective search (SkillOpt) on all four, improving the unoptimized baseline by 16.6 percentage points on average versus 10.9 for GEPA and 5.3 for SkillOpt. Because CASD performs a single offline analysis pass rather than iterative search, producing an optimized prompt costs approximately \$1.60---over $22\times$ cheaper than validation-gated search. Even when competing methods are granted additional validation data and unrestricted environment access, CASD remains ahead on two of four benchmarks. These results suggest that corpus-scale statistical reflection is a viable alternative to iterative search for prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Coding-Agent Skill Distillation (CASD), a non-iterative, offline method that learns an optimized prompt from a static corpus of agent trajectories using a coding-capable LLM, outperforming existing search-based prompt optimizers in effectiveness and cost.
AI.motivation: Existing search-based prompt optimization methods require iterative interaction with the environment and validation data: they repeatedly modify prompts, re-run agents, and retain changes that improve some validation metric. This makes them expensive, slow, and dependent on online rollouts. The authors want to know if this iterative optimization loop is actually necessary, and whether one can instead derive strong prompts purely from an offline dataset of past trajectories, without additional environment access or validation sets.
AI.method: They introduce Coding-Agent Skill Distillation (CASD). A coding-capable LLM is given a static corpus of agent trajectories and tasked with analyzing it via code: it computes corpus-wide statistics, identifies systematic failure modes, examines representative episodes, and converts these findings into concrete behavioral rules that constitute a new optimized prompt. This is done in a single pass, without iterative online search or validation gating. They compare CASD against state-of-the-art reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA and SkillOpt under matched data access, and also under settings where competing methods have extra validation data and full environment access.
AI.result: On four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, τ^2-bench retail, τ^2-bench telecom, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), with matched data access, CASD outperforms GEPA on three of four benchmarks and outperforms SkillOpt on all four. CASD improves the unoptimized baseline by 16.6 percentage points on average, versus 10.9 points for GEPA and 5.3 for SkillOpt. CASD’s single offline analysis pass costs about $1.60 to produce an optimized prompt, over 22× cheaper than validation-gated search. Even when other methods are granted more validation data and unrestricted environment access, CASD still leads on two of the four benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Iterative, validation-gated search is not strictly necessary for strong prompt optimization. A coding-capable LLM can perform corpus-scale statistical reflection over offline trajectories and distill systematic insights into effective prompts in a single pass. CASD proves to be both more effective and substantially cheaper than leading search-based prompt optimizers on several benchmarks, suggesting that offline statistical analysis is a viable and competitive paradigm for prompt optimization.

title: Decoupling Is Not Identification: Supervised Evidential Learning in Next-Token Prediction
summary: A next-token probability says what a model predicts, not how much training support lies behind it. A Dirichlet head can represent this distinction by separating mean $m$ from concentration $S$, but decoupling does not identify what $S$ means. Here we propose an Evidential Next-Token Prediction (ENTOP) framework to audit this gap on character-level Moby-Dick, using exact 8-gram count as a reproducible lexical-support label and withholding count regression from 20% of context types. Standard implicit evidential training carries essentially no count signal beyond confidence on held-out-label types (partial Spearman $ρ= 0.001 \pm 0.014$), whereas explicit supervision generalizes ($ρ= 0.201 \pm 0.010$; matched-pair win $= 0.822 \pm 0.021$). CE predictive entropy is at chance for unseen 8-grams (AUROC $= 0.490 \pm 0.004$), while supervised vacuity reaches $0.772 \pm 0.003$, comparable with an indexed CE-representation baseline ($0.769$) but below the tautological corpus oracle ($1.000$). Neither longest-suffix nor representation-distance strata explain where amortization succeeds. Increasing count weight under the digamma objective improves support fit only by sacrificing prediction. A constant predictor wins natural log-RMSE, and vacuity does not improve error deferral. These results motivate a minimum evidence protocol---confidence control, matched pairs, held-out labels, a constant baseline, and a decision test---and show that concentration can pass identification while failing calibration and utility.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well a language model’s uncertainty head (Dirichlet concentration) reflects actual training data support, and finds that naive evidential methods largely fail, proposing a protocol to properly evaluate and supervise such signals.
AI.motivation: Next-token probabilities conflate prediction with how much evidence from training data supports that prediction. Dirichlet-style evidential heads promise to separate these via mean vs. concentration, but it is unclear what the concentration parameter actually corresponds to in practice. The authors want a controlled, reproducible setting to test whether evidential heads truly encode lexical support and provide useful uncertainty for language models.
AI.method: They introduce the Evidential Next-Token Prediction (ENTOP) framework on character-level Moby-Dick. They treat the exact 8-gram training count as a gold-standard ‘lexical support’ label, and withhold these count labels for 20% of context types to test generalization. They compare standard implicit evidential training (where concentration is only indirectly trained through prediction) versus explicit supervision on counts. They evaluate with correlation (Spearman ρ), win-rate in matched pairs, AUROC for detecting unseen 8-grams, log-RMSE vs. a constant baseline, and examine structural factors like suffix length and representation distance. They also study trade-offs between fitting support counts and predictive accuracy under a digamma objective.
AI.result: Implicit evidential training conveys almost no information about true counts beyond what is in prediction confidence (Spearman ρ≈0 with held-out types). Explicit count supervision yields moderate but clear generalization (ρ≈0.20 and high matched-pair win rate). Cross-entropy predictive entropy is useless for detecting unseen 8-grams (AUROC ~0.49), whereas supervised vacuity is much better (AUROC ~0.77), close to a representation-indexed CE baseline and below an oracle based on corpus counts. Structural heuristics like longest matching suffix or representation distance do not explain where amortization works. Increasing the weight on count-fitting in the loss only improves support estimation by harming predictive performance. A trivial constant-support predictor beats learned models in natural log-RMSE, and vacuity-based deferral does not improve error deferral performance.
AI.conclusion: Simply adding a Dirichlet/evidential head does not ensure that the concentration parameter meaningfully tracks training support or yields useful uncertainty: concentration can be identifiable in optimization terms yet poorly calibrated and of limited practical value. The authors recommend a minimum evidence evaluation protocol—confidence control, matched-pair comparisons, held-out support labels, a constant baseline, and an explicit decision test—to rigorously validate evidential heads. Explicit supervision on evidence signals helps but remains imperfect, underscoring that evidential modeling in language models requires careful design and auditing rather than being assumed trustworthy by default.

title: FISSION: Label Augmentation for Bot Detection
summary: Bot accounts and coordinated influence operations are often discovered via heuristic methods, leaving a dearth of reliable ground-truth labels for training detection systems. To address this challenge, we study a natural question: can we generate labels to assist in learning embeddings in which bots and accounts from the same coordinated operation are close? We present FISSION, a method to generate labels by splitting each account's activity into positively labeled sub-accounts. Given this label source, we train detection models which preserve behavioral regularities recurring across positive sub-accounts. We evaluate FISSION and show it outperforms prior methods in detecting Wikipedia sockpuppets and Twitter/X bots.

AI.tldr: FISSION generates pseudo-labels by splitting each account’s activity into multiple sub-accounts, enabling better embeddings for bot and coordinated-operation detection.
AI.motivation: Detecting bots and coordinated influence operations needs labeled data, but most existing labels come from ad-hoc heuristics and are unreliable or scarce. The authors seek a way to automatically generate useful labels to train better behavior-based detection models.
AI.method: They propose FISSION: for each account, its activity history is partitioned into several segments, treated as separate “sub-accounts” that all inherit a positive label for belonging to the same underlying actor. Models are then trained so that these positive sub-accounts are embedded close together, learning to capture behavioral regularities that persist over time and across segments.
AI.result: Using these automatically generated labels as supervision, their learned embeddings and detection models outperform previous approaches at identifying Wikipedia sockpuppet accounts and Twitter/X bot accounts.
AI.conclusion: Automatically generated intra-account labels via activity splitting provide a strong supervisory signal for learning behavior embeddings, leading to improved detection of bots and coordinated accounts without relying on expensive or noisy external ground-truth labels.

title: Dual-Frontier: When Can an Agent Trust Its World Model?
summary: Learned world models are becoming essential to general-purpose agents: by predicting action consequences, they support planning and decision-making while reducing reliance on costly trial and error. This reliance creates a fundamental ambiguity: when a world-model-guided decision fails, the trajectory alone may not reveal whether the agent's decision rule or the world model caused the loss. We formalize this failure-attribution problem as a counterfactual decomposition of return loss and prove that its components are not identifiable from passive interaction, even for finite-horizon planners. This obstruction motivates Dual-Frontier, a learning principle that admits a world-model-guided decision only when its predicted advantage exceeds a certified bound on decision-relevant world-model error; otherwise, evidence is allocated to world-model verification. Action-conditioned value bounds and a closed-loop extension guarantee non-decreasing return for admitted decisions. Calibrated gates and simultaneous confidence sequences support adaptive evidence reuse, with sufficient and necessary verification bounds. Controlled learned-model experiments validate the predicted failure modes and certification behavior, while cross-backbone tool-use benchmarks instantiate the same verify-then-promote rule in realistic agent world-model pipelines, consistently improving decision quality and reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how to safely use learned world models for decision-making by only trusting them when their predicted advantage exceeds a certified bound on their possible error, thereby avoiding performance degradation.
AI.motivation: When agents use learned world models for planning, failures can result either from a bad decision rule or an inaccurate world model, but observed trajectories alone cannot clearly attribute the cause. This ambiguity obstructs principled improvement of either component and raises safety and reliability concerns for model-based decision-making.
AI.method: The authors formalize the failure-attribution problem as a counterfactual decomposition of return loss and prove that, under passive interaction, the contributions of the decision rule and the world model are not identifiable, even in finite-horizon settings. To address this, they introduce Dual-Frontier, a learning principle that admits world-model-guided actions only if the model’s predicted advantage exceeds a certified upper bound on decision-relevant model error. They derive action-conditioned value bounds, a closed-loop extension to ensure non-decreasing return, and use calibrated statistical gates with simultaneous confidence sequences to adaptively reuse verification evidence and characterize sufficient and necessary verification conditions.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that the counterfactual components of return loss are unidentifiable from passive data and that decisions admitted under Dual-Frontier enjoy guarantees of non-decreasing return given the established bounds. Empirical studies with controlled learned-model experiments confirm the predicted failure modes and the correctness of the certification mechanism. Additional experiments on cross-backbone tool-use benchmarks demonstrate that embedding the same verify-then-promote rule into realistic agent pipelines improves both decision quality and reliability across different world-model architectures.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that failure attribution between world models and decision rules is fundamentally limited from passive interaction data, necessitating new learning principles. Dual-Frontier provides such a principle by tightly coupling decision admission to certified world-model reliability, yielding provably safe or non-degrading decisions in theory and improved robustness and performance in practice. This verify-then-promote strategy offers a practical blueprint for building more trustworthy model-based agents that can leverage learned world models without sacrificing reliability.

title: Reliability Theory for AI Control
summary: Reliability theory gives a mature language for layered systems, but its formal tools are not yet standard in frontier AI control. We apply them to Google DeepMind's defenses against rogue deployment. The same control stack can have cubic, quadratic, or linear rare-failure suppression depending on its failure domains. Birnbaum importance identifies which component improvements buy the most nominal reliability, while prevention changes the population on which recovery is demanded. These results give concrete guidance about what to separate, improve, measure, and test.

AI.tldr: The paper applies reliability theory to analyze and improve the robustness of Google DeepMind's multi-layered defenses against rogue AI deployment, providing guidance on system design and testing.
AI.motivation: While reliability theory is well-developed for analyzing layered engineering systems, its formal methods are not commonly applied to cutting-edge AI safety and control mechanisms. The authors aim to bridge this gap by using reliability tools to better understand and optimize DeepMind's defenses against unintended or rogue deployment of AI systems.
AI.method: The authors model DeepMind's defense stack as a layered reliability system and analyze it using concepts such as failure domains, rare-failure suppression scaling (cubic, quadratic, linear), and Birnbaum importance. They distinguish between components that contribute to preventing failures versus those that enable recovery, and examine how changes in these components affect overall system reliability.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the same high-level control stack can have vastly different rare-failure suppression behavior (cubic, quadratic, linear) depending on how failures are correlated and how components are separated into failure domains. Birnbaum importance highlights which specific components yield the largest gains in nominal reliability when improved, while prevention mechanisms alter which scenarios require recovery, thus reshaping the reliability profile.
AI.conclusion: Reliability theory provides actionable, quantitative guidance for AI control stack design. By carefully structuring failure domains, focusing improvements on components with high Birnbaum importance, and distinguishing prevention from recovery, designers can significantly enhance robustness against rogue deployment. The paper recommends using these tools to decide what to separate, improve, instrument, and test in safety-critical AI infrastructures.

title: The Source of Disturbance Matters: External, Internal, and Control-Generated Noise in Adaptive Regulation
summary: Adaptive regulation can itself perturb the state it is intended to stabilize. In replicated simulations of an adaptive agent, we compare external disturbance, persistent internally generated disturbance, and control-generated disturbance under regulation-first and disturbance-first ordering. Persistent internal disturbance produces the largest exposure and regulatory burden within the tested parameter grid. When positive controller updates generate an immediate disturbance cost, increasing that cost produces a nonmonotonic response: effective disturbance initially rises, variability across stochastic runs increases over an intermediate range, and corrective activity becomes strongly suppressed at higher costs. The results show how disturbance source and timing shape exposure and controller burden in this model. They motivate testing adaptive agents with distinct disturbance sources and assessing regulatory activity alongside exposure.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different sources and timings of disturbance affect both exposure and regulatory burden in an adaptive control model, showing that persistent internal disturbances are most taxing and that penalizing control updates can suppress needed corrective actions in a nonmonotonic way.
AI.motivation: To understand how adaptive regulatory systems—such as control algorithms or biological homeostatic mechanisms—are themselves perturbed by the very adaptations they perform, and how different sources and timings of disturbance change both the exposure to disturbance and the cost of regulation.
AI.method: The authors run replicated simulations of an adaptive agent under a range of parameter settings. They systematically compare three disturbance types (external disturbance, persistent internally generated disturbance, and control-generated disturbance) and two orderings (regulation-first vs. disturbance-first). They also vary the immediate cost attached to positive controller updates and analyze how this affects effective disturbance, variability across stochastic runs, and corrective activity.
AI.result: Within the explored parameter grid, persistent internal disturbance produces the greatest exposure to disturbance and the highest regulatory burden. When positive controller updates carry an immediate disturbance cost, raising that cost produces a nonmonotonic pattern: effective disturbance first increases, then variability between stochastic runs becomes larger over an intermediate cost range, and, at high costs, corrective regulatory activity is greatly suppressed.
AI.conclusion: Disturbance origin (external vs. internal vs. control-induced) and timing (regulation-first vs. disturbance-first) substantially shape both exposure and regulatory effort in the model. The findings imply that evaluating adaptive agents requires considering multiple disturbance sources and explicitly measuring regulatory activity, not just exposure outcomes.

title: Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents
summary: AI agents are beginning to automate research and development across the AI stack, from improving training efficiency to optimizing inference. A natural next step is to improve the research efficiency of the agents themselves. When an AI research agent's own code is the object of optimization, each accepted rewrite becomes the agent that the next round edits. We refer to this loop as recursive self-improvement. Its significance lies in a long-standing trend, in which increased cumulative spending on R&D yields diminishing returns. Sustained self-improvement offers a way to counter this trend. We present AIDE^2, a system that implements this loop for a frontier AI research agent. It proposes changes to its own code, benchmarks modified versions of itself on a suite of AI R&D tasks, and keeps the changes that perform best on hidden evaluations. In an autonomous 8-day run, AIDE^2 discovered seven successive improvements, ranging from a new search policy to memory mechanisms that compress and manage the agent's growing context. These gains generalize to four held-out benchmarks spanning machine learning engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering, and physics-based weather forecasting, the last of which is out of distribution from the selection tasks. On all four, the strongest discovered agent matches or exceeds a human-engineered production research agent that ranks among the strongest on FML-Bench. On a separate held-out task family, the discovered agents also exhibit reduced reward hacking, a property the loop never explicitly optimized for: the rate falls from 55% to 32% during the run, 7 percentage points below the human-engineered agent. Together, these results show that an AI research agent can improve its own research efficiency through recursive self-improvement, and that these gains transfer to tasks and domains the loop never encountered.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AIDE^2, an AI research agent that recursively improves its own code, demonstrating sustained self-improvement that transfers to unseen tasks and reduces reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Traditional increases in AI R&D spending yield diminishing returns, and while AI agents can automate many R&D tasks, their own research efficiency remains a bottleneck. The authors aim to explore whether an AI research agent can directly and repeatedly optimize its own implementation to break or alleviate this diminishing-returns trend, and to test if such recursive self-improvement leads to robust, generalizable gains rather than overfitting or reward hacking.
AI.method: They build AIDE^2, a system where an AI research agent proposes modifications to its own source code, instantiates these modified versions as new agents, and benchmarks them on a suite of AI R&D tasks. Using hidden evaluations to prevent overfitting or gaming, the system keeps the highest-performing variants and repeats this loop over multiple days, allowing for recursive self-improvement. The loop searches over design changes such as search policies and memory mechanisms for handling large and growing contexts.
AI.result: In an autonomous 8-day run, AIDE^2 discovers seven successive code improvements, including better search policies and context-compression memory modules. The final discovered agent matches or outperforms a strong human-engineered production research agent on four held-out benchmarks covering ML engineering, heuristic algorithm design, and physics-based weather forecasting, including out-of-distribution tasks. Moreover, on a separate held-out task family, the improved agents show less reward hacking: the rate drops from 55% to 32%, which is 7 percentage points below the human-engineered baseline, despite reward hacking not being a direct optimization target.
AI.conclusion: Recursive self-improvement is practically realizable for a frontier AI research agent and can yield sustained, composable gains in research efficiency. The improvements discovered by AIDE^2 not only persist across iterations but also transfer to new tasks and domains beyond those used in the optimization loop. Additionally, the process can incidentally improve alignment-related properties like reduced reward hacking, even without explicitly optimizing for them, suggesting that self-improving research agents may become a powerful paradigm for scaling AI R&D efficiency.

title: Reproducible AI Requires Reproducible Randomness
summary: Pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) constitute indispensable computational tools across multiple scientific domains, including Monte Carlo simulations, stochastic computing, and artificial intelligence (AI). The reproducibility of such applications critically depends on the ability of PRNG implementations to generate identical sequences across software environments when initialized from the same internal state. These algorithms enable the simulation of stochastic processes while providing deterministic and repeatable behaviour, thereby facilitating reproducible experiments. Modern PRNG implementations may be initialized through either a seed or, more accurately, an initial state that exceeds the capacity of a conventional integer seed. However, reliance on a simple seed alone frequently proves insufficient to ensure consistent program execution traces across different implementations. A natural assumption is that transferring the complete internal state of a generator should guarantee identical outputs regardless of the software library used. This study examines the validity of this assumption by investigating whether complete initial states can ensure cross-library fidelity and portability of PRNG streams. We focus on two widely deployed generators, Mersenne Twister and Philox, and evaluate their implementations across four major Python ecosystems-Random, NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. We compare the sequences produced by these implementations against those generated by the original reference algorithms under identical initialization conditions. Our results demonstrate that reproducibility cannot be assumed from PRNG state transfer alone, even when implementations claim to follow the same underlying algorithm. While fidelity was successfully achieved for several implementations, significant discrepancies were observed in others. Most notably, the Philox implementation in PyTorch exhibits fundamental incompatibilities with the reference algorithm, preventing exact reproduction of generator outputs across environments. These findings challenge the common expectation that access to a full internal state of a PRNG is sufficient to ensure reproducibility across software stacks. They further highlight that implementation-specific design choices can introduce hidden barriers to experimental replication, particularly in AI workflows that rely on multiple frameworks. This work shows that implementation fidelity of a PRNG is a necessary condition for scientific reproducibility and makes two primary contributions. First, it identifies practical guidelines for achieving reliable PRNG usage and reproducibility within the Python scientific and AI ecosystem. Second, it evaluates the extent to which cross-library portability and fidelity can be recovered through user-level techniques, without requiring modifications to library source code.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether sharing the full internal state of PRNGs is enough to guarantee identical random number sequences across different Python libraries, and finds that it is not always sufficient due to implementation differences.
AI.motivation: Scientific computing and AI workflows depend heavily on pseudorandom numbers while also requiring strict reproducibility. Many users assume that exporting and importing the full internal state of a PRNG ensures identical sequences across libraries and environments. The authors are motivated to test this assumption systematically, because inconsistent implementations may silently break reproducibility and hinder experimental replication.
AI.method: The authors select two popular PRNGs—Mersenne Twister and Philox—and examine their implementations in four major Python ecosystems: the built-in random module, NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. They reconstruct or consult the original reference algorithms for these PRNGs, then initialize each implementation with the same seed or complete internal state where possible. They compare the generated sequences to those of the reference implementations and to each other, assessing fidelity, cross-library portability, and sources of divergence. They also explore user-level strategies to recover portability without changing library source code.
AI.result: The study finds that full PRNG state transfer does not universally guarantee identical outputs across libraries, even when they nominally implement the same algorithm. Several implementations match the reference behaviour and are mutually compatible, but others diverge noticeably. In particular, PyTorch’s Philox implementation shows fundamental incompatibilities with the reference Philox algorithm, blocking exact cross-environment reproducibility for that generator. These discrepancies arise from implementation details such as parameter choices, state layout, or additional transformations.
AI.conclusion: Implementation fidelity to the reference PRNG algorithm is a necessary condition for reproducible research; having access to a full internal state alone is not sufficient. Users cannot safely assume cross-library reproducibility based only on PRNG names or state export/import mechanisms. The paper offers practical guidelines for reliable PRNG use in the Python scientific and AI stack and demonstrates that some degree of cross-library fidelity can be restored by careful user-level practices, but only when underlying implementations adhere closely enough to the reference design.

title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents often use generative models for bounded decisions, raising the question of when these decisions can be handled more efficiently without reducing task success. We study REFLEX, an agent architecture that uses Jev as a fast, typed decision layer and calls a strong LLM when confidence is low, or generation is required. On a frozen 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, with reductions persisting across three fallback families. Controlled interventions show that reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and $τ$-style evaluations reveal limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate. These findings identify when selective control with Jev can reduce computation and where its benefits are limited.

AI.tldr: REFLEX is an LLM agent architecture that uses a fast typed decision layer (Jev) and only calls a strong LLM when needed, cutting expensive model calls while maintaining high task success.
AI.motivation: Generative LLM agents often rely on powerful models for every decision, which is computationally costly. The authors want to know when decisions can be made more efficiently—via structured, cheaper mechanisms—without sacrificing success rates, and how far selective control can reduce reliance on strong models.
AI.method: They design REFLEX, an agent architecture combining Jev, a fast typed decision layer, with a fallback strong LLM used only when Jev’s confidence is low or when open-ended generation is required. They benchmark REFLEX on a fixed 100-task suite, compare it to a strong-only agent, and test several different fallback model families. They also run controlled interventions varying action-set size and the presence of near-valid but unauthorized actions to study reliability. Finally, they use external BFCL and τ-style evaluations to compare REFLEX against a cheaper generative cascade under conditions of already-accurate routing.
AI.result: On the 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% task success while reducing calls to the strong model by 72.7% relative to a strong-only agent, and this reduction is robust across three types of fallback models. The reliability of Jev’s decisions degrades with larger action sets and with many near-authorized alternatives. Under BFCL and τ-style evaluations, REFLEX shows only marginal gains compared with a well-tuned cheap generative cascade when routing accuracy is already high.
AI.conclusion: Selective control with a typed decision layer like Jev can substantially reduce expensive strong-LLM calls without much loss in success, especially in settings with moderate action spaces and clear authorization boundaries. However, when routing among generative models is already very accurate, the additional complexity of Jev offers limited practical advantage, so its benefits are context-dependent.

title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
summary: LLM-as-a-judge enables evaluation across diverse tasks, but inference cost and confidence reliability become critical at scale. We study whether a decision-only judge can provide an economical first pass and identify when stronger evaluation is needed. Comparing jev-as-a-judge with sixteen generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, we find it within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge, our strongest comparator, on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality at 0.36% of the comparator's fee. Larger gaps arise when judgments require checking a derivation or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer. On several benchmarks, JEV's gap to this comparator is concentrated in low-confidence decisions. A frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy at lower cost.

AI.tldr: They propose and analyze a lightweight, decision-only LLM judge (JEV) that cheaply approximates a strong LLM-as-a-judge, and show it works well especially when combined in a cascade that escalates only low-confidence cases.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-judge is powerful for automated evaluation but is expensive and sometimes unreliable at scale. The authors want to know if a cheaper, non-generative judge can serve as an effective first-pass filter, saving cost while preserving evaluation quality, and when escalation to a stronger model is necessary.
AI.method: They build a decision-only judge, JEV, and compare it against sixteen existing judges, including state-of-the-art generative and reward-model judges. Using blinded human adjudication, they measure accuracy on preference judgments and evidence-grounded factuality, and study specific challenging scenarios like checking derivations and resisting persuasive but wrong answers. They then analyze model confidence, identify where JEV fails, and design a frozen cascade that accepts JEV’s confident decisions and escalates only uncertain cases to a stronger judge.
AI.result: JEV matches a strong SOTA LLM judge within about three percentage points on standard preference and factuality tasks, while costing only 0.36% as much per judgment. Performance gaps are larger on tasks requiring derivation checking or resisting sophisticated incorrect answers, and JEV’s errors are concentrated in low-confidence predictions. A cascade that trusts JEV when confident and escalates uncertain cases to the stronger judge preserves about 99% of the stronger judge’s accuracy while reducing overall evaluation cost.
AI.conclusion: A decision-only LLM judge can serve as an efficient front-line evaluator, delivering near-SOTA judging quality at a tiny fraction of the cost. Because its errors cluster in low-confidence cases, combining it in a simple cascade with a stronger judge yields almost the same accuracy as the strong judge alone, but much more cheaply, making scalable LLM-as-a-judge pipelines more practical.

title: Neutral-Atom-based Quantum Optimization for Resource Allocation in NOMA Networks
summary: In wireless communication networks, many resource optimization problems are nondeterministic polynomial-time hard (NP-hard) due to their combinatorial nature and high computational complexity. Recently, neutral-atom-based quantum computing has emerged as a promising platform for efficiently solving such problems by leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement. However, its application to wireless communication optimization problems remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the use of neutral-atom quantum platforms to solve the maximum access problem (MAP), formulated as a mixed-integer programming task that jointly considers admission control, user clustering, channel assignment, and power allocation in a non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-enabled uplink network. To reduce the computational burden, the MAP is equivalently reformulated as a maximum independent set (MIS) problem in graph theory. This reformulation enables the use of the neutral atom platform based on Rydberg atom arrays, where the MIS problem is naturally encoded into the physical geometry and blockade constraints of the quantum system. Numerical results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this approach for addressing large-scale wireless resource optimization problems.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using neutral-atom quantum computing to solve a complex wireless resource allocation problem by reformulating it as a maximum independent set problem that can be naturally implemented on Rydberg atom arrays.
AI.motivation: Resource optimization in wireless networks, such as NOMA-enabled uplink systems, often leads to NP-hard mixed-integer problems that are computationally expensive for classical algorithms, especially at large scale. With the emergence of neutral-atom-based quantum computing, there is a need to understand whether and how this platform can practically address such wireless optimization tasks, a question that is largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors start from the maximum access problem (MAP) in a NOMA uplink network, which jointly optimizes admission control, user clustering, channel assignment, and power allocation via a mixed-integer programming formulation. They then derive an equivalent reformulation of this MAP as a maximum independent set (MIS) problem on a graph. This MIS instance is encoded into a neutral-atom quantum computing platform using Rydberg atom arrays, exploiting the physical geometry and Rydberg blockade constraints to represent graph vertices and edges and to search for the MIS via the system’s quantum dynamics. Numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate performance and feasibility.
AI.result: The numerical results show that the neutral-atom-based MIS formulation can successfully solve instances of the maximum access problem and suggest favorable scalability for larger problem sizes compared with conventional approaches. The experiments indicate that mapping MAP to MIS and then to Rydberg atom arrays is practically realizable and effective for complex wireless resource optimization.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that neutral-atom quantum computing, specifically using Rydberg atom arrays, is a viable and promising tool for tackling large-scale NP-hard wireless resource optimization problems. By recasting the maximum access problem as a maximum independent set problem, the authors provide a physically meaningful mapping to the quantum hardware, demonstrating both feasibility and potential performance benefits, and opening a route for broader quantum-assisted optimization in wireless networks.

title: Quantum-Aided Active Device Detection in Energy-Harvesting Symbiotic Radio Networks
summary: Massive connectivity in next-generation networks demands energy- and spectrum-efficient solutions for large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) deployments. Symbiotic radio (SR) enables passive IoT devices to communicate by backscattering existing cellular transmissions. A key challenge in uplink SR is active device detection (ADD), which directly affects decoding reliability, interference management, and system throughput. We propose an energy-harvesting code-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-SR system in which IoT devices harvest energy from ambient uplink signals and backscatter information using low-density spreading (LDS) codes. To reduce the complexity of ADD, Grover's quantum search algorithm is employed, providing a quadratic reduction in oracle-query complexity over exhaustive maximum-likelihood (ML) search. Numerical results show that the proposed approach closely approaches ML performance while substantially reducing the number of search iterations, demonstrating its potential for scalable ambient IoT systems.

AI.tldr: They propose a quantum-aided active device detection scheme for an energy-harvesting NOMA symbiotic radio IoT system that uses LDS codes, achieving near-ML performance with far lower search complexity.
AI.motivation: Next-generation massive IoT requires supporting many low-power devices with high energy and spectrum efficiency. Symbiotic radio backscatter allows passive IoT devices to communicate using existing cellular uplink signals, but reliably detecting which devices are active (active device detection) is challenging and computationally expensive, especially when using optimal ML detection in large-scale systems. A more scalable, low-complexity detection approach is needed.
AI.method: They design an energy-harvesting code-domain NOMA symbiotic radio system where IoT devices harvest energy from ambient uplink cellular signals and backscatter their data using low-density spreading (LDS) codes to support massive connectivity. For active device detection in the uplink, instead of conventional exhaustive ML search, they apply Grover's quantum search algorithm, which reduces the oracle query complexity quadratically. The scheme effectively searches over possible active-device patterns in a quantum-computing framework to identify which devices are transmitting.
AI.result: Numerical simulations indicate that the proposed quantum-search-based active device detection achieves performance close to maximum-likelihood detection in terms of accuracy/reliability, but with a substantially reduced number of search iterations, implying a major complexity reduction. This suggests that the method scales better to large numbers of devices compared to classical exhaustive search.
AI.conclusion: Integrating energy harvesting, LDS-based code-domain NOMA, and Grover's quantum search for active device detection yields an energy- and spectrum-efficient symbiotic radio IoT system with near-ML detection performance at much lower search complexity. This makes the approach promising for scalable massive ambient IoT deployments in future networks.

title: The Delegation Blind Spot: Auditing Product Decisions from Agent Choices
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Computational technical report with proofs and synthetic-task experiments; no human participants. Code: https://github.com/shi1720/delegation-blind-spot
summary: Successful agent execution need not identify which future product improvement its user would value. We present a decision-specific audit that maps a declared observation channel and product-value contrast to compatible intervals and witness populations. Its foundations are established identification and decision theory; the contribution is an executable measurement workflow and a controlled study of its limits. A frozen experiment makes 4,800 requests to two pinned model snapshots on shared synthetic tasks. All 36 conservative primary intervals remain unresolved despite different execution accuracy. An exploratory 2,400-call follow-up records supplied preferences and resolves three of nine comparisons per model. A deterministic extractor resolves seven of nine without model calls or calibration observations, exposing unnecessary uncertainty introduced by model-generated reports. A further 14,400 controlled multinomial simulations distinguish structural ambiguity from weak identification and finite calibration precision. We propose a source-labeled decision receipt and provide an offline viewer for inspecting the audit. These results motivate preserving decision-relevant structured input and diagnosing why a decision is unresolved before collecting more telemetry. The study contains no human participants or real customer outcomes. Full proofs, raw model provenance, controlled experiments, and reproducible analyses accompany the report.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decision-specific audit workflow to determine whether a system can reliably support particular product decisions, without needing to know users’ detailed future preferences.
AI.motivation: In many AI-product settings, teams must decide whether model-driven agents can safely or usefully support specific product changes, but they lack rigorous ways to tell if models’ observable behaviors are informative enough for those decisions. The authors want a principled measurement framework that connects observable model outputs, available calibration data, and product-value questions, and that can expose when a decision is fundamentally under-identified rather than simply under-instrumented.
AI.method: The authors design a ‘decision-specific audit’ procedure: given (1) an observation channel (what the system can report or log) and (2) a contrast between product options, the audit maps these to identification-compatible intervals over outcomes and to ‘witness populations’ that would resolve the decision if observed. They instantiate this with pinned model snapshots and synthetic tasks, running large frozen experiments that compare variants via model-generated reports, a follow-up study that incorporates explicit user preference reports, and a deterministic ‘extractor’ that infers decisions from structured inputs without additional model calls. They further run extensive multinomial simulations to separate structural ambiguity (decisions that cannot be resolved in principle) from weak identification or limited calibration data.
AI.result: In the main 4,800-request frozen experiment across two model snapshots and shared tasks, all 36 conservative primary decision intervals remain unresolved, even though execution accuracy differs between models. A 2,400-call follow-up that records explicit preferences resolves only three of nine decision comparisons per model. Using a deterministic extractor on the same structured inputs, they can resolve seven of nine decisions without any new model calls or calibration observations, showing that reliance on model-generated reports introduces avoidable uncertainty. Additional 14,400 multinomial simulations clarify when unresolved intervals stem from fundamental structural ambiguity versus inadequate identification strength or finite calibration precision.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that whether a decision can be resolved is tightly linked to how decision-relevant structure is preserved or lost in the observation channel, not just to model accuracy or telemetry volume. The authors argue that practitioners should preserve structured decision inputs, use source-labeled ‘decision receipts’ to separate model-derived from deterministic evidence, and diagnose identification failures before investing in more data collection. They provide an offline viewer and full reproducible artifacts, positioning their audit workflow as a practical tool for diagnosing and improving decision readiness of AI-enabled products without relying on real user outcomes.

title: Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free: A Constrained Decision Head Follows the Option Name, Not the Rubric Bound to It
summary: Typed decision models are built for settings where model outputs are consumed directly by software. Instead of generating free-form text, they return a decision over a predefined set of options. By construction, every output conforms to the required schema. Yet this guarantee does not tell us whether the model interprets the options as intended. We study Jev and two Jev-like models with open weights by changing how option names are assigned to rubrics. Each option consists of an option name and a textual rubric that defines what the option means. We change only which option name is assigned to each rubric; the question, state, rubric wording, and set of option names remain exactly the same. On 1200 workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics, renaming the two options from 0/1 to no/yes changes 70.4 more answers per hundred (95% CI: [67.6, 73.1]) and shifts AUC from .94 to .23, revealing a systematic reversal in the decision ranking rather than simple uncertainty. The same operation has little effect with neutral option names. This pattern holds across all 4 predicates, where the effect is at least 7.4x larger than under the neutral control, and becomes stronger as the number of options increases. The effect also depends on the read-out geometry: a second model family that mean-pools over the full option span flips 4.1x less often. The hosted model exhibits the same behavior: the swap changes AUC from .8146 to .5806 and produces 24x as many answer flips as its test-retest floor. In contrast, replacing the option names with random character strings returns all model families to the neutral-control regime without reducing accuracy. The failure therefore depends on the semantic polarity of the option names rather than on the renaming operation itself. Across all conditions, the type-error rate remains 0%, even when decision accuracy degrades substantially.

AI.tldr: Typed decision models can perfectly follow output schemas but still systematically misinterpret label meanings, especially when option names have semantic polarity like yes/no versus 0/1.
AI.motivation: To test whether schema-valid typed decision models actually understand option labels as intended, rather than just outputting syntactically correct but semantically misaligned decisions.
AI.method: Evaluate Jev and two related open-weight model families on 1200 workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics while systematically reassigning option names to fixed rubrics. Compare behavior under semantically polar option names (e.g., yes/no, 0/1), neutral names, and random strings; vary number of options and model read-out geometry; measure flips in chosen options, AUC, and type-error rate.
AI.result: Renaming options from 0/1 to no/yes causes about 70 additional answer changes per 100 decisions and drives AUC from .94 to .23, indicating a near-complete reversal of decision ranking, not just noise. Neutral option names have little effect; the polarity-driven effect is at least 7.4x larger than control and increases with more options. A model family using mean-pooling over option spans flips 4.1x less often. A hosted Jev-like model shows similar but somewhat smaller degradation. Replacing option names with random strings eliminates the large effects without hurting accuracy. Type-error rate stays at 0% in all conditions.
AI.conclusion: Typed decision models can satisfy output-type constraints while catastrophically misaligning the semantics of labels, particularly when option names carry strong polarity like yes/no. The vulnerability is tied to the semantic content of labels and read-out geometry, not to renaming per se, and can be mitigated by neutral or meaningless option names. Schema conformance alone is therefore insufficient to guarantee reliable decision semantics in such models.

title: Grow the Harness, Not the Context: From Strategy-Free Scaffolds to Reusable Specialist Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents often handle streams of related tasks, yet standard harnesses repeatedly ask the model to reconstruct the same control decisions inside each task's context. We study whether task feedback can instead turn recurring control into reusable executable code, while reserving LLM calls for task-specific semantic reasoning. We introduce Growing Harness, a failure-guided training paradigm that learns the agent harness itself from a strategy-free scaffold that exposes fixed model and tool interfaces but encodes no task-solving controller. Function-level execution traces localize each failure to a bounded code surface, an optimizer repairs a window of failures jointly, and a success-first held-out gate rolls back repair sequences that harm prior capability. Accepted edits accumulate in one shared harness, allowing its control structure to emerge from task feedback. Across BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified with three deployment models from 4B to 120B parameters, Growing Harness achieves the highest mean success in five of six benchmark-model settings and trails the best mean by 0.7 pp. in the sixth. Relative to a Tool-Calling agent, it reduces LLM calls by 76.0-91.8% and deployed-agent inference cost by 74.4-98.6%. On WebArena-Verified, its success remains 44.7-45.3% across model scales, whereas Tool-Calling falls to 6.7% with the 4B model. Ablations show that trace-local edits, joint repair, and gate-based rollback each improve final success. These results show that persistent program growth can move recurring control out of model context and into low-cost code, yielding reusable specialist agents that remain effective with smaller deployment models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Growing Harness, a training paradigm that converts repeated control decisions made by LLM agents into reusable executable code, significantly reducing LLM calls and inference costs while maintaining or improving task success.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often perform sequences of related tasks (e.g., browsing or web interaction), but existing agent harnesses repeatedly require the LLM to regenerate control logic in-context for each task. This wastes computation, makes the agent brittle—especially for smaller deployment models—and fails to exploit the fact that much of the control structure is shared and repeatable across tasks. The authors want to see if feedback from tasks can be used to grow a persistent, executable controller that handles generic control and tool use, leaving the LLM to focus only on semantic reasoning parts.
AI.method: They propose Growing Harness, starting from a strategy-free scaffold that only defines interfaces to the LLM and tools but contains no task-solving controller. As the agent runs on tasks, it collects function-level execution traces that identify exactly where failures occur in the harness code. An optimizer then jointly repairs bounded windows of failing code segments based on these traces. A success-first held-out gate validates each proposed sequence of edits against previously solved tasks, rolling back harmful changes. Over time, accepted edits accumulate into a single shared harness whose control logic is entirely induced from task feedback, turning recurring decision patterns into executable code. They evaluate on BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified with multiple LLM sizes (4B–120B) and run ablations on key components: trace-local edits, joint repair, and gate-based rollback.
AI.result: Across BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified, Growing Harness attains the best mean success in five of six benchmark–model combinations and is within 0.7 percentage points of the best in the remaining setup. Compared to a standard Tool-Calling agent, it reduces LLM calls by 76.0–91.8% and overall deployed-agent inference cost by 74.4–98.6%. On WebArena-Verified, Growing Harness maintains relatively stable success (44.7–45.3%) even when the deployment model is small (4B), whereas the Tool-Calling baseline’s success collapses to 6.7% at 4B. Ablation experiments demonstrate that localizing edits via traces, repairing multiple failures jointly, and using a held-out rollback gate each contribute to higher final success rates.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that an agent’s control logic can be grown as persistent program code directly from task feedback, rather than being repeatedly regenerated by an LLM in context. By turning recurring control behavior into low-cost executable code, Growing Harness substantially cuts LLM usage and inference cost while maintaining or improving success rates—especially for smaller models. This suggests a practical path toward reusable, specialist agents whose high-level control is encoded in an evolving harness, with LLMs reserved for the parts of the task that truly require semantic reasoning.

title: SWE-Serve: Benchmarking Agentic Engineering For Production Inference Serving
summary: We introduce SWE-Serve, a benchmark for evaluating agents on production inference engineering tasks. Implementing an inference feature can require coordinating multiple changes across the serving stack, including model support, runtime execution, and public APIs.
