Existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of production inference engineering: repository-level software engineering benchmarks do not target inference, while general terminal-agent benchmarks include only a few inference tasks. Dedicated inference benchmarks, meanwhile, focus primarily on isolated kernel generation or performance optimization rather than repository-scale production feature implementation. SWE-Serve provides 53 repository-grounded tasks derived from recent production changes to SGLang, spanning six inference engineering families. Each task executes on either CPU or a single GPU (H100) and is evaluated with hidden functional and regression tests, including, where applicable, end-to-end (E2E) serving tests and calibrated performance gates. Executable no-op and oracle controls, adversarial verifier review, and closed-book execution support task validity and evaluation integrity. Across 11 models and 31 model-effort configurations, the best-performing configuration achieves 75% mean pass@1. SWE-Serve exposes a substantial gap between completing tasks locally and achieving production correctness. On 19 tasks with end-to-end coverage, model-serving E2E tests reject roughly one-third of patches that pass every other test (45.9% under the verifier versus 69.4% with E2E tests excluded from scoring), with pass rate increasing for each model's best-performing configuration. By making the production correctness gap directly measurable, SWE-Serve enables the field to track whether future agents move beyond completing tasks locally to achieving production correctness.

AI.tldr: Introduces SWE-Serve, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on realistic production inference engineering tasks in model serving systems.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of benchmarks that truly capture the complexity of real-world production inference engineering: existing software-engineering benchmarks are not inference-specific, generic terminal-agent benchmarks have very few serving tasks, and current inference benchmarks focus on narrow kernel/perf problems rather than end-to-end feature implementation in large repositories.
AI.method: Construct 53 repository-grounded tasks based on real production changes in the SGLang serving stack, covering six families of inference engineering problems. Each task runs on CPU or a single H100 GPU and is evaluated via hidden functional and regression tests, plus, when relevant, end-to-end serving tests and performance thresholds. They add no-op/oracle controls, adversarial verifier review, and closed-book execution to ensure validity and integrity. They then evaluate 11 models across 31 configurations and report pass@1 and detailed pass-rate differences with and without E2E tests.
AI.result: The best model/configuration reaches 75% mean pass@1 overall, but there is a large gap between local task completion and true production correctness. For 19 tasks with full end-to-end coverage, about one-third of patches that pass all non-E2E tests still fail E2E serving tests; the pass rate appears as 69.4% if E2E tests are excluded but only 45.9% under the stricter verifier including E2E tests. Performance improves when each model is run in its best configuration, but the production gap remains clearly measurable.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Serve successfully exposes and quantifies the “production correctness gap” between passing local tests and achieving fully correct, production-grade inference features. By providing repository-scale, E2E-evaluated serving tasks, it offers a more realistic benchmark and a way to track whether future AI agents can handle genuine production inference engineering rather than just isolated or local coding tasks.

title: CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: Agents often work on complex problems that require millions of tokens of context, which necessitates compacting across sessions due to limited context windows. We develop CliffCompaction, an autocompaction technique that reduces cost by up to 50% under a bounded context while maintaining or improving performance on Terminal-Bench and achieving new levels of efficiency for test-time scaling and state-of-the-art results on KernelBench. The per-rollout savings of CliffCompaction make the performance--cost trade-off of test-time scaling more efficient, adding over 10 percentage points on Terminal-Bench for less than the cost of two full-context runs. Under parallel test-time scaling, CliffCompaction lets Kimi K2.6 match Opus 4.7, and exceed Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex at lower cost. The key to CliffCompaction's effectiveness is that it keeps compacted information faithful by only truncating or dropping content, never rephrasing or rewriting it. We never compact a compaction---each pass operates only on original content, and prior compacted output is discarded, preventing context drift from accumulating. These properties sustain continual learning over sessions exceeding a million tokens: on KernelBench, CliffCompaction reaches CUDA kernel speedups of $2.23\times$ after 200 steps and $3.58\times$ after 400 steps, surpassing specialized search algorithms and trained agents despite being a general-purpose compaction technique. We open-source a scaffold-agnostic API-proxy implementation of CliffCompaction usable with Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses.

AI.tldr: CliffCompaction is an autocompaction method that halves context costs for long-horizon agent tasks while maintaining or improving performance on benchmark suites like Terminal-Bench and KernelBench.
AI.motivation: LLM agents tackling complex, long-horizon problems often need to reason over millions of tokens across multiple sessions, but current context windows are limited and naive compaction either loses important information or causes context drift, making test-time scaling expensive and inefficient.
AI.method: The authors introduce CliffCompaction, an automatic compaction strategy that operates only by truncating or dropping original content, never rewriting it, and crucially never compacts already-compacted summaries. Each compaction pass uses only original-context material, discarding previous compacted outputs, which ensures faithfulness and prevents drift over many sessions. They integrate this into a scaffold-agnostic API-proxy that can sit in front of code-oriented agents such as Claude Code or Codex, and evaluate it under both single-rollout and parallel test-time scaling settings on benchmarks like Terminal-Bench and KernelBench.
AI.result: Under bounded context, CliffCompaction cuts cost by up to 50% while maintaining or improving performance on Terminal-Bench, improving the performance–cost frontier of test-time scaling by more than 10 percentage points for less than twice the cost of a full-context run. In parallel scaling experiments, integrating CliffCompaction allows Kimi K2.6 to match or outperform larger or more capable systems like Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, and GPT-5.3 Codex at lower cost. On KernelBench, it enables continued learning over million-token sessions, reaching CUDA kernel speedups of 2.23× after 200 steps and 3.58× after 400 steps, surpassing specialized search algorithms and trained agents despite being a general-purpose compaction mechanism.
AI.conclusion: CliffCompaction provides an efficient, faithful, and general-purpose way to manage extremely long contexts for LLM agents, making test-time scaling more cost-effective and enabling sustained performance gains over very long interaction horizons. Its simple design—drop/truncate-only, no rewriting, and no compaction-of-compactions—avoids context drift and works across different scaffolds via an open-source API-proxy implementation.
